sections.heading: Word limits: the ceiling on every written component
paragraphs: Written components in the Diploma are capped, and the caps are enforced. Work over the limit risks the examiner stopping at the limit, which means a conclusion that never gets read. Al Bateen students planning an Extended Essay a year out benefit from knowing the ceiling before the research question is fixed, because an over-broad question produces an essay that cannot be finished inside the words available.

The limits are the reason the Extended Essay goes wrong more often than any other component. Four thousand words sounds generous until a student has written two thousand words of background. A narrow question with a defensible method fits; an interesting but sprawling one does not. That is a planning problem, and it is solvable in a single session six months before the deadline.

The pattern repeats across subjects at smaller scale. Three Economics commentaries at eight hundred words each reward discipline in selecting the article. A History Internal Assessment at two thousand two hundred words leaves no room for narrative. An English Higher Level essay between one thousand two hundred and one thousand five hundred words is a tight argument, not a survey.

Treat the figures below as indicative and confirm each one against the current subject guide through your child's IB coordinator, because subject guides are revised on a cycle and this page does not republish board documents. sections.heading: What a specialist costs in Abu Dhabi, and what to check before paying it
paragraphs: The figures below are market rates in the UAE, drawn from providers' own published pricing and from a published 2026 Dubai tutoring rate survey by Bestimate. They are presented as the market, not as an IB Gram price list. For Al Bateen households, the relevant use of the table is sanity-checking a quote for a narrow subject, where the pool of people who can teach it is small and prices drift upward.

Three things move a rate: the level, the format, and whether travel sits inside the hour. Published examples run from roughly AED 45 to 65 an hour at the budget online end, AED 150 for IGCSE and AED 200 for IB from one agency publishing its rates, AED 270 from a UK-based agency, a survey band of AED 200 to 450 and above for specialist exam-year work, and AED 650 at the premium named end. In-home visits in Abu Dhabi are published between roughly AED 180 and AED 500, with the journey priced into the hour.

Monthly packages are easier to compare than hourly rates if you count sessions. Published examples include around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions. The same survey put weekly one-hour tuition at roughly AED 240 to 600 a month at budget level, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support.

The checks worth making before paying any of it are specific. Ask which board and syllabus code the tutor teaches. Ask whether the person holds a MoHRE private tuition work permit. Ask what happens to a missed session. Ask whether the quoted figure includes VAT, and do not accept a general statement about the tax treatment of tuition without a Federal Tax Authority reference. A provider who answers all four plainly is usually the one worth booking.

sections.heading: Online tuition versus an in-home tutor on the western island
paragraphs: Families in Al Bateen searching for a home tutor are asking a sensible question, and the geography here is genuinely favourable to in-home work compared with the outer communities. The district is central, the island roads are short, and a tutor living on the island can reach most Al Bateen addresses in fifteen minutes. The travel objection that dominates in the mainland communities is weaker here.

The objection that remains is depth of pool. The narrow subjects Al Bateen asks about most, Arabic A at Higher Level, a bilingual diploma grid, Paper 3 in Analysis and Approaches, are taught well by a small number of people. Restricting the search to those willing to drive to the western island on a Tuesday evening shrinks a small pool to a very small one. That is a real academic cost, not a logistical one.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere in the UAE, and does not operate a centre in the emirate. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, with a shared screen for working through papers and texts and a written note to the parent afterwards. For a Standard Arabic literature session or a Paper 3 walkthrough, the shared screen is arguably better than a kitchen table, because both parties annotate the same document.

The table sets out the trade honestly, including where in-home has the advantage. For a Grade 2 child who needs an adult present to stay on task, in-home provision is a reasonable choice and this page is not going to pretend otherwise.

sections.heading: Is the person teaching your child legally permitted to do it?
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated, and the rule is not obscure. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published, so no amount is quoted here.

The eligible categories are broad, which surprises parents who assume the permit is only for qualified teachers. They include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18, and university students. MoHRE's own service page for the permit is Issuance of a New Work Permit for Private Tutor Licensing, listing no fees and a two-working-day completion time, applied for through the MoHRE smart app, website and e-services system.

Two conditions matter more than the permit itself. The permit carries a code of conduct that bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school, and press reporting on ADEK's professional-ethics rules describes a prohibition on Abu Dhabi private and charter school staff providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school. Verify the current wording against ADEK's published policy before relying on it. The practical conclusion is the same either way: do not arrange for your child's own class teacher to tutor them privately.

A tutoring operation with premises and staff is a different legal animal from an individual tutor and needs an institutional permit from the emirate's education regulator. In Dubai that is a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute, with initial approval first, a maximum of six months to complete the permit and licence steps, and annual renewal requested at least thirty days before expiry. IB Gram holds no such permit and no approval, accreditation or licence from ADEK, KHDA, SPEA, MoHRE, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and nothing on this page should be read as implying otherwise.

sections.heading: Mid-year arrivals, mid-year departures and the diplomatic calendar
paragraphs: Al Bateen has a steady trickle of households arriving and leaving outside the normal academic cycle, because diplomatic and corporate postings do not respect September. A child joining a Diploma Programme cohort in January, or leaving in March, faces problems that no amount of general tutoring solves and that specific planning does.

Arriving mid-year into DP1 is the harder case. The six-subject grid is already set, Internal Assessment work has started in several subjects, and the Extended Essay supervisor has been allocated. The useful response is triage: identify which components have hard deadlines in the next twelve weeks, work on those, and accept that general catch-up in the remaining subjects happens over the summer rather than immediately.

Leaving mid-year raises a different question, which is what the child carries with them. Internal Assessment work completed at one school does not automatically transfer in usable form, and a change of board between Cambridge and Pearson changes the papers even when the subject name is identical. Ask the departing school for the component records, the syllabus codes and the forecast grades in writing before the last day.

Online delivery is a practical fit for both situations for an obvious reason: the tutor does not change when the address does. A student who starts work in Al Bateen in February and moves to another country in July keeps the same specialist through the transition, which is worth more during an exam year than any other form of continuity.

process.title: Name the language stream, not just the language
process.description: Arabic A, Arabic B and ab initio are separate courses with separate assessments. The same applies to English A and English B. Stating the stream in the first message avoids the single commonest mismatch in bilingual Al Bateen households, where a heritage speaker is matched to a second-language tutor or the reverse.

process.title: Ask for a written diagnostic before the first paid session
process.description: For a language placement, a short piece of analytical writing in the target language settles the level in one reading. For a Mathematics route question, a single past-paper section does the same. Both are more reliable than a predicted grade and far more reliable than a conversation about how the student feels.

process.title: Fix the destination before the subject grid
process.description: Write down the degree subjects your child might apply for, read the published entry requirements on each university's own admissions pages, and choose Higher Levels and the Mathematics route from that. This is a Year 11 or MYP 5 job. Reversing it in DP2 is usually not possible.

process.title: Work backwards from the school's internal deadline
process.description: Coursework support should be planned from the school's own internal deadline, not from the board's final submission date, because the two can be months apart. Ask the coordinator for the internal calendar and build the session plan from it before booking a block.

process.title: Check the permit and the paper, then book
process.description: Two questions filter most of the market: which syllabus code do you teach, and do you hold a MoHRE private tuition work permit. Clear answers to both, plus a stated cancellation policy, are a better signal than any rating. Review the match after four sessions rather than at the end of term.

whyPoints.title: Language streams are treated as separate subjects
whyPoints.description: Arabic A and Arabic B are matched separately, after a written diagnostic rather than a conversation. In a district where bilingual households are the norm, that single step prevents the most common and most expensive mismatch in the Diploma.

whyPoints.title: Published rules, quoted and sourced
whyPoints.description: The equivalency, permit and mandatory-subject detail on this page is quoted from the published sources and attributed. Where a figure is not verified, including any IB points threshold for equivalency, it is left out rather than guessed at.

whyPoints.title: Route advice checked against prerequisites, not opinion
whyPoints.description: The Mathematics route and Higher Level grid are discussed against the degree requirements a family names, with the instruction to confirm each one on the university's own admissions pages. Nothing is presented as settled when it is a matter of a specific institution's policy.

whyPoints.title: A small specialist pool is not narrowed further by geography
whyPoints.description: Arabic A at Higher Level and Analysis and Approaches Paper 3 are taught well by relatively few people. Because sessions run over live video, the choice is made among all of them rather than among those willing to drive to the western island.

whyPoints.title: Continuity through a posting change
whyPoints.description: Households here move in and out of the emirate mid-year more than most. The tutor does not change when the address does, which matters most in the term before a terminal exam, when a change of teacher is the last thing a candidate needs.

faqs.question: Should a bilingual child in Al Bateen take Arabic A or Arabic B?
faqs.answer: Decide it on written evidence, not on how fluently the child speaks at home. Arabic A: Language and Literature is a literature course assessed in Standard Arabic, with unseen textual analysis and comparative essay work. A heritage speaker may be completely fluent in conversation and have had no instruction in literary terminology or written register. Ask the school for a short piece of analytical writing on an unseen Arabic text and read it. If the comprehension is strong and the structure weak, Arabic A with support is often right. If the script itself is slow, Arabic B is the honest placement.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a tutor to homes in Al Bateen?
faqs.answer: No. Lessons for Al Bateen families are delivered one-to-one over live video, and IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE. Independent tutors and agencies in Abu Dhabi do travel, and published in-home rates in the emirate run from roughly AED 180 to AED 500 an hour with the journey inside the rate. The reason online suits this district is not travel time, which is short on the island, but pool depth: the narrow subjects Al Bateen asks about are taught by a small number of specialists, and geography should not shrink that number further.

faqs.question: How many IGCSE subjects does a student need for UAE equivalency?
faqs.answer: The published British-track requirement is five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count. A student also needs one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or better, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. One tutoring site ranking for this market states six subjects, which does not match the published rule. Confirm the current requirement on moe.gov.ae or with the emirate's attestation authority before planning a subject grid.

faqs.question: Are Arabic and Islamic Education counted towards the equivalency subject total?
faqs.answer: No. The published requirements state that Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects for the GCSE or IGCSE count. That does not make them optional at school, because they are mandatory subjects in UAE private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum. It does mean a student needs five other accredited subjects at the stated minimum grade. Families planning a narrow subject grid in Year 10 sometimes discover this late, which is why it belongs in the conversation before options are chosen rather than after results.

faqs.question: What does the Ministry require from an American-curriculum student instead?
faqs.answer: Test scores rather than a subject count. The published English-proficiency requirement is a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL internet-based test, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT. Mathematics requires at least 450 in the SAT Mathematics test before applying. These are thresholds to be met, so they can be planned for and retaken, unlike a subject choice made two years earlier. Verify the current figures on moe.gov.ae, and note that IB Gram neither performs nor guarantees any part of the equivalency process.

faqs.question: Is there an IB points figure Al Bateen families can plan equivalency around?
faqs.answer: Not one that this project has been able to verify on the Ministry's own site, and no figure is published here for that reason. The British-track numbers are sourced and quoted elsewhere on this page; the IB equivalent is not. Any points threshold you are shown by a tutoring provider should be traced back to moe.gov.ae or to the emirate's attestation authority before you plan around it. If a figure cannot be sourced to one of those, treat it as unverified. Ask your school's IB coordinator, who deals with the attestation route directly.

faqs.question: Which Mathematics route keeps the most degree options open?
faqs.answer: Analysis and Approaches is accepted more broadly, including by mathematics, physics and engineering courses that name it specifically in their published prerequisites. Applications and Interpretation is a rigorous course and is accepted for a wide range of degrees, but a minority of quantitative courses exclude it. The method that works is unglamorous: list the three or four degree subjects your child might apply for, read the published entry requirements on each university's own admissions pages, and pick the route that keeps all of them live. Do that in Year 11, not DP2.

faqs.question: Why does Paper 3 cause so much trouble at Higher Level?
faqs.answer: Because it supplies no method. Papers 1 and 2 ask questions whose shape tells a prepared student what technique to apply. Paper 3 presents an extended problem and expects the candidate to choose the route through it, which exposes anyone who has learned procedures without the reasoning underneath. It is worth a fifth of the Higher Level grade, so the exposure is expensive. The fix is practice on unfamiliar extended problems with the solution withheld, which is slow work and the main reason Higher Level students book a full term rather than a block.

faqs.question: How long can the Extended Essay actually be?
faqs.answer: Four thousand words is the ceiling, and work beyond it risks the examiner stopping at the limit, so a conclusion written at word four thousand two hundred may never be read. That constraint should drive the research question rather than be discovered after a first draft. A narrow question with a defensible method fits inside four thousand words; an interesting but broad one does not. Confirm the current limit and any formatting requirements against the Extended Essay guide through your school's IB coordinator, because subject guides are revised and this page does not republish board documents.

faqs.question: What word limits apply to the other written components?
faqs.answer: Indicatively: the Theory of Knowledge essay is capped at 1,600 words, the TOK exhibition commentary at 950 words across three objects, a History Internal Assessment at 2,200 words, Economics at three commentaries of 800 words each, and an English A Higher Level essay at 1,200 to 1,500 words. Confirm every one of these against the current subject guide through your child's IB coordinator before planning. The habit matters more than the numbers: find the ceiling, then choose a question that can be answered inside it. Most coursework problems start as scope problems.

faqs.question: Does my tutor in Abu Dhabi need a MoHRE permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18 and university students. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published. The application route is MoHRE's own private tutor licensing service, via its smart app, website and e-services system.

faqs.question: Can we hire a teacher from my child's own Abu Dhabi school privately?
faqs.answer: It should be avoided. The MoHRE private tuition permit carries a code of conduct that bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school, and press reporting on ADEK's professional-ethics rules describes a prohibition on Abu Dhabi private and charter school staff providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school. Verify the current wording against ADEK's published policy before relying on it. There is also a practical reason: a tutor from outside the school has no stake in the school's own predicted grades and tends to give more candid feedback on where marks are being lost.

faqs.question: Is IB Gram approved by ADEK or KHDA?
faqs.answer: No, and any provider claiming such approval should be asked for a permit number. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from ADEK, KHDA, SPEA, MoHRE, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson. A tutoring business with premises and staff needs an institutional permit from the emirate's education regulator, which is a specific document issued to training institutes; in Dubai that is a KHDA Educational Services Permit, renewed annually. This page explains what those regulators do because Abu Dhabi families need to understand them, not to imply any endorsement.

faqs.question: Our posting ends in March. What should we ask the school for before leaving?
faqs.answer: Ask in writing for the syllabus codes of every subject, the component records for any Internal Assessment work already completed, the internal deadline calendar, and the current forecast grades. A change of board between Cambridge and Pearson alters the papers even when the subject name is identical, so the codes matter more than the subject list. If the move happens during DP1 or Year 10, triage the components with hard deadlines inside twelve weeks first. Online delivery means the tutor does not change when the address does, which is worth most during an exam year.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with an Extended Essay without breaching academic honesty?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a clear boundary. A tutor explains how each criterion is awarded, asks the questions a supervisor asks about scope and method, and gives feedback on drafts the student has already produced. A tutor does not supply text, data or analysis that enters a submission. The practical safeguard is the calendar: an Extended Essay planned across two terms is a manageable project, while the same work compressed into a fortnight is exactly the situation where the boundary gets tested. Official guides and mark schemes are cited and linked rather than redistributed.

abu-dhabi/al-bateen.closingHeading: Settle the stream and the destination first, then book the teaching
abu-dhabi/al-bateen.closingBody: Most Al Bateen enquiries turn on a decision rather than on a gap: which Arabic stream, which Mathematics route, which Higher Levels, what the Ministry will want to see. Those are answerable with published requirements and a short written diagnostic, and they are far cheaper to settle in Year 11 than in DP2. Once the decision is made, the teaching is matched on the syllabus code and delivered one-to-one over live video, so a narrow specialism is chosen from everyone who teaches it rather than from everyone who can reach the western island on a weekday evening.

abu-dhabi/al-falah.tutorsIntro: Al Falah enquiries usually arrive as a list rather than a single request: a primary child, a middle-years child and an examination candidate, each needing something different. The tutors below each work with one stage properly rather than all of them loosely, one-to-one over live video.

intro.heading: One household, four school timetables
paragraphs: Al Falah sits on the mainland out towards the airport, north-east of Khalifa City and next to Al Shamkha, built as large family villas on generous plots. The housing stock tells you most of what you need to know about tutoring here. These are big households, frequently with four or five children spread from foundation stage to sixth form, and often with two or three different schools in use because the right school for a Year 2 is not the right school for a Year 12.

That produces a scheduling problem of a different kind from the one a two-child apartment faces. The school run has several legs. The children arrive home at different times and in different states. The youngest is ready to work at four and useless by six; the oldest is barely functional at four and at their sharpest at eight. A single family-wide tutoring slot suits nobody, and most of the arrangements that fail in this community fail because they were built as though one existed.

The second feature of a large household is that the children are frequently at different points of a transition at once. One is moving from an MYP school into a Diploma school. One has just arrived from a different curriculum entirely and is meeting command words and tiered papers for the first time. One is choosing between three Higher Levels and three A Levels. Each of those transitions has a specific, nameable gap, and each takes a predictable number of weeks to close.

The third is cost discipline, which works differently here than in a one-child household. The marginal decision is never whether to buy tutoring; it is which child gets the hour this term. Families in Al Falah ask better questions than most about where an hour does the most good, and the honest answer usually involves fewer total hours spread more deliberately, with the youngest on short frequent sessions and the examination candidate on fewer but longer ones. The families who get the most out of a year are the ones who reallocate at each report rather than renewing everything in September and then leaving the whole arrangement untouched until the end of June.

All of it is delivered one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not run home visits in the UAE - home visits are an India-only service - and in a household with this many moving parts that turns out to be the point. Nobody is scheduling around a driver's route, a missed slot can be moved to another evening, and three children can be matched to three different specialists rather than to whichever one tutor was willing to make the journey out to Al Falah.

Children arrive home at different times and in very different states

abu-dhabi/al-falah.programmesIntro: A household here can have children in three of these at the same time. The notes focus on what each stage needs from the family's evening rather than on describing the curriculum.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: No external examination, which is why primary tutoring here is almost always about two specific things: number facts to automaticity and written English. A child can move happily through units of inquiry and reach Year 7 unable to handle fractions without a calculator or structure a paragraph around one idea.
programmes.countryNote: In a large Al Falah household the primary child has an advantage: they get the earliest slot, when the house is loudest but their own attention is at its best. Thirty to forty-five minutes twice a week does far more at this age than a single long session, and it occupies a time of day that the older siblings cannot use productively anyway.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four criteria per subject, each marked out of eight, reported as descriptors rather than percentages. The middle child in a large family is the one whose slide is noticed last, because the primary child is visibly learning and the examination candidate is visibly stressed. A flat middle band for two years is easy to miss.
programmes.countryNote: The transition into or out of the MYP is where Al Falah families lose the most ground, because siblings in different schools follow different reporting languages and parents end up comparing incomparable reports. Taking one marked task and rewriting it against the descriptors in plain English is a two-session job that changes how the student reads every brief afterwards.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge and CAS. The internal assessments carry roughly a fifth to a quarter of most subject grades and are produced at home, which in a busy household means they are produced late. The eldest child needs the latest and longest slot in the evening.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi schools enter the May session, so the autumn of Year 13 carries coursework, the Extended Essay and predicted grades together. For a family running several children's schedules, that term should be protected deliberately: the examination candidate's slot is the one that does not move when something else comes up. Confirm every IB date with the school's Diploma coordinator or on ibo.org.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Eight to ten subjects over two years, tiered in maths and the sciences on Cambridge specifications. The Year 10 tier decision is the most consequential choice in the household in any given year and it has a hard deadline: Cambridge sets final entries for its March 2027 series at 27 November 2026.
programmes.countryNote: Where siblings attend different schools they may well sit different boards, and a family that assumes one set of past papers covers both children will be drilling one of them on the wrong paper structure. Check each child's syllabus code separately - 0580 or 0607 for Cambridge maths, 4MA1 for Pearson - because within one family both can be in use.

abu-dhabi/al-falah.subjectsIntro: The subject list below covers the range a large household typically needs across its stages, from reading fluency to Higher Level technique, with the real failure point named in each case.

subjects.name: Primary mathematics and reading
subjects.description: Number bonds and tables to automaticity, fractions without a calculator, and reading aloud with comprehension questions. The gap that matters at this stage is fluency rather than understanding, and fluency only comes from short frequent practice.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Justification carries the marks: the assumption stated, the step shown, the conclusion tied back. Paper 3 at Higher Level is an extended investigation with no IGCSE equivalent and is the component practised least, because schools rarely have time to set a full one.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The statistical route, and not the soft one. Regression, chi-squared and hypothesis testing on the graphical display calculator decide whole questions, and Higher Level adds matrices, graph theory and Voronoi diagrams that nobody meets at IGCSE.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Uncertainty handling separates the top grades in Paper 2 and again in the internal assessment. Fields and circuits are where the quantitative work hardens and where students who learned definitions rather than relationships stop being able to progress.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms and energetics carry the heaviest Higher Level content load. The internal assessment is a full scientific report with its own criteria, and in a busy household it is the single most reliably late piece of work in the year.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Marks go on precision of language and on the statistics in the internal assessment. A six-mark answer on membrane transport needs the right terms in the right order; a competent description in everyday words scores poorly.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580
subjects.description: Extended sits on Papers 2 and 4, Core on Papers 1 and 3, and material does not cross between them. The Core entry caps the grade, which makes the Year 10 decision the one worth evidencing with a timed paper rather than assuming.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE combined and separate sciences
subjects.description: The choice between separate sciences and a combined award shapes post-16 options, and families with several children often make it differently for each. Electricity, moles and the alternative-to-practical reasoning paper are where marks go.

subjects.name: English: First Language and as a Second Language
subjects.description: Two courses that look similar and grade very differently, with consequences for later university language conditions. Reading inference under time pressure is the part that needs deliberate practice rather than more reading.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language and Islamic education
subjects.levels: The mandatory stream across all stages
subjects.description: Taught and assessed in Standard Arabic for Arab students against centrally prescribed content. Every child in the household carries this stream whatever international curriculum their school is licensed for, and written register is the recurring gap.

abu-dhabi/al-falah.regionsTitle: Al Falah and the communities on the same school runs
abu-dhabi/al-falah.regionsIntro: Al Falah shares its school runs with the mainland districts around it, and the differences between them are mostly about which direction the morning traffic goes.

regions.name: Al Shamkha
regions.note: The immediate neighbour to the south-west, also villa-built and also housing large families. The two communities use overlapping schools and face a near-identical evening timetable.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: West and the main destination for British and IB schooling on this side of the water. For an Al Falah household the run is long enough that the oldest child's slot has to sit after six.

regions.name: Al Reef
regions.note: Towards the airport, mixing villas and apartments around a central souk. A comparable journey and a comparable approach to spreading tutoring hours across several children.

regions.name: Al Raha Gardens
regions.note: South-west along the highway, home to the main full IB continuum school in the corridor. Al Falah children who moved into the Middle Years Programme generally moved in that direction.

regions.name: Al Shahama
regions.note: North, an older community closer to the Dubai road. Families there make a similar airport-side journey and share the same late evening start times.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City
regions.note: South-west and the nearest large concentration of Cambridge IGCSE places. Where a household wants a shorter run for a middle child, this is usually the compromise.

regions.name: Yas Island
regions.note: South-west across the highway, with an American-curriculum academy. Households with one child there and one in a British school are comparing two assessment systems inside one family.

schoolClusters.city: Khalifa City and the Al Raha corridor
schoolClusters.note: The cluster that carries most of the British and IB places used by Al Falah families, and the one that sets the household's latest arrival time. A long run west, which is why examination candidates in this community rarely start before six.

schoolClusters.note: Shorter journeys and lower fee bands, used by Al Falah households particularly for middle and primary children where the longer run is harder to justify. A large share of the Cambridge IGCSE entries on this side of the emirate sit here.

abu-dhabi/al-falah.modesIntro: The three arrangements below are what large households actually use, and most families run two of them at once for different children.

modes.title: Short frequent sessions for the youngest
modes.description: Thirty to forty-five minutes, twice a week, in the earliest slot of the evening. Fluency work - number facts, reading aloud, spelling patterns - responds to frequency rather than duration, and this occupies a time of day the older children cannot use well anyway, so it costs the household nothing in scheduling terms.

Fluency and automaticity rather than new concepts
Fits the hour the examination candidate cannot use

modes.title: Back-to-back hours for two children
modes.description: Two consecutive hours on one evening with two different specialists, so the household only needs to be quiet once. The middle child takes the first hour and the examination candidate the second, which matches both children's actual attention curves and leaves three other weekday evenings clear.

Each child reported on separately
Keeps the rest of the week free for homework and activities

modes.title: A protected block for the examination candidate
modes.description: The one slot in the household that does not move. For a Year 13 carrying coursework and predicted grades, or a Year 11 facing a series, ninety minutes at a fixed time with the understanding that siblings' arrangements flex around it rather than the reverse. In exam terms this is often supplemented by a weekend paper session.

sections.heading: Who gets which slot, and why it matters
paragraphs: In a household with four children the scarce resource is not money and it is not tutor availability. It is quiet evening hours, and there are fewer of them than there are children. The way to use them is to match each child's stage to the part of the evening where that child can actually work, which is a different hour for a seven-year-old and a seventeen-year-old.

A primary child has twenty to thirty minutes of genuine focus after a school day, and it arrives early. Push that child to seven in the evening and the session is wasted whatever the tutor does. A middle-years student has forty to fifty minutes and needs food first. An examination candidate is frequently at their sharpest late, and is the one child in the house for whom an eight o'clock lesson is not a compromise.

That ordering has a second benefit: it means the children do not compete for the same hour. The youngest occupies a slot the oldest cannot use, and the oldest occupies one the youngest should be nowhere near. A household that sequences deliberately can run three children's tutoring through a single evening with no overlap, which is only possible because nobody is travelling to or from the house.

The table below sets out the pattern that works most reliably, with what each slot should be spent on. It is worth planning once at the start of a term and then leaving alone, because the cost of renegotiating a four-child schedule every fortnight is higher than the cost of the lessons.

sections.heading: The transitions that cost marks, and how long each takes to fix
paragraphs: Large families in this community tend to have at least one child mid-transition at any time, and transitions are where grades drop for reasons that have nothing to do with ability. The content is usually continuous. The assessment is not, and nobody sits the student down and explains the difference.

The hardest of them is Cambridge IGCSE into the Diploma Programme. A student finishes Year 11 with grade 8s and 9s, takes three Higher Levels, and produces a 3 or a 4 on the first report. In maths the change is from executing a method to arguing for it. In the sciences it is from knowing content to handling uncertainty, criticising a method and arguing from a graph. In English it is from set texts to unseen analysis and a timed oral. That is roughly eight to twelve weeks of technique work, and it is far cheaper in the summer before Year 12 than in the spring of Year 13.

Arrivals from other systems carry different gaps. A student coming from a national Indian board into Cambridge IGCSE meets command words, extended written answers and practical reasoning papers, and usually has the content but not the answer format. A student moving from an American curriculum into the Diploma meets externally examined papers replacing continuous assessment, and discovers that homework cannot repair a weak examination performance. Both are technique problems with timescales attached.

The reason to name weeks rather than hours is that these gaps close through repeated practice rather than explanation. A single session that explains what Paper 3 wants is useful; six weeks of writing justifications and having them marked is what changes the grade. For a family planning across several children, knowing that a bridge takes two months lets you decide which summer to spend it in.

sections.heading: What a multi-child household actually pays
paragraphs: Pricing advice written for one-child families is close to useless here, because the question is never the hourly rate on its own. It is what a given monthly figure buys across three children, and which allocation of the same money produces the most marks. So here are the market bands in AED, attributed, arranged by household scenario rather than by tier.

The underlying numbers come from published sources. Bestimate's 2026 estimates for one weekly hour are AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 for a qualified subject tutor and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist examination-year support. EdFlik advertises from AED 45 to 65 an hour and Tutopiya from the low thirties. Unitors publishes IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200, and TutorChase shows AED 270. Those are market rates and not IB Gram's quote, which is given after a consultation and trial lesson.

Two patterns are worth knowing before you allocate. First, a second subject for one child costs more than a second child at the same tier, because specialist hours are dearer than general ones - so where two children both have a single at-risk grade, covering both is often better value than doubling up on one. Second, the youngest child's hours are the cheapest useful hours in the household, because fluency work at primary level does not need a specialist and responds to short frequent sessions.

The expensive mistake in a large family is the standing arrangement nobody reviews. Three children on open-ended weekly hours from September to June is a large annual figure for a set of needs that change by term. A better pattern is a diagnostic, a defined block for whoever needs it most, then a reassessment at each report. That costs less and allocates better.

sections.heading: Weekends, and why they are the most valuable hours you have
paragraphs: In a large Al Falah household the weekend is where the work that needs a clear head has to live. A ninety-minute coursework review or a complete timed paper cannot realistically happen on a Tuesday evening after a long run back from Khalifa City, with two siblings needing the same room at different points. On a Saturday morning it can.

The particular case for weekend paper practice is that pacing is a skill and it has to be trained in a state resembling the examination. A student who only ever practises tired learns to perform tired. They produce marks that understate what they know, draw the conclusion that they are weaker than they are, and lose confidence on top of marks. A paper sat at ten on a weekend morning with a visible clock measures the student rather than the week.

Weekends also solve the sibling collision. Two children who both need a long session can have one each across two mornings without competing for the household's quiet hour, which in term time is a single slot that cannot be subdivided. For families running three or more children's arrangements, moving the long work to the weekend and keeping weekdays for short focused sessions is the pattern that holds together across a whole year.

The one thing worth protecting is that the weekend does not become school. Two long sessions on a Saturday and another on a Sunday is a route to a student who resents the subject, which costs more in May than the extra hours earn. One long session per child per weekend, with the rest of the time genuinely off, is the arrangement families here sustain.
bullets: Long work - papers, coursework reviews - belongs at the weekend, not after a long commute
Pacing has to be practised in a fresh state, or the mark measures the week rather than the student
Two children can each have a long session across two mornings without competing
One long session per child per weekend; more than that breeds resentment

sections.heading: Choosing subjects when siblings are in different systems
paragraphs: A recurring Al Falah conversation is a parent trying to compare two children's reports from two different schools using two different assessment languages. One comes home with criterion scores out of eight. One comes home with percentages. One has predicted grades on a points scale. They are not comparable, and the attempt to compare them usually produces either unwarranted panic or unwarranted calm.

What is comparable is the external measure. A timed paper marked against a published mark scheme gives a number that means the same thing in any household. A criterion score tells you how a specific descriptor was met. A predicted grade tells you what the school thinks, which is useful information about the school's expectations as well as the child. Reading each report in its own terms, rather than translating them into one scale, is the first step.

The subject choices themselves differ by system in ways that matter later. The Diploma requires six subjects with no weak link permitted and a heavy coursework load, which suits a broadly strong and organised student. A Level narrows to three or four and allows a weakness to be dropped, which suits a clear direction. For maths specifically, the Analysis and Approaches route is the one most engineering and physical-science degrees expect, while Applications and Interpretation suits economics, business and social-science routes - and that choice should be made against a degree intention rather than against which looks easier.

For UAE equivalency the British route has published requirements: five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count, plus one Advanced Level subject at no less than E or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade. No IB points figure is published here because no official source was read for one. Check your own case with the Ministry rather than with any tutoring site.

sections.heading: What online delivery changes for a large villa household
paragraphs: The advantages of online delivery scale with the number of children, which is why this community notices them more than most. With one child, a tutor who drives to the house is an inconvenience priced into an hourly rate. With four children at four stages, a tutor who drives is a scheduling impossibility: you would need four different specialists willing to make the same journey on four different evenings.

What happens instead is that each child is matched to a specialist for their own stage and subject, and the household supplies four separate hours rather than four separate parking spaces. A villa in Al Falah generally has the rooms for it, which is one genuine advantage this housing stock has over apartment districts: two lessons can run simultaneously if the connection supports it, in rooms far enough apart that headphones are a courtesy rather than a necessity.

The practical requirements are the same for every child. A laptop or tablet rather than a phone, so written working can be seen as it appears. Headphones. Pen and paper in frame, or a second device propped to show the page. A door that closes. And a household rule that the hour is quiet, which in a large family needs stating in advance rather than hoping for.

To be explicit about what is not on offer: IB Gram does not send tutors to UAE addresses. Home visits exist only in the India service. Everything described on this page is one-to-one tuition over live video, and the reason it suits Al Falah is arithmetic rather than ideology.

sections.heading: Tutor availability across four stages, and what happens when a subject is not covered
paragraphs: No competing page found in this market discloses a coverage limit, which is strange, because every tutoring service has one. A household needing four specialists across four stages is the case most likely to run into it, so here is the honest position rather than a claim that everything is always available.

Mainstream requests are reliably covered in UAE evening hours: primary maths and English, lower secondary across the board, Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE maths and the three sciences, Diploma maths in both routes, the three sciences, English A, economics and business management, and Arabic in both streams. For those, a match and a trial lesson is usually arranged within a few days of the brief being clear.

Narrower combinations take longer and sometimes cannot be met in the slot a family wants. A second-language option taught by few schools, a Higher Level subject needed at a specific hour that a specialist already teaches, or a niche Diploma subject with a small teaching population worldwide. In those cases the available answers are a different slot, a tutor working from another time zone whose evening overlaps yours, or waiting. What is not an available answer is putting a general science teacher into a Higher Level chemistry slot and letting the family discover it in February.

Where a fallback applies, it is disclosed before the trial rather than after it. That matters more than it sounds: two ranking competitors in this market route UAE parents to numbers outside the Emirates without saying where the teaching happens. A parent is entitled to know which country their child's tutor is in, what hours that creates, and whether the rate differs.

sections.heading: Academic honesty when siblings study the same subject
paragraphs: This is a problem specific to large households and it is rarely discussed anywhere. Two siblings a year apart, in the same subject, at the same school, with the same tutor, are in a position to produce internal assessments that resemble each other. Even with no intent to cheat, a younger sibling who has watched the older one's work and discussed it at the kitchen table can write something that similarity checking flags.

The consequences fall on the students. Under IB rules this is malpractice territory, supervisors sign authenticity declarations, and the sanction can reach the diploma itself. A family that has not thought about it can create the problem accidentally, which is why it is worth a paragraph rather than a footnote.

The practical safeguards are simple. Research questions must be genuinely different, and where two siblings take the same subject the younger one should choose a different context, dataset or text. The older sibling's finished work should not be available to read. A tutor supervising both should keep the sessions separate and should not discuss one student's approach with the other. And no coursework session should ever be run for two students together, whatever the saving.

On the wider boundary, the same rules apply here as everywhere. A tutor teaches the subject, explains each criterion and what its descriptors require, challenges a research question that is too broad, gives feedback on a draft the student has written, and teaches referencing. A tutor does not supply text that reaches the submitted document, and heavy line-editing is that same breach in a politer form. At least one site competing for these searches sells completed Internal Assessments outright; buying one puts the student, not the seller, at risk.
bullets: Siblings in the same subject can produce similar work without intending to

process.title: List the children, the stages and the schools
process.description: Not one request but the whole household: who is in which year, at which school, on which board, and what each report last said. For an Al Falah family this usually changes the recommendation, because the child the parent is most worried about is not always the one where an hour would do the most good.

process.title: Map the evening before matching anybody
process.description: What time each child is home, which evenings are already taken by activities, how many rooms can be quiet at once, and whether the connection supports two lessons at the same time. The sequence that results - youngest early, candidate late - is usually the whole solution to a scheduling problem the family thought was a budget problem.

process.title: Identify the transitions in progress
process.description: A child moving from IGCSE to the Diploma, arriving from another curriculum, or facing a tier decision has a named gap with a known timescale. Those get priority over general support, because they are the cases where a defined block of work produces a visible change rather than a gradual one.

process.title: Match each child separately, then trial
process.description: One specialist per child per subject, each with a trial lesson against the matched tutor rather than a coordinator. Each child is reported on separately afterwards, because a household-level progress summary tells a parent nothing actionable about any individual student.

process.title: Reassess at every school report
process.description: Rather than a standing arrangement from September to June, the plan is reviewed when each school report arrives and the hours are reallocated. In a large family that is the single biggest lever on value, because the child who needed the hour in October is rarely the child who needs it in February.

whyPoints.title: Built for several children, not one
whyPoints.description: The recommendation covers the household: who gets which slot, which transition takes priority this term, and where an hour does the most good. That is a different conversation from matching a single subject, and it is the one most Al Falah families actually need.

whyPoints.title: A specialist per child, per stage
whyPoints.description: A tutor who is genuinely good with a Year 4's reading fluency is not the tutor for Higher Level chemistry. Because delivery is online, each child gets the right person rather than the one person who was prepared to drive out to the community.

whyPoints.title: Transitions with timescales attached
whyPoints.description: IGCSE into the Diploma, another curriculum into IGCSE, MYP into DP: each has a nameable gap and a realistic number of weeks. Knowing it takes eight to twelve weeks lets a family choose which summer to spend on it rather than discovering the gap in a January report.

whyPoints.title: Hours reallocated, not renewed
whyPoints.description: Plans are reviewed at each report and the hours moved to whoever needs them. A standing three-child weekly arrangement nobody reviews is the most expensive pattern available and rarely the most effective one.

whyPoints.title: Sibling coursework handled carefully
whyPoints.description: Where two children take the same subject, research questions are kept genuinely separate and supervision sessions are never shared. That protects both students from a similarity problem a family can create without ever intending to.

whyPoints.title: No travel, no minimum session
whyPoints.description: UAE lessons are one-to-one over live video, so a thirty-minute primary session is a real option rather than something priced out by a drive, and a missed slot moves to another evening without re-planning anyone's route.

faqs.question: We have four children at four different stages. Where do we start?
faqs.answer: With the evening rather than the subjects. Map what time each child is actually home, which evenings are already committed, and how many rooms can be quiet at once. Then sequence by stage: the youngest takes the earliest slot while their focus is still available, the middle child takes early evening after food, and the examination candidate takes the latest hour, when they are usually sharpest. That ordering means the children do not compete for the same hour, and it often resolves what looked like a budget problem.

faqs.question: Which of our children should get the tutoring hour this term?
faqs.answer: Usually whoever is mid-transition rather than whoever is lowest. A child moving from IGCSE into the Diploma, arriving from a different curriculum, or facing a tier decision has a specific gap that closes with a defined block of work. A child who is quietly average in a settled year gains less per hour. The second consideration is cost efficiency: primary fluency work is the cheapest useful hour in the household, so a small allocation there often costs little and pays off for years.

faqs.question: How long does the jump from IGCSE to the IB Diploma take to fix?
faqs.answer: Eight to twelve weeks of technique work, and it is much cheaper in the summer before Year 12 than in the spring of Year 13. The content is continuous; the assessment is not. In maths the change is from executing a method to arguing for it, with Paper 3 at Higher Level being an extended investigation with no IGCSE equivalent. In the sciences it is from knowing content to handling uncertainty and arguing from data. In English it is from set texts to unseen analysis and a timed oral.

faqs.question: Can two of our children have lessons at the same time in an Al Falah villa?
faqs.answer: Often yes, which is one genuine advantage of this housing stock. Two live video lessons can run simultaneously in rooms far enough apart, provided the connection supports both streams. The usual limit is bandwidth rather than space. Where the connection is marginal, back-to-back hours on one evening work just as well and mean the household only needs to be quiet once. Each child still gets their own specialist matched to their own stage and subject.

faqs.question: Is a 30-minute session worth booking for a primary child?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for fluency work it is better than an hour. Number facts, reading aloud and spelling patterns respond to frequency rather than duration, so thirty to forty-five minutes twice a week does more than a single long session. It also uses a part of the evening the older siblings cannot work in anyway, so it costs the household nothing in scheduling terms. Because nobody is travelling to the house, there is no minimum session length needed to justify a journey.

faqs.question: How do we compare reports from two children at two different schools?
faqs.answer: Do not translate them into one scale. A criterion score out of eight tells you how a specific descriptor was met. A percentage tells you about one assessment at one school. A predicted grade tells you what the school expects, which is information about the school as well as the child. The measure that travels between households and systems is a timed paper marked against a published mark scheme, which is why a diagnostic paper is often the first useful thing to do with a sibling comparison.

faqs.question: Should our Year 11 take Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation?
faqs.answer: Decide it against the degree intention rather than against which looks easier. Analysis and Approaches is the route most engineering and physical-science degrees expect, and at Higher Level it adds proof, complex numbers and an extended investigation paper. Applications and Interpretation is the statistical route and suits economics, business and social-science directions, with matrices, graph theory and Voronoi diagrams at Higher Level. Neither is the soft option; they are different subjects. Check the specific entry requirements of the universities on your shortlist before committing.

faqs.question: Do you offer weekend lessons for Al Falah families?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for large households the weekend is usually where the valuable work goes. A ninety-minute coursework review or a full timed paper cannot realistically happen on a weekday evening after a long run home with siblings needing the same room. A Saturday morning session with a visible clock measures the student rather than the week. Two children can each have a long session across two mornings without competing for the household's single quiet weekday hour.

faqs.question: What does tutoring cost for a household with three children?
faqs.answer: At the mid band, three weekly hours sit roughly between AED 1,800 and 3,600 a month, using Bestimate's 2026 estimate of AED 600 to 1,200 a month per weekly hour for a qualified subject tutor. At budget tier, two children at one hour each sit nearer AED 480 to 1,200, with EdFlik advertising from AED 45 to 65 an hour. Most families reduce that by moving the youngest to twice-weekly short sessions and reviewing the allocation at each school report rather than running three standing arrangements.

faqs.question: Can one tutor teach two of our children in the same subject?
faqs.answer: Where the subject, the board and the stage genuinely match, yes - siblings a year apart in Cambridge IGCSE maths is the common case. It should never be done for coursework. An internal assessment is individual work with an individual research question, and two siblings supervised together is a direct route to submissions that resemble each other, which similarity checking flags. If both children take the same Diploma subject, keep the sessions separate and the research questions genuinely different.

faqs.question: Our older child's internal assessment was good. Can the younger one read it?
faqs.answer: Better not. Even with no intention to copy, a student who has read a sibling's finished work on the same subject can produce something that similarity checking flags, and the consequence falls on the student rather than on anyone else. The safeguards are straightforward: different research questions, different contexts, datasets or texts, the older sibling's finished work kept out of circulation, and a tutor who does not discuss one student's approach with the other.

faqs.question: Will a tutor rewrite our Year 13's essay if the deadline is close?
faqs.answer: No. A tutor may teach the subject, explain each criterion, challenge a research question that cannot be answered in the word count, read a draft the student has written and say where the argument fails, and teach referencing properly. Supplying text that reaches the submitted document is malpractice under IB rules, and heavy line-editing is the same breach in a more respectable form. Where a deadline is close, the useful intervention is a review of what exists plus a realistic plan for the remaining weekends.

faqs.question: How many hours a week is reasonable for an examination-year student?
faqs.answer: One to two, in most cases, plus a weekend paper session in the final term. More than that and the limiting factor becomes the student's own practice time, not the teaching: a tutor can mark a paper but cannot sit it for them. Anyone recommending four or five weekly hours before looking at marked work is guessing at the problem. The more useful question is which two or three specific causes account for most of the lost marks, because each of those has a short fix.

faqs.question: Do you report separately on each child, or as a household?
faqs.answer: Separately, always. Each child gets a short note after each session saying what was covered, what was marked and what to practise, with the annotated work attached. A household-level summary tells a parent nothing actionable about any individual student. What you will not get is a weekly percentage, because a number invented by the person being paid is not evidence; the measures worth tracking are external, such as timed paper marks, criterion scores and mock results.

faqs.question: Will a tutor travel out to Al Falah if we pay more?
faqs.answer: No. Home visits are not part of the UAE service at any price and exist only in the India service. For a household at this distance with children at four stages, travel would also be the wrong trade even if it were offered: you would need four specialists each willing to make the same long journey on four separate evenings. Online delivery is what makes it possible to match each child to the right person for their own stage rather than to whoever was prepared to drive.

abu-dhabi/al-falah.closingHeading: Plan the household, not the child
abu-dhabi/al-falah.closingBody: For an Al Falah family the useful first conversation covers everybody: who is in which year, at which school, on which board, and what time each one is actually home. From there the plan builds itself - youngest in the earliest slot on short frequent sessions, the examination candidate in the protected late hour, the child mid-transition getting the defined block of technique work, and the long jobs moved to a weekend morning. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, each child gets their own specialist and their own written note, and the allocation is reviewed at every school report rather than renewed by default.

abu-dhabi/al-ghadeer.tutorsIntro: Al Ghadeer enquiries come from both sides of the border: a Year 11 at a Dubai school sitting Cambridge papers, a Diploma student at an Abu Dhabi campus, and often siblings in both at once. The tutors below teach one-to-one over live video, matched to whichever specification each child is actually entered for.

intro.heading: One household, two regulators
paragraphs: Al Ghadeer sits at the top corner of Abu Dhabi emirate, pressed against the Dubai boundary, closer to the industrial and Expo-side districts of Dubai than to anything in central Abu Dhabi. The community exists because of that location, and so do its particular problems. A household here may hold an Abu Dhabi address, work in Dubai, and send one child to a school licensed in Dubai and another to a school licensed in Abu Dhabi. Everything downstream of that is slightly more complicated than it is for a family living squarely inside one emirate.

The most common confusion is about who regulates what. Dubai's private schools sit with the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, which is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. Abu Dhabi's sit with the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools there. Those are different bodies publishing different material, and a parent reading KHDA guidance about a school licensed in Abu Dhabi is reading the wrong document, however sensible the guidance is.

Some things, usefully, do not change at the border. The private tuition work permit a tutor needs is issued federally by the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, so the permit question is identical whichever side of the line you live on. Equivalency and attestation are run federally through the Ministry of Education, so a British-curriculum student's requirements are the same wherever the school was licensed. And the federal baseline on curriculum - Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside whatever international curriculum a school delivers - applies in both emirates.

The practical cost of the border is the school run. A cross-boundary journey in the afternoon is a highway journey, and it is longer and less predictable than the distance implies. For an Al Ghadeer household that shapes everything about when academic work can realistically happen: a child returning from a Dubai campus and a child returning from an Abu Dhabi one arrive at different times, and the household's usable evening starts with the later of the two. Parents here learn to quote two arrival times rather than one, and a tutoring slot that ignores the second of them will be interrupted every single week by the door opening, a meal starting and the general collapse of quiet that follows a second car coming home.

Lessons here run one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not run home visits in the UAE; home visits are an India-only service. For a community on the boundary that is more than a convenience. A tutor driving to Al Ghadeer is making a highway run from whichever city they live in, which prices the hour up and shrinks the pool to almost nothing for any specific specification. Online delivery means the border is simply not part of the arrangement.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: The qualification with the widest reach on both sides of the boundary, and the most common point of difference between siblings at different schools. Cambridge tiers maths and the sciences into Core and Extended; Pearson's International GCSE specifications are mostly single tier. The code on the entry, not the school's emirate, decides what practice material is useful.

Cambridge allocates centres to one of six administrative zones, so ask the examinations officer which zone applies to your child's centre.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge and CAS. IB places are relatively concentrated: across Dubai's private school market the International Baccalaureate accounts for roughly 7 per cent of enrolment, which is why a border household weighing an IB route often finds the choice of campus narrower than the headline number of schools suggests.

Confirm every IB date with the school's Diploma coordinator or on ibo.org, because no IB session or results date in this project has been verified from the IB's own site and secondary listings disagree with each other.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four criteria per subject, each marked out of eight, with descriptors instead of percentages. Where one sibling is in an MYP school and another in a GCSE school, the two reports are written in different languages and comparing them produces either false alarm or false comfort.
programmes.countryNote: A border family is more likely than most to have children in different systems, because the two emirates' school markets offer different mixes. The useful habit is to read each report in its own terms and to use one external measure that travels: a timed paper marked against a published scheme gives a number that means the same thing in either emirate.

abu-dhabi/al-ghadeer.subjectsIntro: The subjects below are the ones Al Ghadeer households ask about, listed with the specific component that loses marks rather than a description of the course.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580
subjects.description: Extended adds functions, transformations, vectors and harder trigonometry, and sits on different papers from Core. The structured questions on Paper 4 take most of the marks lost, usually because the student completes the hard step and answers a slightly different question from the one set.

subjects.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics 4MA1
subjects.description: A different paper structure and formula provision from Cambridge, with questions phrased in its own way. Siblings at schools in different emirates are frequently entered for different codes, and material does not transfer between them.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625
subjects.description: Electricity and the moments and momentum questions carry most of the marks lost. The alternative-to-practical paper examines experimental reasoning in writing and rewards a student trained to find the flaw in somebody else's method.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620
subjects.description: Mole calculations and the qualitative analysis tables separate the middle grades from the top. The ion tests learned as a memorised list fail under pressure; understood as chemistry they survive, which is where the teaching goes.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Justification carries the marks: assumption stated, step shown, conclusion tied back. Paper 1 is sat without a calculator and Paper 3 at Higher Level is an extended investigation with no IGCSE equivalent on either board.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Technology is assumed throughout and the statistical routines decide whole questions: regression, chi-squared, hypothesis testing. Higher Level adds matrices, graph theory and Voronoi diagrams, none of which appears earlier.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms and energetics carry the heaviest Higher Level load, and the internal assessment is a full written report with its own criteria. The evaluation criterion is where most students leave marks unclaimed.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Uncertainty propagation is examined in Paper 2 and again in the investigation, so a student who can state a relationship but not carry an uncertainty through it loses marks twice for one gap. Fields and circuits are where the quantitative work hardens.

subjects.name: English: First Language, Language and Literature
subjects.description: At IGCSE the losses are in reading inference under time pressure. At Diploma level Paper 1, the guided analysis of an unseen text, carries the widest mark spread and the least classroom time of any component.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language and Islamic education
subjects.levels: The mandatory stream in both emirates
subjects.description: Required alongside every licensed international curriculum under the federal baseline, and taught in Standard Arabic for Arab students. Written register is the recurring gap, and it is examined regardless of which emirate licensed the school.

sections.heading: Who regulates private schools in each emirate
paragraphs: This is the single most useful table on this page for a border family, and it is also content that appears nowhere in the competing results. Across the pages researched for this market, Abu Dhabi's regulator is named by nobody at all and Sharjah's by one provider in passing. For a household whose children may be enrolled in a different emirate from the one they live in, knowing which body publishes which material is not trivia.

The federal position is published plainly. Abu Dhabi's Department of Education and Knowledge supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in that emirate. Dubai's Knowledge and Human Development Authority is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education there. The Sharjah Private Education Authority regulates private education in Sharjah and Ras Al Khaimah's Department of Knowledge does the same in its emirate - and both of those authorities approve tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods, so approval powers reach beyond inspection. The Ministry of Education plays the supervisory role for private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah.

Two things cut across all of it. The private tuition work permit is federal, issued by the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years, with MoHRE's own service page stating a two-working-day completion time. And equivalency sits with the federal Ministry of Education, so the certificate requirements for a British-curriculum student do not vary by the emirate that licensed the school.

What follows for an Al Ghadeer parent is a simple rule. For anything about your child's school - inspection, curriculum approval, mandatory subject arrangements, teacher approval in Arabic and Islamic education - go to the regulator that licensed that school. For anything about the tutor you are paying, or about equivalency, go federal. Nobody should be telling you that a tutoring provider is approved by any of these bodies, because none of them accredits tutoring platforms.

sections.heading: A Dubai-licensed school and an Abu Dhabi-licensed school, in practice
paragraphs: Regulators publish different amounts of detail, and that is the difference a border family notices first. Dubai's authority publishes unusually specific guidance on the mandatory UAE subjects, down to the organisation of classes and the language of instruction. Abu Dhabi's requirements apply to schools it licenses, against the same federal baseline, and the right source for them is ADEK's own material or the school directly.

On the Dubai side, the published requirements include that Arabic, Islamic education and social or moral studies are mandatory in all private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum. Schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic education and social studies, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is the main language of instruction for Islamic education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language. Schools are required to ensure teachers of Islamic education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects, which is a concrete and checkable question to put to a school.

The fee position also differs in what has been published. Dubai's regulator confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees in the emirate for the 2026-27 academic year, under the emirate's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion within a total of AED 2.5 billion. Abu Dhabi operates its own arrangements, so that decision should not be read across the boundary; ask the Abu Dhabi school what has been approved for its own fees.

None of this changes what your child is examined on. Cambridge, Pearson and the IB set the same papers for the same specifications on both sides of the line, and the entry deadlines are the boards' own. The regulator affects the school; the board affects the examination; the Ministry affects equivalency; MoHRE affects the tutor. Keeping those four separate is most of what a border family needs, and it resolves nearly every question that arrives from this community sounding complicated.

sections.heading: Dubai's school market, from the Abu Dhabi side of the line
paragraphs: A border household's real advantage is choice, and it is worth quantifying rather than assuming. Dubai's private school market is large and growing, and an Al Ghadeer family can reach a meaningful part of it by driving north rather than south.

The published figures for 2024-25 are 387,441 students across 227 private schools offering 17 different curricula, with the UK curriculum accounting for 37 per cent of enrolment, Indian curricula 26 per cent, US 14 per cent and the International Baccalaureate 7 per cent. That last number is the one worth noticing: the IB share is small, which means IB places are concentrated in relatively few campuses rather than spread across the market. A family assuming that 227 schools implies wide IB choice will be disappointed by the shortlist.

Capacity is moving, though. Dubai's 2026-27 intake adds seven new private schools - four UK curriculum and three International Baccalaureate - creating 16,846 new places, after six new schools opened during 2025-26 and enrolment rose 6 per cent. For a border family on a waiting list, new IB capacity on the northern side is the most relevant piece of news in that set, and it affects availability more than it affects price.

On price, the anchor is the fee position rather than a tutoring rate: KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that Dubai private school fees would not increase for 2026-27. Set against that, tutoring is the smaller and more controllable line in the budget. Published market rates in AED put a qualified subject tutor online at roughly 150 to 300 an hour and an IB, IGCSE or A Level specialist at 200 to 450 and above, with Bestimate's monthly estimates running 600 to 1,200 for a weekly hour at mid tier and 1,000 to 2,000 and above for examination-year specialist support.
