sections.heading: The cross-boundary school run and the evening it leaves
paragraphs: A border school run is a highway journey, and highway journeys in the afternoon are less predictable than their distance suggests. An Al Ghadeer household driving north into the southern Dubai corridor is making a short run in kilometres and a variable one in minutes; a household driving south to Khalifa City or Al Raha is making a long one in both.

Where the two directions are used by two children in the same family, the household's usable evening starts with the later arrival. That sounds obvious and is routinely ignored when a parent books a lesson. A slot set against the earlier child's arrival will be interrupted by the later one coming through the door, by the meal that has to happen then, and by the general collapse of quiet that follows. Setting the slot against the later arrival, with a margin, is what makes an arrangement last a term.

In practice most families here settle between half past five and seven for secondary students, with primary children taking a slot earlier in the evening while their concentration is still available. Anything demanding - a timed paper, a coursework review - moves to a weekend morning, because after two highway runs nobody is in a state to practise pacing, and practising pacing while exhausted teaches a student to perform tired.

The thing that makes all of this manageable is that no tutor is in the traffic. A session missed because the northbound road closed can become Thursday instead of Tuesday. A slot can shift later during Ramadan, when school hours are reduced across the Emirates and household routines move after Iftar, by agreement rather than by renegotiating somebody's driving route. For a community whose defining feature is a boundary, the useful property of an online lesson is that it does not notice the boundary at all.

sections.heading: Equivalency and attestation, which the border does not complicate
paragraphs: One genuine relief for a border household: the certificate rules are federal, so the emirate that licensed your child's school does not change what the Ministry of Education requires. This is also an area where competing pages are either silent or factually wrong, so it is worth stating precisely.

For the British track, a student must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, and must submit proof of one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five required subjects. The number is five, not six - at least one page ranking for these searches tells UAE parents they need six IGCSE subjects, which does not match the published clarification.

For the American track, English proficiency is met by a score of 5 in the academic IELTS, 61 in the TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, and mathematics requires at least 450 in the SAT Math test before applying. No IB points threshold appears in that source, so none is published here. If a provider quotes you an IB equivalency figure, ask which moe.gov.ae page it came from before relying on it.

Two boundaries of our own. Equivalency and attestation are processes run by the Ministry and the relevant authorities, not services any tutoring provider performs or can guarantee. And tutoring is not a requirement for equivalency, for university admission or for school progression; it is a way of raising a grade. Anyone presenting a regulatory process as a reason you must buy tuition is selling urgency rather than teaching, and that is worth recognising for what it is.

sections.heading: Is your tutor permitted to work in the UAE?
paragraphs: For a border household this is one of the few questions with an identical answer on both sides, which makes it a good place to start. Private tuition in the Emirates requires the work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and issued by the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. It is granted free of charge for two years, and MoHRE's service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time, with applications made through its smart app, website or e-services system.

Eligibility is broad: teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged between fifteen and eighteen. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws. No schedule of amounts has been published officially, so any specific figure quoted on a website should be treated as unverified.

One restriction matters particularly for the Abu Dhabi side of a border household. Professional-ethics rules reported for private and charter school staff in that emirate bar teachers from giving paid private tuition to students enrolled at their own school, and the permit's code of conduct has been reported to carry a similar bar. That is press-reported rather than quoted from a current policy document, so verify it against ADEK's own publication if it matters to a decision. The practical conclusion holds regardless: do not hire the person who teaches and reports on your child at school.

A tutoring operation with premises and staff in Dubai is a different legal category again, needing an educational services permit for a training institute from KHDA, with initial approval first, a maximum of six months to complete the permit and licence steps, and annual renewal requested at least thirty days before expiry. IB Gram holds no such permit, runs no premises in the Emirates, and does not describe itself as approved or accredited by any authority. It matches families with tutors for online one-to-one lessons, and the permit question is one to put directly to whoever takes your money.

sections.heading: Where the marks go, whichever emirate the school sits in
paragraphs: Regulators differ and examinations do not, which is why the diagnosis of a problem is identical on both sides of the boundary. The board sets the paper, the mark scheme awards the marks, and the places students lose them are remarkably consistent.

At IGCSE: in maths at the higher tier, transformations of graphs, vectors, harder trigonometry and the long structured questions where the demanding step is completed and the actual question is not answered. In physics, electricity and the moments and momentum questions. In chemistry, mole calculations and the qualitative analysis tables memorised as a list. In biology, the precision of extended written answers rather than breadth of recall. On Cambridge syllabuses, the alternative-to-practical paper, which is a distinct skill met cold because class time goes on content.

At Diploma level the losses move from content to method. In mathematics it is justification - the assumption unstated, the step unexplained. In the sciences it is uncertainty handling and the evaluation criterion of the investigation, where the available marks go unclaimed because students write about human error instead of about specific weaknesses and their effect. In English A it is Paper 1 on unseen material. In economics it is diagram accuracy under time pressure.

Above all of them sits one loss that dwarfs any topic: questions left blank at the end of a paper. Twelve unanswered marks costs more than any single misunderstood area, and it is a pacing failure rather than a knowledge failure. It is fixed by sitting whole papers to time with a visible clock and marking them against the board's own published scheme, which is uncomfortable, unexciting and the most reliable intervention available in either emirate.

sections.heading: What a tutor may and may not do with assessed work
paragraphs: The rules here come from the examination boards rather than from either emirate's regulator, so they are the same whichever side of the line your child's school sits on. At least one site competing for these searches sells completed Internal Assessments at a published price. Submitting purchased work is malpractice under IB rules, the sanction falls on the student and not the seller, and it can reach the diploma itself.

The legitimate scope is substantial. A tutor can teach the subject content the assessment rests on, read each criterion descriptor and explain in plain language what it requires, interrogate a research question until it is narrow enough to answer in the word count, read a draft the student has written and identify where the argument fails or the data does not support the conclusion, and teach referencing conventions properly.

What cannot happen is text. No paragraph, no processed dataset, no rewritten conclusion, no bibliography typed out for copying. Heavy line-editing is the same breach in a more respectable form, because a sentence composed by the tutor is a sentence the student did not write and the supervisor's authenticity declaration then states something untrue. Similarity checking applies to the submission.

The same principle governs materials. Examination papers, mark schemes, grade boundary tables and syllabus documents belong to Cambridge, Pearson and the IB, so they are referenced by series and question number, linked to the official source, and worked through on screen in the lesson. What the student keeps is their own annotated attempt, which is the artefact with any value in it. The school holds licensed access for everything else, and the subject teacher is usually the fastest legitimate route to a specific paper.

process.title: Say which emirate licensed each child's school
process.description: It changes which regulator's material is relevant to that child, how the mandatory Arabic and Islamic education classes are likely to be organised, and what fee position applies. It does not change the examination, the entry deadline or the equivalency rules, and keeping those two groups separate removes most of the confusion a border household carries.

process.title: Get the board and syllabus code, per child
process.description: Siblings at schools in different emirates are frequently entered for different specifications. Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 need different practice material and different marking. The school's entry confirmation settles it, and for Cambridge candidates the examinations officer can also confirm the administrative timetable zone.

process.title: Set the slot against the later arrival
process.description: Where one child comes back from a northbound run and another from a southbound one, the usable evening starts with the later of the two. A slot booked against the earlier arrival gets interrupted every week. We ask for both times, plus which evenings are already taken, before matching anybody.

process.title: Trial lesson with the matched tutor
process.description: One hour with the specialist who would teach the term, using material from the student's own specification. It ends with a written view on whether the problem is content, technique or pacing and how many sessions it should take. A wrong match is rematched rather than defended.

process.title: Keep the demanding work on a weekend
process.description: Timed papers and coursework reviews go on a weekend morning, because a weekday evening after two highway runs produces marks that understate the student. The weekday hour then does teaching and review, which tolerates tiredness far better than pacing practice does.

whyPoints.title: The regulator map, published properly
whyPoints.description: All five school regulators named with their own published remits, plus the federal bodies for the tutor permit and for equivalency. Across the competing pages researched for this market, Abu Dhabi's regulator is named by nobody and Sharjah's by one provider in passing.

whyPoints.title: Dated, attributed Dubai figures
whyPoints.description: Student numbers, school counts, curriculum shares, the 2026-27 fee position and the new places for the coming intake, each with its period and source. A border family comparing two emirates deserves numbers it can check rather than impressions.

whyPoints.title: The border is not part of the lesson
whyPoints.description: Every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video, so no tutor is making a highway run to Al Ghadeer and no session is lost to a closed road. A missed Tuesday becomes a Thursday without anybody re-planning a route.

whyPoints.title: One specialist per child, per system
whyPoints.description: Where siblings sit different boards or different programmes, each is matched separately rather than covered by one tutor claiming both. Because delivery is online, two tutors on one evening is a scheduling question rather than a cost one.

whyPoints.title: Clear about what is federal
whyPoints.description: The tutor permit and the equivalency rules do not change at the boundary, and neither does the examination. Knowing which of the four authorities governs which part of your child's education is more useful to a border family than any marketing claim.

whyPoints.title: No accreditation claimed
whyPoints.description: No KHDA or ADEK approval, no premises in the Emirates, no self-asserted ratings. KHDA's educational services permit is a specific licence issued to training institutes with premises, and IB Gram does not hold it or imply that it does.

faqs.question: We live in Al Ghadeer but our child's school is in Dubai. Which regulator applies?
faqs.answer: The one that licensed the school. Dubai's Knowledge and Human Development Authority is responsible for overseeing the quality of private education in that emirate, so its published material governs your child's school even though your home address sits in Abu Dhabi. Abu Dhabi's Department of Education and Knowledge supervises licensing and accreditation for schools in its own emirate. Your home address matters for residency paperwork; the school's licence matters for inspection reports, curriculum approval and mandatory subject arrangements. They are separate questions.

faqs.question: Does living on the border change what exams our child sits?
faqs.answer: No. Cambridge, Pearson and the IB set the same specifications and the same papers on both sides of the line, and the entry deadlines are the boards' own rather than any emirate's. Cambridge closes final entries for its March 2027 series on 27 November 2026, with examinations from 3 February to 4 March 2027. Pearson's International GCSE November 2026 final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026. What the emirate affects is the school; what the board affects is the examination.

faqs.question: How many private schools and curricula does Dubai actually have?
faqs.answer: For 2024-25 the published figures are 387,441 students across 227 private schools offering 17 different curricula, with the UK curriculum at 37 per cent of enrolment, Indian curricula at 26 per cent, US at 14 per cent and the International Baccalaureate at 7 per cent. That IB share is the number worth noticing from the Abu Dhabi side of the border: a large total number of schools does not translate into wide IB choice, because IB places are concentrated in relatively few campuses rather than spread across the market.

faqs.question: Has the fee position for 2026-27 been published on the Dubai side?
faqs.answer: The emirate's regulator confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees in Dubai for the 2026-27 academic year, under the emirate's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion within a total of AED 2.5 billion. That decision applies to Dubai-licensed schools. Abu Dhabi runs its own arrangements, so it should not be read across the boundary - ask an Abu Dhabi school directly what has been approved for its own fees rather than assuming either way.

faqs.question: Is there more IB capacity opening near the border?
faqs.answer: Yes, on the Dubai side. The 2026-27 intake adds seven new private schools in the emirate - four UK curriculum and three International Baccalaureate - creating 16,846 new places, following six new schools during 2025-26 and a 6 per cent rise in enrolment. For a border family on a waiting list that is the most relevant piece of information available, because new capacity moves availability more than it moves price. Confirm current openings with the regulator or the schools themselves rather than with a directory.

faqs.question: Does our tutor need a different permit depending on the emirate?
faqs.answer: No, and that is one genuine simplification of life on the boundary. The private tuition work permit is federal, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and issued by the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. It is granted free of charge for two years, and MoHRE's service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. The same requirement applies whichever emirate the tutor or the family is in, and those tutoring without it are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws.

faqs.question: What time can lessons start when one child comes from Dubai and one from Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Set the slot against the later arrival, with a margin. A northbound run into the southern Dubai corridor is short in kilometres and variable in minutes; a southbound run to Khalifa City or Al Raha is long in both. Most border households settle between 17:30 and 19:00 for secondary students, with primary children taking an earlier slot while their concentration lasts. Anything demanding - a timed paper, a coursework review - moves to a weekend morning, because after two highway runs nobody practises pacing well.

faqs.question: Do the UAE equivalency rules differ between Dubai and Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: No. Equivalency sits with the federal Ministry of Education, so the requirements do not vary by the emirate that licensed the school. For the British track a student needs five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count, plus one A Level at E or above or two AS Levels at the same grade. One page ranking for these searches states six IGCSE subjects, which does not match the published clarification. Verify your own case with the Ministry.

faqs.question: Which Arabic and Islamic education arrangements will our school follow?
faqs.answer: Ask the school, because the detail differs in what each regulator publishes. The federal baseline requires private schools to teach Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside whatever international curriculum they deliver. Dubai's published guidance goes further, requiring separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic education and social studies, setting Standard Arabic as the language of instruction for the Arab streams, and requiring that teachers of those subjects hold appropriate KHDA approval. Abu Dhabi schools work to ADEK's requirements.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover siblings at schools in two different emirates?
faqs.answer: Only if they genuinely work to both specifications, which is a question about the board rather than about the emirate. A teacher comfortable with Cambridge 0580 Extended may know Pearson 4MA1 well or barely at all, and the question phrasing and formula provision differ enough to matter at the top grades. Ask any prospective tutor how the long questions differ between the two. Because lessons are online, matching two separate specialists costs the household nothing extra in logistics.

faqs.question: Do you have an office or centre near the border we can visit?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram runs no premises anywhere in the Emirates and does not claim to. A tutoring operation with premises and staff in Dubai needs an educational services permit for a training institute from KHDA, with initial approval first, a maximum of six months to complete the permit and licence steps, and annual renewal requested at least thirty days before expiry. We hold no such permit and no regulator accreditation of any kind. What we do is match families with tutors for one-to-one lessons over live video.

faqs.question: Will a tutor drive out to Al Ghadeer if we pay for the travel?
faqs.answer: No. Home visits are not part of the UAE service at any price and exist only in the India service. For this community the trade would be particularly poor. Published market bands for a tutor travelling to a home run AED 180 to 500 an hour and would apply at the top of that range for a highway run to the boundary, and the real constraint is the pool: a specialist in one specification who is also willing to make that journey on a weekday evening is a very short list. Online delivery removes the problem.

faqs.question: How do we compare two children's reports from schools in different emirates?
faqs.answer: Read each one in its own terms rather than converting them to a single scale. A criterion score out of eight tells you how a specific descriptor was met; a percentage tells you about one assessment at one school; a predicted grade tells you what that school expects. The measure that travels between emirates and systems is a timed past paper marked against the board's own published scheme, which is why a diagnostic paper is often the first genuinely useful thing to do with a sibling comparison.

faqs.question: Is tutoring required for our child to get equivalency or a university place?
faqs.answer: No, and any provider implying otherwise is manufacturing urgency about a regulatory process. Equivalency depends on holding the required certificates at the required grades and is administered by the Ministry of Education and the relevant authorities. Tutoring can help a student reach a grade they would otherwise miss, which is a legitimate reason to hire one. It confers no standing with any authority, forms no part of the procedure, and nobody can guarantee an outcome in a process they do not run.

faqs.question: What happens to lessons during Ramadan on this side of the border?
faqs.answer: They usually move later and often get shorter and more frequent. School hours are reduced across the Emirates during the month and household routines shift, so most families prefer sessions after Iftar. The important part is agreeing the change before the month begins rather than improvising inside it: households that settle the new timing in advance keep the arrangement, while those that leave it open tend to lose three or four weeks to rescheduling. Because nobody is driving, the change is a scheduling decision rather than a negotiation.

abu-dhabi/al-ghadeer.closingHeading: Keep the four authorities separate and the rest is simple
abu-dhabi/al-ghadeer.closingBody: For an Al Ghadeer household the confusion is almost always about who governs what. The regulator that licensed the school governs the school. The examination board sets the paper and the entry deadline. The Ministry of Education runs equivalency. MoHRE issues your tutor's permit. Once those four are separated, the tutoring decision is the same as anywhere: get the syllabus code for each child, set the slot against the later arrival, move the demanding work to a weekend, and match a specialist to the specification. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, and the boundary plays no part in them.

abu-dhabi/al-jubail-island.tutorsIntro: The tutors below cover the Diploma and both IGCSE boards at the levels island families ask for most: Higher Level sciences, Mathematics in both routes, and the English and Economics components where written technique decides the grade. Each match is made against the syllabus your child's school actually teaches.

intro.heading: Who has moved onto Jubail Island, and what that does to study time
paragraphs: Jubail Island sits in the mangrove channel between Saadiyat and Yas, reached by a single bridge from the Sheikh Khalifa highway. It was built as low-density villa land, and the households that took those plots arrived with school-age children before any school opened on the island itself. That one fact shapes every tutoring conversation here. A family on Al Reem or in Khalifa City can walk a teenager to a school gate; a Jubail Island family is in the car twice a day in each direction, and the hours that remain are the hours a tutor has to work inside.

Four recognisable household types have settled here. The first is the capital-sector professional family, often two working parents, children placed on Saadiyat or Yas because the drive is short and the schools are strong. The second is the relocated household, arriving mid-year from the United Kingdom, Singapore or another Gulf city, with a child who has to enter a cohort that started in September. The third is the Emirati or long-resident Abu Dhabi family who moved out from Al Bateen, Al Mushrif or Al Khalidiyah and kept the original school place, so the drive now runs back into the city rather than out to the islands. The fourth is the multi-child household running two different programmes at once, usually a primary child on a British route and an older sibling in the Diploma.

Each of those four asks a different first question. The professional household asks when a lesson can start without colliding with the commute. The relocated household asks what its child has missed and how fast the gap closes. The family driving back into the city asks whether the hour in traffic is worth the school it is driving to. The multi-child household asks whether one tutor can sensibly hold two programmes, and the honest answer is usually no, because a Diploma Higher Level physicist and a Year 5 reading specialist are different people.

What all four share is that the academic pressure point is not the school. Private schools reachable from the island are inspected by the Department of Education and Knowledge, and the stronger ones teach well. The pressure point is the quantity of work a Diploma or IGCSE student has to carry on their own, in a house that is twenty-five minutes from everything, after a day that started before seven. An internal assessment is not taught in class. A past paper is not marked in class. The independent half of the course is where island households lose ground, and it is the half an outside tutor can actually hold.

So this page is organised around the household rather than around the subject list. It names the schools each district actually offers, prices the market in dirhams with the source attached, sets out what the regulator's inspection report does and does not tell you about your own child's subject, and states the line a tutor may not cross on internally assessed work. Tuition itself is delivered as one-to-one online lessons, which is why the bridge does not need crossing twice.
bullets: No private school currently operates on Jubail Island itself; every option is a drive
Saadiyat, Yas and Khalifa City are the three realistic school districts from here

abu-dhabi/al-jubail-island.programmesIntro: Island households split fairly evenly between the IB continuum and a British route that runs IGCSE into A Levels or into the Diploma. The four programmes below are the ones a tutor is asked for from this postcode, with a note on what each means specifically for a family whose school is on the other side of a bridge.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: The PYP is inquiry-led and reports against learner attributes rather than subject percentages, which is why a PYP report can look reassuring while a reading age or a number-bond gap sits underneath it. Tutoring at this stage is diagnostic: establish where phonics, fluency, place value and written number work actually sit, then close the specific gap rather than covering the whole year again.
programmes.countryNote: For a Jubail Island family, the practical issue at primary age is the length of the day. A child leaving the island at seven and arriving home near four has no appetite for a long session. Twenty-five focused minutes on screen, three times a week, does more at this age than a single long block, and it fits between the car and dinner without a second drive.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The MYP marks eight subject groups against four criteria each, lettered A to D, every one scored out of eight. Parents read a 5 and assume a middling child; the number is actually a statement about one named skill, such as inquiring and analysing or communicating. Tutoring here means decoding the criterion the marks are falling against and practising that specific task type.
programmes.countryNote: MYP Year 10 and 11 is where island families most often first call. The Personal Project lands in the same window as the longest commute of the week, and it is the first piece of work a student has to project-manage alone. We coach the process, the research question and the reflection, and the project itself stays entirely the student's own from start to submission.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. In the current science guides the internal assessment carries 20% of the final grade at both Standard and Higher Level, and the Mathematics exploration carries 20% as well. Those are the components a weekly lesson can genuinely protect, because they are coursework with criteria rather than a performance on one morning.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma students on the island are typically at Cranleigh Abu Dhabi, Raha International School, the British International School Abu Dhabi or GEMS American Academy, all of which run a full Higher Level set. The gap is rarely teaching. It is the forty to sixty hours of independent work per subject across two years that has to happen in a quiet room, and that room is here.

programmes.name: IGCSE and A Level
programmes.description: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel both run international GCSEs here, and the papers differ even where the subject name is identical. Cambridge splits Mathematics 0580 into a Core tier sitting papers 1 and 3 and an Extended tier sitting papers 2 and 4, with the Core ceiling at grade C. Pearson's 4MA1 is tiered as Foundation and Higher. Confirming the board and the tier is the first thing a tutor should do.
programmes.countryNote: British-route island families need five accredited IGCSE or GCSE subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3 for Ministry of Education equivalency, with Arabic and Islamic Education excluded from that count of five, plus one A Level at E or two AS Levels at the same grade. That is the file your child carries to a UAE university, so the subject spread matters as much as the grades.

abu-dhabi/al-jubail-island.subjectsIntro: Requests from the island concentrate in the Higher Level sciences and Mathematics, with English and Economics close behind. The descriptions below say what each course actually assesses and where marks leave the page, because that is what a tutor has to aim at.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Standard Level sits two papers at 40% each with the exploration at 20%; Higher Level adds Paper 3, with papers 1 and 2 at 30% each, Paper 3 at 20% and the exploration at 20%. Marks go missing in Paper 3's extended investigation, where students solve correctly but never state the structure of the argument.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: A modelling and statistics route with the graphic display calculator in use throughout. The usual loss is interpretation: a correct regression or confidence interval followed by no sentence saying what it means in context. Examiners award those marks for the sentence, not the calculation.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Papers 1 and 2 carry 36% and 44%, with the scientific investigation at 20%. Island students are usually fine on mechanics and lose ground in fields and in the Higher Level quantum material, where the written explanation has to name the mechanism rather than restate the equation.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Structure and reactivity are examined across the same two papers and the same 20% investigation. Organic mechanisms and energetics are where Higher Level marks go; the fix is a mechanism drill with curly arrows drawn by hand, which is slow work and exactly what a one-to-one hour is for.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The course now runs on unifying themes rather than a topic list, which rewards students who can transfer a concept to an unseen context. Data-based questions in Paper 2 are the reliable loss point, because students describe a trend when the command term asked them to explain a cause.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Standard Level is Paper 1 at 30%, Paper 2 at 40% and the portfolio at 30%; Higher Level adds the quantitative Paper 3. The portfolio of three commentaries is the most coachable part of the course, and the most common failure is a commentary with no diagram doing any analytical work.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 is unseen textual analysis, Paper 2 a comparative essay, and the Individual Oral carries 30% at Standard Level. Higher Level adds the HL essay at 20%. Students who read widely still lose marks by summarising the text instead of analysing the writer's choices.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language
subjects.description: Cambridge 0510 and 0511 assess reading, writing, listening and, in some routes, speaking. The written paper rewards register control and accurate structure over vocabulary display. For relocated students this is often the subject that most needs an outside pair of eyes in term one.

subjects.name: Mathematics (IGCSE)
subjects.description: The Extended tier accesses grades A* to E, the Core tier C to G. Moving a student between tiers in Year 11 is a serious decision with a hard grade ceiling attached, and it should be made on marked evidence rather than on a feeling about confidence.

subjects.name: Combined and Coordinated Sciences
subjects.description: The double-award sciences compress physics, chemistry and biology into fewer papers, so a weak strand drags the whole grade. Diagnosis by strand before buying lessons is what stops a family paying for three sciences when one is the problem.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Arabic runs alongside the international programme in every private school in the emirate under the federal curriculum rules. Non-Arab students are assessed against a different expectation from first-language learners, and the gap that opens is usually script fluency rather than vocabulary.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Higher Level sits Paper 1 at 35% and Paper 2 at 40% with the project at 25%. The project requires real organisational evidence, and students who choose a company they cannot access end up with an analysis built on guesses, which the criteria punish.

abu-dhabi/al-jubail-island.regionsIntro: A tutoring plan from Jubail Island has to account for the surrounding districts, because that is where the school is, where the grandparents are and where the second car goes in the afternoon. These are the areas island households actually move through.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: The closest school district by road, reached without touching the mainland. Cranleigh Abu Dhabi anchors it. A Saadiyat school place is the shortest school run available to a Jubail Island family, which makes a 4.30pm session realistic rather than aspirational.

regions.name: Yas Island
regions.note: Reached in roughly the same time as Saadiyat but on the opposite side, with West Yas Academy and the Yas schools cluster. Yas households add event traffic to the calculation: race weekends and concert nights move the evening, so a fixed weekday slot beats a Friday one.

regions.name: Al Raha Beach
regions.note: On the Khalifa highway corridor between the island and the airport. Families here share the same bridge and the same afternoon window as Jubail Island, and often share a school bus route too, so sibling scheduling patterns transfer directly.

regions.name: Al Raha Gardens
regions.note: Villa community built around Raha International School, which runs the full IB continuum through to the Diploma. Several Jubail Island Diploma students hold places here, which means a commute out along the highway rather than in towards the city.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: The deepest school cluster reachable from the island, including GEMS American Academy Abu Dhabi, the British International School Abu Dhabi and Al Yasmina Academy. It is also the longest drive, and the one that most often pushes a weekday lesson past 6pm.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: A dense apartment island on the other side of the channel with its own school provision. Jubail Island families with older children sometimes keep a Reem school place after moving, which converts a five-minute walk into a bridge-and-highway run.

regions.name: Al Bateen
regions.note: Established city district with long-standing school provision including Al Bateen Academy and the American Community School. Families who moved out to the island from Bateen frequently keep the school, which is the commute that runs back into town.

regions.name: the Corniche
regions.note: Not a school district but the route most city-bound island families take home, and the one where the afternoon is lost. A parent collecting from a Bateen or Khalidiyah school is realistically back on the island after five.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City
regions.note: Mainland residential district with a large Indian and Pakistani curriculum school presence. Relevant to island households whose staff or extended family live there, and to students transferring between a national board and IGCSE.

regions.name: Al Reef
regions.note: Villa and apartment community near the airport, popular with teaching staff. Mentioned here because tutor availability in the emirate is shaped by where teachers live, and Al Reef is one of the places they do.

schoolClusters.city: Saadiyat and Yas Islands
schoolClusters.note: The two island school districts a Jubail Island family can reach without going through the city. Between them they cover the British curriculum, the IB Diploma and an American route, which is why most island school decisions are made inside this cluster first.

schoolClusters.city: Khalifa City and the Al Raha corridor
schoolClusters.note: The mainland cluster at the end of the highway run, and the deepest set of Higher Level Diploma options available to island households. It is also where most of the emirate's British-curriculum capacity sits.
schools: The British International School Abu Dhabi

schoolClusters.note: The schools island families keep after moving out of town. The drive is the longest of the three clusters and the one most likely to make a weekday lesson impossible before six.

abu-dhabi/al-jubail-island.modesIntro: Three delivery patterns cover almost every island household. The choice is driven by the commute and by how many children are being scheduled, not by preference, and it is worth deciding before the first lesson rather than after three.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one over live video
modes.description: A fixed hour each week with the same tutor, held in the slot the school run leaves free. This is the pattern for a Diploma student carrying a Higher Level subject across two years, because the value accumulates: a tutor who saw the mock knows what to look for in the next piece of written work.
bullets: Same tutor, same slot, so the session needs no restart each week
Shared screen for marked scripts, graphs and mechanism drawings
Work set between sessions and reviewed at the start of the next
Slot held through term breaks if the family travels

modes.title: Coursework supervision blocks
modes.description: Short, intense sequences timed to an internal assessment, an Extended Essay or a Personal Project. Three or four sessions placed at the proposal, the data or sourcing stage, and the evaluation stage do more than a vague weekly hour, because coursework fails at identifiable moments rather than gradually.
bullets: Session one on the research question and whether it is answerable
Session two on method, sourcing or data quality before it is collected
Session three on the criteria the draft is currently missing
Feedback only on the student's own text, never new text supplied

modes.title: Sibling stacking across one evening
modes.description: Two children, two programmes, back-to-back slots with different specialists on the same evening. The island household running a primary child and a Diploma student is the commonest multi-child case here, and stacking keeps the disruption to one evening instead of spreading it across four.
bullets: Different tutor per child, matched to level rather than to convenience
Shorter block for the younger child, full hour for the older
One parental handover conversation covering both
Rescheduling handled as a pair when the family travels

sections.heading: Four Jubail Island households, and the question each one asks first
paragraphs: A tutoring enquiry from this island almost always comes from one of four household shapes, and knowing which one you are saves a month of aimless lessons. The capital-sector professional family with both parents working has a time problem rather than an academic one: the child is capable, the school is strong, and the week has no slot in it that anyone has deliberately protected. The relocated household has an alignment problem: the child has arrived into a cohort mid-course, the board may have changed, and nobody has yet written down which specific topics were skipped.

The third shape is the family who moved out from the city and kept the original school place. Their problem is arithmetic. A fifty-minute drive each way removes nearly two hours from the day, and the student is doing independent work in the two hours that remain, at the point of lowest energy. For these families the right answer is often fewer, longer, earlier weekend sessions rather than a weekday hour that keeps collapsing.

The fourth is the multi-child household with two programmes running at once. The temptation is a single generalist who covers everyone. That works at primary level and stops working the moment one child is carrying a Higher Level science, because the content knowledge required is genuinely different. Stacking two specialists into one evening costs the same number of disrupted hours and buys two real matches.

The table below is the version of this we use when a parent first calls. It is not a personality test. It is a way of working out what to buy first, because the wrong first purchase on this island is usually a weekly general session that nobody can keep.
bullets: Time-poor professional household: protect one slot, do not add subjects
Mid-year arrival: diagnose the skipped topics before booking a term
City-school commuter: move the work to the weekend and earlier
Two programmes in one house: two specialists, one evening

sections.heading: An island with no school of its own, and three districts to choose between
paragraphs: There is no private school operating on Jubail Island itself, so every family here has made a school decision that is also a traffic decision. The three realistic districts are the island cluster on Saadiyat and Yas, the mainland cluster through Al Raha and Khalifa City, and the original city schools on Abu Dhabi island. All of them are licensed and inspected by the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate, so the regulatory framework is identical across the three. What differs is the curriculum mix, the Higher Level subject depth and the length of the drive.

The practical consequence for tutoring is that two neighbours on the same street can be on entirely different academic calendars. One child may be sitting Cambridge IGCSE papers in a June series; the next-door student may be in a Diploma cohort working to a May session with internal deadlines set by their own school rather than by the board. A tutor matched to the wrong board wastes the first fortnight discovering it.

It also means school-choice questions arrive here more often than they do in established districts. Parents ask whether the extra fifteen minutes to Khalifa City buys enough additional Higher Level provision to be worth it. The answer depends entirely on the subjects your child wants, which is why the table names programmes offered rather than giving a general ranking.

We publish inspection ratings only where they have been read on the regulator's own listing for the current cycle, and the column below is deliberately left as a pointer rather than filled with numbers we cannot stand behind. Checking a band on the ADEK listing before a school tour takes about five minutes and is more reliable than any table on a tutoring website.

sections.heading: The bridge, the school bus and what is left of the afternoon
paragraphs: Jubail Island has one road connection, and every school run uses it. A bus collecting for Khalifa City is on the island early, because the route then picks up through Al Raha before reaching the school gate. A parent driving to Saadiyat leaves later and gets home sooner. The difference between those two patterns is close to ninety minutes a day, and it entirely changes which tutoring slot is realistic.

Work the afternoon backwards instead of forwards. A secondary school day ending at half past two puts an island child home between three and a quarter past four depending on district and whether the bus or the car is used. Allow thirty minutes for food and decompression, and the earliest honest start is four o'clock for a Saadiyat family and closer to five for a Khalifa City one. A session that starts at five and runs an hour leaves the evening intact. A session that starts at seven competes with sleep, and by the third week it is being cancelled.

Weekends do more work out here than they do in the city. Friday and Saturday mornings are the only blocks in the week that are not downstream of a commute, which makes them the right place for anything cognitively heavy: a Paper 3 investigation, an Extended Essay drafting session, a full timed paper under conditions. Families who put their hardest subject in a Saturday morning slot and keep a short weekday review for consolidation lose far fewer sessions over a term than families who try to carry two heavy weekday hours.

There is also a seasonal shape to this. Ramadan brings shortened school days across the emirate, which temporarily opens an early afternoon window that is otherwise unavailable, and post-Iftar sessions work well for older students. The summer break is long, and it is the only period in which a genuine rebuild of a weak foundation is possible without competing with term deadlines.

Saadiyat families can realistically start at four; Khalifa City families at five
Put the hardest subject in a weekend morning, not a late weekday hour

sections.heading: What tutoring costs around Abu Dhabi, set against the fees already paid
paragraphs: Most tutoring pages in this market publish no price at all. Three of the six competitor pages examined for this project quote no figure, and the two that do quote in US dollars, a currency no UAE family transacts in. The bands below are market rates in dirhams, attributed to whoever published them, and they are not IB Gram's price list. They exist so an island household can tell whether a quote it has received is normal.

The budget end, between AED 45 and AED 150 an hour, is university students and non-specialist generalists; EdFlik advertises from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52 for its lower tiers. A qualified subject tutor working online sits between AED 150 and AED 300, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. In-home one-to-one visits run from AED 180 to AED 500 once travel is inside the figure, on Bestimate's 2026 Dubai rate table and comparable home-tutor listings. A genuine Diploma or A Level specialist is AED 200 to AED 450 and upwards, with TutorChase publishing AED 270 and premium named tutors reaching AED 650.

Those numbers only mean something next to the fees a family is already paying. An Abu Dhabi private school place in the stronger British and IB schools is a substantial annual commitment, and two weekly tutoring hours across a full academic year is a fraction of it. Parents who have never done that arithmetic tend either to over-buy at the top of the market in panic or to under-buy at the bottom and conclude tutoring does not work.

The fair way to think about it is cost per component protected. A Higher Level science internal assessment is 20% of that subject's final grade. If four supervision sessions placed at the right moments are what keeps that component from being mediocre, the arithmetic is straightforward. A general weekly hour with no component attached is much harder to justify, and it is the purchase island families most often regret.

sections.heading: A home tutor on the island against one-to-one online
paragraphs: Parents here search for a home tutor, and the search is reasonable: a villa household with two children and one car would obviously rather someone arrived than add another journey. So it is worth answering the question properly before saying what we actually do. A home tutor on Jubail Island is paying for the crossing in both directions. That travel is inside the rate, which is why in-home figures in this market start around AED 180 and run to AED 500, against AED 150 to AED 300 for an equivalently qualified tutor working online. The second cost is invisible: the tutor pool shrinks to people willing to drive to a low-density island at five in the afternoon, which in practice means generalists rather than Higher Level subject specialists.

IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. Every lesson for an Abu Dhabi family is delivered one-to-one over live video. That is a real constraint and it is better stated plainly than discovered after a deposit.

The case for it on this island is specific rather than general. A Jubail Island family that insists on someone in the room is choosing from whoever is prepared to make the drive. A family on live video is choosing from the people who actually teach the syllabus their child sits, which for a Higher Level chemist or an Economics Paper 3 candidate is a materially different set of people. Screen sharing also suits the work that matters most here: a marked script, a graph, a mechanism drawn step by step and a mark scheme side by side are easier to work through on a shared screen than across a kitchen table.

What online does not fix is motivation or supervision. A twelve-year-old who needs an adult in the room to stay on task is a harder case on video than in person, and we say so rather than selling a format that will not hold. For that age, shorter sessions and a parent within earshot work better than an hour alone with a laptop.

sections.heading: Two children, two programmes, one evening
paragraphs: The multi-child island household is the case that most often goes wrong, and it goes wrong in a predictable way. A parent books one tutor for both children to keep the logistics simple. For a while it holds, because at primary and lower secondary level a strong generalist covers a lot of ground. Then the older child enters the Diploma or Year 10, and the content moves past what a generalist can carry. The family does not notice immediately, because the sessions still happen and the reports are still polite. What they notice is a mock grade in February.

Stacking solves the logistics without the compromise. Two consecutive slots on the same evening, a shorter block for the younger child and a full hour for the older, with a different specialist in each. The number of disrupted evenings stays at one. The parent has a single handover conversation covering both children. If the family travels, both slots move together.

There is an order worth respecting when the budget only stretches to one child at a time. Fund the child with an examined component imminent, because that is the money with a deadline attached. A Year 13 Higher Level subject in January has a harder claim than a Year 5 reading gap, however worrying the reading gap feels, because the Year 5 gap can be closed across a summer and the Year 13 one cannot.

The other thing worth setting up early is a shared view of what each child is actually working on. Island households run busy weeks, and the commonest failure is two tutors each doing good work while nobody knows the school has moved a deadline. A short written note after each session, naming what was covered and what was set, costs nothing and prevents most of that.
bullets: One generalist for two different stages stops working around Year 10
Two specialists in consecutive slots cost the same evening, not two
Fund the child with the nearest examined component first
Ask for a written note after each session, naming what was set

sections.heading: Reading an ADEK inspection report for your own child's year group
paragraphs: The Department of Education and Knowledge licenses and inspects private schools in the emirate and publishes its own ratings. Parents use the overall band as a shorthand, which is understandable and slightly misleading. An overall rating is an aggregate across phases, subjects and a long list of inspection standards. It tells you about the institution. It does not tell you about the Higher Level physics set your sixteen-year-old is sitting in.

The useful reading is narrower. Find the section covering your child's phase, not the school as a whole, because a school can be strong in primary and merely adequate in the sixth form or the reverse. Then read what the report says about attainment against curriculum standards separately from what it says about progress, because those two judgements answer different questions. High attainment with weak progress describes a selective intake that is not adding much. Modest attainment with strong progress describes teaching that is working on a harder cohort.

Then look for the subject-level commentary. Inspection reports routinely name subjects or phases where outcomes lag, and that is the sentence worth photographing, because it is the closest thing a parent gets to an external opinion on whether the specific teaching their child receives is any good. If the report flags a subject your child takes, you have your answer about where an outside hour should go.

What a report cannot do is substitute for the evidence in your own house. A marked mock script tells you more about your individual child than any inspection band, and it is free. Our first session with a secondary student almost always begins with the last thing a teacher marked, for exactly that reason.
bullets: Read the phase section, not just the overall band
Separate attainment from progress; they answer different questions
Look for named subjects flagged as lagging and check against your child's set
A marked mock script beats an inspection rating for your own child

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies alongside an IB or British route
paragraphs: Private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific national curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and they must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That federal baseline is why your child's international programme always runs alongside a set of mandatory subjects, whichever emirate you are in and whichever curriculum the school is licensed for. Families arriving onto the island from the United Kingdom or Singapore are regularly surprised by it, usually in October.

The organisational rules are specific. Expectations differ between Arab and non-Arab students, with Arabic as a first language and Islamic Education taught against different curriculum expectations and in a different language of instruction from the courses non-Arab students take. Dubai's regulator publishes the most detailed public guidance on how this is to be organised, including minimum lesson lengths and a prohibition on combining the two groups, and it is a useful reference even for Abu Dhabi families because the federal requirement underneath is the same.

Two practical consequences for a tutoring plan. First, these subjects occupy real timetable hours, so a Diploma student carrying six subjects plus the core is doing so in a week that also contains mandatory Arabic. When parents say there is no time in the week, this is frequently part of why. Second, and more importantly for British-route families, Arabic and Islamic Education are not counted among the five accredited subjects the Ministry requires for equivalency on the GCSE and IGCSE track. A student who assumes those two count towards the five can finish Year 11 a subject short of what their university file needs.

Tutoring support for Arabic is available as an additional-language stream, focused on script fluency and the specific assessment the school uses. We do not supply or reproduce Ministry-approved content, because for the mandatory subjects the use of different or additional material without prior Ministry permission is not allowed, and that is a line worth respecting rather than working around.
bullets: The federal rule covers Arabic, social studies and Islamic studies in every private school
Arab and non-Arab students follow different expectations and are taught separately
Arabic and Islamic Education do not count towards the equivalency five

sections.heading: Where a tutor stops on internally assessed work
paragraphs: Every programme reachable from this island carries assessed work the student produces outside an exam hall: a Diploma internal assessment in each subject, the Extended Essay at 4,000 words, the Theory of Knowledge essay at 1,600, the MYP Personal Project, IGCSE coursework where a school offers it. That work has to be the student's own, and the rules around it are enforced. A breach is a malpractice finding against the student, not against the tutor, which is why the line matters more to your family than it does to us.

So here is what a tutor does. Interrogates the research question until it is answerable within the limits. Points out that a method will not generate data capable of supporting a conclusion, before the data is collected rather than after. Reads a draft against the published criteria and says which criterion is currently unevidenced. Teaches the skill the draft is missing, then hands it back. Asks why a paragraph is there.

And here is what a tutor does not do. No sentence is ever supplied for a student to paste. No section is rewritten into something better than the student could produce. No draft is edited to completion. No topic, data set or structure is handed over ready-made, and nothing is bought in from anywhere. One operation in this market openly sells finished Diploma internal assessments; that product is an academic-integrity breach and the student carries the consequence.

The practical version of this is about timing. Supervision bought early, at the point where a question is being chosen and a method designed, is both more useful and completely safe. Supervision bought three days before submission is where families end up asking for things nobody should provide. Island households, with their compressed evenings, are especially prone to leaving coursework late, so we flag the dates in the first session and book the supervision blocks against them.
bullets: Research question, method and criteria coaching, as early as possible
Feedback given against the published criteria, on the student's own text
No supplied text, no rewriting to completion, no ready-made topics
Supervision booked at the proposal stage, not the week before submission

sections.heading: Getting started from Jubail Island, and what we say when nobody is free
paragraphs: The first conversation is short and it is about evidence. We ask which school and which district, so we know the board and the calendar. We ask for the most recent thing a teacher marked, because a script shows a problem that a report only describes. We ask what time the child is actually home, since that sets the slot rather than any preference. And we ask what has already been tried, because a family that has had two tutors leave does not need a third identical arrangement.

Then a trial session with the matched tutor, which is a diagnostic rather than a sales appointment. The tutor works through the marked script, establishes whether the problem is content, technique or timing, and writes down what a term of work would actually consist of. If the diagnosis is that tutoring is not the right purchase, we say that. Some students need a conversation with their subject teacher, a set change, or simply a protected hour of their own time, and none of those is something to sell.

Availability has limits and we state them before you plan around us. Niche Higher Level subjects, the less common Diploma languages and some specialist combinations are thin in the UAE time zone, and an island family asking for a Thursday five o'clock slot in a rare subject may find nothing available. When that happens we say so, offer the nearest genuine alternative, and if there is no honest match we tell you rather than putting a generalist in front of a Higher Level paper.

One more thing worth knowing as a parent in this market. Individuals providing private lessons in the UAE need a private tuition work permit from the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years, with eligibility extending to registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Anyone tutoring without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published, so treat any figure you are quoted with suspicion. It costs nothing to ask a prospective tutor whether they hold the permit.
bullets: Send the last marked script before the first conversation
The trial session is a diagnostic and may conclude against buying lessons
Rare Higher Level subjects and languages can be genuinely unavailable
Ask any tutor whether they hold the MoHRE private tuition permit

process.title: Tell us the school, the district and the drive
process.description: Which school, which of the three districts it sits in, and what time your child is genuinely through the door. That triple sets the board, the assessment calendar and the only slots that will survive a term. Guessing at any of the three is how arrangements collapse in week four.

process.title: Send the last marked piece of work
process.description: A marked mock, a returned essay, an internal assessment draft with teacher comments. One marked script tells a specialist more than a page of description, because it shows whether marks are leaving over content, over exam technique or over timing. It also makes the trial session useful instead of introductory.

process.title: Meet the matched tutor in a diagnostic session
process.description: The tutor works through the script with your child, establishes what is actually going wrong, and writes down what a term of work would contain. You get that plan whether or not you continue. If the honest conclusion is that lessons are not what is needed, the tutor says so.

process.title: Fix the slot and the cadence
process.description: One weekly hour, a weekend morning for the heavy subject, or a short supervision block timed to a coursework deadline. The cadence is chosen against the island commute and the school's own deadline calendar, then held, including through term breaks if the family travels.

process.title: Review against the next marked thing
process.description: Progress is checked against external evidence, not against how the sessions felt. The next mock, the next returned essay, the next criterion-marked draft. If the evidence has not moved after a reasonable number of sessions, the plan changes or the tutor does.

whyPoints.title: Matched to the syllabus, not to the postcode
whyPoints.description: An island family choosing a tutor who will drive to Jubail Island is choosing from a small pool of people with cars and spare afternoons. Choosing on live video means choosing from people who teach the exact syllabus your child sits, including the Higher Level sciences and the Mathematics routes where the specialism genuinely matters.

whyPoints.title: Prices published, and attributed
whyPoints.description: Every dirham figure on this page is a market rate with the source named and the month stated. Three of the six competitor pages examined for this project publish no price at all and two quote in dollars. Knowing the bands is what lets you recognise a reasonable quote when you receive one.

whyPoints.title: The regulator explained, not borrowed
whyPoints.description: We name the Department of Education and Knowledge, explain what it licenses and inspects, and show you how to read its report for your own child's phase. IB Gram holds no accreditation, licence or partnership from ADEK, KHDA, the Ministry of Education, the IB or any examination board, and we do not imply one.

whyPoints.title: A coursework line that protects your child
whyPoints.description: Research questions, methods, criteria and feedback on the student's own text. No supplied sentences, no rewriting to completion, no ready-made topics. The consequence of a malpractice finding falls on the student, so this boundary is drawn for their protection rather than for ours.

whyPoints.title: Availability stated before you plan around it
whyPoints.description: Rare Higher Level subjects and the less common Diploma languages have thin coverage in this time zone. We say so at the first conversation, offer the nearest real alternative, and tell you when there is no honest match rather than putting a generalist in front of a Higher Level paper.

whyPoints.title: Built for the island afternoon
whyPoints.description: One bridge, one exit window and a school run of twenty-five to fifty minutes each way. Slots are chosen from what the commute actually leaves, weekends carry the heavy work, and the shortened Ramadan school day is treated as the opportunity it is rather than a disruption.

faqs.question: Is there a school on Jubail Island itself?
faqs.answer: No private school currently operates on Jubail Island. Every family here commutes, and the three realistic districts are the island cluster on Saadiyat and Yas, the mainland cluster through Al Raha Gardens and Khalifa City, and the older city schools on Abu Dhabi island. All of them are licensed and inspected by the Department of Education and Knowledge, so the regulatory position is the same wherever you choose. What differs is the curriculum mix, the depth of Higher Level Diploma provision and the length of the drive, which is the factor that ends up deciding which tutoring slots are possible.

faqs.question: What time can a tutoring session realistically start for an Al Jubail Island family?
faqs.answer: Work backwards from the drive rather than from the school bell. A secondary day finishing at half past two puts a Saadiyat-schooled child home around three, so a four o'clock start is comfortable. A Khalifa City family, especially one using a bus route that collects early and drops late, is realistically looking at five. Allow thirty minutes for food before anything academic begins. Sessions placed after seven get cancelled by the third week, which is why we would rather fix a sustainable hour at the outset than agree an optimistic one.

faqs.question: How much do IB and IGCSE tutors in Al Jubail Island charge per hour?
faqs.answer: Market rates in the emirate run roughly AED 45 to 150 for a budget or university-student tutor, AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor working online, AED 180 to 500 for an in-home visit with travel inside the figure, and AED 200 to 450 or more for a genuine IB or A Level specialist. Those bands come from published competitor pricing and Bestimate's 2026 Dubai rate table, as of October 2026. They are the market, not an IB Gram price list, and they exist so you can judge whether a quote you receive is normal.

faqs.question: Do tutors travel to villas on Jubail Island?
faqs.answer: Ours do not. IB Gram does not make home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India, and every lesson for an Abu Dhabi family runs one-to-one over live video. Independent in-home tutors do work on the island, and their rates reflect the crossing in both directions, which is why in-home figures in this market start near AED 180 and reach AED 500. The hidden cost is the narrower choice: the pool becomes people willing to drive to a low-density island late in the afternoon rather than specialists in your child's actual subject.

faqs.question: Which school districts do Jubail Island children usually attend?
faqs.answer: Three. Saadiyat and Yas give the shortest run and cover British, American and IB Diploma routes. The Al Raha and Khalifa City corridor has the deepest Higher Level Diploma provision and the largest British-curriculum capacity, at the cost of the longest drive. The third group is the city schools in Al Bateen and Al Mushrif, usually kept by families who moved out to the island and did not want to move their children. Knowing which district you are in tells a tutor the board, the calendar and the usable slot.

faqs.question: Can one tutor take both my primary child and my Diploma student?
faqs.answer: At primary and lower secondary level a strong generalist covers a lot of ground, so it works for a while. It stops working around Year 10, when Higher Level or Extended-tier content moves past what a generalist can carry, and the failure usually shows up as a February mock grade rather than as an obvious problem in the sessions. Stacking two specialists into consecutive slots on the same evening costs the same single disrupted evening and gives both children a real match, with one handover conversation covering both.

faqs.question: My child has just moved to Abu Dhabi mid-year. Where should tutoring start?
faqs.answer: With a map of what was actually skipped, not with a general catch-up block. A mid-year arrival into an established cohort has specific unmapped gaps: topics taught in September that the previous school covered later or not at all, and sometimes a different board for the same subject. One diagnostic session per subject, built around the last work the previous school marked, identifies those gaps in a couple of hours. Booking a term of lessons before that diagnosis is how families end up paying to re-teach material the child already knows.

faqs.question: What does an ADEK inspection rating tell me about my own child's subject?
faqs.answer: Less than parents assume. The overall band is an aggregate across phases, subjects and a long list of standards, so it describes the institution rather than your child's set. Read the section for your child's phase, separate the judgement on attainment from the judgement on progress, and look for named subjects flagged as lagging. If a subject your child takes appears in that list, you have a clear answer about where an outside hour should go. A marked mock script still tells you more about your individual child than any band.

faqs.question: How much of a Diploma science grade is the internal assessment worth?
faqs.answer: In the current science guides the scientific investigation carries 20% of the final grade at both Standard and Higher Level, with papers 1 and 2 carrying the remaining 36% and 44%. The investigation is marked out of 24 across four criteria covering research design, data analysis, conclusion and evaluation. Because it is coursework with published criteria rather than a performance on one morning, it is the most reliably improvable component in the subject, and it is where a small number of well-timed supervision sessions has the clearest effect.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help write my child's internal assessment?
faqs.answer: No, and nobody reputable should offer to. A tutor interrogates the research question, checks that the method can generate usable data before it is collected, reads a draft against the published criteria and names the criterion that is unevidenced, then teaches the missing skill and hands the work back. No text is supplied, no section is rewritten, and no topic or data set is handed over ready-made. A malpractice finding falls on the student, not on the tutor, which is why this boundary protects your child rather than us.

faqs.question: Do Arabic and Islamic Education count towards the Ministry of Education equivalency subjects?
faqs.answer: No. On the British track the Ministry requires five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at no less than grade E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five. Candidates also need one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or better, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. One competitor page in this market publishes a six-subject figure, which is wrong. Verify the current requirement on the Ministry's own site before you rely on it for a university application.

faqs.question: Does my child's tutor need a UAE permit, and how do I check?
faqs.answer: Individuals providing private lessons need a private tuition work permit from the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. The permit is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Tutoring without one carries fines and penalties under the applicable laws, though no fine schedule is published. Simply ask a prospective tutor whether they hold it; the answer costs nothing and tells you a lot.

faqs.question: Is a weekend morning session better than a weekday evening out here?
faqs.answer: For heavy work, yes. Friday and Saturday mornings are the only blocks in a Jubail Island week that do not sit downstream of a commute, which makes them the right place for a Paper 3 investigation, a full timed paper under conditions or an Extended Essay drafting session. Keep a short weekday slot for consolidation and setting work rather than for anything cognitively demanding. Families who arrange it this way lose noticeably fewer sessions across a term than those trying to carry two heavy weekday hours.

faqs.question: What happens if no tutor is available for a rare Higher Level subject?
faqs.answer: We tell you, before you plan around us. Coverage for the less common Diploma languages, some Higher Level combinations and a few specialist options is genuinely thin in this time zone, and a request for a specific weekday slot in a rare subject may have nothing behind it. In that case we offer the nearest real alternative, which might be a different day, a different session length or a tutor working from another time zone, and if there is no honest match we say so rather than putting a generalist in front of a Higher Level paper.

faqs.question: Do the shortened Ramadan school days change the tutoring schedule?
faqs.answer: They open a window that is otherwise unavailable. Private schools across the emirate run reduced hours during Ramadan, which puts children home considerably earlier and makes an early afternoon slot possible for the only time in the year. Older students often prefer a post-Iftar session instead, which works well and tends to be calmer than a rushed weekday hour in term time. We move slots deliberately for that month rather than letting sessions quietly lapse, and set the pattern before the month starts rather than during it.

abu-dhabi/al-jubail-island.closingHeading: Start with the marked script, not the subject list

intro.heading: The Airport Road clock, and why it decides whether tutoring works here
paragraphs: Al Karamah sits in the middle of Abu Dhabi island, east of Al Mushrif and south of Al Nahyan, with the Airport Road corridor running along its edge. That road is the island's main artery, and it carries school buses, commuters and the morning and afternoon school runs for a large part of the city. Living beside an artery is convenient at 11:00 and expensive at 07:15 and 15:00. The distances are short; the half hours either side of the bell are not.

For most families here the tutoring question is not which subject or which board. It is which hour. A household can know exactly what their child needs and still fail to get it, because the lesson was booked for a time that assumes a quiet afternoon. A session that starts eight minutes after a car pulls into the compound is a session the student spends the first third of recovering from. Parents here discover that in week two and usually blame the tutor.

The week has more constraints in it than a scheduling form usually captures. There is the school day, which varies by school and by phase. There are activities and sports fixtures. There are prayer times. There is Ramadan, which shifts roughly eleven days earlier each year and changes the school timetable, the evening and the whole shape of an academic term. There are school exam weeks, when a tutor adding work makes things worse rather than better. And there is the simple fact that a younger child and a Diploma candidate in the same household need opposite ends of the evening.

There is also the question nobody asks until it goes wrong, which is what happens when a lesson is missed. A family that has agreed in advance what counts as notice, what happens to a session cancelled because of a fixture or a flight, and whether unused sessions expire, is in a completely different position from a family discovering those terms in week six. Four questions answered before the first booking prevent most of the friction that ends an arrangement which was otherwise working perfectly well.

This page is a scheduling page. There are tables on which time windows actually work and why, on session length and frequency, on Ramadan and term-calendar adjustments, on what a fair reschedule policy contains, on how the market prices by hour, session and month, and on what happens when the right specialist is not in this time zone. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi, because home visits are a service we run only in India, and in a district whose problem is the road that turns out to be the point rather than a limitation.
