abu-dhabi/al-karamah.programmesIntro: Three programme routes dominate Al Karamah enquiries, and each one has a different natural rhythm. Matching the format to that rhythm matters as much here as matching the subject.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Two-year courses assessed by terminal papers, tiered in many subjects. Syllabus codes decide the match: 0580 Mathematics, 0625 Physics, 0620 Chemistry and 0610 Biology for Cambridge, 4MA1 and 4PH1 for Pearson. The work is cumulative, which makes a steady weekly slot more valuable than an intensive block.
programmes.countryNote: An IGCSE student in Al Karamah is usually best served by one fixed sixty-minute slot a week from 16:30 or 17:30 Gulf Standard Time, rising to two sessions in the final term. Consistency beats volume at this level, because the content is broad and the technique has to be built by repetition rather than taught once.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Internally assessed work carries a fifth to a quarter of each subject grade and is produced outside taught time, which means the student's own evening schedule does most of the work.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma students in this district often prefer a 19:30 or 20:00 slot, because that is when they would be working alone anyway and because the earlier evening is taken by the commute, food and activities. Ninety minutes suits Higher Level component work; sixty minutes suits a weekly check on a long-run project.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each, marked from 0 to 8, with no terminal exam unless the school enters eAssessment. Criterion letters rather than percentages appear on reports, so a pattern of lost marks on one criterion can persist unnoticed.
programmes.countryNote: Younger students fade sharply after 19:00, so MYP sessions belong in the 16:30 to 18:00 window even where a parent would find a later slot more convenient. Forty-five minutes of attentive work at 16:30 produces more than ninety distracted minutes at 20:00.

abu-dhabi/al-karamah.subjectsIntro: The notes below pair each subject with the kind of session it actually needs, because a subject that requires sustained working differs from one that benefits from short frequent contact.

subjects.name: Mathematics (IGCSE)
subjects.description: Needs frequent short contact rather than long blocks, because fluency is built by repetition. A sixty-minute weekly slot with twenty minutes of practice between sessions outperforms a two-hour fortnightly session, and the Extended tier adds functions, vectors and harder trigonometry to cover.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Higher Level Paper 3 work needs ninety-minute blocks, because an extended problem cannot be started and abandoned. This is the clearest case on this page for a later evening slot, when a student can sustain concentration without the next activity pressing on it.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics work in sixty-minute sessions, since the tasks are naturally bounded. Marks are lost in interpretation rather than calculation: a correct regression followed by a sentence that misstates what the gradient means earns the calculation and nothing else.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL · Cambridge 0625 · Pearson 4PH1
subjects.description: Problem-solving benefits from longer blocks, because the first fifteen minutes are usually spent reconstructing the method. Electricity is the perennial difficulty, and circuit work in particular rewards an uninterrupted stretch with a shared diagram on screen.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Mole calculations and energetics reward short, frequent drilling; organic mechanisms reward a long block. Splitting a chemistry plan into both kinds of session, rather than treating every week identically, is one of the simplest improvements available.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Content-heavy and penalised for imprecise language rather than for ignorance. Works well in sixty-minute sessions with written answers marked between them, since the gains come from phrasing rather than from extended problem solving.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 unseen analysis needs a full timed sitting, so the practice itself belongs at the weekend with the session used for marking. The individual oral is worth twenty to thirty per cent depending on level and should be rehearsed as an exam rather than discussed.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram work suits short sessions and the three Diploma commentaries, capped at eight hundred words each, suit a defined block timed around the school's internal deadlines. Higher Level adds a quantitative paper worth a fifth of the grade.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: The clearest case for short frequent contact anywhere in this list. Mandatory in UAE private schools and taught in a separate stream from the first-language course, it responds to three twenty-minute exposures a week far better than to one long weekend session.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: An essay capped at one thousand six hundred words marked against a single global descriptor out of ten, plus an exhibition with a nine hundred and fifty word commentary across three objects. A short, finite block of three to five sessions, best scheduled well before the school's internal deadline.

abu-dhabi/al-karamah.regionsIntro: Al Karamah's neighbours matter here mostly as traffic and timing, since the district sits on the island's main corridor. Each note describes what the neighbouring area does to an Al Karamah family's afternoon.

regions.name: Al Mushrif
regions.note: Immediately west, sharing school bus routes and the same afternoon traffic pattern. Lesson timings are effectively interchangeable between the two districts, which is why siblings attending different schools across the boundary can still be stacked into one evening.

regions.name: Al Nahyan
regions.note: North, another dense central district with a heavy school presence. Pick-up traffic from its schools feeds onto the same corridor, which is the main reason a 16:00 start is optimistic in this part of the island and 16:30 is not.

regions.name: Al Wahda
regions.note: North-east, around the Al Wahda interchange, one of the slowest points on the island between 15:00 and 16:00. Families whose school run passes through it should plan for 17:00 rather than 16:30 on weekdays.

regions.name: Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: North-west on the island's western side, with a concentration of tuition centres. Al Karamah families often compare a centre class against one-to-one tuition, and the drive to a centre is itself a second school run in the same afternoon.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: East across the channel, with The British International School Abu Dhabi and Repton Abu Dhabi. From Al Karamah that is a twenty to thirty minute afternoon run, so students at those schools generally need 17:30 or later.

regions.name: Zayed Sports City
regions.note: South across the Airport Road corridor, where many Al Karamah children train. Sports commitments usually fix one or two evenings completely, which makes the remaining nights the only real options and worth identifying before any booking.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Off-island to the east over the bridges. A minority of Al Karamah families commute out there, and for those households the realistic lesson window is 18:00 onwards on weekdays, with heavier work moved to Saturday morning.

schoolClusters.note: This group sits within fifteen minutes of most Al Karamah addresses, but the drive at pick-up is slower than the distance suggests because several schools release within the same half hour onto the same roads. The predictability is the point: a slot that never moves is a slot the student prepares for, and a slot that moves weekly becomes the first thing dropped when the week gets busy.

sections.heading: The time windows that actually work on this corridor
paragraphs: The direct answer: for most Al Karamah families the workable weekday windows are 16:30 to 18:00 for students up to about Year 9, and 18:00 to 21:00 for IGCSE and Diploma students, with 19:30 and 20:00 the most requested slots in the district. The window between 15:00 and 16:15 looks available on a calendar and is not, because it is the school run and the recovery from it.

The reason is that the Airport Road corridor absorbs pick-up traffic from several schools releasing inside the same half hour. A fifteen-minute distance becomes a thirty-minute drive. A family that books a 16:00 lesson will spend most terms starting at 16:12 and apologising, and a tutor who holds the slot open loses the time either way.

The second factor is recovery. A student who has been in school since 07:30 and in a car since 15:00 needs food and twenty minutes before they can think. The difference between a lesson that starts at 16:15 and one that starts at 16:30 is not fifteen minutes of inconvenience; it is the difference between a session that works and a session that is endured.

The third factor is the back end of the evening. Younger students fade sharply after 19:00, and a forty-five-minute session at 16:30 will produce more than ninety minutes at 20:00. Older students are the reverse: a Diploma candidate at 20:00 is already at a desk, and the session simply replaces an hour they would have spent working less efficiently alone.

sections.heading: How long a session should be, and how often
paragraphs: Length is treated as an administrative detail and is actually a teaching decision. Different work has a different natural duration, and the commonest mistake in this district is buying a single weekly ninety-minute session for everything because it feels like better value per booking.

Short frequent contact wins where the goal is fluency. Arabic vocabulary, times-table automaticity, algebraic rearrangement at speed: these improve through repeated short exposure and barely improve at all through one long weekly session, because the skill decays between contacts. Three thirty-minute sessions beat one ninety-minute session for the same total time.

Long blocks win where the work cannot be fragmented. An extended problem-solving paper, a stretch of Internal Assessment data analysis, a full timed essay: all of these need a run-up and a continuous stretch, and a sixty-minute session spends a third of itself reconstructing where the student left off.

Frequency should also change through the year rather than staying fixed. One session a week is right for most of a two-year course. Two or three a week in the final six weeks before a terminal paper is right for a candidate close to a boundary. Holding the same cadence for twenty-four months is a sign nobody is reading the calendar.

There is a cost argument in the same direction. Buying a ninety-minute weekly session for fluency work pays for duration the student cannot use, while buying sixty minutes a week for Higher Level problem solving pays for a session that spends twenty minutes getting back to where it stopped. Matching the length to the work is the cheapest improvement available in this plan.

sections.heading: Ramadan, prayer times and the academic calendar
paragraphs: The UAE academic year has features that a generic study plan ignores, and ignoring them is how a term's tutoring quietly stops happening. Ramadan is the largest. It moves roughly eleven days earlier each year in the Gregorian calendar, so its position relative to mock exams and internal deadlines changes annually, and in some years it lands directly in the heaviest coursework weeks.

During Ramadan schools typically run a shortened day, which changes both the finish time and the student's energy curve. Confirm your own school's adjusted timetable rather than assuming last year's. The practical adjustment that families here make most often is to move sessions to after Iftar, when students are fed and the evening is naturally awake, and to shorten daytime sessions rather than cancel them.

Prayer times are the smaller, steadier constraint, and they move through the year with sunset. A fixed 18:00 slot that works comfortably in December can sit awkwardly in June. Agreeing a slot that can shift by twenty or thirty minutes seasonally, rather than one fixed to the minute for a year, avoids a recurring monthly negotiation.

Two further calendar points matter. School exam and mock weeks are the wrong time to add new work: a tutor's useful contribution during those weeks is marking and technique, not new content, and some families pause entirely. And the long summer break is where transition work belongs, because a bridging block has a clear run at it without a school timetable competing.

sections.heading: Why Saturday morning is the most valuable hour of the week
paragraphs: The school week here runs Monday to Friday and the weekend is Saturday and Sunday, which gives a student exactly one morning that is both free and early. Saturday morning is worth protecting, because it is the only time in the week when a student can sit a full paper to time without a commute before it or an activity after it.

That is the single highest-value piece of exam preparation available, and it almost never happens, because nobody schedules it. A full paper requires an uninterrupted stretch, a willingness to stop at the time limit, and the discipline to mark it afterwards. Attempting it on a Tuesday evening after a school day produces a result that measures tiredness rather than ability.

The arrangement that works is a split week. Saturday morning is used for the paper, written independently with nothing open. A short weekday session is then used to mark it against the official scheme, writing the reason next to each lost mark, and to record the recurring error pattern. The teaching happens in the marking rather than in the sitting.

Sunday is better used for review than for new work, partly because the school week starts the next morning and partly because a student who has just marked a paper has a short list of specific things to fix. Twenty minutes on each of three named errors is a better Sunday than two hours of general revision. It is also a session a tired student will actually start, which general revision is not.

sections.heading: Missed sessions, rescheduling and what a fair policy contains
paragraphs: This is the part of a tutoring arrangement that families in this district ask about last and need first, because the Airport Road corridor generates genuine clashes: a fixture that overruns, a flight, a road closure, a sibling's event. A policy agreed at the start prevents most of the friction that ends an otherwise working arrangement.

A fair policy has four parts. A clear notice period, usually twenty-four hours, with a stated consequence either side of it. A defined treatment of planned pauses, such as exam weeks and Eid, which should not consume paid sessions. An expiry rule for unused sessions in a package, stated in writing. And a tutor-side rule, because the tutor will occasionally need to move a slot too.

The red flags are equally specific. A package with no stated expiry is not generous, it is ambiguous, and ambiguity resolves in the provider's favour. A policy that treats a planned pause and a late cancellation identically punishes the organised family. And any refund arrangement tied to a grade outcome rather than to delivery should be refused, because a result cannot be promised by anyone.

One advantage of online delivery is directly relevant here. A session that would be cancelled because a tutor could not cross the island at 17:00 can simply be moved by an hour on the day, because nobody has a journey to waste. In a district where the road is the problem, removing the road removes most of the cancellations.

sections.heading: How the market prices by hour, by session and by month
paragraphs: Comparing tutoring quotes in Abu Dhabi is harder than it should be because providers price in different units. One quotes an hourly rate, another a per-session fee for a ninety-minute lesson, a third a monthly package with a session count. The figures below are market rates in the UAE, taken from providers' own published pricing and a published 2026 Dubai tutoring rate survey by Bestimate, and they are the market rather than an IB Gram price list.

Published hourly figures run from roughly AED 45 to 65 at the budget online end and AED 33 to 52 from one platform's entry tier, AED 150 for IGCSE and AED 200 for IB from an agency that publishes rates, AED 270 from a UK-based agency, a survey band of AED 200 to 450 and above for specialist exam-year work, and AED 650 at the premium named end. In-home visits in the emirate are published between AED 180 and AED 500, with travel inside the hour.

Monthly packages seen in the market include around AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions. The same survey put weekly one-hour tuition at roughly AED 240 to 600 a month at budget level, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support.

The conversion that makes quotes comparable is cost per teaching minute, one to one. Work it out for each quote before deciding. Then ask two more questions: whether the quoted figure includes VAT, and what the reschedule terms are. Do not accept a general statement about the tax treatment of tuition fees without a Federal Tax Authority reference; the only thing a provider needs to tell you is whether its own quoted AED figure includes it.

sections.heading: An in-home tutor crossing the island at 17:00, compared with online
paragraphs: Families here searching for a home tutor are reacting to a real problem, which is that the afternoon is already full. The difficulty with solving it by having someone come to the house is that the tutor is on the same road at the same hour, and nothing about hiring them changes the traffic.

That produces two recurring failures. The first is lateness: a tutor leaving a 16:00 lesson elsewhere on the island to reach Al Karamah for 17:00 will sometimes arrive at 17:20, and a sixty-minute booking becomes forty minutes. The second is cancellation, because a journey that cannot be made is a lesson that cannot be delivered, rather than a lesson that moves by an hour.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE, and does not operate a centre in the emirate. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, with a shared screen for working through papers. The scheduling consequence is the whole argument on this page: a session can start on the minute, can move by an hour on the day, and is not affected by a closure on the corridor.

In-home tutoring still has a genuine advantage for younger children who concentrate better with an adult physically present, and that is worth stating on a page arguing for something else. For a Year 11 or Diploma student whose problem is that there is no time in the week, the format that removes two journeys is the one that solves the stated problem.

sections.heading: When the right specialist is not in this time zone
paragraphs: Coverage is deep in mainstream subjects and thin in the niches, and an Al Karamah family should be told which group their request falls into before they commit. Mainstream requests, IGCSE Mathematics and the sciences, English, both Diploma Mathematics routes, Economics, Business Management, usually match within one or two working days with a choice of slots.

The thinner areas are predictable: Higher Level Further Mathematics, Arabic as a first language at upper secondary, Music, Film, Visual Arts, and some second-language combinations. Where no UAE-based tutor covers a subject, lessons may be taught by a specialist in another time zone, usually from India, over the same live video format. That is disclosed before booking rather than discovered afterwards.

Time zones matter practically rather than abstractly. India Standard Time runs ninety minutes ahead of Gulf Standard Time, which means a 20:00 slot in Abu Dhabi is 21:30 for the tutor, and a 16:30 slot is 18:00. Both are workable. A 07:00 Abu Dhabi slot is not, and a request for one should be met with a straight answer rather than an attempt.

The honest fallback, when nothing fits, is to say so quickly. A family told within two working days that no Film Higher Level specialist is available can go elsewhere with the term intact. The alternative, which some providers choose, is three weeks of reassurance followed by the same answer in a worse month. Where a match is partial, the sensible compromise is to begin on the component that can be taught now and keep the rest under review rather than holding the whole plan hostage to one subject.

process.title: Write down the week before you ask for a tutor
process.description: List the actual school finish time, the activity evenings, the sports fixtures and the nights that are already gone. Al Karamah households usually discover they have two real options rather than five, and knowing which two shortens matching to a day or two instead of a week of near misses.

process.title: Choose the slot from the day's structure, not the calendar gap
process.description: Pick the hour at which your child can sit down fed and settled, which on this corridor is rarely before 16:30 and often 18:00 or later. A slot chosen because it is empty rather than because it is workable produces three weeks of lessons and then a quiet stop.

process.title: Match the session length to the work
process.description: Ask for thirty to forty minutes two or three times a week for fluency work, sixty minutes weekly for subject teaching, and ninety minutes for extended problem solving or coursework analysis. Buying one long weekly session for every purpose is the commonest avoidable mistake in this district.

process.title: Agree the reschedule terms in writing first
process.description: Notice period, treatment of planned pauses, expiry of unused sessions, and what happens if the tutor moves a slot. Four questions, answered before the first booking. This is the single step that prevents most of the friction that ends an otherwise working arrangement.

process.title: Protect Saturday morning
process.description: Keep one weekend morning for a full timed paper, written independently with nothing open, and use a short weekday session to mark it. It is the only uninterrupted early block in the week and the highest-value piece of exam preparation available anywhere in this plan.

whyPoints.title: The slot is treated as a teaching decision
whyPoints.description: Session time, length and frequency are set from the student's day and the kind of work rather than from whichever hour looks empty. On a corridor that absorbs the island's school traffic twice daily, that is what separates a plan that lasts a year from one that lasts a month.

whyPoints.title: Nothing is lost to the road
whyPoints.description: A sixty-minute online session is sixty minutes of teaching. No tutor is late because of a closure on Airport Road, no lesson is cancelled because a journey could not be made, and a slot can move by an hour on the day without anyone wasting a drive.

whyPoints.title: Ramadan and exam weeks are planned, not improvised
whyPoints.description: Ramadan moves earlier each year and sits in a different part of the academic calendar each time. Sessions shift to after Iftar, daytime slots shorten rather than vanish, and school exam weeks become marking and technique rather than new content.

whyPoints.title: Reschedule terms stated before the first booking
whyPoints.description: Notice period, planned pauses, package expiry and tutor-side cancellation are all stated up front. A refund promise attached to a grade is never offered, because no provider can promise a result and any that does is selling something else.

whyPoints.title: Coverage limits and tutor time zones disclosed
whyPoints.description: Where a subject has no available UAE-based specialist, that is stated along with the tutor's time zone and the slots it allows. A family can then decide with the facts, rather than finding out in week three that the only slot offered is at 07:00.

faqs.question: What is the earliest time a lesson can realistically start in Al Karamah?
faqs.answer: On a normal weekday, 16:30 Gulf Standard Time for younger students and 18:00 or later for anyone whose school run crosses the channel or the bridges. The window between 15:00 and 16:15 looks free on a calendar and is the school run plus recovery. The Airport Road corridor absorbs pick-up traffic from several schools releasing within the same half hour, so a fifteen-minute distance becomes a thirty-minute drive. Add twenty minutes for food and settling, and 16:30 is the first hour at which a student can actually think.

faqs.question: Is a later evening slot acceptable for a Diploma student?
faqs.answer: It is often the best slot available. A Diploma candidate at 20:00 is already at a desk, and the session replaces an hour they would otherwise spend working alone less efficiently. Many Al Karamah Diploma families settle on 19:30 or 20:00 for exactly that reason. The opposite is true for younger students: concentration falls sharply after 19:00, so forty-five minutes at 16:30 produces more than ninety minutes at 20:00 for a Year 7 or Year 8 child.

faqs.question: How long should each session be?
faqs.answer: It depends on the work rather than on the subject. Fluency work such as Arabic vocabulary or arithmetic automaticity improves through repeated short exposure, so thirty to forty minutes two or three times a week beats one long session of the same total length. Subject teaching at IGCSE suits sixty minutes weekly. Extended problem solving, a Higher Level Paper 3 question or a stretch of Internal Assessment data analysis needs ninety minutes, because a sixty-minute session spends a third of itself reconstructing where the student stopped.

faqs.question: Should the number of sessions change through the year?
faqs.answer: Yes, and a plan that never changes cadence is a sign nobody is reading the calendar. One session a week suits most of a two-year course. Two or three a week in the final six weeks before a terminal paper suits a candidate close to a grade boundary. During school mock and exam weeks the useful contribution is marking and technique rather than new content, and some families pause altogether. The summer break is where transition and bridging work belongs, because it has a clear run.

faqs.question: How does Ramadan change the lesson slot for an Al Karamah student?
faqs.answer: Yes, and that is the adjustment most Al Karamah families make. Schools typically run a shortened day during Ramadan, which changes both the finish time and the student's energy curve, so daytime sessions are usually shortened rather than cancelled and the main slot moves to after Iftar when students are fed and the evening is naturally awake. Ramadan shifts roughly eleven days earlier each year, so confirm your own school's adjusted timetable annually rather than assuming last year's arrangement still applies.

faqs.question: How do prayer times affect a fixed weekly slot?
faqs.answer: They move through the year with sunset, which is why a slot fixed to the minute for twelve months causes a recurring negotiation. A 18:00 session that sits comfortably in December can clash in June. The practical solution is to agree a slot that can shift by twenty or thirty minutes seasonally, settled once rather than renegotiated monthly. Tutors working with UAE families are used to this, and it is a reasonable thing to raise when the arrangement is first set up rather than six weeks in.

faqs.question: Why is Saturday morning worth protecting for study?
faqs.answer: Because the school week runs Monday to Friday, Saturday morning is the only block in the week that is free, early and uninterrupted. That makes it the only realistic time to sit a full paper to time, which is the highest-value piece of exam preparation available. Attempting the same thing on a Tuesday evening after a school day measures tiredness rather than ability. The arrangement that works is Saturday for the paper, written independently with nothing open, and a short weekday session to mark it.

faqs.question: What should a fair reschedule policy contain?
faqs.answer: Four things, agreed in writing before the first session. A stated notice period, usually twenty-four hours, with a clear consequence either side of it. A defined treatment of planned pauses such as school exam weeks and Eid, which should not consume paid sessions. An expiry rule for unused sessions in any package. And a tutor-side rule, because the tutor will occasionally need to move a slot too. A policy that binds only the family, or a package with no stated expiry, is ambiguity rather than generosity.

faqs.question: What happens if we need to cancel on the day because of a fixture?
faqs.answer: Ask before booking how many same-day changes are allowed. A reasonable arrangement includes one allowance per term, with same-day cancellations beyond that charged, and anything cancelled with more than twenty-four hours' notice rescheduled within the month at no charge. Al Karamah generates genuine clashes, since fixtures overrun and the corridor closes, so this is worth settling at the start. One advantage of online delivery is that a session can often simply move by an hour on the day, because no one has a journey to waste.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a tutor to our home in Al Karamah?
faqs.answer: No. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, and IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; that service runs only in India. The scheduling reason matters in this district: a tutor travelling to Al Karamah for 17:00 is on the same corridor as everyone else, so a sixty-minute booking becomes forty when they arrive late, and a journey that cannot be made is a lesson lost rather than moved. Published in-home market rates in the emirate run from roughly AED 180 to AED 500 an hour with travel inside the rate.

faqs.question: How do I compare an hourly rate against a monthly package?
faqs.answer: Convert everything to cost per one-to-one teaching minute. Published market figures include roughly AED 45 to 65 an hour at the budget online end, AED 150 for IGCSE and AED 200 for IB from an agency that publishes its rates, AED 270 from a UK-based agency, AED 200 to 450 and above for specialist exam-year work, and packages around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions or AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions. Those are market figures, not IB Gram prices. Then ask whether the session is a full sixty minutes of teaching.

faqs.question: Do quoted tutoring prices in Abu Dhabi include VAT?
faqs.answer: Ask the provider directly about their own quoted figure, and treat any broader claim with caution. The only thing a provider needs to tell you is whether the AED figure it has quoted includes VAT. A general statement about how tuition fees are treated for tax purposes should not be accepted without a Federal Tax Authority citation, because that is a question about UAE tax law rather than about a price list. Get the answer about the quote in writing alongside the reschedule terms.

faqs.question: What if the only specialist for my child's subject is outside the UAE?
faqs.answer: You should be told before booking, along with the slots it makes possible. Where no UAE-based tutor covers a subject, lessons may be taught by a specialist in another time zone, usually from India, over the same live video format. India Standard Time runs ninety minutes ahead of Gulf Standard Time, so a 20:00 Abu Dhabi slot is 21:30 for the tutor and a 16:30 slot is 18:00, both workable. A 07:00 Abu Dhabi slot is not, and the honest answer is to say so.

faqs.question: How quickly can a tutor be matched for an Al Karamah student?
faqs.answer: Mainstream requests usually take one to two working days: IGCSE Mathematics and the sciences, English, both Diploma Mathematics routes, Economics and Business Management all have several available specialists and a choice of evening slots. Higher Level Mathematics with a Paper 3 focus takes three to five working days and is usually evening-only. Narrow subjects such as Arabic as a first language at upper secondary, Music, Film or Visual Arts at Higher Level take longer, and where nothing fits the honest answer is a decline rather than a wait.

faqs.question: Should we pause tutoring during school exam weeks?
faqs.answer: Often yes, and if not, the session should change shape. During a school's own mock or exam week the student's load peaks, and a tutor adding new content makes things worse. What helps during those weeks is marking completed papers, working on timing, and fixing one or two named errors. Many Al Karamah families pause entirely and book a review session for the week after results come back, which is the point at which the component breakdown is available and a plan can be built from evidence.

abu-dhabi/al-karamah.closingHeading: Send the week, and the slot will follow
abu-dhabi/al-karamah.closingBody: Al Karamah families rarely need help identifying the subject. What they need is an hour that exists. Write down the real school finish time, the evenings already committed to activities and fixtures, and the nights the household can protect, and the workable slot usually becomes obvious. From there the session length is matched to the kind of work, the reschedule terms are agreed in writing, and Saturday morning is kept for the one full timed paper nobody otherwise finds time to sit. Lessons run one-to-one over live video, so the corridor stops deciding what is possible.

abu-dhabi/al-khalidiyah.tutorsIntro: Profiles below name the board and the syllabus code each tutor teaches, not just the subject. In a district where neighbouring schools enter different boards for the same subject, that is the only matching detail that reliably prevents a term of near-miss teaching.

intro.heading: Same subject, different board, different paper: the gap nobody explains
paragraphs: Al Khalidiyah is one of the densest parts of Abu Dhabi island, a grid of apartment towers between the Corniche and Al Bateen with Zayed the First Street running through the middle of it. Households here are mixed in nationality and compact in size, children are generally within twenty minutes of school, and the tuition centres along the main street tell you how much demand there is. What they do not tell you is which board any given child is entered with.

That is the gap this page is about. A school teaches a syllabus thoroughly. What it rarely has time to explain is why the assessment is shaped the way it is: why one Physics student sits a practical test and another answers questions about an experiment they never performed, why one Mathematics candidate is capped at a lower grade than the student beside them, why entries for next spring closed last November. Those are board mechanics, and they decide a surprising share of the final result. They are also the part of the system that no report card mentions and no parents' evening has time for.

The practical consequence shows up in tutoring. A competent Physics teacher who has spent ten years on Cambridge 0625 will teach a Pearson 4PH1 student well on content and imperfectly on paper technique, because the papers are not the same shape and the mark schemes do not reward the same phrasing. Families rarely ask about this, and almost nobody volunteers it. The fix costs nothing: read the code off the front of the last mock paper and quote it when you ask for a tutor.

The second part of the gap is what a student does with the information. Tier choices, series choices and resit decisions are made by the school as the examination centre, usually in conversation with the parent, often on a short deadline and with no explanation of the consequences. A family that understands the November route before results day in August behaves very differently from one that discovers it in September. The same is true of tiering: a decision taken quietly in October caps what is available the following June, and it is far easier to question in October than in April.

What follows is organised as board mechanics rather than as subject content. There are tables comparing Cambridge and Pearson for the same subjects, on the Core and Extended decision, on how practical skills are assessed under each board, on the exam series and their entry deadlines, and on what the Abu Dhabi market charges. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE, because home visits are a service we run only in India.

abu-dhabi/al-khalidiyah.programmesIntro: Three routes cover almost every Al Khalidiyah enquiry. The useful difference between them is how the final grade is produced, because that determines what a tutor should be working on in January.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE
programmes.description: Terminal papers at the end of a two-year course, with Core and Extended tiers in many subjects. Sciences add a practical component, sat either as a practical test or as an alternative-to-practical written paper depending on what the centre offers. Syllabus codes are the operative detail: 0580 Mathematics, 0625 Physics, 0620 Chemistry, 0610 Biology, 0500 First Language English.
programmes.countryNote: Cambridge runs a June series and a November series, and every centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones with its own timetable version. Ask your Al Khalidiyah school which zone it sits in and work from the timetable it issues, because Cambridge's own guidance states it cannot accept responsibility for a candidate who misses an exam after using the wrong zone's timetable.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Graded 9 to 1, with Foundation and Higher tiers in subjects such as Mathematics A, where the code is 4MA1. Physics is 4PH1. Practical skills in the sciences are assessed inside the written papers rather than by a separate practical exam, which changes how a student should prepare and what a tutor should drill.
programmes.countryNote: Pearson International GCSE exams are available in May or June and in November each year. The November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, while November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, so always work from the live official PDF.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Internally assessed work carries a fifth to a quarter of each subject grade and is produced outside taught time, which is why it accounts for a large share of recoverable marks.
programmes.countryNote: Al Khalidiyah students who continue into the Diploma usually do so at a school on Al Reem or Saadiyat, and the board mechanics change completely. There is no tiering, no resit series in the same academic year, and the practical work sits inside an internally assessed investigation rather than in a separate paper.

abu-dhabi/al-khalidiyah.subjectsIntro: Each note names the board-specific detail that changes how the subject should be taught, because that is the information missing from most tutoring enquiries in this district.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.levels: Cambridge 0580 Core and Extended · Pearson 4MA1 Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: The tier caps the grade, so the decision matters more than the teaching in Year 10. Extended and Higher include functions, vectors and harder trigonometry. The quiet weakness in this district is non-calculator arithmetic, since students who have always worked with a device do not notice until a paper forbids it.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Cambridge assesses practical skills through a separate practical test or an alternative-to-practical paper. Pearson assesses them inside the written papers. Electricity remains the universal difficulty: students who can state the relationships still misread a circuit with a parallel pair inside a series loop.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Mole calculations, rates and organic families carry the papers. The alternative-to-practical route rewards a student who can describe a method and spot a flaw in somebody else's apparatus, which is a different skill from performing the experiment and needs separate practice.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Content-heavy, and penalised for imprecise language rather than for ignorance. An answer that says a substance moves without naming the gradient, the membrane or the transport protein loses marks the student thinks they earned. Diagram labelling is worth more than students expect.

subjects.name: English as a First Language
subjects.description: Directed writing and reading response, where marks go on purpose and audience rather than on vocabulary. Students over-prepare content and under-prepare timing, then lose the final question. Reading the number of marks before writing is the single most effective habit here.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language
subjects.description: A functional course with listening, reading and writing components, often the right entry for students whose stronger academic language is Arabic or another first language. Being entered for First Language English when Second Language fits better is a common and costly misplacement in mixed districts.

subjects.name: Business Studies
subjects.description: Case-study application rather than recall. Marks come from applying a concept to the specific business in the extract, with figures, rather than from defining the concept. Students who revise definitions and not application reliably score in the middle bands.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy decides the grade. An unlabelled axis or a shift drawn without a new equilibrium caps an answer regardless of the written evaluation around it. At IB level there are also three commentaries capped at eight hundred words each, built on real news articles.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics
subjects.description: Offered by some schools as a bridge into A Level or Higher Level Diploma mathematics, and genuinely demanding. Students who take it alongside 0580 Extended gain real fluency in algebra and calculus foundations, which pays back directly in Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Mandatory in UAE private schools and taught in a separate stream from Arabic as a first language. Students in Al Khalidiyah's mixed towers frequently arrive mid-phase with no Arabic and are placed by year group rather than by level, which is where frustration starts. Short frequent sessions work better than weekend blocks.

abu-dhabi/al-khalidiyah.regionsIntro: Al Khalidiyah sits in the middle of the island's western side, so the practical geography is about which school a family has chosen rather than about distance. These notes describe each neighbour from an Al Khalidiyah address.

regions.name: The Corniche
regions.note: Immediately north, effectively continuous with Al Khalidiyah's western edge. Shared schools and shared bus routes mean afternoon timings are almost identical, and the two districts generate similar requests, though the Corniche skews a little more towards Diploma Programme component work.

regions.name: Al Bateen
regions.note: South along the island's western shore, more established and more bilingual. Requests for Arabic as a first language and for Arabic A in the Diploma come disproportionately from there, which affects which tutors are in demand at the same hours.

regions.name: Al Mushrif
regions.note: Inland and south-east, home to The British School Al Khubairat. One of the shorter school runs available from Al Khalidiyah and a common destination, which is why Cambridge syllabus codes appear more often than Pearson ones in enquiries from this corridor.

regions.name: Al Markaziyah
regions.note: The central business district just to the east, dense and walkable, with a similar tower population. Students there often attend the same schools and sit the same papers, and lesson slots from 16:00 Gulf Standard Time are realistic for both districts.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Across the island to the east, with The British International School Abu Dhabi and Repton Abu Dhabi. A twenty-five to thirty-five minute afternoon run from Al Khalidiyah, so students at those schools generally want sessions from 17:30 onwards.

regions.name: Al Nahyan
regions.note: Central island, between Al Khalidiyah and the eastern waterfront, with a dense school mix and a long-established Arabic-speaking population. Families moving between the two districts often change school and sometimes change board, which is the commonest trigger for a first enquiry.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Over the bridge to the north-east, home to Cranleigh Abu Dhabi. The run is slower at pick-up than at drop-off, so secondary students from Al Khalidiyah attending there tend to settle on later evening slots for exam-technique work.

sections.heading: Cambridge or Pearson: the same subject assessed two ways
paragraphs: The short answer: Cambridge IGCSE and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE are separate qualifications with separate syllabus codes, separate paper structures and separate mark schemes. Universities treat them as equivalent. Teachers and students cannot, because the papers do not ask questions the same way.

The clearest difference is in the sciences. Cambridge assesses practical skills through a dedicated component, either a practical test or an alternative-to-practical written paper, and the centre decides which one candidates sit. Pearson assesses practical skills inside the written papers, through questions about method, apparatus and data. A student prepared for one route and entered for the other loses marks that have nothing to do with their physics.

The second difference is tiering vocabulary. Cambridge uses Core and Extended; Pearson uses Foundation and Higher. Both cap the maximum grade available at the lower tier. Schools sometimes enter a whole class at one tier and a small group at the other, and the decision is made on mock performance in Year 10, which is early.

There is a quieter difference in grading vocabulary too. Pearson International GCSE reports on a 9 to 1 scale, while Cambridge subjects may report on letters or numbers depending on the syllabus and the region, so two siblings can bring home results that look incomparable and are not.

The practical instruction for an Al Khalidiyah parent is one sentence long. Look at the front cover of your child's most recent mock paper, read the four-character code, and quote it when you ask for a tutor. It takes thirty seconds and it removes the commonest cause of a wasted term. Teachers in this district will confirm the code without hesitation, because it is printed on everything they issue.

sections.heading: Core or Extended: a decision made in Year 10 that caps the grade
paragraphs: Tiering is the most consequential IGCSE decision a family is barely consulted on. In tiered subjects the lower tier has a maximum attainable grade, so a student entered at Core cannot reach the top grades however well they perform. Schools make the call on mock evidence, often in the first half of Year 10, and it is usually presented as a protective measure rather than as a ceiling.

Both readings are fair. Entering a struggling student at Extended can produce a worse grade than a strong performance at Core, because the paper is harder and the marks are not there to be had. Entering a capable student at Core forecloses the grades a sixth form will ask for. The decision therefore needs evidence rather than instinct.

The evidence is cheap to produce. Have the student sit one past paper at each tier, to time, and mark both against the official schemes. The gap between the two scores answers the question in a way no predicted grade can, and it also shows whether the problem is content, timing or command terms, each of which has a different remedy.

Timing matters because entries are submitted by the centre months before the exam. A tier change requested after the entry deadline may not be possible. If you intend to challenge a tier decision, do it in the term the school proposes it, with the two marked papers in hand. A late change may also carry a charge set by the board and the centre, which is another reason the autumn conversation is the cheap one.

sections.heading: How practical science is assessed when your child studies partly online
paragraphs: This question comes up constantly in Al Khalidiyah, partly because so many families here supplement with online tuition and partly because the two boards handle it differently. The answer is that practical skills are always assessed, but not always by performing an experiment.

Under Cambridge, the sciences carry a dedicated practical component. A centre may enter candidates for a practical test, performed under exam conditions in a laboratory, or for the alternative-to-practical written paper, which asks about method, apparatus, data and sources of error without the student handling equipment. The centre decides. Ask your school which one your child is entered for, because preparing for the wrong one is a straightforward waste of revision time.

Under Pearson, practical skills are assessed within the written papers. There is no separate practical exam, which means questions about planning a method, identifying a variable, reading an instrument or spotting a flaw in somebody else's procedure appear throughout the theory papers and must be prepared as part of them.

For a tutor working online, the implication is useful rather than limiting. The alternative-to-practical and the embedded practical questions are written exercises, and they are taught well on a shared screen: a diagram of apparatus with a deliberate error in it, a table of results with an anomaly, a method with a missing control. What online work cannot replace is the laboratory time a practical test requires, and that is the school's job. Any provider suggesting it can substitute for a laboratory is overselling, and a family should treat the claim as a warning rather than a convenience.

sections.heading: The exam series, the entry deadlines and the resit route
paragraphs: Families consistently underestimate how far ahead entries close. The decision that fixes next year's exams is typically made two to three months before the first paper, and it is made by the school as the examination centre rather than by the parent. Knowing the shape of the calendar lets you have the conversation at the right time.

Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level exams in a June series and a November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. Ask your Al Khalidiyah school which series it enters candidates for, since not every centre offers both. The gap between entry and exam is best illustrated by Cambridge's published March series key dates: for March 2027 the exam period runs 3 February to 4 March 2027, final entries were due 27 November 2026, forecast grades 27 February 2027, results on Cambridge Direct 13 May and certificates in late June.

Pearson Edexcel International GCSE exams are available in May or June and in November each year. The November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson also publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, so work from the live official PDF rather than from a restated date.

There is also a zone trap. Every Cambridge centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, and Cambridge states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. For IB sessions, Abu Dhabi Diploma candidates sit the May session, but confirm every IB date with your school's coordinator or on ibo.org, because no IB date is restated here.

sections.heading: Entering as a private candidate from Al Khalidiyah
paragraphs: Some families in this district need to enter a subject their child's school does not offer, or need to sit a resit after leaving a school. That means entering as a private candidate through a registered examination centre, and the practical constraints are worth understanding before promising a child they can take the subject.

A centre has to be willing to accept private candidates for that specific syllabus and series, and that willingness is not universal. Science subjects are the hardest case, because a practical test requires laboratory access that a private candidate may not have. Where a centre offers only the practical test route rather than the alternative-to-practical, the subject may simply not be available to an external candidate.

Deadlines are stricter rather than looser for private entries, and fees are set by the centre on top of the board's own charges. Start the conversation a full series ahead: for a November entry, that means asking in the spring, not in September. Ask the centre which syllabus code it is entering, which practical route applies, and what the final entry date is in writing.

What tutoring can do here is specific. It can prepare a candidate for the written routes thoroughly, including the alternative-to-practical paper, and it can build the error-pattern repair that a resit needs. What it cannot do is substitute for laboratory access or arrange an entry on a family's behalf, and any provider suggesting otherwise should be asked exactly which centre and which series they mean.

sections.heading: Grade boundaries, and why a target should be a mark rather than a grade
paragraphs: Grade boundaries are set after each series, on the evidence of that series' papers and candidate performance. They move. That is the whole reason a student should be working to a raw mark target rather than to a grade, because a grade target silently assumes a boundary nobody has published yet.

The practical method is straightforward. Take the boundaries published for recent series in that syllabus, through the school, which holds proper access to them. Add a margin of several marks. Work to that total across the components, weighted by how much each one is worth. A student who knows they need roughly this many marks on Paper 4 behaves more precisely than one aiming at a letter.

This is also why component-level results matter more than the overall grade on results day. Two students with the same grade can have completely different profiles, one strong on theory and weak on the practical component, the other the reverse. A resit plan built on the overall grade repeats everything; a resit plan built on component marks targets the twenty per cent that went wrong.

Boundary tables, past papers and mark schemes belong to the boards that publish them. The right route is through the school and the boards' own official pages, cited rather than copied. IB Gram does not host or distribute board documents, and a provider offering a download library of them is telling you something about how it operates.

sections.heading: What IGCSE support costs in Abu Dhabi, in AED
paragraphs: The numbers here are market rates in the UAE, drawn from providers' own published pricing and from a published 2026 Dubai tutoring rate survey by Bestimate. They are the market, not an IB Gram price list. Al Khalidiyah has a visible concentration of tuition centres, so a family here is usually comparing a centre quote against an online one, which is a fairer comparison than it looks only if you count contact minutes per student.

Published hourly figures run from roughly AED 45 to 65 at the budget online end and AED 33 to 52 from one platform's entry tier, AED 150 for IGCSE and AED 200 for IB from an agency that publishes its rates, AED 270 from a UK-based agency, a survey band of AED 200 to 450 and above for specialist exam-year work, and AED 650 at the premium named end. In-home visits in the emirate are published between roughly AED 180 and AED 500, with travel inside the hour.

Priced by the month rather than the hour, the same survey data reads differently. Eight online sessions are advertised at around AED 799, while four two-hour in-home sessions are quoted at AED 1,599 to 1,799 - roughly double, for half the contact hours. Weekly one-hour tuition works out at about AED 240 to 600 a month at budget level, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more where specialist exam-year support is involved.

A group class at a centre looks cheaper per hour and is often more expensive per minute of attention. Eight students and one teacher means roughly seven minutes each in an hour of individual feedback. That is fine for content revision and poor for the error-pattern work a borderline candidate needs. Ask any centre how many students are in the class before comparing its rate with anything.

sections.heading: A tutor coming to an Al Khalidiyah tower, compared with online delivery
paragraphs: The honest position first. Al Khalidiyah is central, dense and well connected, so a tutor living on the island can reach most addresses here in fifteen minutes. The travel argument that dominates in the outer communities is weak in this district, and families asking for a home tutor are not being unrealistic.

What does differ is matching precision. Everything on this page turns on the board: 0625 against 4PH1, Core against Extended, practical test against alternative to practical. Tutors who are genuinely fluent in a specific code and component are not evenly distributed across the island, and restricting the search to those willing to visit a particular tower at a particular hour narrows a useful pool for no academic benefit.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere in the UAE, and does not operate a centre in the emirate. Tuition is delivered one-to-one over live video, with a shared screen for marking papers against the official scheme. For the kind of work this page describes, annotating the same paper simultaneously is a practical advantage, and the student keeps the annotated copy.

The table compares the realistic options. In-home tutoring has a genuine edge for younger children who need an adult present to stay on task, and a centre group class has a genuine edge on price for general revision. Neither of those is the situation most Al Khalidiyah IGCSE enquiries describe, which is a Year 11 student with thorough content coverage losing marks on a specific component of a specific specification.

sections.heading: Coursework, honesty and what a tutor may do at IGCSE and beyond
paragraphs: Most IGCSE subjects are now assessed entirely by terminal examination, which removes the coursework temptation that used to dominate this conversation. Where a coursework or portfolio route still exists under a particular board and centre, and in the Diploma where internally assessed work carries a fifth to a quarter of each subject grade, the boundary matters a great deal.

The rule is simple and not negotiable. Assessed work must be the student's own. A tutor explains how the criteria are awarded, asks the questions a supervisor asks about scope and method, teaches the referencing convention, and gives feedback on a draft the student has already produced. A tutor supplies no text, no data and no analysis that enters a submission.

One researched competitor in this market sells completed Internal Assessments. The consequence of using such a service falls on the student, because a malpractice finding can cost a diploma rather than a grade, and no provider carries that risk afterwards. That is worth stating plainly on a page that parents may be comparing against one of those sites.

The protective measure is timing rather than policy. Work planned across months has room for a method that fails and a redraft that improves. The same work compressed into a fortnight is the situation in which honesty gets tested. Booking a component block early is a cheaper safeguard than any written assurance. It is also the version that produces a better mark, because a draft that has been through two rounds of honest feedback scores higher than one written quickly and corrected by somebody else.

process.title: Read the code off the paper, then ask
process.description: Find your child's most recent mock paper and read the four-character syllabus code on the front: 0580, 0625, 4MA1, 4PH1. Quote it in the first message along with the tier. This one detail removes the most common cause of a near-miss match and shortens the search to a day or two.

process.title: Ask the school three questions in writing
process.description: Which series is my child entered for, which tier, and which practical route in the sciences. Schools answer these readily and the answers change what a tutor should be teaching in January. Getting them in writing also fixes the entry deadline you need to work back from.

process.title: Sit two timed papers before a tier decision
process.description: One past paper at each candidate tier, written to time and marked against the official schemes, settles a Core or Extended argument with evidence. The score gap also reveals whether the underlying problem is content, timing or command terms, which need three different remedies.

process.title: Build the plan from component marks, not the grade
process.description: After a mock or a results day, work from the component breakdown rather than the overall grade. A resit plan built on the grade repeats the whole syllabus; one built on components targets the paper that went wrong and usually takes a third of the time.

process.title: Review at four sessions and decide
process.description: Four sessions is enough to judge whether the board match is right and whether the student is doing the work between lessons. Changing tutor then is free. Discovering a mismatch in May, three weeks before a paper, is not.

whyPoints.title: Matched on the code, not the subject name
whyPoints.description: Cambridge 0625 and Pearson 4PH1 are both called Physics and are not the same teaching job. Matching starts from the code on the student's own paper, which is the difference between a tutor who teaches the content and one who teaches the paper.

whyPoints.title: Tier and series decisions backed by marked papers
whyPoints.description: A Core or Extended recommendation comes with two timed papers marked against the official schemes and the score gap quantified, in writing. That is something a family can take to the school, which a tutor's opinion is not.

whyPoints.title: Practical routes explained before revision starts
whyPoints.description: Whether a child sits a practical test or the alternative-to-practical paper changes how the component is prepared. Establishing which one the centre entered, early, prevents the straightforward waste of revising for the wrong assessment.

whyPoints.title: Costs compared on attention, not on headline rate
whyPoints.description: A centre class at a lower hourly rate can deliver a few minutes of individual feedback per student. This page sets out the market bands and asks the question that actually decides value, which is how many students share the hour.

whyPoints.title: Board documents cited, never redistributed
whyPoints.description: Past papers, mark schemes and boundary tables come through the school and the boards' official pages. IB Gram does not host them, holds no approval or accreditation from Cambridge, Pearson or any UAE regulator, and says so rather than implying otherwise.

faqs.question: How do I find out whether my child sits Cambridge or Pearson papers?
faqs.answer: Read the front cover of their most recent mock or past paper. Cambridge syllabuses carry a four-digit code such as 0580 for Mathematics, 0625 Physics, 0620 Chemistry or 0610 Biology. Pearson International GCSE codes look different, such as 4MA1 for Mathematics A and 4PH1 for Physics. Schools in Al Khalidiyah sometimes enter different boards for different subjects within the same child's timetable, which is legitimate and common. Quote the code when you ask for a tutor, because the content overlaps heavily while the paper structure and mark-scheme phrasing do not.

faqs.question: Are Cambridge and Pearson International GCSE equivalent qualifications?
faqs.answer: Universities and the UAE equivalency route treat them as comparable qualifications at the same level. Teaching them is not interchangeable. The paper structures differ, the tier labels differ, Cambridge uses Core and Extended while Pearson uses Foundation and Higher, and the sciences assess practical skills by different routes. A tutor with ten years of Cambridge 0625 experience will teach a 4PH1 student well on content and imperfectly on technique unless they have specifically taught that specification. Match on the code and the problem disappears.

faqs.question: What does Core or Extended entry actually mean for my child's grade?
faqs.answer: The lower tier caps the maximum grade available, so a student entered at Core cannot reach the top grades however well they perform on the day. Extended covers more content, including functions, vectors and harder trigonometry in Mathematics, and carries a real risk of a lower outcome for a student who is not ready. Schools decide on mock evidence, often early in Year 10. If you want to challenge it, bring two past papers, one at each tier, sat to time and marked against the official schemes, and do it before the entry deadline.

faqs.question: Can a tier decision be changed after the school has entered my child?
faqs.answer: Often not, which is why the conversation has to happen early. Entries are submitted by the school as the examination centre, typically two to three months before the first paper, and a change after that date may not be possible or may carry a late-entry charge set by the board and the centre. Ask the school in writing for its own entry deadline and work backwards from it. If you intend to contest a tier, produce the evidence in the term the decision is proposed rather than in the term before the exam.

faqs.question: How is practical physics assessed if my child is tutored online?
faqs.answer: It depends on the board, and in both cases the written preparation works well online. Under Cambridge the sciences carry a dedicated practical component, entered by the centre either as a laboratory practical test or as the alternative-to-practical written paper, which asks about method, apparatus, data and error sources without handling equipment. Under Pearson, practical skills are assessed inside the theory papers. Ask the school which route applies. Flawed-method questions, anomalous data tables and apparatus diagrams are taught effectively on a shared screen; laboratory time itself is the school's job.

faqs.question: Which Cambridge exam series will my Al Khalidiyah school enter?
faqs.answer: Ask, because not every centre offers both. Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level exams in a June series and a November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. The November series is the usual route for resits and for a subject entered late. Each centre is also allocated to one of six administrative zones with its own timetable version, and Cambridge states it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong zone's timetable.

faqs.question: When does Pearson publish results and timetables for the November series?
faqs.answer: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE exams are available in May or June and in November each year. The November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. For the summer series, June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026. November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson also publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, including future November series, so always work from the live official PDF on the Pearson support pages rather than from a restated date.

faqs.question: Why do entry deadlines sit so far before the exam?
faqs.answer: Because the board has to timetable, print and distribute papers worldwide and collect forecast grades from every centre. Cambridge's published key dates for its March 2027 series show the gap clearly: the exam period runs from 3 February to 4 March 2027, while final entries were due 27 November 2026 and forecast grades 27 February 2027, with results on Cambridge Direct 13 May and certificates in late June. The practical lesson for a parent is that subject and tier conversations belong in the autumn term, not in the spring.

faqs.question: Can my child sit an IGCSE subject their school does not offer?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, as a private candidate through a registered examination centre that accepts external entries for that syllabus and series. The hard case is the sciences, because a practical test needs laboratory access a private candidate may not have, and where a centre offers only that route the subject may be unavailable externally. Deadlines are stricter and the centre sets its own fees on top of the board's. Start a full series ahead, and ask the centre in writing for the syllabus code, the practical route and the final entry date.

faqs.question: Should my child aim at a grade or at a number of marks?
faqs.answer: At a mark total, with a margin. Grade boundaries are set after each series on the evidence of that series, so they move, which means a grade target silently assumes a number nobody has published. Take the boundaries for recent series in that syllabus, obtained through the school which holds proper access, add several marks of margin, and distribute the target across components by weighting. A student who knows roughly how many marks they need on a specific paper prepares far more precisely than one aiming at a letter.

faqs.question: After results day, how should we plan a resit?
faqs.answer: From the component breakdown, not the overall grade. Two candidates with the same grade can have opposite profiles, one strong on theory and weak on the practical component, the other the reverse. A plan built on the grade repeats the entire syllabus and takes a year. A plan built on components targets the twenty or thirty per cent that went wrong and is usually a dense block of error-pattern repair and timed papers over two or three months, aimed at the next available series.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a tutor to apartments in Al Khalidiyah?
faqs.answer: No. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, and IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; that service runs only in India. Independent tutors and agencies in Abu Dhabi do travel, and published market rates for in-home work run from roughly AED 180 to AED 500 an hour with the journey inside the rate. The reason to choose online here is not travel time, which is short on the island, but code-specific matching: fluency in 0625 or 4MA1 is unevenly distributed, and geography should not narrow the choice further.

faqs.question: Is a tuition centre group class cheaper than one-to-one tuition?
faqs.answer: Per hour, usually yes. Per minute of individual feedback, often no. Eight students sharing one teacher for an hour works out at a few minutes each of personal attention, which is adequate for content revision and poor for the error-pattern work a borderline candidate needs. Al Khalidiyah has a visible concentration of centres, so this comparison comes up often. Ask the centre how many students are in the class before comparing the rate with anything, and ask which syllabus code the class is taught against.

faqs.question: Can a tutor provide past papers and mark schemes for my child's syllabus?
faqs.answer: They should not need to. Syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables belong to Cambridge, Pearson and the IB, and the proper route is through your child's school, which holds authorised access, and through the boards' own official pages. IB Gram does not host or distribute board material, and a provider advertising a download library of it is telling you something about how it operates. Sessions work from material the student brings from school, with the official source cited.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram hold any Cambridge or Pearson approval?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from Cambridge, Pearson, the IB, ADEK, KHDA, SPEA, MoHRE or the Ministry of Education, and any provider claiming such status should be asked for a document number. Private tutors in the UAE do need a MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years, and it is reasonable to ask a tutor whether they hold one. A tutoring business with premises needs a separate institutional permit from the emirate's regulator.

abu-dhabi/al-khalidiyah.closingHeading: Start with the code, the tier and the series
abu-dhabi/al-khalidiyah.closingBody: Almost every IGCSE problem an Al Khalidiyah family brings is traceable to one of three facts nobody wrote down: the syllabus code, the tier and the series. Those three answers take one email to the school and they change what a tutor should be teaching this term. Once they are settled, teaching is matched to the exact specification and delivered one-to-one over live video, with papers marked line by line against the official scheme on a shared screen the student keeps afterwards.

abu-dhabi/al-manaseer.tutorsIntro: The tutors below cover the Diploma and IGCSE subjects Al Manaseer households ask for most: Diploma mathematics and sciences at Higher Level, IGCSE double award sciences, and Arabic alongside an international curriculum. Each teaches one subject at one level rather than a general timetable.

intro.heading: The bus leaves before seven, and that decides everything else
paragraphs: Al Manaseer sits in the western third of Abu Dhabi island, a dense grid of mid-rise apartment blocks wedged between Al Khalidiyah and Al Bateen, with Zayed the First Street running straight through the middle of it. It has shops, clinics and mosques within walking distance of almost every building. What it does not have, because island land ran out decades ago, is a large campus with playing fields. So the school run here runs outward. Children board a contracted bus and travel off the district, and in many cases off the island altogether.

That single fact shapes a tutoring plan more than any subject choice does. A child catching a bus at 06:40 for a campus in Khalifa City or on the Al Raha side is not home at 15:30. Add the return leg, the walk up from the bus bay and twenty minutes to eat, and the first honest moment a lesson can start is closer to quarter to five. Book a four o'clock slot and you will spend half of it waiting, and the other half teaching a child who has not put their bag down.

The second fact is that Al Manaseer afternoons are full. This is a district where after-school life is close enough to walk to: Quran classes at the neighbourhood mosque, swimming at a club on the Corniche, football, extra Arabic for a child in the first-language stream. Those commitments are fixed by someone else's timetable. A tutoring slot has to fit between them, which usually means one firm hour on a named weekday rather than a vague promise of two sessions a week.

The third is subject supply. The schools Al Manaseer children attend are strong, but a Higher Level Diploma group in Physics or Chemistry at any one campus may be a handful of students taught by one teacher who also carries Standard Level and the MYP. If your child needs that teacher's subject explained a second way, there is no second teacher on site to ask. A tutor who lives nearby solves a travel problem, not a specialism problem. A tutor on a screen can be the person who taught that exact syllabus for a decade.

This page is written for the parent working out when a lesson can realistically start, what the hour costs in this market, and what the regulator expects of the person teaching it. Everything IB Gram delivers to Al Manaseer is one-to-one and online over live video. IB Gram does not run home visits anywhere in the UAE; that is an India-only service. The comparison table further down sets the two formats against each other on cost, travel and tutor choice, and lets you decide on the numbers.
