abu-dhabi/al-manaseer.programmesIntro: Al Manaseer households are split between the Diploma, the British route to IGCSE and A Level, and the American diploma with Advanced Placement. The four programmes below are the ones families on this side of the island actually ask about, with what each one demands of an afternoon.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Transdisciplinary units rather than separate subjects, assessed by teacher judgement against learning outcomes with no external papers. Reports describe approaches to learning and conceptual understanding, which is why a parent can read one twice and still not know whether their child can subtract confidently. Support at this stage is diagnostic: find the arithmetic or reading gap, close it, and leave the rest of the programme alone.
programmes.countryNote: Several campuses used by Al Manaseer families run PYP in the primary years and switch to a British secondary route, so a child can leave a conceptual programme at eleven and meet subject-by-subject marks at twelve. The useful work in Year 6 is number fluency and writing stamina, both of which travel across any transition.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups marked against four criteria per subject, each criterion scored out of eight and converted to a 1-7 grade. Criterion labels are letters, not topics, so a child can be strong on knowledge and weak on inquiry and finish mid-band. The Personal Project in the final year is the first long independent piece most students meet.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi MYP cohorts often contain children who joined from a CBSE or American middle school where marks came from tests. The adjustment is to criterion language: a report that says criterion C is a four is telling you about communication of findings, not about effort, and that distinction is where most of this year's recoverable marks sit.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects at Higher or Standard Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Internal assessment typically carries twenty to thirty per cent of a subject grade and is marked by the teacher against published criteria before external moderation. The written papers carry the rest, and students lose most of their marks to command terms rather than to content.
programmes.countryNote: Al Manaseer Diploma students are usually travelling to one of a small number of island or mainland IB campuses, which means a long day before any coursework begins. Internal deadlines at those schools tend to cluster in the same weeks, so an Extended Essay draft and two internal assessments can land inside a fortnight unless the year is planned backwards.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson International GCSE
programmes.description: Two-year courses examined by terminal papers, tiered in several subjects as Core and Extended or Foundation and Higher. The tier a school enters a child for sets a ceiling on the grade before a single paper is sat. Cambridge syllabuses carry four-digit codes such as 0580 for Mathematics and 0625 for Physics; Pearson uses forms like 4MA1 and 4PH1.
programmes.countryNote: Families on this side of the island frequently discover in Year 11 that the sibling at a different Abu Dhabi school sits a different board for the same subject. The papers, the formula sheet and the practical arrangements differ, so revision material has to be chosen by syllabus code rather than by subject name.

abu-dhabi/al-manaseer.subjectsIntro: Requests from Al Manaseer skew towards the subjects where one teacher carries a whole level at a campus, and towards Arabic, where the first-language and additional-language streams are genuinely different courses. Each entry below names what the subject assesses and where the marks go missing.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Proof, calculus and algebraic fluency, with a Higher Level paper that assumes manipulation happens without hesitation. Marks go on unjustified steps and on the exploration, where a student picks a topic they cannot actually model. Work starts with algebra speed before any new topic is opened.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling, statistics and technology-heavy questions. Students who chose it to avoid calculus meet regression, hypothesis testing and a calculator that must be driven accurately under time. The common loss is interpretation: a correct test statistic followed by a conclusion that does not answer the question asked.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Mechanics, fields, thermal and waves, with a Higher Level extension that rewards comfort with algebraic rearrangement. Most lost marks are not conceptual; they are in unit handling, significant figures and the practical skills paper. Data analysis is drilled with real tables rather than described in the abstract.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: The subject where an island cohort is most often taught by a single specialist. Organic mechanisms and energetics carry the Higher Level burden, and the internal assessment is where students invent an investigation with no controllable variable. Sessions separate what must be memorised from what must be derived.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Volume is the problem, not difficulty. Students who revise by rereading notes score below students who answer past questions and compare against mark schemes. Statistical reasoning in the practical paper is routinely untaught in the pressure of covering content, and it is quick to fix.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy decides grades more than essay style. A correctly labelled and correctly shifted diagram earns marks that three paragraphs of prose cannot recover. The commentary portfolio needs an article chosen for the theory it permits, not for how interesting it reads.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Tool application under time pressure, from decision trees to ratio analysis, plus a research project built on a real organisation. Students lose marks by describing a framework instead of using it on the case material in front of them.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Unseen analysis, the comparative essay and the individual oral on a global issue. The oral fails on structure far more often than on insight, because students arrive with observations and no argument. Preparation is rehearsal against a timer with a marked transcript.

subjects.name: Arabic A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The first-language route for students who have been schooled in Arabic, assessed on literary analysis in formal Standard Arabic. Fluent household speech does not carry a student through it; written register and literary terminology do, and those are taught rather than absorbed.

subjects.name: Arabic B and Arabic ab initio
subjects.description: The additional-language routes, assessed on prescribed themes, productive writing and a conversation. Placement errors are common in Abu Dhabi: a child who speaks dialect at home but never studied Arabic formally sits uncomfortably between the streams, and the fix is a placement check before Year 12.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.description: The grade ceiling sits in the tier, so the first question is which paper your child is entered for. Extended and Higher papers assume algebraic confidence that Year 9 may not have delivered. Topic order is rebuilt around the specific paper structure the school uses.

subjects.name: Combined and Coordinated Sciences
subjects.description: Three sciences compressed into two or three IGCSE grades, with content from each discipline on shared papers. Students fall behind in whichever discipline is timetabled thinnest, usually physics. Support targets the weakest discipline rather than spreading evenly across all three.

abu-dhabi/al-manaseer.regionsIntro: Al Manaseer children are schooled across the island and out onto the mainland corridor, and the journey time to each destination is what decides a session slot. These are the clusters that come up in enquiries from this district, with the practical effect of each run.

regions.name: Al Bateen
regions.note: The nearest school cluster to Al Manaseer and the only one a child might reach without a long bus run. A Bateen campus can mean a child home before four, which is the one case where a mid-afternoon session genuinely works.

regions.name: Al Mushrif
regions.note: A short hop inland and a common destination for British-curriculum families from this district. Traffic on the connecting roads at pick-up is the variable, so slots are set at 16:45 rather than 16:15 to avoid a weekly apology.

regions.name: the Corniche
regions.note: Not a school cluster but an activity one. Swimming and club sport along the waterfront take the early evening for many Manaseer children, which pushes tutoring either earlier or onto the weekend.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Reached by bridge, with a bus run that starts early and ends late. Families sending a child here plan around a return after 16:30 at the earliest, and often choose a Saturday morning session for the heavier Higher Level subject.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Another bridge crossing, with tower-based campuses and a tight drop-off window. The practical consequence for study is noise and space at home rather than travel, since apartments here and in Al Manaseer share the same constraint.

regions.name: Yas Island
regions.note: The longest island-to-island run from this district. A child on a Yas bus leaves early and arrives home tired, and a ninety-minute session on a weekday evening rarely survives past October.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Off the island and over the bridge, and the single most common destination for Manaseer families who want a large campus with grounds. Door-to-door is routinely over an hour in the afternoon peak.

regions.name: Al Raha Beach and Al Raha Gardens
regions.note: The airport-road corridor, with several IB and British campuses. The return leg crosses the same bottleneck as the commuter traffic, so the earliest honest lesson start for this run is closer to five.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City
regions.note: A mainland destination for families whose school choice is driven by fees rather than proximity. Long run, early departure, and a strong case for stacking tutoring into the weekend instead.

regions.name: Al Reef
regions.note: Beyond the airport and a long way from this district, but it appears in enquiries where a family has moved and kept the child's school. Online delivery is what keeps the same tutor through that kind of move.

schoolClusters.city: Western island: Al Manaseer, Al Khalidiyah and Al Bateen
schoolClusters.note: The schools closest to this district, including long-established British and American campuses. Enquiries from here concentrate on IGCSE sciences in Year 11 and on Diploma mathematics in Year 12, with Arabic first-language support running alongside in a large share of households.
schools: American Community School of Abu Dhabi

schoolClusters.city: Mainland corridor: Khalifa City, Al Raha and the airport road
schoolClusters.note: The larger campuses Al Manaseer families bus to when they want space and a full co-curricular programme. These are the runs that push a lesson start past half past four, and the ones where the weekend becomes the serious study time.

schoolClusters.city: Bridge destinations: Saadiyat, Al Reem and Yas
schoolClusters.note: Newer campuses reached by crossing water, with the earliest bus departures of any run from this district. Diploma students here carry the longest days, which is why coursework blocks are scheduled into term breaks rather than squeezed into term weeks.
schools: Sorbonne-linked and other Saadiyat campuses used by island families
Yas Island campuses used by commuting households

IB Gram has no affiliation, partnership or endorsement arrangement with any of them, and none is a client; confirm any school's current curriculum and inspection position with the school and with ADEK.
abu-dhabi/al-manaseer.modesIntro: Three delivery patterns cover almost every Al Manaseer enquiry, and the choice between them is driven by the bus more than by the subject. All three are one-to-one over live video, with the student sharing their own work on screen.

modes.title: One fixed weekday hour, set from the bus drop
modes.description: A single named slot on a single weekday, starting after the child is home, fed and sitting down. One subject, one level, the same tutor each week. This is the pattern that survives a full academic year, because it competes with nothing else in the afternoon and nobody has to renegotiate it in November.
bullets: Start times set between 16:45 and 18:30 after the first week is measured
Sixty minutes for a single subject; ninety only in an exam term
The slot is held for the year rather than rebooked weekly

modes.title: Saturday morning depth on the heaviest subject
modes.description: The one block in an Al Manaseer week that is not fighting the school run, a club session or a Quran class. Mornings suit Higher Level work that needs a long unbroken run: a derivation, a full past paper under time, or a mechanism sequence that cannot be covered in forty minutes between other commitments.
bullets: Ninety to one hundred and twenty minutes without a hard stop

modes.title: Coursework clinics around the school's internal deadlines
modes.description: Short blocks booked against the dates your child's own school has set for internal assessment drafts, the Extended Essay and the Theory of Knowledge essay. The tutor reads the student's own draft, questions it and teaches against the criteria. The writing stays the student's work, which is the only version of this that is permissible.
bullets: Scheduled from the school's internal calendar, not a generic one

sections.heading: Where Al Manaseer children actually go to school, and what each run costs in time
paragraphs: An honest tutoring slot starts with a measured journey, not an assumed one. Parents in this district rarely know the real door-to-door figure, because the bus contract quotes a pick-up time and nothing else. For the first week of any arrangement, write down three numbers: the time the bus left, the time your child walked back into the flat, and the time they were genuinely ready to work. The third number is the only one a tutor can book against.

The pattern across Al Manaseer enquiries is consistent. A school in Al Bateen or Al Khalidiyah gives a child back a usable afternoon. A school in Al Mushrif costs around half an hour each way once the pick-up queue is counted. Anything across a bridge or out on the airport road turns a nominal 15:30 finish into a 16:30 arrival, and that is before an older sibling on a different run has been collected.

The table below is a planning tool rather than a timetable. Bus departures and arrivals vary by operator, route order and the position of your building on the route, and they change when a new family joins the run. What does not vary is the direction of the effect: the further the campus, the later the first workable lesson, and the stronger the argument for moving the heavier subject to Saturday morning.

One further consideration applies specifically here. Al Manaseer blocks are dense, and many children share a room with a sibling. A session booked while the whole household is home is a session with a door opening in it. Where the flat is tight, the early evening slot often works better than the one straight after the bus, because by then one child is at a club and the other has the table.
bullets: Measure the bus drop for a week before fixing a slot
Add twenty minutes for food and a change of clothes, not five
Count the collection of a sibling on a different route
Where two children share a room, stagger the two slots

sections.heading: The two windows a dense island district actually has
paragraphs: Once the arrival time is known, an Al Manaseer week has two usable windows and no more. The first is the stretch between the bus drop and the evening meal, which in practice is one hour and not two. The second is the early evening after prayer and before the day collapses, which is reliable in term time and unreliable in the fortnight before a long weekend. Everything else parents imagine is available is already spoken for.

The first window suits consolidation. It is the right place for last week's class content, a set of exam questions on a topic already taught, or a worked example the child did not follow in school. It is the wrong place for a first encounter with a difficult new idea, because a child who left the flat before seven has limited capacity for novelty at five. Treat the weekday hour as repair work, and the weekend as construction.

The second window suits a written component. Drafting, planning an essay, or reading a mark scheme against the student's own answer all work better when the household has finished eating and the phone has been handed over. Many Manaseer families find that an 18:30 start on one weekday is the only slot in the entire week that nobody else is competing for.

What does not work, and is worth saying plainly, is two separate subjects on the same weekday evening. The second hour is reliably worse than the first, the child knows it, and attendance decays by half term. One hour, one subject, one named day, repeated for the year, outperforms any arrangement that looks more ambitious on paper.

sections.heading: Activities, prayer times and the slot they quietly take
paragraphs: Al Manaseer is walkable, which is a genuine advantage and a scheduling complication. Because the mosque, the clinic, the sports club and the shops are all within a few streets, children here carry more fixed after-school commitments than children in a far-flung villa community. Quran classes, extra Arabic for a child in the first-language stream, swimming at a Corniche club and football all land in the same early-evening band, and none of them moves for a tutor.

The practical approach is to write the whole week down before booking anything, including the commitments that only run for part of the year. A football season that ends in March frees a Tuesday that was unavailable in November, and a family that did not notice keeps revising around a slot that no longer exists. Prayer times shift through the year as well, so an 18:00 start that works in January sits awkwardly in June.

Ramadan changes the shape of the week more than any other factor in the UAE calendar. School hours shorten, afternoons are for rest, and useful study happens late. Sessions move to post-Iftar timing, usually between 20:30 and 22:00, and the sensible plan reduces frequency rather than pretending the normal pattern still works. Families who agree that shift in advance keep momentum; families who improvise lose a month.

Term breaks are the other overlooked resource. The UAE academic year carries a long winter break and a spring break, and both fall close enough to the examination series to be useful. A block of three or four consecutive sessions inside a break achieves more on a weak topic than six weekly sessions across a term, because nothing interrupts and the student is not tired.
bullets: List every fixed commitment, including seasonal ones, before booking
Expect to re-time the slot twice a year as prayer times move
Plan Ramadan as post-Iftar and lower frequency, agreed in advance
Use winter and spring breaks for consecutive-day blocks on one weak topic

sections.heading: Reading an ADEK inspection report before you choose a tutor
paragraphs: Private schools in Abu Dhabi and Al Ain are licensed and accredited by the Department of Education and Knowledge, which also inspects them and publishes outcomes. The u.ae government portal states that ADEK supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. That makes the inspection report the single most useful free document a parent in Al Manaseer has, and most families read only the overall rating on the front.

The overall band is the least informative part. Inspections report on separate areas, and a school can be strong on students' personal development while being weaker on teaching in a particular phase or on assessment practice. A school rated well overall can still have a thin science department in the sixth form, and a school with a middling overall band can have an outstanding mathematics team. The decision you are making is about a subject and a year group, not about a brand.

Read the report for three things. First, what it says about teaching and assessment in your child's phase rather than across the school. Second, whether the recommendations from the previous inspection were acted on, because an unaddressed recommendation is a pattern rather than an incident. Third, any comment on provision for the specific subject group your child depends on. Those three paragraphs tell you whether the gap is your child's or the department's.

None of this means a weaker band requires tutoring or a stronger band removes the need for it. Those are different questions. A good report tells you where the school's own capacity sits, which lets you aim private support at the thing the school cannot cover rather than duplicating what it does well. That alone usually cuts the number of hours a family books.

sections.heading: What the Abu Dhabi market charges, and who published the number
paragraphs: Three of the six most visible tutoring pages in this market publish no price at all, and two of the ones that do quote in US dollars, a currency no Abu Dhabi family transacts in. That is why the figures below are given in AED and attributed. They are market rates collected from providers' own published pages and from a published rate survey; they are not an IB Gram price list, and your own quote should come from a consultation rather than from a table on a website.

The bands are wide for a reason. A university student revising IGCSE mathematics with a Year 10 child and a Diploma Chemistry specialist preparing a Higher Level student for Paper 3 are not the same product, and treating them as interchangeable is how families end up paying mid-range money for entry-level teaching. Ask what the person has taught, for how long, and on which board, and then judge the rate against the answer.

The in-home column exists because it is the honest comparison point, not because IB Gram sells it. A visiting tutor is pricing travel into the hour. In this district that travel is short if they live on the island and substantial if they do not, and the rate reflects it either way. Online delivery removes that line from the invoice entirely, which is a large part of why the online band sits below the in-home band at every level.

One piece of local context is worth having in front of you. Private school fees are the dominant education cost in an Abu Dhabi household, and tutoring is a small fraction of it. Reading the two together usually changes the conversation from whether to book an hour to which single hour would do the most good, which is the better question.

sections.heading: A tutor driving into Al Manaseer against a specialist on a shared screen
paragraphs: Parents searching for a home tutor in this district are asking a reasonable question, and it deserves a direct answer rather than a redirect. In-home tutoring in Abu Dhabi exists, it is widely advertised, and the market rate for it sits between AED 180 and AED 500 an hour depending on level, with travel priced into that figure. What you buy is a person in the room, which some children genuinely need, and a tutor pool limited to whoever can reach your building and still get home.

That pool limit is the part families underestimate. Al Manaseer is central, so the pool is larger here than in an outer community, but it is still defined by a drive. If your child needs Higher Level Chemistry, you are choosing from the specialists who happen to live within a workable distance of Zayed the First Street at five in the afternoon, which may be a very short list. Online, the same child is matched to someone who has taught that syllabus for years, and the drive is irrelevant.

IB Gram does not sell home visits anywhere in the UAE, and nobody will be sent to a residential address here; those visits are a service offered only in India. Every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video, with the student sharing their own exercise book or screen, writing while the tutor watches, and keeping the recording or the annotated work afterwards. That last point matters more than it sounds: a parent can review what happened in the hour, which is not possible with a closed door.

The table sets the two formats against each other on the things that actually differ. Neither column is universally better. A Year 4 child who will not sit still for a screen is better served in a room. A Year 13 student working on an internal assessment, where the tutor needs to see the data file and the write-up side by side, is better served online, and the cost difference buys more hours in the term that matters.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies in a Manaseer household
paragraphs: Private schools in the UAE are not required to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That federal baseline is why a child doing the Diploma or IGCSE in Abu Dhabi also carries subjects that belong to no international syllabus. In a district like Al Manaseer, where a large share of households speak Arabic at home, this is the half of the timetable families ask about least and worry about most.

The first thing to establish is which stream your child is in. Arabic as a first language and Arabic as an additional language are different courses with different expectations, and placement is made by the school. A child who speaks dialect fluently at home but has never studied formal Standard Arabic can be placed in the first-language stream and struggle badly with literary register, while a child placed in the additional-language stream can coast and lose the chance to take Arabic A at Diploma level.

The second is that these subjects sit outside the Ministry of Education's equivalency count for British-curriculum leavers. Equivalency for that track requires five accredited IGCSE or GCSE subjects at no less than grade E or 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five. That is a frequent surprise in Year 11, and it changes which subjects a family protects when the timetable gets tight.

The third is a constraint on tutoring itself. For the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry is not allowed. So support in these subjects is reading, structure, vocabulary and examination technique on the school's own material. A tutor who offers an alternative syllabus for Islamic Education or Social Studies is offering something that should not be accepted.
bullets: Confirm in writing which Arabic stream your child is placed in

sections.heading: The permit question, and how a Manaseer parent checks it
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, and it is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged fifteen to eighteen and university students. The official route is MoHRE's own service, Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, applied for through its smart app, website and e-services system.

Two things follow for a parent. First, a tutor who tells you a permit is unnecessary, or that it costs a fee, is wrong on both counts. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit from MoHRE are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no schedule of amounts is published, so no figure circulating online should be treated as fact. Second, because the permit is free and takes a short time to process, there is no good reason for a working tutor not to hold one.

There is a separate point specific to Abu Dhabi, and it is the one families stumble into with good intentions. Press reporting on ADEK's professional-ethics rules describes a prohibition on private and charter school staff providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, with the MoHRE permit's code of conduct pointing the same way. Verify the current wording against ADEK's own policy before relying on it, but do not go looking for your child's own class teacher as a paid tutor.

A tuition operation with premises and staff is a different legal animal again, requiring an educational services permit from the relevant authority. IB Gram holds no regulator approval, accreditation or licence from ADEK, KHDA, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, operates no office or centre in the UAE, and describes itself as an independent tutor-matching platform. Any provider telling you otherwise about itself is making a claim worth checking.

sections.heading: Coverage, fallback and the honesty line on coursework
paragraphs: No tutoring platform covers every subject at every level at every hour, and a page that implies otherwise is setting up a disappointment. The subjects where availability is tightest are the ones where cohorts are smallest everywhere: Higher Level Physics and Chemistry, the less common Diploma languages, Music, and Design Technology. If a request lands in one of those, the honest answer at the first conversation is a named match time or a clear no, not a holding pattern.

Where no UAE-based specialist is free, the fallback is a tutor based elsewhere teaching the same syllabus over the same live video, scheduled to Gulf Standard Time. That is disclosed before any booking rather than discovered in the first lesson. Several providers in this market conceal non-UAE delivery behind a local-looking contact route; stating it in advance is a small thing that is nonetheless rare here.

The academic honesty line is the other place where a provider either tells you the truth or sells you a problem. A tutor may teach the skills a piece of coursework needs, explain the assessment criteria, ask questions about a draft the student has written, and point at a section that does not yet answer the question. A tutor may not write, draft, complete or edit to completion an internal assessment, an Extended Essay, a Theory of Knowledge essay or a Personal Project. One page in this market sells finished internal assessments outright; that is a malpractice trigger for the student, and the student is the one who pays for it.

The same restraint applies to materials. Official syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables belong to the awarding bodies and are not ours to redistribute. A tutor cites and links the official source, and works with what your child's school has legitimately issued. If the only thing a provider can offer is a folder of copied papers, there is nothing being taught.
bullets: Tight-availability subjects are named at the first conversation, not later
Non-UAE-based delivery is disclosed before a booking, not after

Official papers and mark schemes are cited and linked, not redistributed

process.title: Measure the week before you book anything
process.description: Write down the bus departure, the real arrival time and every fixed commitment for seven days, including the ones that only run for part of the season. The slot that comes out of that exercise is the slot that lasts. Almost every abandoned tutoring arrangement in this district was booked against an assumed arrival time rather than a measured one.

process.title: Name the subject, the level and the board
process.description: Not mathematics, but Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, or Cambridge 0580 Extended. Not physics, but Pearson 4PH1. Matching is only as good as the specificity it is given, and a wrong board means the wrong paper structure, the wrong formula sheet and wasted hours before anyone notices.

process.title: Diagnostic first session, with a written outcome
process.description: The first hour establishes where the marks are being lost, using the student's own last assessment and a short set of exam questions. It produces three named priorities and an honest view of how long they will take. If the honest answer is that the school is already covering it well, that is said rather than hidden.

process.title: Fix the slot and hold it for the year
process.description: One named weekday hour, plus a weekend block where the commute makes the weekday unworkable. The slot is held rather than rebooked each week, which is what keeps it from being eaten by a club season or an exam week. Ramadan timing is agreed in advance, not improvised in the first week of it.

process.title: Review against the school's own calendar
process.description: Progress is checked against your child's school assessments and internal deadlines, not against a feeling that lessons are going well. If a tutor cannot name the next thing your child's school will mark, they are working blind, and the review is the point at which that becomes visible.

whyPoints.title: The slot is built from your bus, not from a template
whyPoints.description: Scheduling here starts with a measured arrival time from a specific campus, which is why a Khalifa City family is offered a different starting point from an Al Bateen family. That sounds obvious and is almost never done, which is why so many afternoon slots in this district quietly stop being attended by November.

whyPoints.title: One tutor, one subject, one level
whyPoints.description: A Higher Level Chemistry hour is taught by someone who teaches Higher Level Chemistry, not by a generalist covering six subjects across four year groups. Depth in one syllabus is what moves a Paper 3 mark, and it is the thing a small school department genuinely cannot supply a second time.

whyPoints.title: Rates in AED, with the source named
whyPoints.description: Every figure on this page is in the currency you pay in and attributed to whoever published it. Market bands are presented as market bands rather than as our price, and your own quote comes from a conversation. Three of the most visible competitors in this market publish no price at all.

whyPoints.title: The coursework boundary is stated before you ask
whyPoints.description: Teaching, criteria explanation and questioning on a draft the student wrote: yes. Writing, drafting or completing an internal assessment, Extended Essay or Theory of Knowledge essay: never. That boundary protects your child from a malpractice finding, which is a consequence they carry and nobody else does.

whyPoints.title: No regulator claim, no office, no invented numbers
whyPoints.description: IB Gram is an independent tutor-matching platform with no ADEK, KHDA, SPEA, Ministry, IB, Cambridge or Pearson approval, no UAE premises, and no self-published rating or success statistic. Where a figure appears on this page it carries its source, and where something is unverified it is marked unverified.

whyPoints.title: Delivery is disclosed, including when it is not local
whyPoints.description: Lessons are one-to-one over live video. Where no UAE-based specialist covers a subject, the tutor may be based elsewhere and teaching to Gulf Standard Time, and you are told that before booking rather than after. No home visits are sold in the UAE at all.

faqs.question: When can a tutoring session realistically start for a child in Al Manaseer?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on which campus the bus goes to. A child at a school in Al Bateen or Al Khalidiyah can be ready by around quarter past four. A child bussing to Al Mushrif is closer to quarter to five. A run across a bridge to Saadiyat or Al Reem, or out to Khalifa City and the Al Raha corridor, pushes the first honest start to half past five or later once the return leg, the walk up and twenty minutes to eat are counted. Measure your own arrival time for a week before fixing anything, because the bus contract's pick-up time tells you nothing about the afternoon.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a tutor to apartments in Al Manaseer?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not sell home visits anywhere in the UAE, and nobody will be sent to a residential address in this district or any other. Home visiting is a service offered only in India. Every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video, with the student sharing their own exercise book or screen and writing while the tutor watches. The practical trade is that you give up a person in the room and gain a tutor chosen for the exact syllabus and level rather than for living within a workable drive of Zayed the First Street at five in the afternoon.

faqs.question: Why should a session be one hour rather than two on the same evening?
faqs.answer: Because the second hour is reliably worse than the first, and the child knows it. A student who left Al Manaseer before seven in the morning has limited capacity for new material by early evening. One focused hour on a single subject, on a named weekday, held for the whole year, outperforms a two-hour block that looks more serious on paper and stops being attended by half term. Where a family needs more coverage, the better answer is a second slot on a different day, or a longer Saturday morning block when nothing is competing with it.

faqs.question: What is the single best hour in an Al Manaseer week for a Higher Level subject?
faqs.answer: Saturday morning. It is the only block in the week that is not competing with a school run, a club session, a Quran class or the evening meal, and it is long enough to do work that cannot be done in forty minutes. A full past paper under timed conditions followed immediately by mark-scheme comparison needs an unbroken ninety minutes to be worth anything. Using the weekend for the heaviest subject also frees the weekday slot for a lighter second subject, which is how families cover two subjects without booking two evening hours.

faqs.question: How should the schedule change during Ramadan for a student on the island?
faqs.answer: School hours shorten, the afternoon becomes rest time, and the useful study window moves late. Sessions typically shift to post-Iftar timing between about half past eight and ten in the evening, and the frequency usually drops rather than holding steady. The families who keep momentum through the month are the ones who agree that shift in advance, in writing, before Ramadan begins. The ones who try to keep a normal four o'clock pattern and improvise week by week generally lose most of the month, and then try to recover it in a fortnight that is already full.

faqs.question: My child goes to school in Khalifa City. Is a weekday slot worth booking at all?
faqs.answer: Yes, but a short one and for a specific purpose. With a return across the bridge in the afternoon peak, a weekday hour starting around half past five works as consolidation: last week's class content, a set of exam questions on a topic already taught, or a worked example the child did not follow in school. It is the wrong slot for a first encounter with a hard new idea. Put the construction work, meaning new topics and timed papers, into a Saturday morning block, and treat the weekday hour as repair.

faqs.question: Which part of an ADEK inspection report should I read before booking a tutor?
faqs.answer: Not the overall band on the front page. Read what the report says about teaching and assessment in your child's specific phase, whether recommendations from the previous inspection were acted on, and any comment on the subject group your child depends on. A school rated strongly overall can still have a thinly staffed sixth-form science department, and a school with a middling band can have an excellent mathematics team. You are making a decision about one subject in one year group, so read the paragraphs that describe that.

faqs.question: What do tutors charge per hour in Abu Dhabi, and are those your prices?
faqs.answer: Those are market rates, not ours. As published by the providers themselves, budget online tutoring starts around AED 45 to 65 with EdFlik and AED 33 to 52 with Tutopiya; Unitors lists IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200; TutorChase shows AED 270; the Bestimate rate survey puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350 and specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above; BartyED publishes AED 650. Monthly packages in this market run around AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour home visits. IB Gram's own figure comes from a consultation, not a table.

faqs.question: Is my child in the right Arabic stream, and how would I know?
faqs.answer: Ask the school in writing which stream they are placed in and why. Arabic as a first language and Arabic as an additional language are different courses with different expectations. A child who speaks dialect fluently at home but never studied formal Standard Arabic can be placed in the first-language stream and struggle with literary register and written formality. A child placed in the additional-language stream can coast and quietly lose the option of taking Arabic A at Diploma level. A placement review before Year 12 is the moment that decision is still cheap to change.

faqs.question: Do Arabic and Islamic Education count towards the Ministry equivalency subjects?
faqs.answer: Not for the British curriculum track. Equivalency on that route requires five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects. That surprises families in Year 11 and it changes which subjects you protect when the timetable gets tight. Verify the current requirement with the Ministry before relying on it for a university application.

faqs.question: Can a tutor teach my child's Islamic Education or Social Studies syllabus?
faqs.answer: Support in those subjects is limited to reading, structure, vocabulary and examination technique on the school's own material. For the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry is not permitted. So a tutor can help a student organise an answer, build subject vocabulary and practise the format of the assessment, working from what the school has issued. A tutor offering an alternative syllabus or their own content for these subjects is offering something a parent should decline, however convenient it looks.

faqs.question: Does the person tutoring my child need a permit, and can I see it?
faqs.answer: Yes, and yes. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and is applied for through MoHRE's smart app, website and e-services system under Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing. Eligible categories include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Asking for the permit reference is reasonable. Anyone telling you a permit is optional, or that it carries a fee, is wrong on both points.

faqs.question: Can we hire my child's own class teacher privately in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: You should not try. Press reporting on ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff describes a prohibition on providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct points the same way. Treat that as press-reported and verify it against ADEK's current policy document before relying on the exact wording, but the direction is clear enough that no reputable provider will arrange it. The practical alternative is a specialist who teaches the same syllabus somewhere else entirely, which also removes the awkward conflict over your child's own grades.

faqs.question: Our flat is small and two children share a room. Where does the lesson happen?
faqs.answer: Usually at the dining table, with the slot staggered rather than shared. In a dense district like this one, the common fix is to put one child's session in the window when the sibling is at a club or a mosque class, and the other child's on a different evening. A session booked while the whole household is at home is a session with a door opening in it. Headphones, a wall to face rather than a room to face, and a cleared table do more for the hour than any amount of software, and all three are free.

faqs.question: Suppose nobody covers my child's Higher Level subject from the UAE. Then what?
faqs.answer: You are told at the first conversation, with either a named match time or a clear no. Availability is tightest in the subjects where cohorts are small everywhere: Higher Level Physics and Chemistry, the less common Diploma languages, Music and Design Technology. Where no UAE-based specialist is free, the fallback is a tutor based elsewhere teaching the same syllabus over live video and scheduled to Gulf Standard Time, and that is disclosed before any booking rather than discovered in the first lesson. A holding answer that never resolves is worse than a no, so you will not be given one.

faqs.question: Exactly what can a tutor do with an internal assessment draft?
faqs.answer: A tutor can teach the skills the task needs, explain what each assessment criterion is asking for, ask questions about a draft the student has already written, and point at a section that does not yet answer its own research question. A tutor cannot write, draft, complete or edit to completion an internal assessment, an Extended Essay, a Theory of Knowledge essay or a Personal Project. The spoken-feedback rule is the practical test: if comments are going into the document rather than into the conversation, the line has been crossed. The student carries the malpractice consequence, which is why the boundary is not negotiable.

abu-dhabi/al-manaseer.closingHeading: Start with the arrival time, then the subject
abu-dhabi/al-manaseer.closingBody: Tell us which campus your child travels to from Al Manaseer, what time they actually walk back in, and the exact subject, level and board they need. From those three things we can tell you whether a weekday hour or a Saturday morning block is the right shape, what the market rate for that level is, and whether a specialist is free. If the honest answer is that your child's school is already covering the gap, we will say so. Lessons are one-to-one over live video; IB Gram does not run home visits in the UAE, and we hold no regulator approval of any kind. The first conversation costs nothing and ends with a named next step.

abu-dhabi/al-maryah-island.tutorsIntro: Tutors matched to Al Maryah Island households are selected for reliability across a calendar that moves: a specialist who can hold the same weekly slot through term time, exam season and a fortnight when the family is in London or Mumbai. Each teaches one named board and level.

intro.heading: Nobody goes to school here, which inverts the whole day
paragraphs: Al Maryah Island is Abu Dhabi's central business district: the Abu Dhabi Global Market free zone, The Galleria, Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi, two large hotels and a set of residential towers, all on a compact island connected by bridges to the Al Zahiyah side of the main island and onward towards Al Reem. It was planned as a financial and commercial centre with residences attached rather than as a family suburb, and the consequence for anybody raising teenagers here is simple: there is no school on the island.

That produces a daily pattern families do not experience anywhere else in the emirate. In most communities the parent commutes and the child's school is close. Here it is reversed. A parent can walk to an office in the ADGM or across to The Galleria, while a child is driven or bussed across a bridge to Al Mushrif, Al Bateen, Al Nahyan, Saadiyat Island or out to Khalifa City. The parent is frequently home before the child, which sounds like an advantage and in practice creates its own problem: the supervising adult is available at four o'clock and the student is not.

The second feature of this population is mobility. Al Maryah households are weighted towards finance, legal, consulting and healthcare professionals, often on international assignments, often travelling for a week here and a fortnight there. School, by contrast, does not move. A Diploma student's internal assessment deadlines, mock weeks and coursework checkpoints are set by the school months in advance, and the damage a travelling household takes is almost never missed teaching. It is a deadline that fell during a trip nobody checked against the school's own calendar.

The third is the apartment itself. A high floor on a CBD island is a pleasant place to live and an ambiguous place to study. The view is a distraction, the layout is open, the acoustics of a shared living space carry, and the building adds time at both ends of every journey because the drop-off point is not the front door. None of that prevents serious work. It means the study arrangement has to be designed once, properly, rather than improvised around whichever surface is clear.

What follows works through those four things in order: the real door-to-door times to the schools Al Maryah children attend and the earliest session each one supports, the inverted supervision problem and what to do about it, how to hold a weekly slot across time zones when the family travels, how to set up a tower apartment for genuine study, what a mid-year transfer between island campuses actually costs, what tutoring spends look like over a two-year programme in AED, and the honest answer to the home-tutor question.

abu-dhabi/al-maryah-island.programmesIntro: Al Maryah children attend schools across four or five districts, which means several programmes per building. These four cover almost all of them, and each reacts differently to a household that travels.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led primary schooling reported against learner attributes and approaches to learning rather than percentages, which makes progress genuinely hard to read for a parent used to grades. Assessment is continuous, so a fortnight away costs specific tasks rather than an examination, and that makes the PYP the most travel-tolerant programme a mobile household can be in.
programmes.countryNote: Several PYP and IB continuum schools sit within reach of Al Maryah Island, mostly on Saadiyat Island, in Al Raha and in Khalifa City. For a primary-age child here the honest first question is the commute rather than the curriculum: a long daily crossing does more damage to a seven-year-old's learning than most of the things parents buy tutoring for.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four published criteria marked out of eight, converted to a grade from 1 to 7. Deadlines are internal and spread across the year rather than concentrated in a series. That spreads risk for a travelling family, and it also means nothing externally fixed forces the catching-up, which is where a weekly slot that survives the travel earns its place.
programmes.countryNote: MYP 5 carries the Personal Project, which is self-directed, supervised and assessed on process as much as on product. It is the component most commonly damaged by a mobile year, because it has one deadline a long way off and no intermediate structure, so it loses every scheduling contest it enters.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, normally three Higher and three Standard Level, with Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Internal assessment carries 20% in the sciences and both mathematics courses, and Higher Level mathematics adds a third paper worth 20%. It is the least travel-tolerant of these programmes because the deadlines are cumulative and set by the school rather than by the family.
programmes.countryNote: For a mobile Al Maryah household the most valuable fifteen minutes of the year is spent putting the school's internal deadline sheet next to the family's travel plans and looking for collisions. Where one exists there are three options, all of them easy in advance and none of them easy afterwards.

programmes.name: IGCSE at Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel
programmes.description: Cambridge splits most subjects into Core and Extended, with Core capped at grade C; Pearson Edexcel tiers mathematics as Foundation and Higher with a grade 9 ceiling. Both are end-of-course qualifications. Cambridge runs June, November and March series, and Pearson Edexcel runs May or June and November, which gives a mobile family more entry flexibility than the Diploma does.
programmes.countryNote: The detail that matters for an internationally mobile household is the timetable zone. Every Cambridge centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, each with its own timetable version, and Cambridge states it is essential to use the correct one and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after the wrong version was used. Work only from the timetable the school confirms.

abu-dhabi/al-maryah-island.subjectsIntro: These notes describe each subject in terms of how well it survives a disrupted fortnight, because for households here that is the variable that decides what needs support and when.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Cumulative and unforgiving of gaps: a fortnight missed in calculus affects everything that follows. It is also the subject that recovers fastest with short frequent practice, so a travelling household should protect continuity here above almost anything else. The exploration is 20% at both levels.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics with the calculator assumed throughout, including on the first paper. More modular in feel than Analysis, so a missed fortnight is more easily absorbed. The exploration needs a real dataset, which a travelling student can often source more interestingly than a settled one.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Two written papers plus one scientific investigation worth 20% at both levels. Problem-solving practice survives interruption well; the investigation does not, because it depends on laboratory access and a data collection window that the school sets. Plan that component around travel rather than in spite of it.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms and equilibrium reward drilled practice that works in short sessions anywhere. The investigation carries 20% and has a 3,000 word ceiling, and it is the component most frequently damaged by a trip, because data collection and write-up both sit inside term time.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Content-dense and decided by command terms, which makes it highly portable: a student can make real progress from a hotel room with a set of marked questions and a connection. The statistical treatment expected in the investigation is the specific gap for students arriving from a double award background.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: The internal assessment is a portfolio of three commentaries built on published news articles, worth 30% at Standard Level and 20% at Higher. Because each commentary is a discrete piece of work, it suits a mobile household unusually well: one commentary per quiet fortnight, planned against the school's own deadlines.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Case-study command and calculation accuracy decide the grade. The Higher Level research project rests on a real organisation within an 1,800 word limit, and a student in a household with professional parents often has better access to a willing organisation than most, which is a genuine advantage if used early.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 is a timed guided analysis of an unseen non-literary text, which is ideal for a compressed session anywhere in the world: one text, one timed attempt, one honest marking. The Higher Level essay runs to 1,200 to 1,500 words and needs a longer planned block.

subjects.name: English B and English as a second language
subjects.description: Productive skills respond to frequency rather than duration, which suits short sessions across a travelling year. Listening components need a quiet room and headphones, something worth arranging deliberately in a shared tower apartment rather than assuming.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies form the federal baseline that private schools must deliver whatever curriculum they are licensed for. Script fluency and vocabulary retention are the realistic aims for a non-Arabic-speaking student, and both decay quickly over a long trip, which makes continuity more important here than in most subjects.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: An exhibition of three objects with a 950 word commentary plus a 1,600 word essay on a prescribed title, both assessed and contributing to the matrix points. Thinly timetabled and almost always deprioritised in a disrupted term, which makes it the component most often rescued by a protected weekend hour.

abu-dhabi/al-maryah-island.regionsIntro: What matters about Al Maryah's neighbours is the bridge crossing and the time of day. These notes describe the journey rather than the district.

regions.name: Al Zahiyah and the Tourist Club area
regions.note: The immediate mainland neighbour across the short crossing, dense and long-established. A short hop at most hours, though the approach roads carry a lot of commercial traffic during the working day, which matters for an afternoon collection rather than a morning one.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Connected on the other side, with its own residential towers and school provision. For an Al Maryah family this is often the nearest alternative when school capacity on the main island is tight, and the crossing between the two is the shortest in this set.

regions.name: Al Mushrif and Al Nahyan
regions.note: Inland on the main island, where several long-established schools sit. These are the most common destinations for Al Maryah children and the crossings are predictable in the morning and variable in the afternoon, which is what sets a realistic session start.

regions.name: Al Bateen
regions.note: The western side of the main island, with established international provision and a longer run from Al Maryah through the island's internal roads. Households with children here usually find that any session before half past four is optimistic.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: North across the bridges, with premium campuses and IB provision. The journey is straightforward outside peak hours and considerably longer during them, and it is the longest regular crossing most Al Maryah children make.

regions.name: The Corniche
regions.note: The western waterfront, reached in minutes, with a concentration of clinics, clubs and activity providers. These are the real competitors for a weekday evening study slot, because an activity is usually in the diary before any tutoring is considered.

regions.name: Khalifa City and Al Raha
regions.note: Off-island towards the airport, with several large international campuses including IB continuum provision. The longest run from Al Maryah, and the one that usually pushes a family towards a weekend morning for anything substantive.

schoolClusters.city: Main island: Al Mushrif, Al Nahyan and Al Bateen
schoolClusters.note: The nearest cluster across the bridge and the destination for most Al Maryah children. Long-established international provision with a mix of British-curriculum and IB routes, and the crossings that make a weekday session possible rather than theoretical.

schoolClusters.note: The second ring, reached across the longer bridges, including premium campuses and IB continuum provision. These produce the latest arrivals home and are the main reason Al Maryah households move substantive work to a weekend morning.

Short and defended, because the value of this format is that it happens most weeks rather than two in three, which is what an optimistically early slot delivers from an island with two bridges.

sections.heading: The bridge, not the bell, decides when a lesson can start
paragraphs: Scheduling from Al Maryah Island begins with a number almost nobody has measured: the time a child is actually at a desk, fed, on an ordinary weekday. Parents estimate it from the school's finishing time, which is wrong twice over. The crossing is between the school and the island, and the building is between the drop-off and the apartment. Between those two, most families underestimate by twenty to thirty minutes, and that error is the reason an agreed four o'clock slot becomes a four twenty-five start three weeks in a row and then an argument.

The table below gives door-to-door windows for the schools Al Maryah children most commonly attend. These are planning figures drawn from the households we work with rather than published timetables, and they assume an ordinary afternoon rather than a bad one. Two patterns stand out. The main island cluster in Al Mushrif, Al Nahyan and Al Bateen supports a session from around half past four, which is workable. The Saadiyat and off-island campuses do not reliably support anything before five or half past, which is the strongest argument available for moving substantive work to a weekend morning.

The practical instruction is to measure your own number before booking anything. For two weeks, write down the time the child is at a desk rather than the time they came through the lobby. Average it, add fifteen minutes for food, and that is the slot. Then hold it, because consistency beats optimism: a session that happens thirty-six times across a year is worth considerably more than a better-looking slot that happens twenty-four times and is resented on the other twelve.

sections.heading: The inverted school run, and the supervision it does not provide
paragraphs: In most households the parent gets home after the child, and the supervision problem is the hours before they arrive. On Al Maryah Island the reverse is common. A parent working in the ADGM or across at The Galleria can be back in the apartment at four, with the child still crossing a bridge. That looks like an advantage, and in one sense it is: there is an adult present when the student arrives. In another sense it quietly removes the structure that longer parental absence creates, because a student who knows somebody is home tends to defer starting work until asked.

The second half of the inversion is less obvious. A parent who has finished a working day at four has the energy to supervise at half past four. A child who has been in school since eight and in a car since half past three does not have the energy to be supervised then. The two availability windows overlap at exactly the wrong moment. Families here frequently describe an evening in which the parent is ready and the student is not, followed by an evening in which the student finally settles at nine and the parent is finished.

What works is to stop treating supervision and teaching as the same thing. Supervision is the short, defined, unglamorous routine: thirty to forty minutes of the same task type each weekday, written down rather than spoken, checked briefly afterwards. Teaching is the weekly hour with a specialist. The useful arrangement sets the daily task inside the weekly session and checks it at the start of the next one, so the student's accountability runs to a fixed external point rather than to whichever parent happens to be in the room and in what mood. For an inverted household that distinction does more than any change in timing could.

sections.heading: Holding one weekly slot across three time zones
paragraphs: Mobility is the defining feature of this population, and it is a solvable problem rather than a reason to stop. Abu Dhabi sits four hours ahead of UTC all year and does not observe daylight saving, which means the difference between Abu Dhabi and a European city changes by an hour twice a year while the Gulf clock stays still. That single fact causes more missed sessions in travelling households than anything else, because a slot agreed in February quietly moves relative to London in March.

The fix is to pre-agree the session time for each destination rather than renegotiating on arrival. The table below gives the arithmetic for the destinations Al Maryah households travel to most. The principle is to keep the session in the student's afternoon or early evening wherever they are, and to accept that one or two destinations will require a morning slot for the tutor or for the student. Both are usually possible if asked for in advance and rarely possible if asked for on the day.

There is one thing to settle before the first trip: whether travel weeks are a pause or a continuation. Either answer is fine as long as it is a decision rather than a drift. A pause with a defined catch-up session booked before departure works well for shorter trips. A continuation works well for longer ones, particularly where the student has coursework in train, because an internal assessment does not pause and nor does the school's deadline. What does not work is leaving it open, because an open question becomes four weeks of nothing and a scramble on return.

sections.heading: Setting up a high-floor apartment for actual work
paragraphs: A tower apartment on this island is a good place to take a lesson and a poor place to study by default, and the difference is worth engineering once rather than negotiating weekly. The default study position in these flats is the dining table in an open-plan living space, facing a view, in earshot of everything. It works for twenty minutes. It does not work for the ninety-minute block that an exploration or a timed paper requires, and no amount of willpower from a sixteen-year-old fixes an arrangement that is structurally against them.

Four decisions solve it, and together they cost less than one hour of tutoring. A desk that faces a wall rather than the window, even if it is a small one in a bedroom. Over-ear headphones with a boom microphone, so the student can be heard without raising their voice over a shared room and can hear without the room intruding. A wired connection, or at minimum the 5 GHz band rather than whatever the laptop joined by default, because a dropped connection costs more than any processor upgrade would return. And a second phone or tablet propped as a document camera, so the tutor sees the written working rather than the student's face.

The document camera is the one families consistently skip and consistently regret. In mathematics and the sciences, almost everything a tutor needs to diagnose is in the working rather than in the answer: a rearrangement done in the head, a unit dropped three lines earlier, a graph with an axis chosen badly. Without a view of the page, a session becomes a conversation about answers, which is the least useful version of one-to-one teaching. With it, the tutor is marking in real time, which is the most useful version. An old phone and a stack of books is sufficient.

sections.heading: What a mid-year transfer between island campuses actually costs
paragraphs: Al Maryah households change schools more often than settled communities do, for reasons that have nothing to do with dissatisfaction: a posting extends, a sibling gets a place somewhere better placed, a commute that looked acceptable in September proves unsustainable in February. Abu Dhabi's private schools are licensed and inspected by the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate, and the market offers genuine choice. The cost of moving is rarely the fee. It is the curriculum mismatch nobody audits until afterwards.

The specifics matter more than the general principle. Moving a Year 10 student between two British-curriculum schools can still mean moving between Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel entries, which creates content gaps running in both directions and makes two terms of past papers useless. Moving a Diploma student means finding six subjects at matching levels, and a single mismatch at Higher Level can cost most of a year's content. Moving between an IB continuum school and a British one at fourteen means moving between criterion-based assessment and tiered written papers, which is a change of skill set rather than of syllabus.

The table below sets out what each transfer actually breaks and roughly how long it takes to repair with focused one-to-one work. The useful discipline before accepting a place is to ask the new school three questions in writing: which board and syllabus code is each subject entered with, which topics has the class already covered, and are the required subjects and levels available in the student's year group. The third question is the one that occasionally produces an answer that should change the decision, and it is almost never asked until the uniform has been bought.

sections.heading: Tutoring spend in context, over a two-year programme
paragraphs: Most pages in this market quote an hourly rate or nothing at all. Three of the six competitor pages reviewed for this project in October 2026 published no price, and two quoted in US dollars. An hourly figure is also the least useful number for a household planning a two-year Diploma, because the decision being made is not what an hour costs but what a programme of support costs across twenty-four months. The table below converts the published market bands into programme-level figures in AED.

The bands themselves come from published platform and agency rate pages surveyed in October 2026 and from Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table. They are market rates rather than an IB Gram price list, and no figure here is a quote. Published monthly estimates for a single weekly hour run roughly AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 in the middle and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support, with package offers seen at around AED 799 per month online for eight sessions.

Reading the table, two decisions produce most of the variance. The first is how many subjects are supported, and the honest answer for most students is one or two rather than four; a Diploma student with four tutors has no free evenings and tends to resent all of them. The second is whether the support is continuous or targeted, because an internal assessment supervision block and a pre-series paper block together cost a fraction of two years of weekly lessons and address the two components where marks are most recoverable. Ask any provider, including us, whether a figure is per hour or per session, whether VAT is included, and what happens to a prepaid balance if you stop.

sections.heading: Why Al Maryah searches say home tutor, and what is delivered
paragraphs: The home-tutor search is not irrational from a CBD island. A household where a parent travels wants somebody reliable who turns up, and a concierge building makes an arranged visit straightforward. For younger children, physical presence genuinely helps with attention in a way a screen does not. These are real reasons and they deserve a direct answer rather than a deflection into sales language.

The market picture is this. Published in-home rates in the UAE run roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour with the tutor's travel inside the fee, against AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor working online and AED 200 to 450 for a specialist. On an island reached by bridge, the travel component is not a rounding error: a tutor crossing in the late afternoon spends a meaningful share of the booked hour in a car, prices accordingly, or declines. The people who accept tend to be those with diary gaps rather than specialists with full ones. And for a household that travels, an in-home arrangement ends at the airport.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE. Home visits are a service we run only in India, and nobody will be sent to an Al Maryah Island address. Lessons are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video, with screen sharing for marked work and a document camera for written working. For this population the delivery model is the point rather than a compromise: the same specialist, the same slot and the same plan continue across a bridge, across a posting and across a time zone, which is not something a person who had to drive here can offer.

sections.heading: Coursework integrity when the tutor is in another country
paragraphs: Online delivery across borders makes one boundary more important rather than less, so it is worth stating precisely. Under IB academic honesty rules an internal assessment, an Extended Essay and a Theory of Knowledge essay must be the student's own work, authenticated by a supervisor at the school and declared by the school. A malpractice finding falls on the student. At least one site ranking for these searches sells completed Internal Assessments at a published price, and for a travelling household under time pressure that offer is designed to look like a solution.

What a tutor can legitimately do is extensive and does not change with distance. Read the published criteria with the student line by line and explain what each band rewards. Read a draft the student produced and return written comments and questions on it. Ask the question that exposes a method the student cannot yet explain. Check notation, units, axis labelling and statistical treatment. Plan dated checkpoints backwards from the school's internal deadline and hold the student to them, which for a mobile family is the single most useful service on offer, because the deadline does not move when the family does.

What a tutor must never do is become the author. No sentence, calculation, diagram or restructured paragraph should reach a submitted assessment unless the student made it. We also do not distribute board materials: syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables belong to Cambridge, Pearson and the IB, and the correct behaviour is to cite and link the official source rather than send a copy. If any provider offers your child finished coursework, the correct response is not a negotiation about price.
