sections.heading: Starting from Al Maryah Island, with limits stated
paragraphs: Send four things: the school, the board and syllabus code, the level or tier, and one measured figure, which is the time your child is actually at a desk on an ordinary weekday. If you have travel planned, send the dates too, along with the school's internal deadline sheet if you have it, because checking those two documents against each other takes a few minutes and prevents the most expensive mistake a mobile household makes. We then name the tutor who would teach, where they are based and what they have taught at that level, before any payment.

The limits are worth hearing up front. Coverage is uneven in narrow Higher Level subjects, in less common languages and in uncommon Pearson Edexcel options, and the honest answer is one of three things: a different hour of the week where the right specialist is free, an adjacent level or board where the overlap is real and the gap can be named, or a plain statement that we cannot cover it. Time zones add a second limit: a destination eight or nine hours behind the Gulf needs a tutor whose own day matches, which is not always available at short notice and is usually available if asked for a fortnight ahead.

On money and data: the rate is agreed before the first paid session, nothing on this page is a quote, and there is no outcome-linked refund scheme. Any condition attached to a trial is stated before you book it. We hold no office, centre or branch in the UAE. Forms on this site collect a parent's contact details and the child's year, board and subject, which is what matching needs; a photograph, a grades history and a teacher's name are not required. UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on Personal Data Protection governs how that information is handled, and the privacy link explains how to have it removed.

process.title: Measure the crossing for a fortnight
process.description: Write down the time your child is actually at a desk, fed, rather than the time school ended or the car arrived in the lobby. Average that across two weeks and add fifteen minutes. From an island reached by bridge, that figure is usually twenty to thirty minutes later than a parent would guess, and it is the single number a timetable should be built on.

process.title: Put travel dates next to the school's deadline sheet
process.description: Before anything is booked, lay the family's travel plans alongside the school's internal deadline dates and look for collisions. Where one exists the options are to move the trip, agree an earlier submission with the school, or book a defined block of work before departure. All three are easy in advance and none is easy on return.

process.title: Send the board, code and level
process.description: Cambridge 0580 Extended and Pearson Edexcel 4MA1 Higher are both called IGCSE Maths in conversation and are different examinations with different papers and calculator rules. The code on the school's entry confirmation removes the guesswork, and for a Diploma student the Higher or Standard split decides which components matter most.

process.title: We name the tutor, and the time zone, before payment
process.description: You are told who would teach, where they are based, which board and level they cover and whether they can hold your slot through term time and through travel. Where you plan to be in a distant time zone, we say in advance whether a matching tutor is available rather than discovering it during the trip.

process.title: Split the week: short midweek, substance at the weekend
process.description: After a bridge crossing the weekday hour is best used for marked practice of material already understood, and the substantive work belongs in a weekend morning. Households here consistently get more from one long weekend block plus one short weekday slot than from three identical evening sessions, two of which underperform.

whyPoints.title: Scheduled from a measured crossing, not a bell
whyPoints.description: The slot is built from two weeks of recorded data about when the student is genuinely at a desk, which on an island reached by bridge with a tower lift at the end is twenty to thirty minutes later than the obvious estimate. Getting that right is what makes an arrangement last a term rather than three weeks.

whyPoints.title: The slot follows the household
whyPoints.description: The same specialist and plan continue from London, Mumbai or Singapore, with the offset agreed in advance rather than renegotiated on arrival. Abu Dhabi does not observe daylight saving, so a European slot shifts twice a year; we build that in rather than discover it.

whyPoints.title: Deadlines checked before trips are booked
whyPoints.description: The damage a mobile family takes is almost never missed teaching; it is a submission date that fell inside a trip. Laying the school's internal deadline sheet next to the travel plans takes minutes and is the highest-return administration available to a Diploma household here.

whyPoints.title: Supervision and teaching treated separately
whyPoints.description: On this island the parent is often home before the child, and parental availability peaks when student capacity is lowest. The weekly session sets a short written daily task and checks the previous one, so accountability runs to a fixed external point rather than to whoever is in the apartment.

whyPoints.title: Stated limits, including on time zones
whyPoints.description: Coverage in narrow Higher Level subjects is uneven and a destination nine hours behind the Gulf needs a tutor whose own day matches. You get the real position before paying, including a plain no, rather than a match that works on paper and collapses in the second week of a posting.

faqs.question: Are there any schools on Al Maryah Island?
faqs.answer: No. The island was planned as a central business district with residences, hotels, a hospital and a retail centre rather than as a family suburb, so every school-age child here crosses a bridge twice a day. The nearest cluster is on the main island in Al Mushrif, Al Nahyan and Al Bateen, with Al Reem Island on the shorter eastern crossing, Saadiyat Island further north, and the larger off-island campuses towards Khalifa City. Which direction you travel in sets the earliest hour a tutoring session can realistically start.

faqs.question: What time is my child realistically home from school here?
faqs.answer: Later than the school's finishing time suggests, because there are two delays rather than one: the bridge crossing and the building. For the main island cluster in Al Mushrif, Al Nahyan and Al Bateen, most secondary students are at a desk between four and ten to five. For Saadiyat campuses it is nearer half past four to a quarter past five, and for off-island Khalifa City later again. Measure your own figure across a fortnight, record the time at the desk rather than in the lobby, and add fifteen minutes for food.

faqs.question: I get home before my child does. Does that help with homework?
faqs.answer: Less than you would expect, because your availability and their capacity peak at different hours. A parent who finished work at four is ready to supervise at half past four; a child who has been in school since eight and in a car since half past three is not. The arrangement that works separates the two jobs: a short written daily task of thirty to forty minutes set inside the weekly tutoring session and checked at the start of the next one, so accountability runs to a fixed point rather than to a parent's mood.

faqs.question: Can we keep the same tutor while we are in London for three weeks?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is worth agreeing the timing before you go rather than on arrival. Lessons are delivered online over live video, so the same tutor and subject continue from anywhere. Abu Dhabi sits four hours ahead of UTC and does not observe daylight saving, so the gap to London is three hours in summer and four in winter, which means a slot agreed in February quietly shifts in March. Pre-agree the London time, keep the session in the student's late afternoon, and book any catch-up session before departure.

faqs.question: How do we stop a trip from clashing with a coursework deadline?
faqs.answer: Put the school's internal deadline sheet next to the travel plans once a term and look for collisions. Schools set those dates themselves, months in advance, and publish them; almost nobody reads the sheet before booking flights. Where a clash exists there are three options: move the travel, agree an earlier submission with the school, or book a defined block of work before departure. For a Diploma student this is the highest-value fifteen minutes of administration a parent can spend, because the deadlines are cumulative.

faqs.question: Does a time difference of eight hours make online tutoring impractical?
faqs.answer: Not impractical, but it needs a tutor whose own working day matches. A destination eight or nine hours behind the Gulf cannot be served comfortably by a tutor on Gulf or South Asian time, because one side ends up at an hour where nobody is useful. The solution is a tutor in a matching time zone, which is usually available with a fortnight's notice and often not available at a day's notice. Say where you will be and when, and that gets solved before you leave rather than during the trip.

faqs.question: What is the best study setup in a high-floor apartment?
faqs.answer: Four decisions, made once, costing less than one hour of tutoring. A desk facing a wall rather than the view, even a small one in a bedroom. Over-ear headphones with a boom microphone rather than earbuds, so the student can be heard without competing with an open-plan room. A wired connection or the 5 GHz band rather than whatever the laptop joined automatically. And an old phone propped as a document camera, so the tutor sees the written working rather than the face, which in mathematics and the sciences is where every diagnosis actually lives.

faqs.question: We may change schools mid-year. What does that cost academically?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on what changes. A move between two British-curriculum schools on the same board in Year 9 breaks option blocks and set placement, worth four to eight hours of repair. A move between boards in Year 10 invalidates two terms of past paper work and takes ten to sixteen hours per examined subject. A Diploma transfer mid-programme is the serious case: six subjects must be matched at matching levels, and a single Higher Level mismatch may not be repairable. Audit the subjects and levels in writing before accepting a place.

faqs.question: What should we ask a new school before accepting a place?
faqs.answer: Three questions, in writing. Which board and syllabus code is each subject entered with, because two British-curriculum schools can sit different boards. Which topics has the class already covered this year, which converts a vague fear of being behind into a finite list. And are the required subjects available at the required levels in my child's year group, which is the question that occasionally produces an answer that should change the decision and is almost never asked until the uniform has been bought.

faqs.question: What does two years of Diploma support actually cost?
faqs.answer: Working from published market bands rather than hourly rates: one weekly hour with a qualified subject tutor is roughly AED 600 to 1,200 a month, and with an IB or IGCSE specialist roughly AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more in an exam year. Across a two-year Diploma that is around seventy to eighty sessions in one subject. A targeted alternative, an internal assessment supervision block of eight to twelve sessions plus a pre-series paper block of ten to fifteen, costs a fraction of that and addresses where marks are most recoverable.

faqs.question: Can a tutor come to our apartment on Al Maryah Island?
faqs.answer: Not through us. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India, and nobody will be sent to an Al Maryah Island address. Lessons are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video. Published in-home rates in the UAE run roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel inside the fee, and on an island reached by bridge a late-afternoon crossing consumes a real share of the booked hour. For a household that travels, an in-home arrangement also ends at the airport.

faqs.question: Which internal assessment is worth supporting first?
faqs.answer: Whichever carries the most weight and has the least supervision, which in practice usually means a science investigation or a mathematics exploration, both worth 20% of the subject grade. They run over months, the school's realistic involvement is a lesson on criteria plus comments on one draft, and the marks are highly legible once the published criteria are read properly. For a travelling household they are also the components most at risk, because they depend on data collection windows and school deadlines that do not move.

faqs.question: Who regulates the schools my child might move between in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: The Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate and publishes inspection outcomes. Dubai's equivalent is the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, Sharjah has the Sharjah Private Education Authority, Ras Al Khaimah has its Department of Knowledge, and the Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. That map matters for a mobile family, because a move between emirates means a different regulator, a different inspection framework and a different set of published information.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help write an internal assessment if we are short of time?
faqs.answer: No, and any provider who says yes is selling your child a malpractice risk. Under IB academic honesty rules an internal assessment, an Extended Essay and a Theory of Knowledge essay must be the student's own work, authenticated by a school supervisor and declared by the school, and the consequence of a finding falls on the student. What a tutor can do is substantial: read the criteria line by line, comment in writing on a draft the student produced, check statistical treatment and notation, and hold dated checkpoints. The student authors every word.

abu-dhabi/al-maryah-island.closingHeading: Two numbers and a date list
abu-dhabi/al-maryah-island.closingBody: To get something workable from here, send the school, the board and syllabus code, the measured time your child is actually at a desk, and your travel dates for the term. Those four things produce a slot that survives a bridge crossing and a posting, the name of someone who teaches that exact specification, and a check against the school's own deadlines before anything is booked. Lessons run online, one-to-one, over live video, and they follow the household. If a time zone makes the slot unworkable, you will hear that before you pay rather than during the trip.

intro.heading: Two languages in one household, and the marks that depend on it
paragraphs: Al Muroor is one of the established interior districts of Abu Dhabi island: apartment blocks along and behind Muroor Road, neighbours in Al Nahyan, Al Karamah, Al Mushrif and Al Manaseer, schools within a short drive rather than a long bus run. The households here are mostly long-settled rather than newly arrived. Many are Emirati; many more are Arab, South Asian and Filipino families who have been in the city for a decade or longer, with children who were born here and have never studied anywhere else.

That matters for one reason. In an Al Muroor household the language of the classroom and the language of the home are usually different, and that difference is where the marks go. Not because the students are weak — a great many are genuinely bilingual — but because the examination system makes a series of quiet decisions about which language course a bilingual child is entered for, and those decisions cap grades years before anyone looks at them.

The first of them happens in Year 9 or Year 10, when a school decides whether a child sits First Language English or English as a Second Language at IGCSE. Those are different qualifications. One assumes English is the student's main language and examines reading, directed writing and composition at that level. The other is a second-language qualification, perfectly respectable, with a different paper structure and a different reception from some sixth forms and some universities. Families are rarely told the choice is being made, and almost never told what it affects.

The second happens in DP1, when the school places the student in Language A: Literature, Language A: Language and Literature, Language B or Language ab initio. The difference between a Language A and a Language B placement is enormous. A student doing two Language A subjects earns a bilingual diploma. A genuinely bilingual student placed into Language B is sitting a course below their level, which feels comfortable and costs points. A student placed into Language A on the strength of fluent speech, with no experience of literary analysis, meets Paper 1 unseen commentary for the first time in a mock and falls apart.

Add the subjects every private school in the country must teach alongside the international curriculum — Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies — and an Al Muroor family can easily be managing three language streams at once, each with its own grading logic. This page is about getting those decisions right, what the market charges to support them, and what a tutor may and may not do with a piece of writing. Lessons are delivered online, one to one, over live video; IB Gram does not run home visits in the UAE, which is a service we offer only in India.

abu-dhabi/al-muroor.programmesIntro: Al Muroor children sit a wider spread of programmes than most Abu Dhabi districts, because the schools within reach include British, IB and Indian-board campuses as well as schools following the Ministry curriculum. These four cover most of what we are asked for.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Two-year courses with a syllabus code that determines the papers, the tier and, in English, the qualification itself. Cambridge tiers several subjects so that a Core entry caps the grade while Extended runs the full range. Pearson International GCSE is linear in most subjects with its own codes and paper structures. The two are not interchangeable in revision terms.
programmes.countryNote: For an Al Muroor family the English entry is the decision worth checking first. Read the statement of entry: 0500 and 0990 are First Language English, 0510, 0511 and 0991 are English as a Second Language, and 4EA1 and 4ES1 are the Pearson equivalents. The school chooses, usually on the basis of a Year 9 assessment, and a parent who asks early can sometimes have that choice revisited.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS, for a maximum of 45 points. Every subject carries an internally assessed component. In the language subjects that component is an individual oral, and in Higher Level it is joined by an essay on a studied text.
programmes.countryNote: The bilingual diploma is the part Al Muroor families most often have not heard about. It is awarded to a student who completes two Language A subjects, or a Language A plus a group 3 or group 4 subject studied in a second language. For a child who genuinely reads and writes Arabic as well as English, that is a realistic and valuable outcome, and it is decided by a placement conversation in DP1 rather than by anything that happens in DP2.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each, marked 1-8. Language acquisition and language and literature are separate subject groups with separate criteria, and the phase a student is placed in for language acquisition is the middle-years version of the same decision the Diploma makes later.
programmes.countryNote: MYP reporting hides the language question rather than exposing it, because a criterion level of 5 looks the same whichever phase the student is in. An Al Muroor parent reading an MYP report should ask which phase the child sits in for language acquisition and whether the school expects them to move up, because phase placement at MYP 4 shapes the Diploma placement two years later.

programmes.name: AS and A Level, after IGCSE
programmes.description: Three or four subjects studied in depth, assessed by examination with some coursework depending on the subject. For UAE equivalency purposes the British track requires one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level with the same grade, on top of five accredited subjects at GCSE or IGCSE.
programmes.countryNote: Al Muroor families weighing the Diploma against A Levels for a bilingual student should know that the two reward language differently. The Diploma makes a second language compulsory and rewards it with points and a bilingual award. A Level lets a student drop languages entirely after Year 11, which suits some students and wastes a real asset in others.

abu-dhabi/al-muroor.subjectsIntro: Our enquiries from Al Muroor are weighted towards the language courses and the subjects where writing quality decides the mark. Each entry says what is assessed and where the marks tend to go.

subjects.name: Language A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 is a guided analysis of an unseen non-literary text, Paper 2 a comparative essay on studied works, plus an individual oral and, at Higher Level, an essay. Students who speak fluently but have never been taught to analyse a text structurally lose most of their marks on Paper 1.

subjects.name: Language A: Literature
subjects.description: Literary analysis across studied works and unseen passages. The common failure is retelling the plot instead of discussing how a writer produces an effect. That shift is a teachable skill and it is the difference between a 4 and a 6.

subjects.name: Language B
subjects.description: Productive and receptive skills in an acquired language: a writing paper, a listening and reading paper, and an individual oral. It is a second-language course, and placing a genuinely bilingual student in it leaves points on the table rather than securing them.

subjects.name: Arabic A and Arabic B
subjects.description: The route matters more than the level. Arabic A is a first-language literature or language-and-literature course; Arabic B is acquisition. A student who speaks Gulf Arabic at home but has never studied Modern Standard Arabic formally sits awkwardly between the two, and the placement should be made on written evidence.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language
subjects.description: Reading, writing and listening at second-language level, with a speaking component that is counted in or endorsed depending on the code. It is a real qualification with a real ceiling, and some sixth forms and universities treat it differently from First Language English.

subjects.name: First Language English
subjects.description: Reading response, directed writing and composition at first-language level. Marks are lost on the directed-writing task more than anywhere else, because students write well but ignore the audience, form and purpose the question specified.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.levels: IGCSE Core and Extended; DP AA and AI
subjects.description: Word problems are a reading test before they are a mathematics test. Bilingual students who can do the algebra routinely lose marks on multi-clause questions, and the repair is a comprehension method rather than more algebra practice.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.levels: IGCSE and DP HL and SL
subjects.description: The most language-dense of the sciences. Precision verbs decide marks: describe, explain, suggest and compare each demand a different answer shape, and a student answering in the wrong shape scores nothing however correct the biology is.

subjects.name: Business Management and Economics
subjects.description: Case-study subjects where the examined answer has to apply a named concept to the stimulus in front of it. Diagrams earn marks in Economics that prose cannot. Both carry internally assessed written work with strict word limits.

subjects.name: History
subjects.levels: IGCSE and DP HL and SL
subjects.description: An essay discipline in a second language, which is the hardest combination in the Diploma. Marks sit in argument structure and use of evidence, not in the amount remembered, and both are explicitly teachable in an hour a week.

abu-dhabi/al-muroor.regionsTitle: Al Muroor and the island districts around it
abu-dhabi/al-muroor.regionsIntro: Al Muroor sits in the interior of the island with short runs to several school clusters, which is why the tutoring constraint here is the evening timetable rather than the commute. These are the neighbouring districts that come up in our enquiries.

regions.name: Al Nahyan
regions.note: Directly adjacent, with a similar apartment-and-villa mix and several long-established schools. Families often have children at two different campuses in the two districts, running two different reporting systems in one household.

regions.name: Al Karamah
regions.note: Interior district on the same corridor. The school run is short enough that a six o'clock slot holds comfortably, which is unusual in Abu Dhabi and worth using rather than wasting on a four o'clock session with a tired child.

regions.name: Al Mushrif
regions.note: Villa district with established British and IB provision and a high proportion of long-settled households. Sibling groups spread across phase boundaries are common, which makes stage-specific advice more useful here than general tutoring.

regions.name: Al Manaseer
regions.note: Dense island district with a short run to the Corniche schools. Activity blocks and prayer times shape the evening more than traffic does, so the question is which single slot can be defended every week.

regions.name: Al Wahda
regions.note: Central and heavily built, with large cohorts in several campuses. Set placement and class size are frequent subjects of our first conversations with families here, and they are questions for the school before they are questions for a tutor.

regions.name: Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: Western island district with a long-standing IGCSE presence. Pearson and Cambridge entries sit side by side across these campuses, so the syllabus code is the first thing to establish.

regions.name: Al Mushrif and Al Bateen corridor
regions.note: The run towards the western end of the island, where several Diploma schools sit. Students here come home later because of after-school programmes, which pushes the realistic start time past half past six.

regions.name: The Corniche
regions.note: Established schools along the waterfront serving the interior districts. Named here because Al Muroor children are enrolled across them, and because the distance is short enough that families underestimate how much of the evening the return trip still takes.

schoolClusters.city: The island interior: Al Muroor, Al Nahyan and Al Karamah
schoolClusters.note: A dense cluster of long-established campuses running British, IB and Indian-board curricula within a short drive of each other. This is where most Al Muroor children are enrolled, and the curriculum mix inside one district is the reason a family here often has two children on two incompatible grading systems.
schools: Al Ain English Speaking School, Abu Dhabi campuses

schoolClusters.city: The western island and the Corniche
schoolClusters.note: Reached in a short run from Al Muroor, and where several of the emirate's Diploma cohorts sit. Named as the ecosystem an Al Muroor student studies in rather than as any form of relationship with IB Gram.

abu-dhabi/al-muroor.modesIntro: Three patterns cover nearly every language-led enquiry we take from this district. All are delivered online, one to one, over live video, with the student's own writing on a shared screen.

modes.title: A placement diagnostic before anything else
modes.description: One or two sessions whose only purpose is to establish which course a bilingual student should actually be sitting. The tutor sets a piece of timed writing and an unseen reading task, marks them against the published criteria for both candidate courses, and writes down what the evidence says. That note is what you take to the school.

A written opinion on First Language versus Second Language, or Language A versus Language B
Something concrete to put in front of the head of department rather than an impression

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one on a language or writing-led subject
modes.description: A standing slot on the subject where writing quality is costing marks, worked from the student's own returned essays and the examiner's annotations. Writing improves by rewriting one paragraph properly, not by producing more essays nobody marks closely.
bullets: Sixty or ninety minutes in the same slot each week, booked for a term
Work from the last marked piece, not from the next topic
One paragraph redrafted properly each session beats three essays skimmed

modes.title: A block on the individual oral or an internally assessed essay
modes.description: A short, dense series timed to the school's internal deadline for the individual oral, the Higher Level essay or a written assignment. The tutor coaches the student's own extract choice, global issue and structure, and gives criterion-referenced feedback on what the student has produced.
bullets: Four to six sessions scheduled backwards from the school's deadline
Feedback against the published criteria, line by line, on the student's draft

sections.heading: Who lives in Al Muroor, and what the enquiry turns out to be about
paragraphs: Our enquiries from this district fall into four household shapes, and each one arrives describing a different problem from the one it actually has. The first is an Emirati or Arab family whose child is strong in conversation and weak on paper in both languages, and who has been told the child needs English support. The second is a long-settled South Asian household whose child is academically solid but sitting an English as a Second Language entry nobody discussed with them. The third is a family with children at two campuses on two different curricula, trying to compare a criterion level of 5 with a grade 6 and finding it impossible. The fourth is a Diploma family who have just discovered that a bilingual diploma was available and that their child was placed in Language B.

What unites them is that the presenting complaint is a subject and the real issue is a placement. Tutoring a child harder inside the wrong course is the most expensive mistake available in this market, because it produces visible effort, modest improvement and a ceiling that never moves. The useful first hour is almost always diagnostic rather than instructional: find out what course the student is entered for, find out what they can actually do in writing under timed conditions, and see whether the two match.

That is a cheap thing to establish and an expensive thing to leave unexamined. A timed piece of writing and one unseen reading task, marked against the published criteria of both candidate courses, settles the question in about ninety minutes. If the evidence says the student is sitting below their level, a parent has something concrete to take to the head of department rather than a feeling. If it says the placement is right, the family stops worrying about it and spends the money on the component that is actually losing marks.

The table below is the version we use on first calls from this part of the island. It is not a description of who lives here in any statistical sense — we do not publish demographic figures we cannot source — but it is an honest account of the four shapes our own enquiries from Al Muroor take and what each one should look at first.

sections.heading: English in the classroom, another language at the dinner table
paragraphs: A child who has lived in Abu Dhabi since birth, attended an English-medium school throughout, speaks English with friends and Arabic or Urdu or Malayalam at home is not a second-language learner in any ordinary sense. They are bilingual. But examination systems do not have a category for bilingual. They have first-language courses and acquisition courses, and every bilingual student gets sorted into one or the other by somebody making a judgement.

The judgement is usually made on fluency, and fluency is the wrong evidence. Spoken fluency develops first and develops fast. Academic writing — the ability to hold an argument across four paragraphs, to use subordination deliberately, to vary sentence length for effect, to analyse how a text produces meaning rather than what it says — develops years later and only when it is taught. A great many bilingual students in this district sound like first-language speakers and write like second-language ones, which is why a conversation-based placement decision goes wrong so often in both directions.

The second thing that gets missed is that the gap is narrow and closable. The specific skills examiners reward in a first-language English paper are a finite list: reading for implication, selecting evidence, writing to a specified audience and form, controlling register, and structuring a composition. None of them requires a childhood in English. All of them are teachable inside a term of weekly work on the student's own writing. What does not work is more reading in general, or vocabulary lists, or practice essays nobody marks closely. One paragraph rewritten properly with a tutor beats five essays returned with a grade on them.

For families where Arabic is the home language there is a parallel and less-discussed version of the same problem running in the other direction. A student may speak Gulf Arabic confidently and have very little formal command of Modern Standard Arabic, which is the language the examination is in. That student is not a first-language candidate in the examination's terms and not an acquisition candidate in the family's terms, and the placement needs written evidence rather than a conversation in the corridor.

sections.heading: First Language English or English as a Second Language: the entry that sets a ceiling
paragraphs: At IGCSE these are two different qualifications, not two difficulty settings of one. Cambridge First Language English is 0500, or 0990 on the 9-1 scale: reading response, directed writing and composition, assessed on the assumption that English is the candidate's main language. Cambridge English as a Second Language is 0510, 0511 or 0991 depending on how speaking is handled: reading, writing and listening at acquisition level, with a different paper structure and different mark schemes. Pearson's equivalents are 4EA1 for English Language A and 4ES1 for English as a Second Language.

The school decides, usually from a Year 9 or early Year 10 assessment, and it is often not presented to parents as a decision at all. The consequences arrive later. Some sixth forms set First Language English as an entry requirement for essay-based A Levels. Some universities treat a second-language English IGCSE differently from a first-language one when assessing language competence. And for UAE Ministry of Education equivalency, the British track requires five accredited subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic Education excluded from that count — so the English entry is one of the five that has to be there.

The practical advice is unglamorous and effective. Read the statement of entry and write the code down. If it is a second-language code and you believe your child is capable of the first-language paper, ask the head of English what evidence the placement was based on and whether it can be reviewed, and ask early, because entries close months before examinations. Cambridge's final entry deadline for the March 2027 series, for instance, was 27 November 2026 — the decision window shuts long before anybody is thinking about papers.

Where the evidence genuinely points to the second-language entry, take it and stop worrying. It is a proper qualification, it counts, and a student who scores highly in it is better served than one who scrapes through a first-language paper. The error to avoid is not the second-language entry; it is nobody having checked.

sections.heading: Language A, Language B and the bilingual diploma nobody mentioned
paragraphs: In the Diploma the same decision reappears with higher stakes. A student takes a studies-in-language-and-literature subject, which is a Language A, and a language-acquisition subject, which is a Language B or an ab initio course. A student may also take two Language A subjects instead, dropping acquisition altogether — and a student who completes two Language A subjects is awarded a bilingual diploma. So is one who takes a Language A plus an individuals-and-societies or sciences subject studied in a different language.

That award is a real, free, permanent credential for a child who already reads and writes two languages, and in our experience most families in districts like this one have never been told it exists. It is decided in a placement conversation at the start of DP1, which is to say it is decided while everyone is thinking about something else. If your child genuinely reads and writes Arabic, Hindi, Urdu, Malayalam, French or Tagalog at an academic level, ask the Diploma coordinator in DP1 whether a second Language A is available at your school — some offer it taught, some through the school-supported self-taught route at Standard Level.

The reverse error is just as common and more damaging. A student placed into Language A: Literature or Language and Literature on the strength of fluent speech, with no prior teaching in textual analysis, meets Paper 1 — a guided analysis of an unseen text — as a genuinely unfamiliar task. They can read every word and have nothing to say about structure, voice, register or effect. That gap closes with teaching, but it needs to be identified in DP1 rather than after the first mock in DP2.

The table sets out the component structures as we understand the current guides. Confirm every percentage against your school's copy of the subject guide before planning around it, because language guides are revised on their own cycle and a school may still be running a cohort under an older specification.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies alongside the international curriculum
paragraphs: Every private school in the country teaches Arabic, social studies and Islamic studies alongside whatever international curriculum it is licensed for. The UAE government's own guidance states that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That is the federal baseline behind the requirement, and it applies in Abu Dhabi as elsewhere.

The published detail is clearest in Dubai's own documentation, and it is worth reading even for an Abu Dhabi family because it shows the shape of the rules. Dubai's regulator requires separate classes by group: for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and social studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and combined classes for both groups are stated to be strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. It also requires Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, and sets the instructional time against a forty-minute lesson unit, advising that no mandatory-subject lesson should run shorter than twenty-five minutes. For anything binding in Abu Dhabi, check ADEK's own current circulars rather than assuming Dubai's wording applies.

Two practical points follow for an Al Muroor household. First, your child is probably in the Arab stream or the non-Arab stream for these subjects and the streams are not interchangeable; a tutor needs to know which. Second, for the mandatory subjects the published Dubai guidance states that the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry is prohibited, which is a genuine constraint on what any tutor may legitimately teach from. We work from the student's own school material for these subjects rather than importing a syllabus of our own, and we say so.

One more thing families are relieved to learn: for Ministry of Education equivalency on the British track, Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects. They still have to be studied, and they still appear on the school report, but they do not have to be among the five accredited subjects at grade E or 3 that the equivalency count is built from.

sections.heading: Where a bilingual student actually loses marks
paragraphs: The losses are specific and they repeat. In mathematics they are in the multi-clause word problem: a student who can solve the equation reads the question twice, extracts the wrong quantity and loses three marks on a question whose mathematics they had. The repair is a comprehension routine applied to the question, not more algebra. In the sciences they are in command terms. Describe, explain, suggest, compare, evaluate and justify each demand a different answer shape, and a student who answers the wrong shape earns nothing however accurate the content. Both of these are reading problems wearing a subject's clothing.

In the essay subjects the loss is structural. Bilingual students often write fluent, pleasant paragraphs that do not answer the question, because nobody has taught them that an examination paragraph has a job: make a claim, give evidence, explain how the evidence supports the claim, connect it to the question. Four sentences doing four jobs beat a page of good prose doing one. This is the single most profitable thing to teach a strong bilingual student, and it transfers across every subject at once.

In the language courses themselves the loss is in register and task compliance. Directed writing tasks specify an audience, a form and a purpose, and students write a good piece of the wrong thing. Individual orals lose marks when a student describes the extract rather than connecting it to the global issue they chose. Higher Level essays lose marks when the line of inquiry is too broad to be answered inside the word limit. None of these is a language deficiency. They are task-reading failures, and a tutor who marks against the criteria rather than the general impression catches all of them in a session or two.

The thing a parent can do without buying anything is ask for the last three marked pieces of written work and look for the pattern in the annotations rather than at the grade. If the comments say the same thing three times, that is the brief. If they say nothing except a number, that is also information — about the school's marking rather than the student.

sections.heading: What language and writing support costs around Al Muroor, in AED
paragraphs: Three of the six ranking pages for this kind of search publish no price at all, and the ones that do quote dollars. So here are market bands in dirhams with the source of each, read in October 2026. They are market figures, not an IB Gram price list. Our own arrangement begins with a free consultation and a trial session, and what applies to your child depends on the subject, the level and how scarce the specialism is.

Language work has a particular cost shape worth understanding. A placement diagnostic is one or two sessions and then nothing, which is the cheapest high-value purchase on this page. A writing-improvement block is genuinely slow: a term of weekly work on the student's own paragraphs, because writing does not respond to intensity the way content recall does. Cramming three sessions a week into April will raise a content grade and will not raise a writing grade. Buy the diagnostic first and the long slow block second, in that order.

Set those numbers against the dominant figure in any family's education budget, which is school fees. Dubai's regulator confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees in that emirate would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year, under an economic incentives package; Dubai's private sector was reported at 387,441 students across 227 schools offering seventeen curricula in 2024-25. Tutoring is usually a small fraction of what a family already spends on school, which is a more honest way to judge an hourly rate than looking at it alone.

One caution. A low rate in this market often means a university student working without the private-tuition work permit that national rules require. That is not a bargain; it is an arrangement with no recourse if it goes wrong, and the person tutoring your child is the one exposed. Ask the question before the first paid hour.

sections.heading: A tutor crossing the island against one-to-one online
paragraphs: Al Muroor is better placed than most Abu Dhabi districts for an in-person arrangement. It is interior, central, and within a short drive of several school clusters, so the travel objection that settles this comparison on Saadiyat or in Masdar City is weaker here. A family at this address who wants somebody in the room has a genuine local market, publishing roughly AED 180-500 an hour, and we are not going to pretend otherwise. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE — that service exists only in India — so what follows compares two models rather than selling one.

Where the comparison still tilts is supply of the specific thing. A general English tutor is findable within a short drive of Al Muroor. Somebody who has taught Language A: Language and Literature at Higher Level under the current guide, or Arabic A literature, or a self-taught Language A route, is a different search entirely. The narrower the requirement, the less relevant geography becomes, and language placements are among the narrowest requirements in the Diploma.

The second thing online delivery changes for writing work specifically is the record. Every annotation sits on a shared screen and survives the session, so the student has the marked paragraph and the tutor's comments afterwards rather than a memory of a conversation. For a writing-improvement block, where the whole method is redrafting the same paragraph against criteria, that record is most of the value. A pen on paper in a living room produces one marked copy and no history.

What is genuinely better with somebody in the room is attention management for younger children, and the fact that a parent can see what is happening without asking. We say that rather than claiming the formats are equivalent. For a Year 7 child who drifts, an adult physically present is worth something real. For a DP2 student working on an individual oral, the screen is better.

sections.heading: Honesty on a piece of writing, including when the parent is the editor
paragraphs: Writing is the component where the honesty line is hardest to see, because the help that crosses it looks exactly like the help that does not. A tutor may teach how a paragraph is built, show the student what the criteria reward, read what the student has produced and say which band it sits in and why, ask the questions that expose a weak claim, and teach the student to redraft. A tutor may not supply sentences, restructure a draft so completely that the voice changes, or hand over phrasing to be pasted in. The difference is authorship, and the Diploma asks the student to sign that the work is their own.

This lands differently in a bilingual household, because there is usually a competent adult at home who could improve the English and who wants to help. Our advice to Al Muroor parents is specific: read it, say what you did not understand, and hand it back. Saying "I lost the thread in your third paragraph" is useful and legitimate. Rewriting the third paragraph is not, and it also teaches the student that the fix for unclear writing is somebody else's sentence. For internally assessed work there is a further reason to be careful: schools compare a student's submitted writing with their classroom writing, and a draft that reads above the student's known level invites a question nobody wants asked.

We also do not send families syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes or subject guides. Those belong to the boards and the IB, we link to the official pages instead, and reproducing them would be a copyright problem regardless of how convenient it is. The essay mills competing for these searches sell completed internal assessments outright. That is an academic-integrity breach with the student's diploma attached to it, and no amount of deadline pressure makes it a reasonable purchase.

One regional boundary to add. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from giving paid private tuition to students enrolled at their own school, and the national private-tuition work permit carries a code of conduct that also bars serving students affiliated with the teacher's own school. Treat that as press-reported and verify it against ADEK's current policy document. The practical effect in Al Muroor, where the school is often a short walk away, is that hiring your child's own English teacher privately is not available to you however convenient it would be.

sections.heading: Starting from Al Muroor, with the placement question first
paragraphs: The first call is a free consultation. For a language-led enquiry we ask four things: which code is on the statement of entry, which language courses the school has placed the child in, what the home language is, and whether you can send two recent pieces of marked written work. Those four answers usually tell us whether the problem is placement, technique or content, and they change what we would recommend buying first.

If the answer is placement, we would rather sell you one diagnostic session than a term of weekly work. A timed piece of writing and an unseen reading task, marked against the published criteria of both candidate courses, produces a written opinion you can take to the head of department. That is a cheap purchase with a large effect, and it sometimes ends the enquiry entirely, which is fine.

If the answer is technique, the honest plan is a term of weekly work on the student's own writing with a review at the halfway point against something measurable — a timed paper marked to criteria, a criterion band on the oral, a redrafted paragraph compared with the original. Writing improves slowly and visibly. Anybody promising a rapid grade shift in an essay subject is selling you something they cannot deliver, and we are not permitted to make that kind of claim about an outcome in any case.

On coverage: common combinations match quickly. Arabic A literature, less widely taught first languages, and the school-supported self-taught Language A route are narrower, and sometimes we cannot cover them this term. We say so on the call. Where a UAE-based specialist is not available we will offer somebody from the wider pool delivering the same one-to-one online lesson from another time zone, and we tell you that before anything is booked, including what it means for holding a weekly evening slot from Al Muroor.

process.title: Send the statement of entry and two marked pieces
process.description: The statement of entry carries the syllabus code, which decides what is actually being examined. Two recent pieces of marked written work show whether the same comment keeps appearing. Together they take five minutes to find and replace about half an hour of guessing on the first call.

process.title: A free consultation about placement before method
process.description: We establish which courses the school has placed your child in and whether the evidence supports that placement, before discussing tutoring at all. Working harder inside the wrong course is the most expensive error available in this market, and it is the one we see most often from bilingual households.

process.title: A diagnostic session that produces something written
process.description: A timed piece of writing and an unseen reading task, marked against the published criteria of both candidate courses, with a written note of what the evidence says. If that note says the placement is right, you have stopped worrying. If it says otherwise, you have something concrete for the head of department.

process.title: A term-length writing block with a measured review
process.description: A standing weekly slot on the student's own work, with a halfway review against a timed paper or a criterion band rather than against a feeling. Writing improves slowly, so the review exists to confirm the direction of travel and to end the arrangement when it has done its job.

whyPoints.title: We look at the entry code before the subject
whyPoints.description: First Language English and English as a Second Language are different qualifications. Language A and Language B are different courses with different ceilings and different awards attached. Asking which one your child is actually entered for takes one question, and it changes the plan more than any teaching decision that follows.

whyPoints.title: Bilingual is not the same as second-language
whyPoints.description: Spoken fluency arrives years before academic writing, and placement decisions made on conversation go wrong in both directions. We mark a timed piece of writing against the real criteria and tell you what the evidence says, which is a different thing from telling you what you hoped to hear.

whyPoints.title: The bilingual diploma is worth asking about
whyPoints.description: Two Language A subjects, or a Language A plus a group 3 or group 4 subject studied in another language, earn a bilingual diploma. For a child who already reads and writes two languages at an academic level this is a real credential, and it is decided in a DP1 placement conversation most families do not know is happening.

whyPoints.title: Figures carry their source and their date
whyPoints.description: Every AED band on this page names the provider that published it and the month it was read, and every regulatory statement names the authority it came from. We publish no satisfaction percentage, no student count and no star rating, because we cannot show you the data behind one.

whyPoints.title: The authorship line is set before the first session
whyPoints.description: We teach structure, read the student's own draft and give criterion-referenced feedback. We do not supply sentences, restructure a draft into a different voice, or send you past papers and mark schemes. On internally assessed work that boundary protects the qualification the student is working towards.

faqs.question: How do I find out whether my Al Muroor child is on First Language English or English as a Second Language?
faqs.answer: Read the statement of entry the school issues for the examination series, and write the code down. Cambridge First Language English is 0500 or 0990; English as a Second Language is 0510, 0511 or 0991. Pearson uses 4EA1 for English Language A and 4ES1 for English as a Second Language. If the statement has not been issued, ask the examinations officer rather than the class teacher, because entries are an examinations-office function. Then ask the head of English what evidence the placement was based on, and ask early: entries close months before papers are sat.

faqs.question: Can a second-language English IGCSE limit my child's options later?
faqs.answer: It can affect some routes, which is why it is worth knowing about rather than discovering. Some sixth forms set First Language English as an entry requirement for essay-based A Levels, and some universities assess language competence differently depending on which qualification a candidate holds. For UAE Ministry of Education equivalency on the British track, five accredited subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3 are required, with Arabic and Islamic Education excluded from that count, so an English entry has to be among the five. Check the specific requirement with each destination rather than relying on a general rule.

faqs.question: What is a bilingual diploma and does my child qualify for one?
faqs.answer: It is awarded to a Diploma student who completes two studies-in-language-and-literature subjects, which are Language A courses, or a Language A plus an individuals-and-societies or sciences subject studied in a second language. For a child who reads and writes two languages at an academic level it is a free, permanent credential. Whether it is available depends on what your school offers, including whether it runs the school-supported self-taught Language A route at Standard Level. Ask the Diploma coordinator in DP1, because the placement that decides it happens then.

faqs.question: My Al Muroor child speaks Arabic at home but struggles in Arabic lessons. Why?
faqs.answer: Almost always because the examination is in Modern Standard Arabic and the home language is a spoken dialect. Those are related but not the same, and a student can be entirely confident in conversation and have little formal command of the written academic register. The first thing to establish is which Arabic route the school has placed them in, because Arabic as a first language and Arabic as an additional language have different expectations and, under the published Dubai guidance, are taught in separate classes. The placement should rest on written evidence rather than on how the child speaks.

faqs.question: Do your tutors come to apartments in Al Muroor?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not run in-home visits anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. Every lesson for an Al Muroor family is delivered online, one to one, over live video, with the student's own writing on a shared screen. The in-home market does exist in central Abu Dhabi and publishes rates of roughly AED 180-500 an hour, and because this district is central the travel objection is weaker here than elsewhere in the emirate. What online delivery buys you is the match: a Language A Higher Level specialist rather than whoever is nearby.

faqs.question: Which Al Muroor schools do your students attend?
faqs.answer: Our students in this district are spread across the long-established campuses on the island interior and the western island, running British, IB and Indian-board curricula. We name schools on this page only as context for the environment a student studies in, with no affiliation, endorsement or partnership implied. For a tutoring plan the school name matters less than three facts: which curriculum, which syllabus codes, and what time your child is actually home. Check any school listing against ADEK's own published directory, since provision changes each year.

faqs.question: Can a tutor fix my child's written English in one term?
faqs.answer: A term of weekly work on the student's own writing reliably improves structure, task compliance and paragraph discipline, which is where most of the marks sit. What it does not do is produce a different writer, and nobody should promise you a particular grade. The method that works is slow and unglamorous: one paragraph redrafted properly each week against the published criteria, with the previous marking visible. Writing does not respond to intensity the way content recall does, so three sessions a week in April will not produce what one session a week from September would have.

faqs.question: Should a bilingual student take the IB Diploma or A Levels?
faqs.answer: The two treat a second language very differently, which is the part worth weighing. The Diploma makes a language subject compulsory, rewards genuine bilingualism with points and offers a bilingual diploma. A Levels allow a student to drop languages after Year 11 and concentrate on three or four subjects, which suits a student whose strengths are narrow and deep. Neither is better in the abstract. Decide on your child's evidence and on what the destination they want actually asks for, read on that institution's own admissions page.

faqs.question: How much does Language A or writing support cost for an Al Muroor family?
faqs.answer: Market rates read in October 2026 put a qualified online subject tutor at roughly AED 150-300 an hour and an IB or IGCSE specialist at AED 200-450 or more, with in-home one-to-one at AED 180-500 because travel is inside the rate. Those are other providers' published figures. The cheapest high-value purchase in a language-led plan is usually a single placement diagnostic rather than a standing weekly slot. Our own arrangement starts with a free consultation and a trial session, and the figure depends on the subject, the level and the scarcity of the specialism.

faqs.question: What does the individual oral actually require, and can a tutor help with it?
faqs.answer: The student chooses an extract from a studied work and a global issue, then speaks about how the work and the extract explore that issue, followed by questions. Marks are lost when a student describes the extract rather than connecting it to the global issue, or chooses an issue too broad to be discussed in the time. A tutor can teach the structure, read the student's own outline and give criterion-referenced feedback, and run practice under timing. A tutor may not supply the extract choice, the global issue or the phrasing.

faqs.question: My two children are on different curricula. How do I compare their reports?
faqs.answer: You largely cannot, and trying to is how households misallocate attention. Middle Years Programme reporting gives criterion levels marked 1-8 against four criteria per subject, with no percentages and no raw marks. IGCSE reporting gives grades on an A*-G or 9-1 scale derived from marks. A criterion level measures performance against a descriptor; a grade measures marks against boundaries. Ask each school what the child's next step is in each subject and compare those answers instead, because they are the only commensurable thing in the two documents.

faqs.question: Are Arabic and Islamic Education counted in the equivalency subject total?
faqs.answer: No. The published clarification of UAE equivalency requirements for British-curriculum students states that Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects, which must be accredited subjects passed at no less than grade E or grade 3, alongside one Advanced Level at E or two Advanced Subsidiary Levels at the same grade. They are still compulsory to study and still appear on the report. Verify the current requirement on the Ministry's own pages before relying on it, and treat equivalency as a process the authority runs rather than something a tutor can influence.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover both English and a content subject for an Al Muroor student?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and for a bilingual student it can be the efficient choice, because the skill transferring between them is the same: reading a question accurately and answering in the shape it demands. A tutor working on Biology extended responses and on directed writing is teaching one underlying competence twice. Where it stops working is at Higher Level, where component technique becomes specialist. Our general preference is a language specialist for the language courses and a subject specialist for the subject, with the overlap handled by both knowing what the other is doing.

faqs.question: What time can lessons realistically start from Al Muroor?
faqs.answer: Al Muroor is better placed than most Abu Dhabi districts because the school run is short, so a slot from half past four onwards is often workable rather than the half past six that outer communities are stuck with. The real constraints here are activity blocks and prayer times rather than traffic. Pick the one slot you can defend every week for a whole term instead of the earliest one that is free, because consistency does more for a writing block than frequency does. A slot that collapses in week four was the wrong slot.

faqs.question: Is it a problem if I correct my child's English before they submit it?
faqs.answer: For internally assessed work, yes, and it is worth being careful about. The Diploma asks the student to declare the work is their own, and schools compare submitted writing against classroom writing. A draft that reads above the student's known level invites a question nobody wants asked. What is entirely legitimate, and genuinely useful, is reading it and telling your child where you lost the thread or could not follow the argument, then handing it back unedited. That teaches them to fix it; rewriting it teaches them that someone else will.

abu-dhabi/al-muroor.closingHeading: Check the entry code before you buy anything
abu-dhabi/al-muroor.closingBody: If you are in Al Muroor and considering support for a bilingual student, the most valuable thing you can do costs nothing: find the statement of entry, note which English or language code is on it, and ask the school which language courses your child has been placed in and on what evidence. Send us that plus two recent pieces of marked written work and we will tell you whether the issue is placement, technique or content, and what is worth buying first. Lessons are delivered online, one to one, over live video. If a placement looks wrong, we will say so even when it means recommending nothing.

abu-dhabi/al-mushrif.tutorsIntro: The profiles below cover the phases an Al Mushrif household is most likely to need at the same time: upper primary, lower secondary, IGCSE and the Diploma. Each one names the phase and the board, because a tutor who is excellent with a Year 11 candidate is not automatically the right person for a Year 7 who has just changed school.

intro.heading: A household district, and the transitions that keep showing up in it
paragraphs: Al Mushrif sits inland on the southern half of Abu Dhabi island, a settled grid of villa compounds and low-rise blocks between Airport Road and Khaleej Al Arabi Street. It has one of the longest-tenured populations on the island. Families here tend to arrive and stay, which means a household often has a child in the Diploma, one in Year 9 and one in upper primary, all of them at the same school or at two schools a few minutes apart.

That shape changes the enquiry completely. In a district of short-stay apartments, a tutoring request is usually about one student and one subject. In Al Mushrif it is more often about a household: three children, two boards, four subjects, and one evening a week the family is willing to give up. Scheduling is a real part of the problem rather than an afterthought, and so is consistency of approach between siblings who compare notes at dinner. A plan that works for the eldest and is then stretched to cover the younger two usually fails for both of them.

The academic pressure points are also predictable here, and they are transitions rather than subjects. Children who stay in one school for a decade meet three reliable dips: the move from primary into secondary, where a single class teacher becomes eight subject teachers; the move into the IGCSE years, where coursework-free terminal assessment arrives with command terms nobody has explained; and the move into the Diploma or a sixth form, where independent work becomes most of the grade. Each of those dips is read at home as a loss of effort, and each of them is structural.

There is a fourth transition that this district sees disproportionately, which is the arrival of a cousin or a relative's child from another system entirely. Extended families in Al Mushrif frequently host a student partway through CBSE, an American high school or a national curriculum, who then joins a British or IB school mid-phase. That gap is specific, measurable and closable, and it responds badly to general tutoring and well to a mapped plan. The student is almost never behind in ability; they are behind in a named list of skills the new course assumed and the old one did not teach.

This page is built around those transitions. There are tables mapping curriculum gaps subject by subject, setting out what changes at each phase boundary, placing tutoring cost beside published school-fee figures, listing which authority regulates schools in each emirate for families who may move within the UAE, and comparing post-IGCSE routes. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi, because home visits are a service we run only in India.

abu-dhabi/al-mushrif.programmesIntro: Four programme phases appear in Al Mushrif households simultaneously more often than they do elsewhere, so the notes below are written as a sequence rather than as alternatives.

programmes.name: IB Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led learning organised around transdisciplinary themes, with no external examinations and descriptive rather than graded reporting. The Grade 5 or 6 Exhibition is the first substantial independent project most children attempt. Specific gaps in number fluency or written structure can sit unnoticed behind generally positive reporting.
programmes.countryNote: In an Al Mushrif household the useful PYP question is comparative: a parent with an older child in secondary can usually see whether the younger one has the arithmetic fluency and writing stamina the next phase will demand. Acting on that in Grade 5 is far cheaper than acting on it in Year 8.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups, each marked against four criteria from 0 to 8. Reports show criterion letters rather than percentages, so a student can be consistently losing marks on one criterion across several subjects without that pattern ever being named at home. There is no terminal exam unless the school enters eAssessment.
programmes.countryNote: The transferable skill worth building here is reading a criterion descriptor and working out what a task is marked on. Students who learn that in MYP 4 arrive in the Diploma able to interpret an assessment brief, which is the single cheapest advantage available in the whole programme.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Two-year courses assessed by terminal papers, tiered in many Cambridge subjects as Core and Extended and in Pearson subjects as Foundation and Higher. Codes decide what a tutor needs: 0580 Mathematics, 0625 Physics, 0620 Chemistry, 0610 Biology for Cambridge, 4MA1 and 4PH1 for Pearson.
programmes.countryNote: The transition into Year 10 is where Al Mushrif households most often ask for help, and it is rarely about content. What changes is the arrival of command terms with specific mark values, and the expectation that a student writes to a mark allocation rather than writing everything they know.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS, which together carry up to three additional points. Internally assessed work is worth a fifth to a quarter of each subject grade and is produced largely outside taught time.
programmes.countryNote: For a student moving up inside the same Al Mushrif school, the shock is the volume of independent work rather than the difficulty of the content. A student who coped comfortably at IGCSE by revising thoroughly can struggle in DP1 simply because nobody is setting the deadlines they need.

abu-dhabi/al-mushrif.subjectsIntro: This selection reflects what an Al Mushrif household typically needs across several children at once, with the transition point at which each subject tends to go wrong.

subjects.name: Mathematics (lower secondary)
subjects.description: The phase where arithmetic fluency either becomes automatic or quietly stops developing. Students who still count on fingers for times tables in Year 8 are not weak at mathematics; they are carrying a load that makes algebra feel impossible. Fixing it here costs weeks and later costs terms.

subjects.name: Mathematics (IGCSE)
subjects.description: The tier decision caps the grade, and it is usually made on Year 10 mock evidence. Extended adds functions, vectors and harder trigonometry. The silent weakness across this district is non-calculator arithmetic, which only surfaces when a paper forbids the device.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Assumes algebraic fluency from the first lesson, which is why the IGCSE-to-Diploma gap in this subject is the widest of any. Higher Level adds Paper 3, an extended problem-solving paper worth a fifth of the grade that supplies no method at all.

subjects.name: English (lower secondary to IGCSE)
subjects.description: Reading comprehension carries primary; purpose, audience and structure carry IGCSE. Students who were praised for descriptive writing in Year 8 often underperform in Year 10 because the marks moved to analysis. Reading the mark allocation before writing is the habit that closes the gap.

subjects.name: Combined and Coordinated Sciences
subjects.description: The route many schools use for students not taking three separate sciences. Content is broad and shallow, which suits some students and frustrates others, and the decision between this and three separate sciences is a real one that affects sixth-form options.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL · Cambridge 0625 · Pearson 4PH1
subjects.description: The transition subject that exposes mathematical gaps fastest. A Year 10 student who cannot rearrange an equation confidently will appear to struggle with physics when the problem is algebra. Electricity remains the universal difficulty at every level and in every board.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Mole calculations are the gatekeeper at IGCSE and energetics and organic mechanisms at Diploma level. Students arriving from another system often have strong descriptive chemistry and no calculation practice, which is a four-week gap rather than a two-year one.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Penalised for imprecise language rather than for ignorance. Answers that describe movement without naming the gradient, the membrane or the transport protein lose marks the student believes they earned. Diagram labelling carries more weight than students expect.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language
subjects.description: A mandatory subject taught in separate classes from the additional-language stream, with Standard Arabic as the language of instruction. For long-established Al Mushrif households this is a core academic subject rather than an add-on, and the written register is where marks go, not comprehension.

subjects.name: UAE Social Studies and Moral Education
subjects.description: Mandatory alongside the licensed international curriculum, with the language of instruction set by whether a student is in the Arab or non-Arab group. Tutoring here has to work from the school's own approved material, because additional content without Ministry permission is not allowed.

abu-dhabi/al-mushrif.regionsIntro: Al Mushrif is inland and central, which makes most of the island reachable. These notes describe each neighbouring district in terms of what it adds or costs for a household here.

regions.name: Al Bateen
regions.note: North-west across Khaleej Al Arabi Street, a more bilingual and waterfront-facing district. Several Al Mushrif families use its schools, and the run is one of the shortest on the island, usually under fifteen minutes even at pick-up.

regions.name: Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: North of Al Mushrif, dense with apartment towers and tuition centres along Zayed the First Street. Families here compare centre group classes against one-to-one tuition more often than elsewhere, and Al Mushrif households are frequently making the same comparison.

regions.name: Al Nahyan
regions.note: North-east, a central island district with a long-established Arabic-speaking population and a dense school mix. Requests for Arabic as a first language come heavily from this corridor and from Al Mushrif itself, often for the same year groups.

regions.name: Al Karamah
regions.note: Immediately east along the Airport Road corridor. The two districts share school bus routes and traffic patterns, so lesson timings are effectively interchangeable and siblings at different schools can still be stacked into one evening.

regions.name: Al Mushrif's southern edge towards Zayed Sports City
regions.note: Across the Airport Road corridor, where sports commitments shape the week as much as school does. Households with a child in a competitive training programme usually need one fixed late slot rather than flexible timing.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Across the island to the north-east, with The British International School Abu Dhabi and Repton Abu Dhabi. For Al Mushrif that is a twenty-five to thirty-five minute afternoon run, which pushes lesson slots for those students to 17:30 or later.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Off-island to the east over the bridges, with several British and American schools. A minority of Al Mushrif families commute out there, and those households are the ones for whom stacking siblings into a single evening makes the largest difference.

schoolClusters.city: Schools inside or adjacent to Al Mushrif
schoolClusters.note: These are the campuses reachable in fifteen minutes or less from most Al Mushrif addresses, covering British and IB provision across the full age range. Because households here often have children in two different phases at the same school, the useful conversation with a tutor spans phases rather than one year group.

modes.title: Stacked sibling evening
modes.description: Consecutive one-to-one slots on a single evening, one child per slot, each with the tutor matched to their own subject and phase.
