sections.heading: Who lives in Al Mushrif, and what that means for a tutoring plan
paragraphs: The direct answer: Al Mushrif households are long-tenured, often large, and usually need support across more than one phase at the same time. The planning question here is not which tutor is best for one child, but how a household with three or four students buys teaching without giving up four evenings a week.

The district's character explains it. This is settled inland Abu Dhabi, built as family housing and still used that way, with a mix of Emirati family compounds and expatriate households that have been in the emirate for a decade or more. Children frequently complete their entire schooling at one institution, which produces a different relationship with the school than a two-year posting does.

Two practical consequences follow. The first is that parents here have seen a phase transition before, usually with an older child, and can often predict the next one accurately. That makes them unusually good at describing the problem, which shortens matching. The second is that siblings compare. A tutor who works well with the eldest sets an expectation, and inconsistency between siblings' experiences is noticed.

The third consequence is scheduling, and it is the one that decides whether tutoring survives past a month. Stacking sessions into one evening, one child per slot, is the arrangement that holds in this district. Spreading four children's lessons across four nights looks flexible on paper and collapses in week three, because the household has run out of evenings.
bullets: Support is usually needed in two or three phases simultaneously
Parents here often predict the next transition accurately from an older child
Siblings compare, so consistency of approach matters
One stacked evening survives; four spread evenings do not

sections.heading: The curriculum transition map, subject by subject
paragraphs: This is the table nobody publishes, and it is the one Al Mushrif households need most, because mid-phase arrivals from other systems are common in extended families here. A transition is not a general disadvantage. It is a specific list of topics and skills the new course assumes and the old one did not teach, and that list is short enough to write down.

The widest gaps are rarely where parents expect. A student arriving from a system with strong computational mathematics usually has more algebraic fluency than their new classmates and less practice in written explanation, so they lose marks on method and communication rather than on calculation. A student arriving from a system with heavy written coursework has the opposite profile.

The gaps that genuinely take time are the dependency chains. Algebraic rearrangement underlies physics; mole calculation underlies most of quantitative chemistry; the ability to read a command term underlies every written paper in both boards. Teach those in order and the subject-specific content follows quickly. Teach the content first and the same lesson has to be repeated.

The week counts in the table are indicative ranges based on one or two sessions a week with work completed between them, and they assume the gap is diagnosed rather than guessed. The point of the table is to convert a vague worry about being behind into a list with an end date, which is a far easier thing for a student to carry.

sections.heading: What actually changes at each phase boundary inside one school
paragraphs: Children who stay at one school for a decade still meet three distinct cliff edges, and the dip that follows each one is usually read as a motivation problem when it is a structural one. Naming the structure is the first useful intervention, because a student who understands what changed stops concluding that they have become worse at school.

The move from primary into secondary replaces one adult who knew the child with eight subject specialists who do not yet. Homework arrives from several directions with no coordinating hand, and the organisational load jumps before any academic demand does. Many Year 7 dips are entirely administrative, and they respond to a system rather than to teaching.

The move into Year 10 introduces terminal assessment and, with it, command terms that carry specific mark values. A student who has been rewarded for writing everything they know now loses marks for it. This is the transition where parents in this district most often seek help, and it is also the fastest to fix, because command-term technique is a fortnight of marked questions rather than a year of content.

The move into the Diploma or a sixth form shifts most of the grade into work nobody sets a weekly deadline for. The content difficulty rises, but the thing that breaks is scheduling. A student who coped at IGCSE by revising thoroughly the week before an exam has no method for a project that is due in four months, and that is a planning skill, not an academic one.

sections.heading: Tutoring cost beside school fees: the context nobody provides
paragraphs: A household with three children in private school is already spending a substantial amount on education, and a tutoring decision is made against that backdrop rather than in isolation. Very few pages in this market give a family any way to place a tutoring quote in that context, so this one does, using published figures and attributing each.

On scale, the published Dubai figures give a sense of the sector a UAE family is buying into: 387,441 students across 227 private schools in 2024-25, offering seventeen different curricula, with the UK curriculum at thirty-seven per cent of the total enrolment, Indian at twenty-six, US at fourteen and the International Baccalaureate at seven. KHDA also confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees in Dubai for the 2026-27 academic year, under the emirate's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion. Abu Dhabi families should check ADEK's own published fee framework rather than assuming the same position.

On tutoring, published market figures run from roughly AED 45 to 65 an hour at the budget online end and AED 33 to 52 from one platform's entry tier, AED 150 for IGCSE and AED 200 for IB from an agency that publishes its rates, AED 270 from a UK-based agency, a survey band of AED 200 to 450 and above for specialist exam-year work, and AED 650 at the premium named end. In-home visits in the emirate are published between AED 180 and AED 500 with travel inside the rate.

Monthly comparisons are more useful than hourly ones for a large household. Published market packages include around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions, and a published 2026 survey put weekly one-hour tuition at roughly AED 240 to 600 a month at budget level, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support. None of these are IB Gram's prices; they are the market, cited so a quote can be judged.

sections.heading: Siblings on different boards in one household
paragraphs: It is normal in Al Mushrif for one child to be sitting Cambridge papers, another to be in the MYP, and a third to be in upper primary. Parents reasonably assume a single tutor could cover two of them. Sometimes that is true and often it is not, and the deciding factor is the board and the phase rather than the subject.

A tutor who teaches Cambridge 0580 Mathematics well can usually also teach lower-secondary mathematics competently, because the content is a subset. The reverse is not true. A tutor comfortable with Year 8 mathematics is not automatically ready for Extended tier questions or for Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, which assumes fluency the lower phases do not build.

Across boards the picture is sharper. Cambridge and Pearson International GCSE cover similar content and assess it through differently shaped papers with different mark-scheme phrasing, so a single tutor covering one child on each board has to hold both specifications in mind. That is possible and it should be asked about explicitly rather than assumed.

The practical arrangement that works is one tutor per child, matched to that child's phase and board, with the sessions stacked consecutively on one evening. The coordination is on timing only. Each child gets their own written note, which also prevents the comparison problem, because progress is reported individually rather than as a household average.

One exception is worth making. Where two children sit the same board and the same subject one year apart, a single tutor is genuinely efficient, because the specification and the mark-scheme habits carry straight over. Ask for that deliberately rather than assuming it.

sections.heading: Which authority regulates schools in each emirate
paragraphs: Families in Al Mushrif who have been in the UAE for years frequently consider a move between emirates, and the regulator changes with the address. That matters because inspection reports, fee frameworks and curriculum approvals sit with the emirate's own authority rather than with one national body.

The map is complete and published. Abu Dhabi and Al Ain fall under the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. Dubai falls under the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education there. Sharjah's private schools are regulated by the Sharjah Private Education Authority, and Ras Al Khaimah's by its Department of Knowledge.

The Ministry of Education plays the supervisory role for private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. It is also worth knowing that in Sharjah and Ras Al Khaimah the authorities approve tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods, so curriculum and fee approval, not just inspection, sits with the emirate regulator.

The federal baseline underneath all of it is that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That is the rule behind every emirate's mandatory-subject requirement, and it is why those subjects appear on a British or IB timetable in every emirate regardless of which authority inspects the school.

sections.heading: After IGCSE: the sixth-form decision an Al Mushrif household faces repeatedly
paragraphs: Because households here are long-tenured, the post-IGCSE decision comes round every few years with a different child, and the answer is not the same each time. The routes differ in breadth, in how the grade is produced, and in what they ask of a student who is organised or disorganised.

The Diploma is broad and prescriptive: six subjects across groups, three at Higher Level, plus a core carrying up to three points. It suits a student who is reasonably strong across the board and can manage long-run independent work. It punishes narrow strength, because a weak sixth subject still counts, and it punishes poor scheduling hardest of all.

A linear A Level programme is narrow and deep, typically three subjects, with most of the grade from terminal papers. It suits a student with clear strengths and a specific degree target, and it can rescue a candidate whose IGCSE profile is uneven, because the weak subjects simply stop. The trade is loss of breadth, which matters for some university systems and for MoE equivalency planning.

Whichever route is chosen, check the equivalency and admissions implications before the subject grid is signed. The published British-track equivalency requirement is five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3, excluding Arabic and Islamic education, plus one Advanced Level at E or two Advanced Subsidiary Levels at the same grade. Confirm current requirements on moe.gov.ae, and note that IB Gram neither performs nor guarantees any part of that process.

sections.heading: A tutor visiting an Al Mushrif villa, compared with online delivery
paragraphs: The fair version of this comparison for a large household is not about one lesson. It is about four. An in-home tutor serves one child per visit, and a household with three or four students needing different subjects at different phases would be scheduling several visits a week, each with its own travel window.

Al Mushrif is central and the roads are short, so travel time itself is not the main objection here. The objection is arithmetic. Four children at four different phases means four specialists, and the number of people prepared to drive to a specific villa compound at a specific hour, four times a week, who also happen to teach the right phase and board, is small.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE, and does not run a centre in the emirate. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, which is why stacking is possible: three consecutive slots on one evening involve three different specialists and no journeys at all. The household gives up one night instead of four.

In-home provision still has a real advantage, and it is worth stating on a page recommending something else. A child in the early primary years often concentrates better with an adult physically present, and a parent who wants to overhear a lesson can do so. For a Year 10 or Diploma student losing marks on a specific component, the quality of the subject match matters far more than the room.

sections.heading: What a tutor may and may not do with assessed work
paragraphs: Every household that reaches the Diploma meets this question, and in a district where siblings follow each other through the same school it is worth settling once rather than three times. Assessed work belongs to the student. That applies to an Internal Assessment, an Extended Essay, a Theory of Knowledge essay and an MYP personal project alike.

A tutor's legitimate role is substantial. Explain how each criterion is awarded and what the mark allocation rewards. Ask the questions a supervisor asks about scope, method and evidence. Teach the referencing convention. Read a draft the student has already written and say precisely why a section will not score. All of that moves marks and none of it involves supplying material for a submission.

What a tutor must not do is provide text, data or analysis that enters assessed work. One researched competitor in this market sells finished Internal Assessments outright. The consequence of using such a service falls on the student, because a malpractice finding can cost a diploma rather than a grade, and no provider carries that risk afterwards.

Board material is the related question. Syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables belong to the boards that publish them, and the correct route is through the school, which holds authorised access, with the official source cited. IB Gram does not host or distribute board documents, and a provider advertising a library of them is telling you how it operates.

process.title: Map the household before booking anything
process.description: List every child, their year group, their board and the subject in question. A household plan is quicker to match than four separate enquiries, and it lets the slots be arranged consecutively on one evening from the start rather than retrofitted after the first month falls apart.

process.title: Diagnose against the target course, not the previous one
process.description: For a transition, the diagnostic has to use material from the course the student is moving into. Testing a new arrival on what they already studied measures the old system. Testing them on the first unit of the new one produces the list of named gaps that a plan can be built from.

process.title: Ask for the gap list in writing, with a week count
process.description: A transition block should begin with a written list of specific gaps and an estimated number of weeks to close them. That converts a vague worry into something with an end date, which students carry far better, and it gives the family something to measure the block against.

process.title: Fix one evening and protect it
process.description: Choose the single evening the household can genuinely give up and stack the sessions consecutively. Protect it against everything except illness. Households that keep one fixed night sustain tutoring for terms; households that reschedule weekly stop within a month.

process.title: Re-test at the end of the block
process.description: A transition block should end with the same diagnostic material it started with, so the gap closure is visible rather than asserted. If the re-test shows the gap is still open, that is useful information about the match, and it is better learned in week eight than in May.

whyPoints.title: One tutor per child, one evening per household
whyPoints.description: Each student is matched to their own phase and board, and the sessions run consecutively on a single night. Four children do not need four evenings, and the arrangement that respects that is the one families here actually keep.

whyPoints.title: Transitions treated as a named list, not a general lag
whyPoints.description: A curriculum or phase change produces a specific list of gaps with a dependency order and an estimated week count. That is a plan a student can finish, which is different from an open-ended arrangement that nobody can tell is working.

whyPoints.title: Progress reported per child
whyPoints.description: Each student gets their own written note after each session. In households where siblings compare, individual reporting avoids the comparison problem and gives each child credit for their own work rather than a household average.

whyPoints.title: Cost placed next to published figures
whyPoints.description: Market rate bands and published school-sector figures are set out with their sources so a household can judge a quote in context. No IB Gram price list is invented, and no figure is presented as ours when it belongs to the market.

whyPoints.title: Regulators explained, not claimed
whyPoints.description: The emirate regulator map and the mandatory-subject rules are quoted from published sources because long-tenured families need them. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation or licence from ADEK, KHDA, SPEA, MoHRE, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover two of my children in Al Mushrif?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and the deciding factor is phase and board rather than subject. A tutor who teaches Cambridge 0580 Extended Mathematics can usually also teach lower-secondary mathematics well, because the content is a subset. The reverse is unreliable: a Year 8 specialist is not automatically ready for Extended tier questions or Higher Level Analysis and Approaches. Across different boards, one tutor has to hold two specifications in mind, which is possible but should be asked about directly. The arrangement that works best is one tutor per child with consecutive slots on one evening.

faqs.question: How do we schedule tutoring for four children without losing every evening?
faqs.answer: Stack the sessions. Consecutive one-to-one slots on a single night, one child per slot, with a different tutor matched to each child's phase and board. A typical pattern is 16:30, 17:45 and 19:00 Gulf Standard Time. The household gives up one evening rather than four, and each child still gets an individual session and their own written note. Spreading lessons across four nights looks flexible and reliably collapses by the third week, because an Al Mushrif household has other commitments on those nights too.

faqs.question: My nephew is joining a British school here from CBSE. What is the actual gap?
faqs.answer: Usually not content. Students arriving from CBSE often have stronger computational mathematics than their new classmates and much less practice in written explanation, so marks are lost on method, command terms and mark allocation rather than on the subject. The closable list is specific: reading a command term and answering only what it asks, writing to the number of marks available, and sitting a full paper to time. Expect roughly ten to fourteen weeks of one or two sessions a week with work completed in between, starting with one subject and transferring the technique.

faqs.question: Why does my child dip in Year 7 after a strong primary record?
faqs.answer: Because the structure changed, not the child. One class teacher who knew them well is replaced by eight subject specialists who do not, and homework arrives from several directions with no coordinating hand. The organisational load rises before any academic demand does, which is why many Year 7 dips are entirely administrative. The effective response is a written weekly system the child maintains themselves, reviewed rather than managed by a parent. Teaching content at this point often misses the actual problem.

faqs.question: What changes between Year 9 and Year 10 that catches students out?
faqs.answer: Terminal assessment arrives, and with it command terms that carry specific mark values. A student previously rewarded for writing everything they know now loses marks for doing exactly that, because a question asking them to explain one factor awards nothing for the other three. This is the transition Al Mushrif households ask about most and also the quickest to fix: roughly two weeks of marked exam questions in one subject, with the reason written next to each lost mark, usually transfers to the others with much less input.

faqs.question: Why do strong IGCSE students struggle in the first term of the Diploma?
faqs.answer: Because most of the grade moves into work nobody sets a weekly deadline for. Internally assessed components carry a fifth to a quarter of each subject, the Extended Essay runs across two terms, and the Theory of Knowledge essay has a word limit but no homework diary entry. A student who coped at IGCSE by revising hard the week before an exam has no method for a project due in four months. That is a scheduling skill rather than an academic one, and it is teachable in a few sessions.

faqs.question: How wide is the gap between IGCSE Mathematics and Higher Level Analysis and Approaches?
faqs.answer: It is the widest transition gap in the Diploma. Analysis and Approaches assumes fluent algebraic manipulation from the first lesson and adds proof technique, which most IGCSE courses barely touch. Higher Level also carries Paper 3, an extended problem-solving paper worth a fifth of the grade that supplies no method. Expect eight to twelve weeks of bridging work over the summer or the first term, concentrated on manipulation at speed and on proof, before subject content support becomes the right use of a session.

faqs.question: How should we judge a tutoring quote against what we already pay in school fees?
faqs.answer: Compare monthly rather than hourly. Published market figures put weekly one-hour tuition at roughly AED 240 to 600 a month at budget level, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support, with package examples around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions. Those are market figures from a published 2026 survey and from providers' own pages, not an IB Gram price list. For a multi-child household, the number that matters is the household monthly total against a defined end point for each block.

faqs.question: Did school fees change in the UAE for 2026-27?
faqs.answer: In Dubai, KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees for the 2026-27 academic year, under the emirate's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion. That is a Dubai measure and should not be assumed to apply elsewhere. Abu Dhabi private schools are licensed and overseen by the Department of Education and Knowledge, so Al Mushrif families should check ADEK's own published fee framework and their school's communications rather than relying on a Dubai announcement.

faqs.question: Which authority would regulate our school if we moved to another emirate?
faqs.answer: It changes with the address. Abu Dhabi and Al Ain fall under the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises licensing and accreditation of private schools. Dubai falls under the Knowledge and Human Development Authority. Sharjah is regulated by the Sharjah Private Education Authority and Ras Al Khaimah by its Department of Knowledge, both of which also approve tuition fees, curricula, courses and assessment methods. The Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. Inspection reports sit with the emirate authority, not with one national body.

faqs.question: Should our next child take the Diploma or A Levels after IGCSE?
faqs.answer: It depends on the profile rather than on which is harder. The Diploma is broad and prescriptive, six subjects with three at Higher Level plus a core worth up to three points, and it suits a student who is strong across the board and can self-schedule. A linear A Level programme is narrow and deep, usually three subjects assessed mostly by terminal papers, and it can suit a student with clear strengths and an uneven IGCSE profile. Check the equivalency and admissions consequences before the grid is signed.

faqs.question: What does UAE equivalency require if we choose the A Level route?
faqs.answer: The published British-track requirement is proof of one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, together with five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five. Confirm the current requirements on moe.gov.ae or with the emirate's attestation authority. IB Gram neither performs nor guarantees any part of the equivalency process and does not publish an unverified IB points figure.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send tutors to villas in Al Mushrif?
faqs.answer: No. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, and IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; that service runs only in India. For a household with several children the arithmetic is the real point: an in-home tutor serves one child per visit, so four students at four phases would mean several visits a week, each needing a specialist willing to travel at that hour. Online delivery allows three consecutive slots with three different specialists on one evening, with published in-home market rates of AED 180 to 500 an hour for comparison.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with an MYP personal project or a Diploma Internal Assessment?
faqs.answer: Within a clear boundary, yes. A tutor explains how each criterion is awarded and what the mark allocation rewards, asks the questions a supervisor asks about scope, method and evidence, teaches the referencing convention, and gives honest feedback on a draft the student has already written. A tutor supplies no text, data or analysis that enters assessed work. The protection is timing: a project planned across months has room for a failed method, while the same work compressed into a fortnight is where academic honesty gets tested.

faqs.question: How do we know whether a transition block is actually working?
faqs.answer: Ask for the gap list and the re-test. A transition block should start with a written list of named gaps, in dependency order, with an estimated number of weeks for each, and end with the same diagnostic material it began with so closure is visible rather than asserted. Review at four sessions to judge the match and at the end of the block to judge the outcome. If the re-test shows the gap is still open, that is useful information, and week eight is a much better time to learn it than May.

abu-dhabi/al-mushrif.closingBody: The useful first message from an Al Mushrif family lists every child, their year group, their board and the problem, along with the one evening the household can genuinely protect. abu-dhabi/al-nahyan.tutorsIntro: The profiles below separate subject teaching from core support, because they are different jobs. A tutor who teaches Chemistry Higher Level well is not automatically the right person to help a student structure an argument about knowledge, and the two requests should be matched separately.

intro.heading: The part of the Diploma that has no lesson on the timetable
paragraphs: Al Nahyan is a dense central district on Abu Dhabi island, running inland from the Airport Road corridor, with a long-settled population and a cluster of schools close enough that children from the same building often attend three different ones. Families here are typically well informed about school choice. The thing they most often have not been told about is the Diploma core, which carries real points and almost no teaching.

Every Diploma candidate has to complete three things that sit outside subject teaching. Theory of Knowledge, which has some timetabled discussion but no body of content to revise. An Extended Essay of up to four thousand words, supervised rather than taught. And CAS, which is not graded at all and can still prevent a diploma being awarded if it is not completed and documented. Between them, the first two carry up to three points, awarded on the combination of the two grades.

Those three points are not decoration. At the margins of a university offer, three points is the difference between a conditional met and a conditional missed, and the core is also where a diploma most often fails outright, because an unacceptably low grade in either of the first two components is a failing condition regardless of how strong the six subject grades are. Parents discover that fact at different points, and the earlier the better.

Despite that, the core is the least supported part of the programme in almost every school, and not through negligence. There is no syllabus to teach, and no textbook a parent can buy to help. A supervisor meets a student a handful of times across two terms, and the number is usually stated in advance. The work in between, choosing a question, reading, structuring an argument and writing to a word limit, is independent work by design. For a self-organised student that is a fair design. For most seventeen-year-olds it is a project with no scaffolding, due at the same time as six subjects' worth of internally assessed work.

This page is about that gap specifically. There are tables on what each core component demands and who is responsible for it, on the division between a supervisor's role and a tutor's, on the Theory of Knowledge components and their limits, on the academic-honesty boundary in practical detail, on what a student should have completed by each term, and on the language demands the core places on a student writing at length in a second language. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, and IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi, since home visits are a service we run only in India. For review work on a document that suits the format well.

abu-dhabi/al-nahyan.programmesIntro: Three routes appear in Al Nahyan enquiries. The core described on this page belongs to the Diploma, but the habits it demands are built earlier, which is why the MYP and IGCSE notes matter here too.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus the three core components. Subject grades run 1 to 7 and the core adds up to three further points. Internally assessed work inside each subject carries a fifth to a quarter of that subject's grade, so the total amount of independently produced work across a Diploma is substantial.
programmes.countryNote: Al Nahyan Diploma candidates attend a spread of schools across the island and across the bridges, each with its own internal deadline calendar for the core. Ask the coordinator for that calendar in writing: the school's internal date for an Extended Essay draft is often months ahead of anything the board publishes.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups, each assessed against four criteria from 0 to 8, culminating in the MYP 5 personal project. That project is the first long-run independent piece most students attempt and the clearest predictor of how they will handle the Diploma core two years later.
programmes.countryNote: The personal project is worth treating seriously for that reason rather than for its own mark. A student who has learned to plan a long project, keep a process journal and meet an interim deadline in MYP 5 arrives in DP1 with the one skill the core most depends on, and it cannot be taught in a fortnight.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Terminal papers at the end of two years, tiered in many subjects, with codes that decide the match: 0580, 0625, 0620 and 0610 for Cambridge, 4MA1 and 4PH1 for Pearson. Most subjects now have no coursework at all, which is part of why the Diploma core comes as a surprise.
programmes.countryNote: An IGCSE student who has never produced an extended piece of independent writing is the student who struggles most with the Diploma core. Where a school offers any extended project route in Year 11, taking it is worth more to an Al Nahyan family than an additional subject grade.

abu-dhabi/al-nahyan.subjectsIntro: This selection is weighted towards the subjects in which Al Nahyan students most often base an Extended Essay or an Internal Assessment, with a note on what that component specifically demands.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: A popular Extended Essay subject and a demanding one, because the essay must argue rather than narrate and must evaluate the origin, purpose and content of its sources. The Internal Assessment is capped at two thousand two hundred words with fifteen of its twenty-five marks in the investigation itself.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Three Internal Assessment commentaries at eight hundred words each, built on real news articles, with explicit marks for diagram accuracy and for the use of a key concept. A frequent Extended Essay choice where students underestimate how much data access the question will require.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The scientific investigation carries twenty-four marks across research design, data analysis, conclusion and evaluation. As an Extended Essay subject it demands either genuine experimental access or a defensible database approach, and the choice between those should be made in the first fortnight.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Energetics and organic mechanisms carry the written papers. For the investigation, the data-analysis criterion rewards honest uncertainty treatment, which costs planning rather than equipment. An ambitious experiment with no quantifiable outcome scores worse than a modest one with clean data.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 unseen analysis, Paper 2 comparative essay, and the individual oral built on a global issue. Higher Level adds an essay of one thousand two hundred to one thousand five hundred words on a studied text, which is useful practice for the sustained argument the core demands.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: The right entry for students whose stronger academic language is Arabic or another first language. The course assesses conceptual understanding of text type, audience and purpose as much as accuracy, and students coached only on grammar underperform on the writing tasks.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The exploration is marked out of twenty, with six of those marks for the use of mathematics, which is why a beautifully presented exploration built on thin mathematics underperforms. Higher Level adds Paper 3, worth a fifth of the grade and supplying no method.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics, with the same exploration weighting. A common and sensible Extended Essay base because data is accessible, provided the question commits to a real analysis rather than to describing a dataset.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: An Internal Assessment capped at two thousand two hundred words based on a replication of a published study. Students lose marks on the treatment of the data and on ethical considerations rather than on the write-up, and ethics approval constraints should be checked before a topic is fixed.

subjects.name: Arabic A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: A literature course taught and assessed in Standard Arabic, significant in a district with a long-established Arabic-speaking population. Marks go on written register and literary terminology rather than on comprehension, and spoken fluency at home is not the same preparation.

abu-dhabi/al-nahyan.regionsIntro: Al Nahyan sits in the middle of the island with schools on several sides, so these notes are about which school communities a family here is likely to be part of and what that implies.

regions.name: Al Karamah
regions.note: Immediately south along the Airport Road corridor, sharing bus routes and traffic patterns. Lesson timings between the two districts are effectively interchangeable, and the same 16:30 and 18:00 windows apply after the afternoon run.

regions.name: Al Mushrif
regions.note: South-west, a settled villa district with long-tenured households. Families there often have several children in different phases, and Al Nahyan households moving into larger housing frequently move there, keeping the same schools and the same tutors.

regions.name: Al Wahda
regions.note: North-east around the Al Wahda interchange, one of the slowest points on the island between 15:00 and 16:00. Al Nahyan families whose school run passes through it should plan for 17:00 rather than 16:30 on weekdays.

regions.name: Al Zahiyah
regions.note: North-east towards the eastern waterfront, dense with older apartment blocks. The two districts share a similar school mix and a similar profile of enquiries, with Al Zahiyah skewing a little more towards IGCSE and Al Nahyan towards the Diploma.

regions.name: Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: West across the island, with a visible concentration of tuition centres. Al Nahyan families comparing a centre class against one-to-one core support should note that the core is not a subject a group class can teach well.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: East across the channel, home to The British International School Abu Dhabi and Repton Abu Dhabi. A twenty to thirty minute afternoon run from Al Nahyan, which puts core sessions for students there at 17:30 or later.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: North-east over the bridge, home to Cranleigh Abu Dhabi. The longest regular run from Al Nahyan, and the group most likely to want a 20:00 slot for Extended Essay work, when the student would be at a desk anyway.

sections.heading: The three core components and who is actually responsible for each
paragraphs: The direct answer: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS are all compulsory, the first two are graded and together award up to three points, and CAS is ungraded but must be completed and documented or the diploma is not awarded. None of them is taught as a subject with a body of content to revise.

Responsibility is distributed in a way that confuses families. The school appoints a Theory of Knowledge teacher, an Extended Essay supervisor and a CAS coordinator, and each has a defined and limited role. A supervisor is not a teacher of the essay's subject matter; the role is to check progress, give a bounded amount of feedback and confirm the work is the student's own. A CAS coordinator checks documentation rather than organises activities.

The consequence is that the student is the project manager, usually for the first time in their life, across two years and three components with interim deadlines set by three different adults. The commonest failure in this district is not a weak essay. It is a student who has not begun, in February of DP1, because nobody set a weekly piece of homework for a task due in November.

The table below sets out the division of labour as it actually works. Use it to ask the right adult the right question, and to notice early where nobody is covering something. A family that knows a supervisor will read one full draft and no more plans very differently from one that assumes continuous feedback.

sections.heading: Supervisor or tutor: who does what on an Extended Essay
paragraphs: This is the question Al Nahyan families ask most often about the core, and the confusion is understandable, because the two roles overlap in appearance and not in substance. The supervisor is appointed by the school, is accountable to the programme, and confirms that the work submitted is the student's own. A tutor has no standing in that process at all.

What a supervisor does is bounded deliberately. The role includes discussing the choice of topic, checking that the research question is viable, meeting the student a small number of times, reading a limited amount of draft work and providing written comment on it, and conducting the reflection conversation at the end. A supervisor is not available for weekly feedback, and most schools state the number of meetings in advance.

What a tutor can legitimately add is the teaching the supervision model does not include: how an argument is built, how a criterion is awarded, how to narrow a question so it can be answered inside four thousand words, how a referencing convention works, and how to read the examiner's comment on a draft and act on it. That is instruction rather than supervision, and none of it displaces the supervisor.

What neither may do is produce the work. The essay is the student's own from the research question onwards, and the integrity declaration at the end is theirs to sign. A tutor who supplies paragraphs is exposing the student to a malpractice finding, which can cost a diploma rather than a grade. The division in the table below is the one worth agreeing in writing before any core support starts.

sections.heading: Theory of Knowledge: an essay and an exhibition, both unlike anything else
paragraphs: Theory of Knowledge defeats capable students for a specific reason: it has no content to learn. A Chemistry student can revise bonding. A Theory of Knowledge student cannot revise anything, because the assessment rewards the quality of an argument about knowledge rather than the recall of material. That is a skill, and it is teachable, but it is not taught by reading more.

There are two assessed pieces. The essay responds to one of a set of prescribed titles and is capped at one thousand six hundred words, marked against a single global descriptor out of ten. The exhibition requires three objects linked to an internal prompt, with a commentary of nine hundred and fifty words in total, which works out at roughly three hundred words per object.

The failure modes are consistent. In the essay, students restate the prescribed title in different words for four hundred words before making a claim, then run out of space for evaluation. They also choose examples from the news rather than from their own subjects, which makes the argument thinner and harder to develop. In the exhibition, they choose objects that illustrate a theme instead of objects that genuinely raise the prompt's question.

The practical fix is small and early. Write two hundred words identifying two or three defensible knowledge claims before writing anything else, and choose examples from the student's own six subjects, where they have real knowledge to draw on. Confirm the current word limits and prompts against the Theory of Knowledge guide through the school's coordinator, because guides are revised and this page does not republish board documents.

sections.heading: CAS: ungraded, and still able to cost a diploma
paragraphs: CAS receives the least attention of the three core components because it carries no grade, and that is exactly why it causes avoidable trouble. It is a completion requirement. A candidate with excellent subject grades and incomplete CAS documentation is a candidate with a problem that no amount of revision solves.

The requirement is about evidence of engagement and reflection over time rather than about hours logged in a spreadsheet, and that is the part students misunderstand. Reflections written in bulk at the end do not demonstrate learning over time, and coordinators recognise them immediately. A short reflection written at the time, honestly, is worth more than a long one written retrospectively.

The second recurring problem is the project. Students frequently complete plenty of activity and never produce the collaborative project element, or produce something that was really an event they attended. Identifying that gap in DP1 is straightforward; identifying it in the final term of DP2 means organising something real while everything else is also due.

The honest scope of outside help here is narrow, and worth stating. A tutor has no role in arranging a student's activities and should not be writing reflections, which are first-person accounts of the student's own experience. What is useful is a review session that checks the documentation against the stated learning outcomes early enough to fix gaps, and that is a single session rather than a programme. Anything longer is either doing the student's reflecting for them or billing for time that produces nothing.

sections.heading: The academic honesty boundary, in practical detail
paragraphs: A page about the Diploma core has to be explicit about this, because the core is precisely where the pressure to outsource is highest. The work is long, independent, unsupervised between meetings, and due at the same time as everything else. One researched competitor in this market sells finished Internal Assessments outright.

The principle is that assessed work must be the student's own, and the consequence of breaching it falls on the student rather than on whoever supplied the help. A malpractice finding can mean a diploma is not awarded, which is a different order of outcome from a lower grade. No provider shares that risk and none of them carries it afterwards.

The boundary is easier to apply than to state in the abstract, which is why the table below works through specific actions. The pattern is consistent: teaching a skill, explaining a criterion, questioning a method and giving feedback on existing work are all legitimate. Supplying content, text, data or structure that enters the submission is not, however it is framed.

The same applies to materials. Syllabus documents, subject guides, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables belong to the boards that publish them, and the right route is through the school, with the official source cited and linked. IB Gram does not host or distribute board documents, and a provider advertising a library of them is telling you something useful about how it operates. The same judgement applies to anyone offering model essays on the prescribed titles.

sections.heading: What a Diploma student should have finished by each term
paragraphs: The core fails on timing far more often than on ability, so the most useful thing on this page may be a calendar rather than an explanation. The dates below are expressed as terms rather than as fixed dates, because every school sets its own internal deadlines and those are the ones that bind.

The principle is to stay a term ahead of the school's own calendar on the heaviest component. A student who treats the school's interim Extended Essay deadline as the start of serious work has already lost the margin that allows a failed approach to be replaced. A student who is a term ahead can change a research question in DP1 without drama.

The second principle is to separate the components in time. The worst outcome, and the common one, is all three core components plus several subject internal assessments landing in one fortnight of DP2. That is avoidable by moving the Extended Essay earlier, because it is the only component with a long enough runway to be shifted.

Ask the coordinator for the school's internal calendar in writing at the start of DP1 and put every date on one page. In a district where children from one building attend several different schools, families with two Diploma candidates frequently discover their deadlines are in different weeks, which is an advantage if it is known and a crisis if it is not. Two candidates sharing one quiet table in the same week is a problem that disappears entirely once the dates are on paper.

sections.heading: Writing at length in a second language across the core
paragraphs: Al Nahyan has a long-established Arabic-speaking population, and a significant number of Diploma candidates here are writing four thousand words of academic English having spoken Arabic at home all their lives. That is a specific, respectable difficulty, and it is not a language-course problem.

The gap is register rather than vocabulary. A student may read academic English comfortably and still write in a conversational register, or over-correct into a dense formality that obscures the argument. Examiners are not marking elegance, but a Theory of Knowledge claim that cannot be identified in the sentence does not score, and that is where second-language writers lose marks disproportionately.

The practical remedies are small and specific. Practise the sentence patterns the core actually needs: stating a claim, introducing evidence, conceding a counter-position, evaluating. Write short pieces to a word limit before attempting a long one, because word-limit discipline in a second language takes practice. And draft in the language of assessment from the start rather than translating later, since translation produces structures that read oddly and cost clarity marks.

It is also worth checking the language pathway itself. A student whose stronger academic language is Arabic may be better placed taking Arabic as a Language A and English as a Language B, which is a decision made in Year 11 or MYP 5, not in DP2. A short written diagnostic in each language settles it faster than any conversation, and it is the one piece of evidence a school will take seriously.

sections.heading: What core support costs, and how long each block should take
paragraphs: Core support is finite work with a defined end, and it should be quoted that way. A Theory of Knowledge essay is one thousand six hundred words. An Extended Essay runs across two terms but needs reviews rather than weekly lessons. Any quote that prices the core as an open-ended weekly commitment is pricing something other than the work.

The figures that follow are market rates in the UAE, drawn from providers' own published pricing and a published 2026 Dubai tutoring rate survey by Bestimate, presented as the market rather than as an IB Gram price list. Published hourly figures run from roughly AED 45 to 65 at the budget online end and AED 33 to 52 from one platform's entry tier, AED 150 for IGCSE and AED 200 for IB from an agency that publishes rates, AED 270 from a UK-based agency, AED 200 to 450 and above for specialist exam-year work, and AED 650 at the premium named end.

In-home visits in the emirate are published between roughly AED 180 and AED 500 with travel inside the hour. Monthly packages seen in the market include around AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions, and the same survey put weekly one-hour tuition at roughly AED 240 to 600 a month at budget level, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support.

The useful question to ask a provider about core work is not the hourly rate but the session count and what each session produces. Spaced reviews are the right shape, because a project needs working time between them. A plan offering twelve consecutive weekly sessions on an Extended Essay is describing supervision the school already provides, or something a student should not be buying.

sections.heading: Why supervision-shaped work suits online delivery
paragraphs: Core support is not a lesson in the usual sense. It is a review of a document, conducted against published criteria, with both people looking at the same text and the same descriptor. That is an activity a shared screen handles at least as well as a kitchen table, and in one respect better, because the annotated version exists afterwards and belongs to the student.

The second reason is matching. Theory of Knowledge is taught well by a relatively small number of people, and an Extended Essay reviewer needs to understand both the criteria and the subject. Restricting that choice to those willing to travel to a particular Al Nahyan address at a particular hour narrows a small pool for no academic benefit.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE, and does not operate a centre in the emirate. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video. For spaced reviews across two terms this also removes the main practical friction, because a review can be moved by a day without anybody wasting a journey.

In-home provision still has a genuine advantage for younger children who concentrate better with an adult present, and for families who want to overhear a lesson. Neither of those describes a seventeen-year-old reviewing an essay draft against a criterion descriptor, which is the work this page is about. For that student the useful question is who understands the criteria best, not who lives nearest.

process.title: Ask the coordinator for the internal calendar in writing
process.description: Every school sets its own interim deadlines for the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge and CAS, and those are the dates that bind. Get them in writing at the start of DP1 and put all of them on one page. Families with two Diploma candidates at different schools frequently find the dates fall in different weeks.

process.title: Settle the Extended Essay subject before the question
process.description: The subject determines which criteria apply and what counts as evidence, so it comes first. A question that would be strong in History can be unanswerable in Biology for want of data access. Decide the subject in DP1 term one, then narrow the question against what the criteria actually reward.

process.title: Read the criteria before writing anything
process.description: The Extended Essay carries thirty-four marks with twelve of them for critical thinking, and the Theory of Knowledge essay is marked against a single descriptor out of ten. Those allocations should shape the plan. Confirm the current figures through the school's coordinator, because subject guides are revised on a cycle.

process.title: Agree the honesty boundary in writing first
process.description: Before any core support begins, state what the tutor will and will not do: criteria explained, methods questioned, feedback on existing drafts, and no content supplied for submission. It protects the student, who is the person a malpractice finding falls on, and it sets expectations on both sides.

process.title: Book reviews, not weekly lessons
process.description: Core work needs working time between contacts, so space the sessions to the school's interim deadlines rather than booking a standing weekly slot. Four to six reviews across two terms is the usual shape for an Extended Essay. A twelve-week consecutive block is a sign something other than the work is being priced.

whyPoints.title: The core treated as three jobs, not one
whyPoints.description: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS have different demands, different adults responsible and different failure modes. Treating them separately, with their own blocks and their own deadlines, is what prevents all three landing in the same fortnight of DP2.

whyPoints.title: The supervisor's role is respected, not duplicated
whyPoints.description: A school supervisor confirms the work is the student's own and provides bounded feedback. Core support adds the teaching that model does not include and stays out of the process the programme owns, which is stated in writing before any session.

whyPoints.title: Spaced reviews instead of a standing weekly slot
whyPoints.description: A project needs working time between contacts. Sessions are timed to the school's own interim deadlines, with a defined session count, so a family can judge the cost against the work rather than against a calendar.

whyPoints.title: Second-language writing treated as a technical skill
whyPoints.description: In a district with a long-established Arabic-speaking population, a student writing four thousand words in English needs register and sentence-pattern work, not a language course. That is specific, teachable and usually overlooked entirely.

whyPoints.title: The honesty line drawn action by action
whyPoints.description: This page states, item by item, what a tutor may and may not do with core work, because the core is where the pressure is highest. Board guides and papers are cited and linked through the school rather than hosted or distributed.

faqs.question: What exactly is the Diploma core, and why does it cause so much trouble in Al Nahyan?
faqs.answer: It is three compulsory components outside subject teaching: Theory of Knowledge, an Extended Essay of up to four thousand words, and CAS. The first two are graded and together award up to three points, and a very low grade in either is a failing condition for the whole diploma. CAS carries no grade and can still prevent a diploma being awarded if it is not completed and documented. It causes trouble because there is no syllabus to teach, so almost all the work happens in a student's own time with a supervisor meeting them only a handful of times.

faqs.question: How many points can Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay add?
faqs.answer: Up to three between them, awarded on the combination of the two grades. At the margin of a university offer three points is the difference between meeting a conditional and missing it, so the core is worth more attention than it usually receives. More importantly, a very low grade in either component is a failing condition regardless of how strong the six subject grades are. Confirm the current points matrix and failing conditions with your school's IB coordinator, because this page does not republish board documents.

faqs.question: What is an Extended Essay supervisor actually responsible for?
faqs.answer: A defined and deliberately limited role. The supervisor discusses the choice of topic, checks the research question is viable, meets the student a small number of times, reads a limited amount of draft work and comments on it in writing, and conducts the reflection conversation at the end. The supervisor also confirms that the work submitted is the student's own, which is the part no outside help can take over. Most schools state the number of meetings in advance. A supervisor is not a source of weekly feedback, and families who assume otherwise plan the two terms badly.

faqs.question: What can a tutor legitimately add on top of school supervision?
faqs.answer: The teaching that supervision does not include. How a sustained argument is built. How each criterion is awarded and what the mark allocation rewards. How to narrow a question so it can be answered inside four thousand words. How a referencing convention works. How to read a supervisor's comment on a section and act on it. All of that is instruction on skills the student then applies to their own work. None of it involves supplying text, data, structure or analysis that enters the submission.

faqs.question: Why do capable students struggle with Theory of Knowledge?
faqs.answer: Because there is nothing to revise. A student can prepare Chemistry by learning bonding; Theory of Knowledge assesses the quality of an argument about knowledge rather than recall of material, so additional reading does not help much. The essay responds to a prescribed title, is capped at one thousand six hundred words and is marked against a single global descriptor out of ten. The usual failure is spending four hundred words restating the title before making any claim, then running out of space for the evaluation that carries the marks.

faqs.question: How should a student approach the Theory of Knowledge exhibition?
faqs.answer: Choose objects that genuinely raise the internal prompt's question rather than objects that illustrate a theme, which is the commonest mistake. The commentary runs to nine hundred and fifty words in total across three objects, so roughly three hundred words each, which means the selection has to do most of the work. Writing to an exact word count is itself worth practising. Confirm the current limits and prompts through the school's Theory of Knowledge teacher, since guides are revised on a cycle and the prompts are set by the board.

faqs.question: Can incomplete CAS really stop my child receiving the diploma?
faqs.answer: Yes. CAS carries no grade, which is precisely why it is neglected, but it is a completion requirement and the documentation has to demonstrate engagement and reflection over time. Reflections written in bulk at the end do not show learning over time and coordinators recognise them immediately. The element most often missing is the collaborative project, with students having completed plenty of activity and no project. One review session early in DP2 finds those gaps while they are still fixable.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with CAS reflections?
faqs.answer: Only in a narrow way, and it is worth being clear about it. Reflections are first-person accounts of a student's own experience, so nobody else should be producing them. A tutor has no role in arranging activities either. What is genuinely useful is a single review session that checks the documentation against the stated learning outcomes early enough that a missing project or a thin strand can still be addressed. That is one session, not a programme, and any provider offering more should be asked what it consists of.

faqs.question: Where is the line between legitimate help and malpractice on the core?
faqs.answer: Teaching a skill, explaining a criterion, questioning a method and giving criterion-referenced feedback on work the student has already written are all legitimate. Supplying content, text, data or a structure that enters the submission is not, however it is framed. The consequence of crossing that line falls on the student, because a malpractice finding can mean a diploma is not awarded rather than a grade being reduced. One researched provider in this market sells finished Internal Assessments, which is exactly the service to avoid.

faqs.question: When should a DP1 student start the Extended Essay?
faqs.answer: In the first term, by choosing a subject and starting to read, with a viable research question settled by the second term and a full first draft produced by the end of DP1. That is deliberately ahead of most schools' internal calendars, and the margin is the point: a student a term ahead can abandon an unworkable question without drama, while a student working to the school's deadline cannot. Ask the coordinator for the internal calendar in writing at the start of DP1.

faqs.question: How do we stop every core component landing in the same fortnight?
faqs.answer: Move the Extended Essay earlier, because it is the only component with a runway long enough to be shifted. Theory of Knowledge follows the taught course and CAS runs to its own documentation deadline, so neither moves far. Mapping all three school calendars onto one page at the start of DP1 shows exactly where the collision is. In this district, families with two Diploma candidates at different schools often find the deadlines fall in different weeks, which is manageable if known in advance.

faqs.question: My child speaks Arabic at home and has to write 4,000 words in English. What helps?
faqs.answer: Register work rather than a language course. The difficulty is usually not vocabulary but writing in an academic register and making a claim identifiable in a sentence, which is where second-language writers lose marks disproportionately. Practise the sentence patterns the core needs: stating a claim, introducing evidence, conceding a counter-position, evaluating. Write short pieces to an exact word limit before attempting a long one. And draft in the language of assessment from the start, because translating later produces structures that cost clarity marks.

faqs.question: Should a strong Arabic speaker take Arabic as Language A instead?
faqs.answer: It is worth examining seriously, and the decision belongs in Year 11 or MYP 5 rather than in DP2. A student whose stronger academic language is Arabic may be better placed with Arabic as a Language A and English as a Language B, which also opens the bilingual diploma route. The reliable way to decide is a short written diagnostic in each language, ideally a piece of analytical writing on an unseen text, rather than a conversation about which language the student prefers speaking.

faqs.question: How many sessions should Extended Essay support take?
faqs.answer: Usually four to six spaced reviews across two terms, timed to the school's interim deadlines, rather than a standing weekly slot. A project needs working time between contacts more than it needs frequent contact. If a provider offers twelve consecutive weekly sessions on an Extended Essay, ask what each one produces, because that shape either duplicates supervision the school already provides or prices something a student should not be buying.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram visit homes in Al Nahyan for Extended Essay reviews?
faqs.answer: No. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, and IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; that service runs only in India. For this particular work the shared screen is a practical advantage rather than a compromise, because both people look at the same draft and the same criterion descriptor, and the annotated version exists afterwards and belongs to the student. Published in-home market rates in the emirate run from roughly AED 180 to AED 500 an hour with travel inside the rate.

abu-dhabi/al-nahyan.closingHeading: Map the core first, then book the reviews
abu-dhabi/al-nahyan.closingBody: The Diploma core is where Al Nahyan families lose points they did not know were available and occasionally lose a diploma outright, almost always on timing rather than ability. Ask the coordinator for the school's internal calendar, put all three components on one page, settle the Extended Essay subject in DP1 term one, and agree in writing what a tutor will and will not do with assessed work. Reviews are then spaced to the deadlines that matter and delivered one-to-one over live video, with the annotated draft staying with the student.

abu-dhabi/al-raha-beach.tutorsIntro: The profiles below are filtered by phase as well as subject, because teaching a seven-year-old to read fluently and teaching a Year 10 student to answer a command term are different jobs done by different people. Tell us the year group and send the latest report.

intro.heading: What a report with no marks on it is actually telling you
paragraphs: Al Raha Beach is a waterfront strip on the mainland side of Abu Dhabi, between the city and the airport: Al Zeina, Al Muneera, Al Bandar and Al Dana, a mix of apartment buildings and townhouses with the beach on one side and the main road on the other. It is a popular first posting for families moving to the emirate, and the household age profile is noticeably younger than in the established villa compounds.

That changes what parents here ask for. A majority of enquiries from these buildings concern children between about five and fifteen, and most of them start with a report. Specifically, a report that describes rather than scores: approaches to learning, conceptual understanding, criterion levels out of eight. The parent can see that something is not where it should be and cannot tell what to act on, which is a reasonable response to a document written for a different purpose.

The IB continuum is genuinely informative once the vocabulary is understood. A Primary Years report describes inquiry, conceptual understanding and transdisciplinary skills because those are what the programme teaches, and it deliberately avoids percentages. A Middle Years report gives levels out of eight on four named criteria per subject, each of which assesses something specific. Neither is vague. Both are unreadable until someone explains the letters.

The second thing worth saying early is that a large share of these enquiries do not need tutoring. A seven-year-old whose reading has stalled usually needs twenty minutes of reading aloud every night with an adult listening, not a paid lesson. A Year 7 student who scored 4 out of 8 on one criterion in one subject may be having an ordinary term. We would rather say so in a first conversation than sell a term of sessions into it, and we say it often.

Where tutoring does help in these years it helps in a narrow set of places: reading fluency and stamina, arithmetic automaticity, writing at length without prompting, and — in the Middle Years — the specific skills that criterion levels measure. Those are teachable, measurable and worth paying for. General homework supervision for a primary child is usually a poor purchase, because it addresses the symptom and builds dependence.

Abu Dhabi's regulator is the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate and publishes inspection outcomes. It regulates schools rather than tutoring providers, and IB Gram holds no permit, approval or accreditation from ADEK or from any examination board. Lessons are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video; IB Gram does not send tutors to addresses in the UAE, and visiting tutors are a service we run only in India.

abu-dhabi/al-raha-beach.programmesIntro: Al Raha Beach children are mostly in the first three stages below, with a smaller group approaching the examination years. Each note describes what the stage actually assesses and where a parent can usefully intervene.

programmes.name: IB Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: An inquiry-led programme organised around transdisciplinary themes rather than separate subjects, with conceptual understanding and approaches to learning at its centre and the Year 6 Exhibition at its end. Assessment is formative and descriptive: teachers report on how a child inquires, communicates and thinks rather than on a percentage. Literacy and numeracy are taught within the inquiries rather than as isolated timetabled blocks.
programmes.countryNote: For an Al Raha Beach household the practical question is what to do when a descriptive report suggests a problem. The answer is almost always to test the two things the programme does not report numerically: can the child read aloud fluently for ten minutes, and are number facts automatic rather than calculated. Both are testable at the kitchen table in fifteen minutes, and both are the foundation everything later depends on.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups, each assessed against four criteria labelled A to D, scored from 0 to 8 against task-specific rubrics. The four levels combine to a total out of 32, which the school converts to a grade from 1 to 7 using published boundaries. The final year carries the Personal Project, an extended independent piece with its own criteria, and some schools run MYP eAssessment for externally validated certification.
programmes.countryNote: Criterion levels are the single biggest source of confusion among families in these buildings, many of whom arrived from a percentage-based system. A 5 out of 8 is not 62%. It is a statement that the student met a described standard on one named skill in one task. Knowing which criterion is low tells you precisely what to work on, which is more actionable than any percentage would be.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Two-year externally examined courses with Cambridge codes such as 0580 Mathematics and 0620 Chemistry and Pearson International GCSE codes such as 4MA1 and 4CH1. Cambridge mathematics and the separate sciences are tiered into Core and Extended, which sets the available grade range before papers are sat. Assessment is concentrated at the end rather than distributed through the course.
programmes.countryNote: Some children in this community switch from an IB continuum school into an IGCSE route at fourteen, usually because of a school move. The change is larger than it looks: criterion-based assessment against task-specific rubrics is replaced by raw mark schemes and timed papers. The useful preparation is sitting timed questions and being marked against a real mark scheme before the change rather than after it.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects across Higher and Standard Level with Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Every subject carries an internally assessed component with published criteria, submitted and moderated before external papers sat in a single window. Offers are typically expressed as a points total with minimum grades named in specific Higher Level subjects.
programmes.countryNote: For a family on the continuum, the Diploma is where the currency changes. Criterion levels out of eight are replaced by raw marks and grade boundaries, and the independent project load increases sharply. Students who have done well in the Middle Years are not automatically ready for that; the ones who struggle are usually strong on process and unpractised at timed written work.

abu-dhabi/al-raha-beach.subjectsIntro: These are the areas Al Raha Beach households ask about most. The list runs younger than on most pages because the community does, and each description names what can actually be worked on.

subjects.name: Reading fluency and stamina
subjects.description: The single most consequential skill in primary education and the one least visible on a descriptive report. A child who reads accurately but slowly will struggle with everything later, because comprehension competes with decoding for attention. Twenty minutes of reading aloud nightly with an adult listening outperforms almost any paid intervention.

subjects.name: Number facts and arithmetic automaticity
subjects.description: Multiplication, division and number bonds have to be automatic rather than calculated. A child who works out seven eights every time has no spare capacity for the method being taught. This is pure rehearsal, measurable in seconds per question, and it is where short frequent sessions beat long ones most clearly.

subjects.name: Writing at length without prompting
subjects.description: The gap between a child who writes three sentences when asked and one who writes a page unprompted widens every year. The teachable parts are planning, paragraph structure and sustaining an idea across a page. Criterion B and C in MYP Language and Literature measure exactly this.

subjects.name: MYP Mathematics
subjects.description: Criterion A knowing and understanding, B investigating patterns, C communicating, D applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Most students are strongest on A and weakest on D, because applying mathematics to an unfamiliar context is the hardest and least practised skill. Knowing which letter is low tells you what to work on.

subjects.name: MYP Sciences
subjects.description: Criterion A knowing and understanding, B inquiring and designing, C processing and evaluating, D reflecting on the impacts of science. The design and evaluation criteria are where levels drop, because they ask for independent experimental thinking rather than recall, and they are the direct ancestors of the Diploma internal assessment.

subjects.name: MYP Language and Literature
subjects.description: Criterion A analysing, B organizing, C producing text, D using language. A student can read perceptively and still score low on B, because organisation is a separate skill from insight. This is the subject where criterion feedback is most actionable and most often ignored.

subjects.name: MYP Individuals and Societies
subjects.description: Criterion A knowing and understanding, B investigating, C communicating, D thinking critically. Thinking critically is the criterion that separates grades at the top, and it means evaluating sources and arguments rather than having opinions. It is taught directly in a handful of sessions.

subjects.name: Mathematics (0580 and 4MA1)
subjects.description: For the students in this community who move onto an IGCSE route. The transition issue is presentation of method: criterion-based work rewards communication, and mark schemes reward specific working. The tier decision is the first thing to check, because Core papers cap the available grade.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.levels: Primary, MYP and IB ab initio
subjects.description: Mandatory in UAE private schools whatever the licensed curriculum, and a subject most children in these buildings started on arrival in the country. Progress depends on short frequent contact — fifteen or twenty minutes several times a week — rather than a single long weekly session, at every age.

subjects.name: English as an additional language
subjects.description: A real need in a community with many recent arrivals. The distinction that matters is between conversational fluency, which comes quickly, and academic language, which does not. A child who chats easily and cannot write a paragraph has an academic-language gap, and that is the thing to teach.

subjects.name: Study skills and organisation
subjects.description: Planning a long task, breaking it into stages, meeting an interim deadline. Approaches to learning are explicitly part of the IB continuum and are reported on, yet almost never taught directly. For a Year 8 or 9 student this is often the highest-return hour available.

abu-dhabi/al-raha-beach.modesIntro: Three formats built for younger students, all delivered online, one-to-one or with a sibling, over live video. None involves a tutor arriving at an address in the UAE.

modes.title: Short, frequent primary sessions
modes.description: Twenty-five to forty minutes, two or three times a week, at a consistent hour shortly after the school run. Young children lose concentration long before an hour is up, and the two things that matter most at this age — reading fluency and number-fact automaticity — respond to frequency rather than length. Each session has a measurable output.
