modes.title: Criterion-targeted MYP sessions
modes.description: A weekly session aimed at one named criterion rather than at a subject. If criterion D in sciences is the low one, the work is experimental design and evaluation, taught directly and practised against task-specific rubrics. This is a far more precise purchase than general subject tutoring and it usually takes fewer sessions.

modes.title: Continuum transition block
modes.description: A defined block for the step from Primary into Middle Years, or from Middle Years into the Diploma or an IGCSE route. Each step changes the currency of assessment, and students who did well in the previous stage are not automatically ready for the next. The block builds the specific habits the next stage assumes.

sections.heading: Who actually lives on Al Raha Beach, and the ages that dominate
paragraphs: Al Zeina, Al Muneera and Al Bandar were built as waterfront family housing and they filled with families at an early stage. The result is a community where the modal child is in primary or lower secondary rather than in an examination year, and where a substantial proportion of households have been in the UAE for fewer than five years. Both facts shape what useful tutoring looks like here.

The dominant enquiry is a parent holding a report they cannot act on. The second most common is a parent whose child is fluent in conversational English and cannot produce academic writing. The third is a household where Arabic started on arrival in the country and is now the weakest line on the report. The fourth, smaller group is examination-year families, who are better served by the pages on the islands and the Khalifa City corridor than by this one.

There is a fifth group worth naming because they are frequently sold the wrong thing: parents of a young child whose homework takes too long. Homework supervision is the easiest product to sell and often the worst purchase, because it treats the symptom and builds a dependence on an adult being present. If homework takes too long, the cause is usually reading speed, number-fact recall or writing stamina, and those are what should be worked on.

Use the table to locate your own situation, then read the section on the relevant document — a descriptive primary report or a criterion-level one. The order of this page runs youngest first, which is the opposite of most tutoring pages and matches this community.

sections.heading: Reading a report that gives no grades
paragraphs: A Primary Years report is written to describe a learner rather than to rank one, which makes it genuinely useful to a teacher and frustrating to a parent who wants to know whether there is a problem. The way to read it is to look for verbs and qualifiers rather than adjectives. 'Is beginning to', 'with support', 'when prompted' and 'is developing' are the phrases that carry information; 'enjoys', 'contributes' and 'is enthusiastic' do not.

Then test the two things the report will not quantify. First, reading: ask the child to read aloud from an unfamiliar book at their age level for ten minutes, and note whether they slow down, substitute words, lose the thread, or need to reread. A child who reads accurately but slowly is working hard enough on decoding that comprehension suffers, and that is the most important finding available from any primary assessment.

Second, number facts. Ask twenty multiplication and division questions and time them. A child who answers in under three seconds each has automaticity; one who visibly computes does not, and that computing consumes the attention the method needs. These two tests take fifteen minutes at a kitchen table and they produce more actionable information than most paid assessments.

If both tests are clean and the report still reads oddly, the next step is a conversation with the class teacher rather than a tutor. Ask what specifically they would like the child to be able to do by the end of the term, in a sentence a parent can act on. Teachers usually answer that question well and are rarely asked it.

sections.heading: The MYP criteria, named by letter with what each one assesses
paragraphs: Middle Years reports give four criterion levels per subject, each scored from 0 to 8 against task-specific rubrics, and the four combine to a total out of 32 that the school converts to a grade from 1 to 7 using published boundaries. Nothing about that is vague. The problem is that the letters are rarely explained, so parents read four numbers and learn nothing from them.

Each letter assesses a different thing, and the pattern across a subject tells you what to work on. In sciences, criterion A is knowing and understanding, B is inquiring and designing, C is processing and evaluating, and D is reflecting on the impacts of science. A student with 7 on A and 3 on B knows the content and cannot design an investigation, which is a precise diagnosis and a teachable one. In mathematics, A is knowing and understanding, B is investigating patterns, C is communicating and D is applying mathematics in real-life contexts.

In Language and Literature, A is analysing, B is organizing, C is producing text and D is using language. A student can read perceptively and score low on B, because organisation is a separate skill from insight. In Individuals and Societies, A is knowing and understanding, B is investigating, C is communicating and D is thinking critically, and D is the criterion that separates the top grades.

The practical move is to collect the criterion levels across subjects and look for the letter that is low everywhere. A student weak on C across several subjects has a communication problem rather than four subject problems, and one hour a week on written communication will lift several grades at once. That is the kind of insight criterion-based reporting makes possible and percentage reporting does not.

sections.heading: The continuum, stage by stage, and the step at the end of each
paragraphs: The IB continuum is three programmes with three different assessment currencies, and almost every difficulty a family meets happens at a join rather than inside a stage. A child who is thriving in the Primary Years meets criterion rubrics for the first time in Year 7. A student with strong Middle Years levels meets raw mark schemes and timed papers for the first time in the Diploma. Neither transition is hard if it is anticipated; both are bruising if it is not.

The useful way to plan is to look one stage ahead and introduce its currency early. A Year 6 child benefits from seeing a task-specific rubric before Year 7 begins. A Year 11 student benefits from sitting a timed paper marked against a real mark scheme before DP1, because the shock is not the content but the absence of a rubric describing what a good answer looks like.

The other thing that changes at each join is the amount of unsupervised work. Primary Years work is almost entirely supervised. Middle Years adds the Personal Project, which is substantially independent and runs to school-set interim deadlines. The Diploma adds six internal assessments, the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge, all produced outside taught periods. Study skills are therefore a continuum subject in their own right, reported on under approaches to learning and taught directly almost nowhere.
Use the table as a planning document rather than a description. The right column is the one that matters: it names what to prepare before the join rather than what to repair after it.

sections.heading: The primary years: what actually matters, and what does not
paragraphs: Three things in primary education predict later performance strongly, and almost everything else is noise. Reading fluency and stamina come first, because a child who reads slowly spends attention on decoding that should be spent on meaning, and that deficit compounds across every subject for a decade. Arithmetic automaticity comes second, for the same structural reason. Writing at length unprompted comes third.

None of the three is best addressed by homework help. Reading improves by reading aloud to an adult who listens and corrects, twenty minutes a night, with books slightly beyond comfortable. Number facts improve by timed rehearsal in short bursts, measured in seconds per question so that progress is visible. Writing at length improves by writing regularly to a prompt with no help, then having it read.

What does not matter as much as parents fear: neat handwriting beyond legibility, the particular reading scheme a school uses, whether a child is in the top group in Year 3, and the apparent pace of the curriculum compared with a cousin's school in another country. Comparisons across systems at this age are close to meaningless, because the sequencing differs and converges later.

What does matter and is often missed: a child who has recently changed language of instruction may be fine cognitively and behind linguistically, which looks identical on a report and needs an entirely different response. In a community with as many recent arrivals as Al Raha Beach, that distinction is worth making before anything is bought.

sections.heading: The Personal Project and MYP eAssessment
paragraphs: The Personal Project is the Middle Years Programme's extended independent piece, assessed against its own criteria, and it is the first substantial self-managed task most students in this community will meet. It runs across months, to interim deadlines set by the school, and it is almost entirely unsupervised between those deadlines. For many students it is their first encounter with having to manage their own timeline.

Where support helps is in the process rather than the product. A tutor can teach the criteria and what each one rewards, help a student test whether their chosen goal is achievable in the time available, and read a draft the student has written and give feedback on structure and evidence. A tutor must not author any part of the submission, supply text to be adapted, or make the artefact. The project is assessed as the student's own work and a breach is treated as malpractice.

The commonest failure is scope. A student picks a goal that is genuinely interesting and far too large, and discovers in month three that the evidence required cannot be gathered. Testing scope in the first fortnight is the single most valuable intervention available, and it takes one session. The second commonest failure is the process journal, which is assessed and is usually reconstructed at the end rather than kept as the work happens.

Where a school runs MYP eAssessment, the final year also carries externally validated on-screen examinations and ePortfolios. That changes the preparation: on-screen examinations reward familiarity with the format as well as the content, and the ePortfolio components run to deadlines earlier than the examinations. Ask the school which components apply to your child's cohort, because practice varies between schools.

paragraphs: Published market rates in the UAE span a wide range, and most of the pages ranking for these searches publish no figure at all. For a primary child the honest answer is that the cheapest effective intervention is free: reading aloud nightly and timed number-fact practice, done by a parent. Where paid sessions help, they are short and frequent rather than long, which means the weekly cost looks different from the hourly rate. Three thirty-minute sessions is an hour and a half, not three hours, and pricing by session rather than by hour matters at this age.

For Middle Years work the purchase is usually narrower than parents expect. A criterion-targeted arrangement aimed at one named letter across two or three subjects often runs for six to eight sessions rather than a year, because the skill transfers once it is taught. That is a better outcome and a smaller invoice than a standing weekly subject lesson, and a provider who proposes the standing lesson without looking at the criterion pattern is not reading the report.

Three questions settle most comparisons: is the rate per hour or per session, is marking of work set between sessions included, and does the rate change in the exam term. Those vary more between providers than the headline numbers do.

sections.heading: The step from criterion levels into raw marks
paragraphs: This is the transition that catches strong students, and it catches them precisely because they are strong. A student who has scored 7s and 8s on Middle Years criteria has been assessed against descriptions of quality: a rubric tells them what an excellent answer looks like, and they produce it. In the Diploma and in IGCSE, no rubric is to hand. There is a mark scheme the student never sees during the examination, awarding marks for specific content and specific phrasing.

The practical consequences are three. Timed writing becomes a skill in itself, because criterion tasks usually allow more time than an examination question does. Command terms acquire precise tariffs, where criterion language described quality in general terms. And partial credit works differently: a mark scheme awards method marks for visible steps, so showing working stops being good practice and becomes the source of marks.

The preparation is straightforward and almost never done. In the year before the join, have the student sit timed questions in their strongest subject and mark them against the real mark scheme, with the student watching the marking. Two or three repetitions is usually enough for the currency change to land. Doing it in the strongest subject matters, because the point is the format rather than the content.

The same logic applies in the other direction for a student moving from an examined system into the Middle Years. They will find rubric language unfamiliar and will under-report their own process, because nothing in their previous system rewarded explaining how they worked. Reading the task-specific rubric aloud before starting a task fixes most of it.

sections.heading: Online lessons for a younger child, honestly
paragraphs: Parents of primary-age children are right to ask whether a screen can hold a seven-year-old, and the honest answer is: for twenty-five to thirty minutes, with an adult within earshot, usually yes, and for an hour, usually not. That is a statement about attention rather than about format, and the same child would not sustain an hour with a tutor in the room either.

What works at this age is short, highly structured sessions with visible activity: reading aloud with the text shared on screen, timed number facts, a short piece of writing typed or photographed and annotated live. What does not work is a lesson shaped like a secondary lesson, with explanation followed by practice. The practice has to be continuous and the tutor has to be visibly reacting to it.

IB Gram delivers tutoring in the UAE as one-to-one online lessons over live video. We do not send tutors to addresses in the UAE; visiting tutors are a service we run only in India. For a very young child, or a child with attention needs that a screen aggravates, a tutor in the room is genuinely the better option, and we will say so rather than taking a booking we do not think will work.

sections.heading: Starting from Al Raha Beach, including when the answer is no
paragraphs: Send the most recent report, the child's year group and programme, and one sample of unaided writing. For a Middle Years student, send the criterion levels across all subjects rather than the one subject that worries you, because the pattern across letters is where the useful diagnosis sits. For a primary child, do the ten-minute reading test and the twenty-question number-fact test first and tell us what happened.

The first conversation is diagnostic and free of charge, and a meaningful share of them end with us saying that tutoring is not the right purchase. A seven-year-old whose reading is slow needs nightly reading aloud with a parent. A Year 7 student with one low criterion in one subject after one term may be having an ordinary term. A recent arrival whose spoken English is fluent and written English is weak needs academic-language work, which is a specific thing rather than general tutoring.

Where we do recommend sessions, the recommendation is narrow: a named criterion, a named skill, a stated number of sessions and a way to tell whether it worked. For continuum students that is usually the next school assessment rather than an arbitrary six-week review, because the school's own task is the honest measure.

On availability: early-afternoon slots suit primary children and are the easiest to get; the post-five weekday window is the most requested across Abu Dhabi and the first to fill. We tell you where a tutor is based whenever you ask. We claim no approval or accreditation from ADEK, the Ministry of Education or any examination board, because we hold none, and we publish no statistic we cannot evidence.

faqs.question: My child's primary report has no grades on it. How do I tell whether there is a problem?
faqs.answer: Read it for qualifiers rather than adjectives: 'with support', 'when prompted', 'is beginning to' and 'is developing' carry information, while 'enjoys' and 'contributes' do not. Then test the two things the report will not quantify. Ask the child to read aloud from unfamiliar text at their age level for ten minutes and note slowing, substitutions or rereading. Then time twenty multiplication and division facts; under three seconds each is automaticity. Fifteen minutes gives you more than most paid assessments.

faqs.question: What does a 5 out of 8 on an MYP criterion actually mean?
faqs.answer: It means the student met a described standard on one named skill in one task. It is not 62%. Each subject group has four criteria labelled A to D, each scored 0 to 8 against a task-specific rubric, and the four combine to a total out of 32 that the school converts to a grade from 1 to 7. The useful information is which letter is low: a 7 on knowing and understanding with a 3 on inquiring and designing is a precise, teachable diagnosis.

faqs.question: Which MYP criterion should we worry about most?
faqs.answer: The one that is low across several subjects rather than the lowest single number. A student scoring poorly on communication in sciences, mathematics and individuals and societies has one problem — putting reasoning into clear written form — not three subject problems, and an hour a week on written communication will lift several grades together. A single low criterion in a single subject after one term is often just a difficult task, and is worth watching rather than buying.

faqs.question: Does an eight-year-old really learn anything in an online lesson?
faqs.answer: In twenty-five to thirty minutes, with an adult within earshot and a highly structured session, usually yes. In an hour, usually not, and the same child would not sustain an hour with a tutor in the room either. What works at this age is continuous visible activity: reading aloud with the text shared, timed number facts, a short piece of writing annotated live. What does not work is a lesson shaped like a secondary lesson, with explanation followed by silent practice.

faqs.question: Do you send tutors to Al Zeina or Al Muneera?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram delivers tutoring in the UAE as one-to-one lessons online, over live video, and we do not send anyone to a residential address in the Emirates; visiting tutors are a service we run only in India. For a very young child, or one whose attention needs are aggravated by a screen, a tutor in the room is genuinely the better option and we will say so rather than taking a booking we do not expect to work.

faqs.question: Homework takes my ten-year-old two hours a night. Should we get a tutor for it?
faqs.answer: Probably not for the homework itself. Homework supervision is the easiest thing to sell and often the worst purchase, because it treats the symptom and builds a dependence on an adult being present. If homework takes too long the cause is usually reading speed, number-fact recall or writing stamina, and those are what should be worked on directly, in short measured sessions. Fix the underlying skill and the homework time falls without anyone sitting beside the child.

faqs.question: My son speaks English fluently but his written work is weak. What is going on?
faqs.answer: Almost certainly a gap between conversational fluency, which arrives quickly, and academic language, which does not. They look identical in a classroom and completely different on a page. Academic language means the vocabulary and sentence structures used to explain, compare, justify and evaluate, and it has to be taught rather than absorbed. In a community with as many recent arrivals as this one, the distinction is worth making before buying anything, because the two need different teaching.

faqs.question: How should we prepare for the step from Year 6 into the Middle Years Programme?
faqs.answer: Introduce the new currency early. A Year 6 child benefits from seeing a task-specific rubric and being shown how it describes quality, because criterion-based assessment is the main change. Beyond that, the three things that carry forward are reading fluency, automatic number facts and the ability to write a page unprompted. Planning a multi-stage task is the fourth, and it is the one the Middle Years Programme assumes and almost no primary school teaches directly.

faqs.question: What support is allowed on the Personal Project?
faqs.answer: Process coaching and feedback, nothing more. A tutor can teach the criteria and what each rewards, help test whether a chosen goal is achievable in the time available, and read a draft the student has written and comment on structure and evidence. A tutor must not author any part of the submission, supply text to be adapted, or make the artefact. The project is assessed as the student's own work. Two practical warnings: scope is the usual failure, and the process journal should be kept as the work happens rather than reconstructed.

faqs.question: Why do strong MYP students sometimes struggle in the first Diploma term?
faqs.answer: Because the currency changes. Criterion rubrics describe what an excellent answer looks like and are available while the student works. A mark scheme awards marks for specific content and phrasing and is never seen during an examination. Timed writing becomes a skill in itself, command terms acquire precise tariffs, and showing method stops being good practice and becomes the source of marks. Two or three timed questions marked against a real mark scheme, in the strongest subject, usually land the change before it hurts.

faqs.question: Which schools do Al Raha Beach families mostly use?
faqs.answer: The nearest run is inland to Al Raha Gardens and the Khalifa City corridor, which holds IB continuum, British and American schools and is where most children from these buildings travel. A minority cross to the island schools or to Yas, with later returns that push tutoring earlier in the afternoon or onto the weekend. The continuum schools in the near corridor are the reason criterion-level reports are the document families here most often bring to a first conversation.

faqs.question: What does short, frequent tutoring cost compared with one weekly hour?
faqs.answer: Compare weekly rather than hourly, because the session shapes differ. Three thirty-minute sessions is an hour and a half of teaching, not three hours. Published market rates put budget online tutoring at AED 45-150 an hour, with EdFlik listing AED 45-65 and Tutopiya AED 33-52, and a qualified subject tutor online at AED 150-300, with Unitors from AED 150. Those are the market's figures with their sources. Ask any provider whether they will price by session rather than by hour for a young child.

faqs.question: Does my child have to study Arabic even at an IB continuum school?
faqs.answer: Yes. Arabic is mandatory in UAE private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, as part of the federal requirement that private schools follow Arabic, social studies and Islamic studies alongside whatever curriculum they are licensed for. It appears on the school report whether or not it is being examined externally. For a child who started Arabic on arrival in the country, short frequent contact of fifteen or twenty minutes several times a week works far better than one long weekly session.

faqs.question: How do we judge whether the tutoring is working for a continuum student?
faqs.answer: Against the school's own next assessment rather than an arbitrary review date. For a Middle Years student that means the next task assessed on the criterion you targeted: if the level has not moved, something needs to change. We prefer that measure because it is the school's judgement rather than ours, and because a criterion level is specific enough to be a real test. Where no further sessions are needed we say so rather than letting an arrangement continue by default.

faqs.question: Can one tutor work with two children of different ages in this household?
faqs.answer: Usually not the same tutor and never the same session, when the ages are far apart. Teaching reading fluency to a seven-year-old and criterion-based science writing to a Year 9 student are different jobs done well by different people. Where two children are close in year group and on the same programme, shared topic teaching can work and saves an evening slot. Either way, each child should get separate session notes, so one progress line does not mask the other.

intro.heading: The hour a short school run gives back
paragraphs: Al Raha Gardens is a gated villa community off the main Abu Dhabi to Dubai road, built in phases with its own retail and community facilities, and sitting beside the wider Al Raha area and Khalifa City. Its defining practical feature is proximity. A school operates within the Al Raha community itself and several more sit minutes away in Khalifa City, which means the school run here is measured in minutes rather than in the half-hours that families on the islands and in the outer mainland communities accept as normal.

That sounds like a lifestyle point and it is really an academic one. A household whose child spends fifteen minutes on a bus each way has roughly an hour a day more available than a household whose child spends forty-five minutes each way. Across a five-day week that is five hours. Across a school year it is the better part of two hundred hours. Nobody plans for it, so it mostly disappears into screens and the ordinary drift of an evening.

The families in this community who do well academically are, with some consistency, the ones who treat that hour as a resource rather than as slack. It does not need to be filled with tutoring. It needs to be allocated: a fixed window for independent work with a defined output, an earlier bedtime that makes the next day work, a second subject that would otherwise never get attention, or genuine rest that a commuting household cannot afford.

The second feature of this community is household size. Al Raha Gardens is villa stock with larger families, which means most tutoring decisions here involve two or three children rather than one. That turns the problem from choosing a tutor into designing a week, and the design has to come first. A household that buys three separate weekly lessons without staggering them discovers in week two that all three want the same hour.

The third is that this community is close enough to the airport corridor and the business districts that parents often return later than the children do. Lessons that need an adult present to admit a visitor are harder to sustain than lessons that need a laptop and a seat, which is one of several reasons the format here is online, one-to-one, over live video. IB Gram does not send tutors to addresses in the UAE; visiting tutors are a service we run only in India.

What follows is a planning document rather than a brochure: what the returned hour is worth in numbers, how to stack two or three children in one evening, the examination year counted backwards from the boards' own published dates, how the UAE academic calendar and Ramadan bend a revision plan, and what a year of tutoring costs at different frequencies with every figure attributed.

abu-dhabi/al-raha-gardens.programmesIntro: Al Raha Gardens children sit across the IB continuum, British and American routes, frequently with siblings on different ones. Each note is written for a household with a short commute and more than one child.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects across Higher and Standard Level plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Each subject carries an internally assessed component marked against published criteria, submitted and moderated ahead of external papers sat in a single window. More of the final result depends on self-managed work than in any other route, which makes a protected independent window unusually valuable.
programmes.countryNote: A Diploma student in this community has the rare luxury of a weekday evening that is not already spent in a car. The highest-value use of it is a fixed ninety-minute independent window with a written output, reviewed in the next tutoring session. Where a household has a Diploma student and younger siblings, the Diploma student should get the protected window and the quiet room, which is a scheduling decision rather than a favouritism one.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Two-year externally examined courses, with Cambridge codes such as 0580 Mathematics and 0620 Chemistry and Pearson International GCSE codes such as 4MA1 and 4CH1. Cambridge mathematics and the separate sciences are tiered into Core and Extended, fixing the available grade range before any paper is sat. Entries close months before the examinations, which is the fact most families discover too late.
programmes.countryNote: The entry calendar is the thing worth planning around here, because Al Raha Gardens households have the time to act on it if they know it. Cambridge's published key dates put final entries for the March 2027 series on 27 November 2026, and Pearson's November 2026 International GCSE timetable runs to 19 November 2026. Take the exact timetable from your school: Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and the zone version is the one that applies.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each, labelled A to D and scored 0 to 8 against task-specific rubrics, combining to a total out of 32 that converts to a grade from 1 to 7. The final year carries the Personal Project, an extended independent piece with its own criteria and school-set interim deadlines that run between taught lessons.
programmes.countryNote: Middle Years students are the ones in a villa household most likely to lose the returned hour, because they have no examination pressure to focus it and plenty of competing attractions. A short protected window with a defined output works better at this age than a long one, and the Personal Project year is where the habit pays off most visibly.

programmes.name: American curriculum and Advanced Placement
programmes.description: Continuous assessment across a grade point average, with Advanced Placement courses taken individually and examined separately on a 1 to 5 scale. The structure rewards steady submission and distributes risk across a year rather than concentrating it in one window, which builds coursework discipline and not examination stamina.
programmes.countryNote: Several schools in the Khalifa City corridor run American routes, so a number of households here have one child on a continuous-assessment system and another facing terminal examinations. Those two children need opposite things from the same evening: one needs deadline discipline, the other needs timed practice, and treating them as a single tutoring problem is the commonest planning error in a villa with siblings.

abu-dhabi/al-raha-gardens.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects Al Raha Gardens households ask about most, with the description aimed at what can be done inside a protected weekday window.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Calculus, algebra and proof, with an optional-topic paper at Higher Level. The work that moves marks is unseen problems done alone with every method line written out, then checked. That is exactly the task a protected hour at home suits, and exactly the task that never happens without one.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics, modelling and calculator technique, with interpretation in context carrying real marks. The habit worth building in an independent window is writing the interpretation sentence after every calculation, because students practise the arithmetic and skip the sentence where the marks sit.

subjects.name: Mathematics (0580 and 4MA1)
subjects.levels: IGCSE Core and Extended · Pearson Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: The most requested subject in this community across both boards. Method marks decide grades: a correct answer with no working loses marks that a wrong answer with sound method keeps. The tier decision should be checked early, because Core papers cap the grade regardless of later improvement.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL · IGCSE Core and Extended
subjects.description: Mechanics, electricity, waves and, at Higher Level, fields and quantum topics. Experimental-design questions are the reliable loss and cannot be learned by reading. Formula provision differs between Cambridge 0625 and Pearson 4PH1, which changes what has to be recalled under pressure.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL · IGCSE Core and Extended
subjects.description: Stoichiometry, energetics, equilibrium and organic mechanisms. Mole arithmetic has to be automatic, which is rehearsal rather than teaching, and the protected window is where rehearsal happens. Mechanism questions want arrows and intermediates drawn repeatedly rather than read once.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL · IGCSE Core and Extended
subjects.description: Physiology, genetics, ecology and data analysis, with the heaviest command-term load of the sciences. Writing full answers to past questions and comparing them against the official scheme is the task that pays, and almost no student does it unprompted.

subjects.name: English Language and Literature
subjects.levels: IB Language A HL and SL · IGCSE First Language
subjects.description: Analysis, comparative writing, the individual oral and the higher level essay. The independent work is writing about what was read, under time, without notes. Students who annotate thoroughly and never write to a timer arrive with understanding and no delivery.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Markets, macroeconomic objectives and the global economy. Diagram accuracy and the evaluation paragraph decide more marks than content recall. Both are suited to short repeated practice in a protected window rather than to long explanation sessions.

subjects.name: Business Studies and Business Management
subjects.description: Marketing, operations, finance and structure, assessed through case studies. Marks come from applying a tool to an unfamiliar business, which is a skill built by repetition on new cases rather than by revising the case studied in class.

subjects.name: Arabic
subjects.description: Mandatory in UAE private schools whatever the licensed curriculum. In a villa household with several children it is the subject most often sacrificed to the louder examination subjects, and it responds better than any other to fifteen minutes a day in a protected window.

subjects.name: Study skills and independent work
subjects.description: Planning a multi-stage task, meeting an interim deadline, producing a defined output in a fixed window. In a community whose main academic asset is time, the skill that converts time into results is the one worth teaching first, and it is taught almost nowhere.

sections.heading: A school inside the community, and the hour it gives back
paragraphs: Put numbers on the advantage and it stops being a vague benefit. A child with a fifteen-minute journey each way spends half an hour a day travelling. A child with a forty-five-minute journey spends an hour and a half. The difference is an hour a day, five hours a week, and comfortably more than a hundred and fifty hours across a school year, before any after-school club is added to either side.

A hundred and fifty hours is not a marginal quantity. It is more than most students spend on any single subject's independent revision in an entire examination year. The question for a family in this community is therefore not whether they have time for tutoring and independent work; they clearly do. The question is whether the hour is allocated or absorbed, and by default it is absorbed.

There is a second, less obvious part of the advantage. A child who has not spent forty-five minutes in traffic arrives home in a working state. Lessons and independent work that begin shortly after a short run start at close to full attention, whereas a post-commute session spends its first ten minutes restarting a tired student. Over a term of weekly sessions that difference alone is worth more than most changes of tutor.

Use the table to see what your own arrangement is worth, then decide deliberately what the returned hour is for. It does not have to be academic. An earlier bedtime that makes the following school day work is a legitimate use of it, and for some students it is the best one available.

sections.heading: What to do with the hour the commute does not take
paragraphs: The default use of a returned hour is a screen, and that is not a moral failing; it is what unallocated time becomes in every household on earth. Converting it into something useful requires three decisions made once rather than daily: what the hour is for, when it happens, and what it produces that somebody will look at.

The most valuable allocation for a secondary student is an independent work window with a defined output. Not 'revise chemistry' but 'this past-paper section, timed, marked against the scheme, with the three largest losses written down'. The output is the whole mechanism, because an hour whose product is reviewed by another person stops being optional. That review is the real function of a weekly tutoring slot and it is almost never how tutoring is sold.

The second most valuable allocation is the subject that would otherwise never get attention. In a villa household with examination pressure somewhere in the building, Arabic and the mandatory UAE subjects are the reliable casualties, and they appear on the school report regardless. Fifteen minutes a day on Arabic in the returned hour outperforms an expensive weekly session scheduled into an already full evening.

The third allocation is rest, and it should be said plainly rather than treated as a consolation. A student sleeping seven hours instead of six, consistently, performs better than the same student with an extra tutored hour and less sleep. Where a family has the time and chooses sleep, that is a good decision, and we will say so when it is the one the evidence supports.
bullets: Decide once: what the hour is for, when it runs, what it produces

sections.heading: Two or three children, one evening: stacking a villa week
paragraphs: Most tutoring decisions in this community involve more than one child, and the scheduling has to be designed before anything is bought. The failure mode is predictable: a household books three weekly lessons at roughly the same convenient time, discovers that the quiet room, the household's attention and the family dinner all collide, and within a fortnight two of the three lessons have become negotiable.

Staggering solves most of it. If the eldest is taught at four and the middle child at five, the middle child works independently on a defined task while the eldest is in a lesson, and the quiet room is used continuously rather than fought over. Each child also gets a tutoring session immediately after a period of independent work, which is the ideal sequence: the work exists, so there is something to mark.

Shared teaching is worth considering only where the board and year group genuinely match. Two children on the same syllabus and one year apart can share topic teaching, and the younger often learns from the elder's questions. What cannot be shared is marked-script review, because its entire value is specificity. The pattern that works is shared topic sessions plus a short individual slot each.

One rule applies regardless of arrangement: separate session notes per child, every time. A single shared note after a shared lesson invites a parent to read two different children as one progress line, which is how a quiet struggle survives a whole term unnoticed. sections.heading: The examination year counted backwards
paragraphs: Families plan forwards from today and examination boards work backwards from a paper, which is why entry deadlines take so many households by surprise. The useful exercise is to write the year out in reverse, starting from the examination window and ending at the decision that has to be made first. For Cambridge and Pearson candidates the dates are published and can be relied on; for the IB Diploma they must come from the school.

Cambridge publishes key dates for each series. For the March 2027 series, final entries are due 27 November 2026, the exam period runs 3 February to 4 March 2027, forecast grades are due 27 February 2027, results reach centres on Cambridge International Direct on 13 May and certificates follow in late June. Cambridge also runs June and November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October.

Pearson Edexcel International GCSE examinations are available in May/June and November each year. The November 2026 final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, so take the live official timetable rather than any restatement of it.

For the IB Diploma we publish no session or results dates anywhere on this site, because they could not be confirmed against the IB's own pages — automated access there is blocked, and an unverified date repeated across thousands of pages multiplies one error many times over. Treat the May session as the one UAE schools sit and take exact dates from your school's Diploma coordinator.

sections.heading: Why entry deadlines sit months before the paper
paragraphs: The gap between an entry deadline and an examination looks like bureaucracy and is actually logistics. A board has to print and distribute question papers to thousands of centres across dozens of time zones, allocate marking capacity, and confirm tier and subject combinations for every candidate. None of that can happen on short notice, which is why a February examination closes entries in the previous November.

The consequence for a family is specific and under-appreciated. Decisions that feel like they belong to the spring — whether to sit a subject at all, which tier to be entered for, whether to take an extra subject as a private candidate — actually belong to the autumn, before the evidence a parent would want to use has been generated. A November decision has to be made on October evidence.

That is an argument for producing evidence earlier than feels natural. If a tier decision will be taken in November, the timed Extended questions that would justify a change need to be sat and marked in October. If a subject might be dropped, the conversation belongs in the same month. Waiting for the mock results is waiting until after the decision.

Cambridge adds one further operational detail worth knowing. Every exam centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, and Cambridge states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for the centre's zone, noting that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong zone timetable. Take the timetable from your school, not from any tutoring website.

sections.heading: Ramadan, Eid and the shape of the UAE academic year
paragraphs: A revision plan built on a European or North American calendar will break in the UAE, because the academic year here has features that plan does not contain. Schools run shortened days during Ramadan, which moves the afternoon return earlier and changes the household rhythm substantially. Eid breaks interrupt the term. The summer break is long and hot, and the cooler months are when families travel and host visitors.

The practical approach is to treat these as known variables rather than disruptions. During Ramadan the usual late-afternoon slot often stops working, and many families move to a later evening session after Iftar or to a mid-morning weekend slot. Plan the change a fortnight in advance and hold the new pattern for the whole period rather than renegotiating each week. Because lessons are online, the change is a calendar edit rather than a renegotiation of anyone's driving route.

The long summer is the most underused academic asset in the UAE. For an Al Raha Gardens household it is the cheapest improvement available, because the school run disappears entirely and the day has room in it. Buy it as a defined block with a written target and a diagnostic at each end, rather than as general sessions to keep a student ticking over, which tend to produce the feeling of progress rather than progress.

The cooler months are the trap. Revision plans assume January and February are quiet and in this part of the world they are the social and travel season, which collides directly with mock examinations and, for Cambridge March series candidates, with the examination window itself. Write the unavailable weekends into the plan in September and move the long sessions rather than losing them.

sections.heading: What a year of tutoring costs at different frequencies
paragraphs: Published market rates in the UAE cover a wide range and most of the pages ranking for these searches publish no figure at all. The table below translates the market's own hourly numbers into an annual commitment at different frequencies, because the annual figure is what a household actually decides about. These are market rates with the provider that published each one, not an IB Gram price list.

Two things fall out of the arithmetic. The first is that frequency matters more than rate: one session a week at a mid-band rate costs less across a year than two sessions a week at the budget end, and usually achieves more because the hour includes marking. The second is that a year at one session a week in one subject is a smaller commitment than most families assume and a far better purchase than a crisis block in the spring.

Put the figures in context. ADEK's remit includes school licensing and the emirate's fee arrangements, and school fees are the dominant educational cost in any household here. Tutoring at one session a week in one subject typically sits at a small fraction of a year's fees, which is the comparison worth making rather than comparing one tutor's hourly rate with another's.

Before comparing quotes, establish three things: whether the rate is per hour or per session, whether marking of work set between sessions is included or billed, and whether the rate changes in the examination term. Those answers vary more between providers than the headline numbers do.

sections.heading: A visiting tutor in the compound against one-to-one online
paragraphs: In a gated villa community a visiting tutor is more practical than it is in a tower or on an island, so the comparison here is genuinely closer than elsewhere in Abu Dhabi. There is parking, there is a room, and a tutor who already visits one household in the compound can reach a second with minimal additional travel. Those are real advantages and they should be weighed honestly.

The costs remain. The pool is still limited to who will drive to the airport corridor in the late afternoon, the rate still carries the travel, and the specialist a Diploma student needs may not be in Abu Dhabi at all. A visiting arrangement is also harder to stagger across three children, because the tutor's own evening route caps how many consecutive slots they can offer in one place.

IB Gram delivers tutoring to Al Raha Gardens as one-to-one online lessons over live video. We do not send tutors to addresses in the UAE; visiting tutors are a service we run only in India. We say that before a parent asks, because in a compound where visiting arrangements are common it would be easy to let an assumption stand.

The table weighs it without tilting the scales. Presence is where the room wins and, in a villa with a spare study, that advantage is larger than it is in an apartment. Reach, cost, the staggering of siblings and whether the marked script still exists next week all go the other way.

sections.heading: Where a tutor stops on assessed work
paragraphs: Every programme represented in this community carries work assessed as the student's own: internal assessments and the core in the Diploma, the Personal Project in the Middle Years, coursework in several IGCSE subjects. Academic-honesty rules treat a breach as malpractice and the consequence falls on the student rather than on whoever helped.

Stated plainly, the line runs here. A tutor may teach the assessment criteria letter by letter with the marks attached to each. A tutor may test a proposed research question for scope and say honestly whether it will generate usable data. A tutor may read a draft the student has produced and give feedback on structure, reasoning, evidence and clarity. A tutor may teach the underlying skills — referencing, uncertainty treatment, graph conventions, evaluation language — using a different example.

A tutor may not author any sentence appearing in a submission, supply text for a student to adapt, build the student's data set, make an artefact, or hand over a model answer to the student's own question. Where a school's rules are tighter than the board's, the school's rules apply, and some schools in this corridor limit external feedback on an assessed draft to one round. Ask at the start of the task rather than at the end.

There is also a copyright line worth stating because competitors cross it. We do not reproduce, host or supply board past papers, mark schemes, grade-boundary tables or syllabus documents; they belong to Cambridge, Pearson and the IB, and unreleased material carries a malpractice exposure as well. We cite and link the official source, and schools will usually release the material their students are entitled to use.

sections.heading: Starting from Al Raha Gardens
paragraphs: Send the year groups and boards for every child who might be involved, the most recent marked script or report for each, and the shape of a typical weekday evening in the house. The last item is the one families leave out and the one that determines whether a plan survives: who is home when, which room is quiet, and what else is already in the diary.

The first proposal you get back from us is usually a schedule rather than a lesson. With two or three children, staggering and the allocation of the returned hour do more for outcomes than the choice of any individual tutor, and they cost nothing. Only after that do we recommend specific sessions, with the subject, the frequency, the session length and a way to judge whether it worked.

Trials are taught rather than sold. A short diagnostic, worked through live, and a written note afterwards naming the specific gaps found. Where the honest answer is that a household does not need paid lessons — because it has time, a quiet room and a student who will use a defined window with light supervision — we will say so and offer a fortnightly review instead of a weekly lesson.

On availability, this community has an advantage worth using: early-afternoon slots are much easier to get than the contested post-five window, and a short school run makes them possible here. For a few niche Higher Level subjects the specialist may be based outside the UAE and teaching into a UAE evening, and we say where a tutor is based whenever you ask. We hold no approval or accreditation from ADEK, the Ministry of Education or any examination board.

process.title: Measure the hour you actually have
process.description: Work out the daily travel time for each child and compare it with the table on this page. Households here usually find an hour a day they had not counted, and naming it is the first step to allocating it rather than letting it be absorbed.

process.title: Design the week before buying a lesson
process.description: With two or three children, staggering matters more than the choice of tutor. Consecutive slots, a defined independent task for whoever is not being taught, and one quiet room used continuously rather than contested.

process.title: Write the entry calendar out in reverse
process.description: Start from the examination window and work back to the decision that has to be made first. Cambridge's March 2027 entries closed on 27 November 2026; Pearson's November 2026 timetable ran to 19 November 2026. Take IB dates from your coordinator.

process.title: Produce evidence before the decision
process.description: If a tier or subject decision falls in November, the timed and marked work that would justify a change has to exist in October. Waiting for mock results means waiting until after the entry has been made.

process.title: Give every independent window an output
process.description: A past-paper section, timed, marked against the scheme, with the three largest losses written down. The output is what makes the hour real, because somebody looks at it in the next session.

process.title: Review at six weeks, or at the school's next task
process.description: A repeat of the same diagnostic, or the school's own next assessment on the targeted criterion. If nothing has moved we change the method or the tutor, and we say when the answer is fewer sessions rather than more.

whyPoints.title: Scheduling first, teaching second

faqs.question: How much time does a short school run actually save a family here?
faqs.answer: Compared with an outer-community or island commute, roughly an hour a day. A ten or fifteen-minute journey each way costs twenty to thirty minutes of travel; a forty-minute journey costs eighty. Across a five-day week that is four to seven hours, and across a thirty-eight week year it runs well past a hundred and fifty hours. There is a second benefit that does not appear in the arithmetic: a child who has not sat in traffic arrives home able to work, so a session that starts early starts at close to full attention.

faqs.question: What is the best use of the extra hour in the evening?
faqs.answer: An independent work window with a defined output is usually the highest-return allocation for a secondary student: a past-paper section, timed, marked against the scheme, with the three largest losses written down. The second-best is the subject that otherwise never gets attention, which in villa households with examination pressure is almost always Arabic. The third is sleep, and that should be said plainly rather than treated as a consolation, because a consistently rested student outperforms a tired tutored one.

faqs.question: We have three children. How should we schedule tutoring without chaos?
faqs.answer: Stagger it, and design the week before buying anything. If the eldest is taught at four and the middle child at five, the middle child works independently while the eldest is in a lesson and the quiet room is used continuously. Each child then gets a session immediately after a period of independent work, which means there is something to mark. Shared teaching only works where the board and year group genuinely match, and marked-script review always stays individual.

faqs.question: When does the Cambridge entry deadline fall for the March series?
faqs.answer: Cambridge's published key dates put final entries for the March 2027 series on 27 November 2026, with the exam period running 3 February to 4 March 2027, forecast grades due 27 February 2027, results on Cambridge International Direct on 13 May and certificates in late June. Read backwards, the subject and tier decision has to be settled in October or early November. Take the exact timetable from your school: Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and the zone version applies.

faqs.question: Why do entry deadlines sit so far before the examination?
faqs.answer: Logistics rather than bureaucracy. A board has to print and distribute papers to thousands of centres across many time zones, allocate marking capacity, and confirm tier and subject combinations for every candidate, none of which can be done at short notice. The practical consequence is that decisions which feel like spring decisions — whether to sit a subject, which tier, whether to add one as a private candidate — belong to the autumn, and have to be made on autumn evidence rather than mock results.

faqs.question: Do tutors come into the compound for lessons?
faqs.answer: Not from IB Gram. We deliver tutoring in the UAE as one-to-one lessons online, over live video, and we do not send anyone to a residential address in the Emirates; visiting tutors are a service we run only in India. In a gated villa community a visiting arrangement is more practical than in a tower, so this is worth saying plainly rather than letting an assumption stand. Published market rates for visiting tutors run AED 180-500 an hour with travel inside the figure.

faqs.question: What does a year of weekly tutoring in one subject cost?
faqs.answer: At published market rates and thirty-eight teaching weeks, a weekly hour with a qualified subject tutor online at AED 150-300 comes to roughly AED 5,700-11,400 across the year, where Unitors lists AED 150 for IGCSE and AED 200 for IB. A weekly ninety minutes with a specialist at AED 200-450, where TutorChase lists AED 270, runs to roughly AED 11,400-25,650. Those are market figures with their sources, not ours. Frequency matters more than rate, because the mid-band hour includes marking.

faqs.question: Can we book an early afternoon slot rather than an evening one?
faqs.answer: In this community, usually yes, and it is worth doing. A short school run means academic work can start before half past three, and the early-afternoon window is far less contested than the post-five slots that most of Abu Dhabi competes for. An early slot also catches a child before the evening fills up and leaves the later part of the evening for the independent window and for rest, which is the sequence that works best for secondary students.

faqs.question: How should a revision plan handle Ramadan in this community?
faqs.answer: Plan the change a fortnight ahead and hold one new pattern for the whole period. Schools run shortened days, so the afternoon return comes earlier and the household rhythm shifts, which often makes the usual late-afternoon slot unworkable. Families commonly move to a later evening session or a mid-morning weekend slot. Because lessons are online, the switch is a calendar edit rather than a renegotiation of anyone's driving route, so there is no reason to improvise it week by week.

faqs.question: Should an Al Raha Gardens family book a block of sessions over the long summer?
faqs.answer: For a household here it is often the cheapest improvement available, because the school run disappears entirely and the day has room in it. Buy it as a defined block with a written target and a diagnostic at each end rather than as general sessions, which tend to produce the feeling of progress rather than progress. Good summer targets are closing specific gaps identified from marked scripts, bridging from IGCSE into the Diploma, or preparing for a resit series.

faqs.question: Which schools do Al Raha Gardens children usually attend?
faqs.answer: Most use the near cluster: a school operating inside the Al Raha community and several more a few minutes away in the Khalifa City corridor, spanning IB continuum, British and American routes. A minority cross to the island schools or to Yas, and those households lose the hour that this page is about. Because several curricula sit within minutes of each other, a tutor should be matched to the exact syllabus code rather than to the subject name.

faqs.question: Do you publish IB session and results dates?
faqs.answer: No. The IB's own site blocks automated access, so no IB session or results date in this project was confirmed from the IB directly, and publishing an unverified date across a large set of pages would multiply a single error many times over. Treat the May session as the one UAE schools sit and take the exact dates from your school's Diploma coordinator. Cambridge and Pearson dates on this page come from those boards' published pages and are attributed where they appear.

faqs.question: Can a tutor supervise the Personal Project or an internal assessment?
faqs.answer: Process coaching and feedback, within clear limits. A tutor can teach the criteria letter by letter with their mark allocations, test whether a chosen question or goal is achievable in the time available, read a draft the student has produced and comment on structure and evidence, and teach the underlying skills on a different example. A tutor cannot author text appearing in the submission, build the data set or make the artefact. Where a school limits external feedback to one round, that limit applies.

faqs.question: Will you send us past papers for practice?
faqs.answer: No, and the reason matters. Past papers, mark schemes, grade-boundary tables and syllabus documents are the copyright of Cambridge International, Pearson and the IB, and unreleased material carries a malpractice exposure as well as a copyright one. We cite them and link the official source. Ask the school first: it holds the material its students are entitled to use and will usually release past papers for revision on request, which costs nothing and keeps everyone on the right side of the rule.

faqs.question: Do we really need weekly lessons if the household has time and a quiet room?
faqs.answer: Often not. Where a student will use a defined independent window with light supervision, a fortnightly review that marks what was produced and sets the next fortnight's work can do most of the job at half the cost. The mechanism that matters is somebody looking at the output, not the frequency of teaching. We will propose that arrangement where the evidence supports it, and we will say when a weekly slot is genuinely the better purchase instead.

abu-dhabi/al-raha-gardens.closingHeading: Design the week, then buy the hour
abu-dhabi/al-raha-gardens.closingBody: The academic advantage in this community is time, and the only question is whether it gets allocated. Send us the year groups and boards for each child, a recent marked script apiece, and the honest shape of a weekday evening in the house. The first thing you get back is usually a staggered schedule and a plan for the returned hour, which costs nothing. Lessons, where they are the right answer, run online, one-to-one, over live video, and we will tell you when a fortnightly review would do the job instead.

abu-dhabi/al-rawdah.tutorsIntro: The tutors below are matched on availability as well as subject, because a specialist who cannot make the one slot your week allows is not a match. Subject, level, board and the actual hour are agreed together before anything is booked.

intro.heading: The hour is the hard part, not the tutor
paragraphs: Al Rawdah sits in the middle of Abu Dhabi island, villas and low-rise housing bounded by Airport Road on one side and the Al Mushrif and Al Karamah districts on the others. It is an established, largely residential district, and the households here are a mix of Emirati families and long-resident expatriates whose children are often in the school cluster a few minutes away in Al Mushrif, or across the island in Al Bateen, or out on Saadiyat.

Almost every tutoring arrangement that collapses in this district collapses for the same reason, and it is not the tutor. A family agrees a time that sounded workable in August, discovers in October that the child is not actually home until twenty past four, pushes the session to seven, and by the first week of November it is being cancelled every second week. Nobody has done anything wrong. The hour was never real.

So this page starts with the afternoon, timed. Schools in and around Al Rawdah finish between about half past one and half past two depending on phase and school. Add the collection, the Airport Road crossing at exactly the wrong time of day, and the ordinary human need to eat something, and the earliest honest start for most households in this district is four o'clock. For a child schooled on Saadiyat or out at Khalifa City it is closer to five. Those two numbers decide everything else, including how long the session should be and what it can be used for.

The second half of the page does the same exercise at a larger scale. Examination years also run backwards, and families plan them forwards. Entry deadlines sit months before papers: Cambridge's final entries for the March 2027 series were due on 27 November 2026 for examinations beginning on 3 February 2027. Forecast grades, mock windows, internal coursework deadlines set by the school rather than the board, and results dates all have their own positions in the calendar, and a plan that does not know them is a plan built on a guess.

There is a third piece of timing nobody asks for and everybody needs, and it is the school's own deadline list. Boards set entry dates and examination windows; schools set coursework submission dates, mock weeks and report dates, and those are almost always earlier than the board's and far more binding on a student's actual week. One email in September produces that list. Families who hold it plan a year; families who do not react to it a fortnight at a time.

Everything here is delivered as one-to-one lessons over live video. For a district where the binding constraint is the clock and the Airport Road junction, a format that adds no second journey to anybody's afternoon is the practical answer as well as the one we offer. It also means a tutor is never the reason a session is missed, which in a district this dependent on one road is not a small thing.

abu-dhabi/al-rawdah.programmesIntro: The programme notes below are written from the scheduling side: what each route demands of a week, and when in the two-year cycle the pressure actually arrives.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. The workload is not evenly distributed: the first year is content-heavy with coursework starting quietly, and the second year front-loads internal assessment deadlines into the months before the papers rather than after them.
programmes.countryNote: For an Al Rawdah Diploma student the crunch is almost always the window from November of the second year to February, when internal assessments, the Extended Essay and mocks all land together. A weekly hour established the previous spring survives that window. An arrangement started in January does not have time to settle before it is needed.

programmes.name: IGCSE
programmes.description: Two-year courses examined externally by Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel, with tiering in several Cambridge subjects that caps the available grade. The pressure point is the second term of Year 11, when past-paper practice should be weekly and is usually monthly.
programmes.countryNote: Year 10 is the cheap year and families rarely use it. A student who builds the habit of timed practice in Year 10 arrives in Year 11 needing supervision rather than rescue, and the difference in total hours bought across the two years is substantial.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups marked against four lettered criteria, each out of eight. The scheduling demand is lower than the Diploma's until the Personal Project arrives in Year 10 or 11, at which point a student needs protected blocks rather than short reviews.
programmes.countryNote: MYP students in this district generally have the best afternoon available to them, because the local school run is short and the homework load is moderate. It is the right stage to establish a sustainable weekly pattern, before the Diploma makes a pattern essential.

programmes.name: A Level
programmes.description: Linear qualifications with everything assessed at the end and little coursework in most subjects. Scheduling is simpler than the Diploma because there are fewer internal deadlines, but the risk concentrates: there is no coursework component to absorb a weak paper.
programmes.countryNote: On the Ministry of Education's British track, candidates need one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or better, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, alongside five accredited IGCSE or GCSE subjects at no less than E or grade 3. That requirement shapes which A Levels are worth protecting.

abu-dhabi/al-rawdah.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects Al Rawdah families most often ask about, described in terms of how much weekly time each realistically needs rather than only what it covers.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Standard Level sits two papers at 40% each with a 20% exploration; Higher Level adds Paper 3 at 20%. Higher Level is the subject most likely to need a full weekly hour for two years rather than a block before examinations, because the content compounds.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics with the graphic display calculator throughout. More forgiving of a shorter weekly session than Analysis and Approaches, because the skills are more modular and a forty-five minute block can complete a whole topic.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Papers 1 and 2 at 36% and 44% in the Diploma, with the investigation at 20%. The written explanation work needs sustained time; a short session can drill calculation but cannot build a mechanism-level written answer.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms require handwritten repetition and immediate correction, which is ideal short-session work. Energetics and equilibrium need longer blocks, so the two halves of the course suit different slots in the week.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Unifying themes with heavy unseen-context questioning in Paper 2. The reliable loss is describing a trend when the command term asked for an explanation, which is correctable in short, frequent sessions rather than long ones.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Standard Level is Paper 1 at 30%, Paper 2 at 40% and the portfolio at 30%, with Paper 3 added at Higher Level. The portfolio needs scheduled blocks at three specific points rather than continuous weekly attention.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Unseen analysis, comparative essay and the Individual Oral at 30% of Standard Level, with an HL essay at 20% added at Higher Level. Essay work needs ninety-minute blocks; a forty-five minute session cannot produce and review a full response.

subjects.name: First Language English
subjects.description: Directed writing and reading response papers rewarding structure and precise reference. The highest-value use of time is a timed response written then dissected, which again means a long slot rather than a short one.

subjects.name: Mathematics (IGCSE)
subjects.description: Tier sets the grade ceiling, with Cambridge Core capped at grade C. Beyond the tier decision, the gains come from timed past papers and self-marking, which is the most schedulable work in any subject.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Higher Level sits Paper 1 at 35% and Paper 2 at 40% with the project at 25%. The project requires real organisational evidence and therefore needs blocks timed around access to that organisation, not around the tutoring calendar.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first and additional language
subjects.description: Mandatory alongside the international programme under the federal rules, with separate provision and different expectations for Arab and non-Arab students. Frequent short sessions suit script and fluency work better than weekly long ones.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: A 1,600-word essay on a prescribed title plus the exhibition with its 950-word commentary. Almost no revision time is allocated to it anywhere, and two or three well-placed sessions on title choice and argument are usually enough.

regions.name: Al Mushrif
regions.note: The adjacent district and the nearest substantial school cluster, including Abu Dhabi International School and Al Muna Academy. A Mushrif school place is the best afternoon available to an Al Rawdah family: home by three, session at four.

regions.name: Al Karamah
regions.note: Directly alongside Al Rawdah with the same road pattern and the same Airport Road crossing. Timings here are effectively identical, which is why families in the two districts tend to share the same workable slots.

regions.name: Al Nahyan

regions.name: Saadiyat Island

regions.name: Al Reem Island

sections.heading: The Al Rawdah afternoon, timed honestly
paragraphs: Do this arithmetic before agreeing any slot, because it is the arithmetic that determines whether the arrangement is still running in November. Start with the school finish time, which across this part of the island runs from about half past one for primary phases to around half past two for secondary. Add the collection itself, which is rarely instant. Add the drive, which for a Mushrif school is a few minutes and for a Saadiyat or Khalifa City school is considerably more, at the hour when Airport Road is least cooperative.

Then add the part families leave out. A teenager who has been in school since half past seven needs to eat and decompress before anything academic is possible, and thirty minutes is the minimum that works. A session that begins the moment the front door closes produces a resentful student and a tutor managing mood rather than content.

The output of that sum is an earliest honest start, and for most Al Rawdah households it is four o'clock. For a child schooled across the island or out at Khalifa City it is nearer five. Those are not ideal times chosen from a brochure; they are the times that survive. A session agreed at seven because it sounded more convenient in August is competing with homework, dinner and sleep, and it loses.

The table below is the version we work through with a parent on the first call. It is deliberately specific about what each slot can be used for, because a half past five start is perfectly good for drilling mechanisms and genuinely poor for writing a timed essay, and treating all hours as interchangeable is how families end up disappointed with a tutor who was doing nothing wrong.

sections.heading: How long a session should be, and what each length can achieve
paragraphs: Session length is treated as a preference and it is really a capability question. Certain work fits inside forty-five minutes and certain work does not, and buying the wrong length is a quiet waste that nobody notices because the session still happens.

Forty-five minutes is enough to mark a past-paper question set against the scheme, drill a mechanism sheet, correct a specific technique or review a coursework draft section. It is not enough to write and dissect a full essay, because the writing alone consumes it. Sixty minutes handles a topic properly, a set of structured questions with discussion, or a focused coursework conversation. Ninety minutes is the only length that supports a full timed paper followed by marking, or a complete essay written under conditions and then taken apart, and it is the length Al Rawdah families most under-use.

For younger children the logic inverts. Twenty-five to thirty minutes, more often, beats a long block every time: attention at nine years old is genuinely finite and a long session produces compliance rather than learning. Three short sessions a week on reading or number work does more than one long one, and it also fits the earlier finish time that primary phases enjoy.

The practical recommendation for a Diploma or Year 11 student in this district is a pairing rather than a single choice: one ninety-minute weekend block for the heavy work, one forty-five-minute weekday slot for consolidation and setting. That combination costs the same as two hours and achieves considerably more than two separate hours placed badly.

sections.heading: The examination year counted backwards from the papers
paragraphs: Families plan examination years forwards from today and the calendar actually runs backwards from the paper. The result is a predictable annual surprise: a deadline that was always there arrives as news. The specific dates below come from the boards' own published pages, and the pattern they show is the point rather than any individual date.

Cambridge's key dates for the March 2027 series are the clearest illustration available. The examination period runs from 3 February to 4 March 2027. Final entries were due on 27 November 2026, more than two months before the first paper. Forecast grades are due on 27 February 2027, results are released on Direct on 13 May and certificates follow in late June. Anyone planning from the examination date alone misses the entry deadline by a wide margin.

There is also a zone trap worth knowing in this region. Every Cambridge centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, each with its own timetable version, and Cambridge states that using the correct version is essential and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after consulting the wrong one. Use the timetable your child's school issues rather than one found through a search.

Pearson Edexcel runs International GCSEs in May and June and again in November, publishing provisional timetables ahead of each series. The November 2026 final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. For the IB we publish no dates: the organisation's own site cannot be verified automatically, UAE schools sit the May session, and the specific dates belong to your child's diploma coordinator.

The most important column in the table below is the last one. Knowing a date is useless without knowing what should already be finished by then, and that is the information families actually need in September.
