abu-dhabi/al-reem-island.tutorsIntro: Profiles are filtered by the system a student is moving into and the specific gap that move creates, not by subject alone. Tell us where your child studied before, where they are now and what the school expects by when, and the shortlist follows from that.

intro.heading: A community that changes system more often than it changes school
paragraphs: Al Reem Island is a tower community: Shams Abu Dhabi, Najmat Abu Dhabi, City of Lights and the developments around Reem Mall, connected to Abu Dhabi island by bridges and to the mainland beyond. The housing is overwhelmingly apartments, the household size is smaller than in the villa communities, and the population turns over faster. Families arrive from India, the Levant, Europe, North America and from elsewhere in the Gulf, often for a posting of a few years.

That profile produces a tutoring problem that is specific and poorly served. A child on Reem has a reasonable chance of having studied in two systems already. A Year 10 student who did Classes 1 to 8 on CBSE and then two years of a British curriculum has gaps that are not random: they sit exactly where the two syllabuses disagree about sequence and emphasis. Nobody at either school is responsible for finding them, and a general tutor will spend a term discovering them one at a time.

The gaps have a pattern. Students arriving from procedural systems are usually ahead on computation and behind on extended written reasoning. Students arriving from American systems are usually comfortable with coursework and continuous assessment and unprepared for a single terminal examination window. Students arriving from a British system into the Diploma are usually fine on content and unready for the independent project load. Each of those is fixable in weeks if named, and expensive if not.

The second thing about a tower household is physical. There is often no spare room, the study surface is shared, and two or three children may need the same table at the same time. That changes session length and session timing more than any subject consideration does: a 45-minute session at a predictable hour with headphones works far better in an apartment than a 90-minute block in a flat that fills up at seven.

The island also has higher education on it. Sorbonne University Abu Dhabi sits on Al Reem Island, which puts the question of what a UAE university actually asks of a school leaver closer to home than it is for most families. The honest answer involves the Ministry of Education's equivalency process, which has published criteria for some tracks and not for others, and which no tutoring provider performs or guarantees.

Everything below is organised around the switch: how to map a transition subject by subject, what changing system at fourteen, sixteen or seventeen costs, how to make an apartment work for lessons, what the market charges with every figure attributed, and what a school leaver has to be able to show. Lessons are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video. IB Gram does not send tutors to addresses in the UAE; visiting tutors are a service we run only in India.
bullets: A tower community with faster turnover, so system switches are the norm here
Gaps from a switch are patterned, not random, and can be mapped in one session
Apartment study space decides session length more than subject choice does
Market rates in AED are published with the provider that quoted each figure
British-track equivalency needs five accredited subjects at no less than E or grade 3
Delivery is online, one-to-one; home visits are an India-only service

abu-dhabi/al-reem-island.programmesIntro: Reem households arrive into all four of the routes below, often partway through. The notes describe what each programme asks of a student who did not start it at the beginning.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects across Higher and Standard Level with Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Each subject carries an internally assessed component with published criteria, submitted and moderated before the written papers. The programme assumes a large amount of self-managed work and rewards consistency across two years rather than a strong final term.
programmes.countryNote: Joining the Diploma late is the hardest of all the transitions available on this island, because the internally assessed components and the core run on school-set deadlines that do not restart for an arrival. A family moving into Abu Dhabi in DP1 should ask the school in writing which components the cohort has already completed and what the plan is for a new student, before any tutoring is arranged around it.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Two-year externally examined courses, with Cambridge codes such as 0580 Mathematics and 0620 Chemistry and Pearson International GCSE codes such as 4MA1 and 4CH1. Cambridge mathematics and the separate sciences are tiered into Core and Extended, which fixes the available grade range before any paper is sat. Several Pearson subjects are modular, allowing a unit to be sat in a different series where the centre permits it.
programmes.countryNote: This is the commonest destination for a system switch on Reem, and the commonest place a switch goes wrong quietly. A student arriving in Year 10 from a different system may be put on a Core entry on the strength of a first term that reflected the transition rather than their ability, and Core papers are capped. Ask which tier your child is entered for and what evidence would change it.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each, labelled A to D, with levels out of eight and task-specific rubrics instead of percentages. The Personal Project in the final year is an extended independent piece with its own criteria. Reports describe skills rather than giving marks, which is informative once the letters are understood and close to unreadable before that.
programmes.countryNote: Families arriving on Reem from a marks-based system routinely misread an MYP report. A 5 out of 8 on one criterion is a specific statement about a specific skill, not a percentage. Before buying any tutoring it is worth having the report translated into plain language, because a meaningful share of enquiries that begin this way turn out not to need tutoring at all.

programmes.name: American curriculum and AP routes
programmes.description: Continuous assessment across a grade point average, with Advanced Placement courses taken individually and examined in a spring window. The structure rewards steady coursework and class participation, and it distributes risk across a year rather than concentrating it in a terminal examination. Students moving out of it meet a single examination window for the first time, which is a change of habit rather than of knowledge.
programmes.countryNote: Several Reem households are on American routes at mainland schools, and a few move into the Diploma or an IGCSE route partway through. The gap that matters is examination stamina and timed-paper technique rather than content. For families staying on the American track, the Ministry of Education's published equivalency requirements include SAT and English-proficiency thresholds, which are set out later on this page.

abu-dhabi/al-reem-island.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects Reem households ask about most, with the description written for a student arriving into the subject partway rather than starting it from scratch.

subjects.name: Mathematics (0580 and 4MA1)
subjects.levels: IGCSE Core and Extended · Pearson Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: The commonest transition subject on the island. Students from procedural systems usually have strong algebra and weak method presentation, losing marks that a wrong answer with visible working would have kept. The tier decision is the first thing to check, because Core papers cap the grade regardless of later improvement.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Calculus, algebra and proof, with a third paper at Higher Level. Students arriving from a system that rewarded speed often skip the justification the mark scheme requires. The exploration is the other pressure point: a topic chosen too broadly cannot be controlled inside the word limit.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics, modelling and calculator technique, with interpretation in context carrying real marks. A frequent destination for students who switched system late and need a route that rewards application over proof. The written explanation of what a model implies is the part to practise.

subjects.name: Physics (0625 and 4PH1)
subjects.levels: IGCSE Core and Extended · IB HL and SL
subjects.description: Mechanics, electricity, waves and, at Higher Level, fields and quantum topics. Formula provision differs between boards, which changes what has to be memorised, and that difference catches transfers immediately. Experimental-design questions are the reliable loss for students new to the system.

subjects.name: Chemistry (0620 and 4CH1)
subjects.levels: IGCSE Core and Extended · IB HL and SL
subjects.description: Stoichiometry, bonding, energetics and organic mechanisms. Transfers usually arrive with the chemistry and without the question-interpretation habits: a mechanism question answered with a description earns very little. Mole arithmetic under time pressure caps more grades than any single topic.

subjects.name: Biology (0610 and 4BI1)
subjects.levels: IGCSE Core and Extended · IB HL and SL
subjects.description: Cells, genetics, physiology and ecology, with the heaviest command-term load of the sciences. For a student arriving from a recall-based system this is the subject where the change of currency is sharpest, because knowing the content and writing the answer are genuinely different skills here.

subjects.name: English as a first and second language
subjects.levels: IGCSE 0500 and 0510 · IB Language A and B
subjects.description: Reading response, directed writing and, in the Diploma, analysis and the individual oral. The decision about which route a transfer should sit on is consequential and often made on arrival with little evidence. A timed piece of unaided writing settles it better than a conversation does.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Markets, macroeconomic objectives and the global economy. Diagram accuracy and the evaluation sentence decide more marks than content recall, and both are teachable quickly. Students joining the Diploma late often need the commentaries explained as a format before any economics is taught.

subjects.name: Business Studies and Business Management
subjects.description: Marketing, operations, finance and structure, assessed through case studies. Application to the business in the stem earns the marks; defining the tool does not. For a Diploma transfer, the research project needs an organisation that will actually supply information, which is worth testing early.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.levels: IB ab initio and Language B · IGCSE 0544
subjects.description: High demand on Reem, where many children started Arabic on arrival in the UAE. Progress depends on short frequent contact rather than long weekly sessions. Arabic is also mandatory in UAE private schools whatever the licensed curriculum, so it appears on the report regardless of the examination route.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Algorithms, data structures and system fundamentals, with pseudocode conventions that differ by board and matter in marking. A common choice for transfers because prior programming experience transfers well, though the written theory papers reward precision of terminology that self-taught coders rarely have.

abu-dhabi/al-reem-island.regionsIntro: Al Reem Island sits between Abu Dhabi island and the mainland corridor, and its families use schools in both directions. The notes describe what each neighbourhood changes for a tower household.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: A planned low-density island to the north with its own school and a bridge connection. Reem and Saadiyat households use several of the same mainland schools, so they share arrival times and compete for the same late-afternoon slots.

regions.name: the Corniche
regions.note: The city-island waterfront across the water, with short school runs and a dense residential core. The commonest crossing destination for Reem children and the reason a late-afternoon slot is realistic for part of this community.

regions.name: Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: Central Abu Dhabi island, mixed residential and commercial, and a major workplace for Reem parents. Households where both parents work there favour lessons that do not need an adult at home to let anyone in.

regions.name: Al Bateen
regions.note: Established island housing with several long-standing schools. One of the main school destinations from Reem, with a crossing that is quick in the morning and slower on the return in the early evening.

regions.name: Yas Island
regions.note: East of the island with its own school and heavy weekend traffic. Reem families on this route have a longer run than those crossing to the city island and tend to book tutoring later in the evening.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Mainland villa communities with a dense school cluster. The longest regular run from Reem, which pushes the first workable lesson past five o'clock for families using those schools.

regions.name: Al Raha Beach
regions.note: Waterfront apartments and townhouses towards the airport road. The closest comparison to Reem in household type, and a community that shares the same demand for Arabic as an additional language.

regions.name: Al Raha Gardens
regions.note: Villa compounds with a school adjacent to the community. The contrast with a Reem tower is instructive: a school inside the community returns roughly an hour a day to the household.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City
regions.note: A large mainland community with a broad curriculum mix and its own schools. Reem and MBZ households rarely share a school but compete for the same specialist tutors in the same evening windows.

regions.name: Al Reef
regions.note: Villa and apartment housing out towards the airport, with long school runs in most directions. Relevant to Reem families comparing a move off the island against the commute it would create.

schoolClusters.note: The schools reached with a single crossing, spanning British, American and IB continuum routes. Reem families use these most heavily because the run is short, and the spread of boards inside one tower is why a tutor has to be matched to a syllabus code rather than to a subject name.

abu-dhabi/al-reem-island.modesIntro: Three formats built for apartment living and for students who arrived partway through a course. All are delivered online, one-to-one or in a small sibling group, over live video; none involves a tutor arriving at an address in the UAE.

modes.title: Transition audit and bridging block
modes.description: A defined block that starts with an audit rather than a lesson: what does the new specification assume that the previous system never taught, what was taught in a different order, and which assessed components has the class already finished. The block then closes gaps in order of paper weighting and ends with a past paper from the new board sat under timed conditions.
bullets: Audit session before any teaching, with a written gap list
Gaps closed by paper weighting rather than chapter order
New board's mark-scheme conventions taught explicitly
Four to eight sessions per subject with a stated endpoint

modes.title: Short apartment-friendly sessions
modes.description: Forty-five minutes at a predictable hour, two or three times a week, designed for a flat where the study surface is shared and the household fills up in the evening. Shorter sessions lose less to interruption, need less space, and suit a student whose concentration is being competed for by siblings and television in the same room.
bullets: 45 minutes, two or three times a week, same hour each time
Headphones and one agreed study surface
Short tasks between sessions rather than long assignments
Works around a tower household's early-evening rhythm

modes.title: Sibling pairs on the same system
modes.description: Where two children in one flat are on the same board and close in year group, shared topic teaching reduces the number of slots a household has to protect and the number of competing demands on the table. Individual script review has to stay individual, because its whole value is specificity, so the usual pattern is shared teaching plus a short individual slot each.
bullets: Shared topic sessions where the year groups are close
Separate short slots for marked-script review
Fewer competing demands on one study surface
Reviewed at six weeks in case one child is being carried

sections.heading: Who actually lives on Al Reem Island, and what each tower household asks for
paragraphs: Five household types recur across Shams, Najmat and City of Lights, and they ask for different things. The recently arrived family wants to know what their child has to make up. The long-resident apartment family wants a grade lifted before a sixth-form application. The dual-career household wants lessons that do not require an adult at home. The multi-child flat wants a schedule that does not put two children at the same table. And the final-year family wants triage.

What unites them is that none of them has a spare room, and most of them have changed system at least once. Those two facts explain most of what works here. Shorter, more frequent sessions beat long blocks. Predictable timing beats flexible timing, because a predictable slot is one the rest of the household can plan around. And an audit before teaching beats a term of discovering gaps by accident.

The turnover also means advice circulates fast and ages badly. A neighbour who used a particular tutor two years ago was on a different board, in a different school, under a different school leadership. In a villa community that advice is roughly transferable. In a tower where families rotate every three or four years it frequently is not, which is why the first question we ask is about the specification rather than about the recommendation.

Find the row closest to your household in the table, then read the transition map that follows it. The order of this page is deliberate: the switch first, because that is what most Reem enquiries are actually about.

sections.heading: A curriculum transition map, subject by subject
paragraphs: A system switch creates gaps in predictable places, and naming them takes one session rather than a term. The table below is the map we use. It is not a substitute for reading your child's own two syllabuses, but it tells you where to look first and roughly how much work each gap represents, which is the information families are never given on arrival.

Two principles govern the repair. The first is sequence by examination weight rather than by textbook order: a transfer has finite hours and the topics carrying the heaviest paper weighting should be closed first, even if that means starting in the middle of a course. The second is that technique gaps close faster than content gaps, so they come first — a student who learns to present method and read command terms gains marks across every topic at once.

The third thing to establish is administrative rather than academic. Which assessed components has the class already completed, and what does the school intend to do for a student who was not there? In the Diploma this question is urgent, because internally assessed work and the core run on school-set deadlines. In IGCSE it affects coursework subjects and the tier decision. Ask in writing and keep the answer.

Weeks of support in the table are indicative and assume one session a week plus work between sessions. A motivated student with a strong prior foundation moves faster. A student also adjusting to a new country, a new language of instruction and a new friendship group moves slower, and planning for that honestly is better than planning for the optimistic case and treating the shortfall as a failure.

sections.heading: Switching at fourteen, sixteen or seventeen: what each age costs
paragraphs: Age at the switch matters more than the distance between the two systems. At thirteen or fourteen, before an examined course begins, almost any transition is manageable: there is time to rebuild habits and no assessed work is at stake. The useful work is technique rather than content, and a term of it usually settles the matter.

At fifteen or sixteen, in the middle of an IGCSE course, the switch is harder in a specific way. The student arrives into a two-year syllabus partway, the tier decision may be made on evidence produced during the disruption, and coursework in some subjects may already be underway. This is the age at which a transfer most often ends up on a capped entry that nobody revisits. The remedy is evidence: timed Extended questions, marked honestly, in front of the subject teacher before the entry is confirmed.

At seventeen, inside the Diploma, a switch is genuinely difficult and should be entered with clear eyes. The internally assessed components, the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge all run on school deadlines that do not restart, and the points total depends on components that may already be partly banked. Families should ask the school exactly what is recoverable before committing, and should consider whether a different route is the better answer rather than a heroic catch-up.

There is one consolation that applies at every age. The gaps created by a switch are narrower than they feel. A student who seems to be failing a new system is usually missing three or four specific things — a way of presenting method, a set of command terms, an examination habit, one or two topics taught in a different year — rather than lacking the subject. Finding out which is a one-session exercise and it changes the mood of the whole household.
bullets: Before an examined course: technique work, a term, low risk
Mid-IGCSE: the tier decision is the risk, and evidence is the remedy
Mid-Diploma: ask in writing what is recoverable before committing
At every age, the real gap is narrower than the first report suggests

sections.heading: An apartment is a study-space problem before it is a tutoring problem
paragraphs: In a tower flat the limiting factor on independent work is rarely motivation. It is surface, quiet and timing. A student working at the dining table in a two-bedroom apartment has a study space until about seven in the evening, after which it becomes a dining table again. Any plan that ignores that produces a student who looks disorganised and is actually dispossessed.

Three cheap interventions do most of the work. Define one study surface and keep it, so that nothing has to be decided each day. Define a window on that surface that the household agrees to protect, ideally before the evening fills up. And give the student headphones, which solve most of the noise problem and signal to everyone else that the window is in progress.

For lessons specifically, shorter is better in an apartment. A 45-minute session loses less to interruption than ninety minutes does, needs less uninterrupted surface, and can be held at a time the household can protect. Two or three short sessions a week beat one long one for almost every subject below Higher Level, and for language work they beat it at every level.

The technical setup takes ten minutes and is worth doing in the trial rather than in week four. A laptop rather than a phone, headphones, and a way to get handwritten work onto the screen — a phone photograph into a shared folder is enough. For mathematics a cheap writing tablet helps. A lesson can continue with the student's camera off if the connection is weak, which matters in a dense tower at peak hours.
bullets: One defined study surface, used every time, decided once
A protected window before the flat fills up in the evening
Headphones solve most of the noise and signal the window to others

sections.heading: Two children, one table: scheduling inside a tower flat
paragraphs: Most Reem households with two or three school-age children have one practical study surface, so the schedule has to be built before any teaching is bought. Staggering is the first move: if one child has a lesson at half past four and the other at half past five, the second child does independent work while the first is taught, and the surface is used continuously rather than fought over.

Where two children are on the same board and close in year group, part of the teaching can be shared. Topic teaching works in a pair: a tutor explaining mole calculations or quadratic methods can hold two students at once, and the second student often learns from the first one's questions. What does not share is marked-script review, because the errors are individual and specificity is the whole point of the exercise.

The pattern that works is therefore a shared topic session plus a short individual slot each. It costs less than two full individual arrangements, uses fewer evening windows, and keeps the part of tutoring that has to be personal personal. We review it at six weeks, because the risk in a pair is that the younger child is carried along or the older one held back, and that is visible in the work rather than in anybody's impression.

One practical warning. Siblings taught together need separate accounts of what happened, sent to the parent separately. A single shared note after a shared session encourages a parent to treat two different children as one progress line, which is how a quiet struggle goes unnoticed for a term.
bullets: Stagger slots so one child works independently while the other is taught
Topic teaching can be shared where the board and year group match
Marked-script review stays individual, always
Separate session notes per child, even after a shared lesson

sections.heading: What tutoring costs for a Reem household, and what the hour buys
paragraphs: Most of the pages ranking for these searches publish no price at all, and the two that do quote in US dollars. The table gives the market's own numbers in AED with the provider that published each one. These describe the market, not an IB Gram rate card; ask us for the trial and the consultation if you want our figures and what sits inside the hour.

For an apartment household buying several short sessions a week rather than one long one, the per-hour figure is less useful than the weekly figure. Three 45-minute sessions is two and a quarter hours, which at the qualified-subject-tutor band is a materially different commitment from a single 90-minute specialist slot. Decide the pattern first and price it second; doing it the other way round tends to produce the wrong pattern.

There is one band worth a specific warning. At the bottom of the market the hour is usually teaching time alone, with no marking of work set between sessions. For a transfer student that is the least useful possible purchase, because the whole value in a transition is someone reading the student's own written work against the new board's mark scheme. Paying less for an hour that excludes the marking is not a saving.

Three questions separate quotes: per hour or per session, is marking included, and does the rate change in the exam term. Those vary more between providers than the headline figures do, and the answers are usually clearer when asked in writing.

sections.heading: Degrees on the doorstep, and what a school leaver has to show
paragraphs: Al Reem Island has a university on it: Sorbonne University Abu Dhabi. For families planning to stay in the UAE for higher education, that proximity makes a question concrete that most tutoring sites ignore entirely — what does a UAE institution actually require from a student finishing an international curriculum here?

Part of the answer is recognition of the school certificate through the Ministry of Education's equivalency process. The British-track requirements have been set out publicly: proof of one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade no lower than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, together with passes in five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no lower than E or grade 3. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects.

On the American track the published requirements are different in kind: English proficiency through a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, and mathematics through at least 450 in the SAT Math test before applying. For the IB Diploma no points threshold is published on this page, because no figure for it could be verified against a Ministry source, and a wrong number repeated across a large set of pages is a large set of errors.

Two cautions. Equivalency is run by the authority and is not something a tutoring provider performs, guarantees or accelerates — we describe it and point to the official channel. And tutoring is not a requirement for it. Any page implying that a student needs tutoring in order to obtain equivalency or a university place is manufacturing urgency about an administrative process, which is a reason to distrust the rest of what it says.

sections.heading: The fork at sixteen: Diploma or A Levels, decided on evidence
paragraphs: Reem families reach this decision with less local history to go on than villa households, because many of them arrived recently and have no sense of how a particular school's sixth form actually runs. The decision is usually made on reputation, which is the weakest available basis for it. It can be made on evidence instead, in about a fortnight.

The evidence is a timed written piece and a timed problem paper in the student's two strongest subjects, marked honestly. A student who writes well under pressure, likes depth and dislikes managing several long independent projects is usually better served by three or four A Levels. A student who manages extended independent work well, needs breadth to stay engaged and tolerates a heavy core is usually better served by the Diploma.

The structural differences matter too and are worth stating plainly. The Diploma spreads risk across six subjects and the core, so one weak subject does not sink the result, but it demands independent project work that some students cannot sustain. A Levels concentrate risk in three subjects with no breadth to absorb a poor grade, but the workload is more predictable and the assessment is nearly all examination.

Where the evidence is genuinely balanced, say so and decide on the school rather than the qualification: the department, the teaching, the subject combination actually available in that school's timetable. A strongly taught A Level cohort beats a thinly staffed Diploma, and the reverse is equally true.

sections.heading: What a tutor may and may not do when the work is new to the student
paragraphs: A transfer student is the most vulnerable person in this market, because they are behind, anxious, and often unfamiliar with the rules of the system they have joined. That is exactly the situation in which an offer to supply finished work is most tempting and most damaging, and at least one operation in this market sells completed Internal Assessments at a published price.

The line is the same for a transfer as for anyone else and it is worth having in writing before a task starts. A tutor may teach the assessment criteria letter by letter with their mark allocations. A tutor may test a proposed research question for scope. A tutor may read a draft the student has produced and comment on structure, reasoning, evidence and clarity. A tutor may teach the needed skills — referencing, uncertainty, graph conventions, evaluation language — on a different example entirely.

A tutor may not author any sentence that appears in a submission, provide text for the student to adapt, build the student's data set, or supply a model answer to the student's own question. Where a school's rules are tighter than the board's, the school's rules apply, and some schools limit external feedback on a draft to one round. For a new arrival, asking that question in the first week is worth more than it sounds, because the answer shapes when support is useful.

There is a second honesty point specific to transfers. A student who has missed taught content cannot be given it by a tutor and then present it as having been learned in class; what they can be given is the content, honestly taught, with the gap acknowledged to the school. Schools generally respond well to a family that says plainly what was missed. They respond much less well to discovering it from a submission that does not match the student's classwork.
bullets: Criteria taught by letter, with the marks attached to each
Research questions tested for scope before data collection
Feedback on drafts the student produced; no authored text in a submission
Tell the school what was missed in a transfer rather than hiding it

sections.heading: Starting from Al Reem Island, and the limits worth hearing first
paragraphs: Send five things: the previous system and school, the current school with board and syllabus codes, the most recent report or marked script, what the school has said about assessed components already completed, and the two time windows the flat can actually protect. For a transfer that last item matters as much as the academic information, because a plan the household cannot physically run is not a plan.

The first session for a transfer is an audit rather than a lesson. The tutor works through short diagnostic tasks across the syllabus, identifies what is missing and where, and sends a written gap list ranked by examination weight. That document is useful even if you never book another session: it is what the two schools between them never produced.

Where the honest answer is that tutoring is not the main problem, we say so. A child who has changed country, language of instruction and friendship group inside six months is carrying a load that an extra hour on a screen does not lighten, and we would rather tell you that in week one than sell a term of lessons into it. Equally, where the gap is real and narrow, we will say that too, because families often arrive expecting the worst.

On availability: the post-five weekday window is the most requested in Abu Dhabi and the first to fill, and January is the tightest month. For a few niche Higher Level subjects the tutor who knows the paper may be based outside the UAE and teaching into a UAE evening; we tell you where a tutor is based whenever you ask. We do not claim accreditation from ADEK, the Ministry of Education or any examination board, because we hold none.
bullets: Previous system, current board and codes, a script, and two protectable windows
The first transfer session is an audit, with a written gap list ranked by exam weight
We say when the problem is the move rather than the teaching

process.title: Name both systems
process.description: Where the child studied before and where they are now, with boards and syllabus codes. The gap after a switch sits exactly where the two syllabuses disagree about sequence and emphasis, so the two names are the starting point for everything that follows.

process.title: Audit before teaching
process.description: The first session for a transfer is diagnostic: short tasks across the syllabus to find what is missing and where. You receive a written gap list ranked by examination weight, which is the document neither school produced and the one the plan is built from.

process.title: Ask the school three questions in writing
process.description: Which tier is my child entered for and what would change it; which assessed components has the class already completed; and what is the plan for a student who was not here. Keep the answers. They determine what tutoring can and cannot achieve.

process.title: Fix the surface and the window
process.description: One study surface, one protected time, headphones. In a tower flat this is the difference between a student who looks disorganised and one who has somewhere to work. It costs nothing and it is usually the highest-return change available.

process.title: Close gaps by weight, not by chapter
process.description: A transfer has finite hours. Technique gaps come first because they pay across every topic at once; then the heaviest-weighted content the student has not met. Starting at chapter one feels orderly and wastes the first month.

process.title: Measure at six weeks
process.description: A past paper from the new board, timed and marked the same way as the first one. If the marks have not moved we change the tutor, the method or the sequence, and we say when the honest answer is that the target or the route needs revising.

whyPoints.title: Built for a switch, not a syllabus
whyPoints.description: Most enquiries from this island involve a change of system, and the gaps that creates are patterned rather than random. We map them in one audit session and give you a written list ranked by examination weight, instead of discovering them one at a time across a term.

whyPoints.title: Designed around apartment reality
whyPoints.description: One study surface, a household that fills up at seven, siblings competing for the same table. Shorter frequent sessions at a predictable hour work in that environment; long blocks do not. We plan the pattern before the price rather than after it.

whyPoints.title: The tier trap flagged early
whyPoints.description: A transfer who had a difficult first term can be placed on a capped Cambridge entry nobody revisits. We ask which tier your child is entered for in the first conversation, and help produce the timed, marked evidence that would change it before the deadline.

whyPoints.title: Equivalency described, never sold
whyPoints.description: We set out the published Ministry of Education requirements by track with the unverified parts marked as unverified. Equivalency is run by the authority; we do not perform it, guarantee it or suggest that tutoring is required for it.

whyPoints.title: Figures attributed, no invented proof
whyPoints.description: Every AED rate here is a market figure with its publisher named. There are no satisfaction percentages, tutor headcounts or star ratings on this page, because we cannot produce the data behind any of them and a number nobody can check is worth nothing.

whyPoints.title: Honest about the transfer that is not academic
whyPoints.description: A child who has changed country, language and friendships in six months is carrying something tutoring does not fix. We will say that in week one rather than sell a term of lessons into it, and we will say equally plainly when the gap is narrow and closeable.

faqs.question: My son moved from CBSE to a British school in Abu Dhabi last year and is struggling. What is actually wrong?
faqs.answer: Usually not the content. Students arriving from CBSE are typically ahead on algebra, trigonometry and numerical work. The gap is in extended written reasoning: command terms carry different tariffs, 'explain' requires a causal chain that 'describe' does not, and 'evaluate' needs a judgement with support. Practical-skills questions are the second shock, asking for control variables and sources of uncertainty. A diagnostic session across the syllabus will name the three or four specific things missing, which is usually a shorter list than the first report suggests.

faqs.question: How long does it take to catch up after changing education system?
faqs.answer: It depends on the move and the age, and indicative ranges help more than a single figure. CBSE or ICSE into IGCSE typically takes six to ten weeks per subject of support. American curriculum into IGCSE runs four to eight, because the gap is examination technique rather than content. IGCSE or MYP into the Diploma is eight to twelve weeks across the programme, since the work is project load and the core rather than any single subject. Those assume one session a week plus work between sessions.

faqs.question: Which schools do families on Al Reem Island use?
faqs.answer: Most cross to Abu Dhabi island for the established British, American and IB continuum schools around Al Bateen, Al Rawdah and the Corniche, and a smaller group travels east or inland to the Yas Island and Khalifa City corridor schools. The practical result is several boards inside one tower, so a tutor has to be matched to the exact syllabus code rather than the subject name. Confirm the board with the school in writing before booking, especially after a recent move.

faqs.question: Do you send tutors to apartments on Al Reem Island?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram delivers tutoring in the UAE as one-to-one lessons online, over live video, and we do not send anyone to a residential address anywhere in the Emirates; visiting tutors are a service we run only in India. In a tower flat the online format has a practical advantage beyond cost: a lesson needs a laptop, headphones and a seat rather than a free room and an adult at the door, which is a much easier thing for an apartment household to supply.

faqs.question: Is 45 minutes long enough, or should we book an hour?
faqs.answer: In an apartment, 45 minutes two or three times a week is usually the better buy than one 60 or 90-minute block. It loses less to interruption, needs a shorter window of protected surface, and suits a student whose attention is competing with the rest of the household. The exception is exam-year timed practice: sitting a paper section and marking it line by line needs ninety minutes, and that session belongs at the weekend when the flat is quieter.

faqs.question: Can my two children share a tutoring session?
faqs.answer: Part of it, yes. Where both are on the same board and close in year group, shared topic teaching works well and the second child often learns from the first's questions. It also frees an evening window, which matters when there is one study surface. What cannot be shared is marked-script review, because its value is entirely in specificity. The pattern that works is a shared topic session plus a short individual slot each, with separate session notes for each child.

faqs.question: My daughter joined DP1 in January. Is the Diploma still realistic?
faqs.answer: Possibly, and the answer comes from the school rather than from a tutor. Ask in writing which internally assessed components the cohort has already completed, what the plan is for a student who was not there, and whether the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge timelines can be adjusted. Those answers determine what is recoverable. If a substantial share is not, it is better to consider an alternative route now than to attempt a heroic catch-up and discover the arithmetic in the second year.

faqs.question: What does a UAE university need from a student finishing IGCSEs and A Levels here?
faqs.answer: Recognition of the certificate generally runs through the Ministry of Education's equivalency process. The published British-track requirements are five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no lower than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from those five, plus either one accredited Advanced Level subject at grade E or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade. Verify the current rules with the Ministry directly. Equivalency is run by the authority and is not something a tutoring provider performs or accelerates.

faqs.question: What are the American-track equivalency requirements?
faqs.answer: The published requirements cover English proficiency and mathematics separately. English proficiency requires a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL iBT test, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT. Mathematics requires at least 450 in the SAT Math test, and the published source states this applies before applying rather than afterwards. The source does not mention EmSAT. For the IB Diploma no points figure is published here, because none could be verified against a Ministry source.

faqs.question: Should my child choose the Diploma or A Levels after IGCSE?
faqs.answer: Decide it on evidence rather than reputation, which takes about a fortnight. Sit a timed written piece and a timed problem paper in the two strongest subjects and have them marked honestly. A student who writes well under pressure, wants depth and dislikes juggling long independent projects usually suits three or four A Levels. One who manages extended independent work and needs breadth usually suits the Diploma. Where the evidence is balanced, choose on the strength of the specific department rather than the qualification.

faqs.question: My child has been put on a Core entry for Cambridge maths. Does that matter?
faqs.answer: It matters a great deal. Core papers are capped in the middle of the grade scale, so improvement across Year 11 cannot show in the final grade, and the entry is often decided on evidence produced during exactly the term a transfer student was adjusting. Ask the subject teacher in writing which tier your child is entered for and what evidence would change it, then produce that evidence: timed Extended questions, marked honestly, before the entry deadline rather than after it.

faqs.question: How much does catch-up tutoring cost in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Published market rates put a qualified subject tutor working online at AED 150-300 an hour, with Unitors listing AED 150 for IGCSE and AED 200 for IB, and subject specialists at AED 200-450 and above, with TutorChase at AED 270. Budget online tutoring runs AED 45-150, where EdFlik lists AED 45-65. For a transfer student the budget band is usually poor value, because the hour excludes the marking of the student's own written work, which is the whole point of transition support.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help my child with an Internal Assessment they started at a different school?
faqs.answer: Within the same limits that apply to anyone, and with one extra step. A tutor can teach the criteria letter by letter, test whether the research question is narrow enough, read a draft your child has produced and give feedback on reasoning and structure, and teach the skills on a different example. No text in the submission may originate with the tutor. The extra step is telling the new school plainly what was and was not completed elsewhere, because a submission that does not match classwork invites a conversation nobody wants.

faqs.question: Do tutors need a permit to teach privately in the UAE?
faqs.answer: Yes. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is granted free of charge for two years, with an eligibility list that includes registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE lists the service as Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing with a two-working-day completion time. Anyone tutoring without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws.

faqs.question: We may move country again in two years. Does that change what we should do now?
faqs.answer: It changes the choice of route more than the choice of tutor. A qualification that travels well and is recognised widely is worth more to a mobile family than a marginally better local fit, and the number of assessed components that cannot transfer matters too: a programme with heavy internally assessed work is harder to move partway through than one assessed mainly by external papers. Say this at the start of a conversation about subject and route choice, because it genuinely changes the advice.

abu-dhabi/al-samha.tutorsIntro: The tutors below are matched against the syllabus a child actually sits, which for a boundary household means confirming the school, the emirate and the examination board before anything else. Two children in the same street here can be on different calendars entirely.

intro.heading: A district at the top of the emirate, schooling in two directions
paragraphs: Al Samha lies in the far north of the Abu Dhabi emirate, along the main corridor that runs up towards the Dubai boundary, with Al Shahama and Al Bahia to the south and the industrial and logistics belt alongside. It is not one kind of neighbourhood. There are villa compounds and family housing, there is substantial industrial and warehousing employment, and there is accommodation tied to that employment. The households are correspondingly varied, and so are the academic questions they bring.

Three household patterns dominate. The first is the family working in the northern industrial and energy sector with children in the Al Shahama, Al Bahia or Khalifa City schools, running a bus route that collects early and returns late. The second is the household that works in Dubai and lives here because the rent is lower, with children schooled over the boundary and a daily commute that crosses an emirate line in both directions. The third is the long-resident family with children in national-curriculum or Indian-board schools nearby, increasingly considering a move into IGCSE for the sixth form and the university route.

The question that catches all three out is regulatory rather than academic, and it arrives at the worst moment. A parent assumes that private schools in the UAE are overseen by one body. They are not. Abu Dhabi, which includes Al Samha, Al Ain and Al Dhafra, is regulated by the Department of Education and Knowledge. Dubai, a short drive north, is regulated by the Knowledge and Human Development Authority. Sharjah has its own authority, Ras Al Khaimah has its own department, and the Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. Those are five different bodies with different inspection frameworks, different published guidance and in some cases different fee-approval powers.

For a boundary household this is not trivia. It determines which inspection report applies to your child's school, which framework its rating came from, which guidance governs the mandatory Arabic and Islamic Education provision, and which authority you deal with if you change emirate mid-course. None of the competitor pages examined for this project names the Abu Dhabi regulator at all, and only one mentions the Sharjah authority, so this information is simply not published in this market.

Alongside that, this page states something most providers conceal: where our coverage actually runs out. A household out here asking for a rare Higher Level subject at a specific hour may find nothing available, and it is better to know that at the first conversation than after a deposit has been taken. Everything we do deliver is one-to-one tuition over live video, which is also what makes the boundary irrelevant to the lesson itself, whichever direction the school bus goes in the morning.

abu-dhabi/al-samha.programmesIntro: Families out here run a wider mix of curricula than most districts, so these notes cover what each programme means for a household that may change school, emirate or board during it.

programmes.name: IGCSE
programmes.description: Two-year externally examined courses offered by Cambridge International and Pearson Edexcel. Cambridge tiers several subjects into Core and Extended, with Core capped at grade C, while Pearson tiers mathematics as Foundation and Higher. The board and the tier together decide what papers a student sits.
programmes.countryNote: Portability is the relevant property for a boundary household. An IGCSE taken in Dubai and one taken in Abu Dhabi are the same qualification from the same board, so a move between emirates does not break the course, provided the new school enters the same board. Confirming that in writing before accepting a place avoids a very expensive surprise.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. In the current science guides the internal assessment carries 20% of the subject grade, and the Mathematics exploration the same, which means a fifth of each grade is work produced at home over months.
programmes.countryNote: The Diploma is the least portable route available to a family that may move. Internal assessments are already in progress, the Extended Essay has a supervisor allocated, and subject combinations differ between schools. A move during the second Diploma year should be avoided if there is any choice in the matter.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups marked against four lettered criteria, each out of eight. It assesses process alongside content, which makes reports harder to read than percentage marks and makes a single session decoding a rubric unusually valuable.
programmes.countryNote: MYP students transfer between IB continuum schools reasonably well, and badly into non-IB systems, because criterion-based reporting has no clean equivalent. A household considering a move across the boundary should ask the receiving school how it places MYP arrivals before committing.

programmes.name: A Level
programmes.description: Linear qualifications assessed at the end of the course, with minimal coursework in most subjects. Three or four subjects studied deeply, which suits a student with examination technique already in place and exposes one who has not built it.
programmes.countryNote: The most portable sixth-form route for a mobile household, and the one that matters for the Ministry of Education's British track: one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or better, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, alongside five accredited IGCSE or GCSE subjects at no less than E or grade 3.

abu-dhabi/al-samha.subjectsIntro: Requests from this district concentrate in the examined core subjects, and availability is the thing worth knowing about as much as content, so each note says something about both.

subjects.name: Mathematics (IGCSE)
subjects.description: Widely covered and quick to match. The decision that matters more than the tutor is the tier, since Cambridge Core caps at grade C and that ceiling is permanent for the session in which it is sat.

subjects.name: Physics (IGCSE)
subjects.description: Well covered at IGCSE level. Electricity and waves are the predictable weak strands, and the alternative-to-practical paper rewards experimental conventions that are rarely drilled anywhere and are learnable quickly.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Well covered at IGCSE and thinner at Higher Level in the UAE time zone. Organic mechanisms need handwritten repetition with immediate correction, which is ideal shared-screen work.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Reliably available. Built on unifying themes at Diploma level with heavy unseen-context questioning, where the standard loss is describing a trend when the command term asked for an explanation.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Standard Level sits two papers at 40% each with a 20% exploration; Higher Level adds Paper 3 at 20%. Higher Level demand exceeds supply in this time zone, so a specific weekday hour may not be available at short notice.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics with the graphic display calculator throughout. Generally easier to match than Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, and more modular, so a short session can complete a topic.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language
subjects.description: Well covered and often the fastest grade movement available per hour for households where English is not the home language. Register control and accurate structure carry more weight than vocabulary range.

subjects.name: First Language English
subjects.description: Reliably available. Directed writing and reading response papers rewarding structure and precise reference, where the work that moves marks is a timed response written and then dissected.

subjects.name: Economics and Business
subjects.description: Both carry internally assessed components with school deadlines attached. Coverage is reasonable at Standard Level and thinner for Higher Level Economics Paper 3, which is quantitative and needs a genuine specialist.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first and additional language
subjects.description: Mandatory alongside the international programme in every emirate under the federal rules, with separate provision and different expectations for Arab and non-Arab students. Availability is good; starting at the correct level matters more than starting quickly.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Increasingly requested from this district and one of the thinner subjects in the time zone, particularly at Higher Level. Worth asking about early rather than assuming a match exists in the slot you want.

subjects.name: Accounting
subjects.description: Rule-based and structured, so marks are lost on presentation conventions as much as on understanding. That makes it unusually responsive to a small number of corrective sessions, and coverage is adequate.

abu-dhabi/al-samha.regionsIntro: This district faces two ways, and the relevant geography is the set of school destinations in each direction rather than a single cluster.

regions.name: Al Shahama
regions.note: The established district immediately south, with local school provision and the nearest shopping and services. The shortest school run available from Al Samha, and the one that leaves the most of the afternoon intact.

regions.name: Al Bahia
regions.note: Coastal district south of Al Shahama with residential provision and schools serving the northern suburbs. Reachable within a manageable run, and a frequent destination for Al Samha families wanting to stay inside the emirate.

regions.name: Al Reef
regions.note: Villa and apartment community near the airport, popular with teaching and aviation staff. Relevant both as a school destination and because tutor availability in the emirate is shaped by where teachers actually live.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: The deepest school cluster in the emirate, with the largest British and IB capacity. From Al Samha it is a committed run, and families who choose it should plan tutoring around weekends from the outset.

regions.name: Yas Island
regions.note: East towards the coast with American and British provision. A realistic destination from the northern suburbs, though event weekends reshape the evening traffic and argue for weekend-morning study blocks.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City
regions.note: Mainland district with the emirate's deepest Indian and Pakistani curriculum provision. The usual destination for families keeping a national board before moving into IGCSE for the sixth form.

regions.name: Al Raha Gardens
regions.note: Villa community built around a full IB continuum school, which appeals to households that want to avoid multiple transitions. From here it is a long but single journey rather than a changing one.

regions.name: The Dubai boundary and Jebel Ali side
regions.note: North of Al Samha the emirate changes, and with it the regulator. Households working in Dubai sometimes school over the line, which puts the child under a different authority and a different inspection framework.

schoolClusters.city: The northern suburbs: Al Shahama, Al Bahia and Al Reef
schoolClusters.note: The nearest provision to Al Samha, spanning national-curriculum, Indian-board and British routes. These are the schools that keep the bus run short, which for a household out here is a genuine academic advantage rather than a convenience.

schoolClusters.city: Khalifa City, Al Raha and Yas Island
schoolClusters.note: The deeper set families travel to for IB Diploma and full British sixth-form provision. The academic case is often strong and the journey is long, which is why weekend study patterns dominate among these households.
schools: The British International School Abu Dhabi

abu-dhabi/al-samha.schoolDisclaimer: Schools are named to describe the educational context around Al Samha and the northern suburbs. IB Gram has no affiliation, partnership or endorsement arrangement with any of them, and none is a client.
abu-dhabi/al-samha.modesIntro: Out here the delivery pattern is dictated by the length of the bus run and by whether the household may move. These three cover almost every case.

modes.title: Weekend-led pattern
modes.description: One ninety-minute block at the weekend carrying the heaviest work, plus a short weekday review. This is the default for any household with a long school run, because it puts the demanding work in the only block of the week that is not downstream of a two-hour commute.
bullets: Long enough for a full timed paper or an essay written and dissected
Weekday slot kept short and single-purpose
Set work between the two, inspected at the start of each session
Survives a late bus far better than a weekday evening hour

modes.title: Portable weekly slot
modes.description: For a household that may move emirate or country, the same tutor and the same hour retained through the change. A student who has already lost continuity at school gains more from keeping their tutor than from any other single decision.
bullets: Tutor retained across a change of school or emirate
Board difference identified before the move, not after
Paused and resumed without losing the match
Works from a temporary address during a relocation

modes.title: Coverage-checked matching
modes.description: Before a plan is built, we confirm whether the subject, level and hour you need actually exist in this time zone. For rare Higher Level subjects and some languages they may not, and the right time to learn that is before you arrange the rest of your week around it.
bullets: Subject, level, board and slot checked together

sections.heading: Who regulates your child's school, emirate by emirate
paragraphs: Private schools in the UAE are regulated at emirate level, and for a household near a boundary that is the single most useful fact on this page. Abu Dhabi, which contains Al Samha along with Al Ain and Al Dhafra, is regulated by the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. Dubai is regulated by the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, described as responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in that emirate.

The other three arrangements are less well known. The Sharjah Private Education Authority regulates private education in Sharjah. In Ras Al Khaimah, the Department of Knowledge regulates private education in that emirate. And the Ministry of Education plays a pivotal role in supervising private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. Those five bodies are the complete map, and a parent who knows which one applies can find the right inspection report, the right guidance documents and the right contact point in a few minutes rather than a few weeks.

There is a further power worth knowing about. Sharjah's and Ras Al Khaimah's authorities approve tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods, so in those emirates curriculum and fee approval sits with the emirate regulator rather than only inspection. That is a meaningful difference from a parent's point of view, because it changes who to approach about a fee question or a curriculum change.

Equivalency is the one process that does not vary by emirate. The Ministry of Education handles the recognition of foreign secondary certificates, so wherever your child's school sits, the equivalency file goes to the same place. That is worth knowing early, because the subject spread that file requires has to be in place two years before anyone asks for it.

sections.heading: ADEK or KHDA: what actually changes over the line
paragraphs: For a household in Al Samha with one child in an Abu Dhabi school and another over the Dubai boundary, or considering a move, the useful comparison is not which regulator is better. Both license and oversee private schools in their emirate and both publish material parents can use. What differs is the detail, and the detail is what causes confusion.

Inspection ratings are the clearest example. Each authority runs its own framework and publishes its own ratings, so a band awarded in one emirate is not directly comparable with a band awarded in the other. A parent comparing two schools across the boundary by their published rating is comparing two different measurements, and the honest conclusion is usually that the two numbers cannot be set against each other at all.

Published guidance also differs in depth. Dubai's regulator publishes unusually detailed public documentation on the mandatory Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies provision, including instructional time calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit, advice that any mandatory subject lesson should run at least twenty-five minutes, and a strict prohibition on combining Arab and non-Arab groups in the same class. Abu Dhabi families sit under a different authority, but the federal requirement underneath is the same, which makes that published detail useful reading wherever your child is schooled.

The practical instruction for a boundary household is short. Establish which authority applies to each child's school, read that authority's own report for that school, and do not attempt to convert a rating from one framework into the other. If you move, expect to repeat the exercise rather than to carry the old assessment with you.

sections.heading: The long bus run, and what it leaves of the evening
paragraphs: A child travelling from Al Samha to a Khalifa City or Yas Island school is on a bus route that collects early and returns late, because the route serves several communities before and after. Two hours a day on a bus is normal for these households, and occasionally more. That is the dominant fact in any tutoring plan out here, and it is bigger than any choice of tutor.

What two hours of commuting does is not simply remove time. It removes the best time. The student arrives home in the late afternoon at the lowest point of their energy curve, having done nothing restful on the bus. Attempting demanding academic work in that state produces frustration and the impression that the child cannot cope, when the honest reading is that nobody could.

So the plan inverts. Weekend mornings carry the heavy work, because they are the only hours in the week that are not downstream of the commute. The weekday slot becomes short, defined and low-friction: a marked question set reviewed, a mechanism sheet checked, a draft section read. Twenty-five to forty-five minutes with one output, not a full hour of ambitious content.

There are two mitigations worth knowing. The bus itself can carry light work for an older student, and some do it well, though it suits review and reading rather than writing. And a school closer to home, even one with a slightly less celebrated reputation, buys back two hours a day for five years, which is a larger academic asset than most parents weigh properly when they choose.
bullets: Two hours a day on a bus is normal from this district

sections.heading: Changing school across the boundary mid-course
paragraphs: Households here move school more often than average, usually because a job changes or a rent does. Moving within the same board and curriculum is manageable. Moving across the boundary, or between boards, during an examination course is where real damage happens, and it is almost always avoidable with two questions asked in advance.

The first question is which examination board the receiving school enters for each subject, with the full syllabus code. Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 are both IGCSE Mathematics and they are different examinations with different papers and different tiering. A student who moves in January from one to the other has lost much of the specific preparation they have done, and nobody tells the family this because nobody thinks to.

The second question is what internally assessed work is already in progress and how the receiving school handles a transfer mid-component. In the Diploma, internal assessments, the Extended Essay supervision and subject combinations are all school-specific, and a move in the second year is genuinely disruptive. If there is any flexibility in the timing of a household move, finishing the examination year where the course started is usually the better decision even at some inconvenience.

If a move cannot be avoided, the sequence that works is the same as for any transfer: collect the previous school's final report and last marked work in every subject, confirm board and tier at the new school in writing, then run one diagnostic session per subject to produce a named list of what was covered and what was missed. That list, not a general catch-up block, is what the bridging work should follow.
bullets: Ask the receiving school for the board and full syllabus code per subject
Ask what internally assessed work is in progress and how transfers are handled
Avoid moving during the second Diploma year if there is any choice
If you must move, diagnose topic by topic before booking any lessons

sections.heading: What tutoring costs out here, and what the drive adds to it
paragraphs: This market publishes very little about price. Three of the six competitor pages examined for this project quote no figure at all, and the two that do quote in US dollars rather than dirhams. The bands below are market rates as of October 2026, attributed to whoever published them, and none of them is an IB Gram price list.

Budget online tutoring, generally university students or non-specialists, runs AED 45 to 150 an hour, with EdFlik advertising from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52 at entry tiers. A qualified subject tutor working online is AED 150 to 300, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. In-home one-to-one visits are AED 180 to 500 with travel inside the figure, on Bestimate's 2026 Dubai table and comparable listings. Genuine IB, IGCSE or A Level specialists are AED 200 to 450 and above, with TutorChase publishing AED 270 and premium named tutors at AED 650.

The geography out here changes the in-home end of that range more than it changes the online end. Al Samha is a long way from where most of the emirate's teaching staff live, and a tutor asked to drive up here for a single hour is pricing an hour of travel in each direction. That pushes a visiting tutor towards the upper part of the in-home band and shrinks the pool to whoever happens to live nearby, which is a filter on availability rather than on quality.

Set against this, the online figure is the same here as it is on Saadiyat Island, because distance is not a cost input. For a household already spending two hours a day on a school bus, a format that adds no further travel to anybody is worth more than the headline rate difference suggests.
bullets: Qualified subject tutor, online, market rate: AED 150 to 300 an hour
In-home visits run AED 180 to 500 with travel inside the rate
Distance from the city pushes in-home rates up and availability down

sections.heading: Coverage and fallback: what happens when nobody covers the subject
paragraphs: No competitor page examined for this project discloses a coverage limit, and several conceal non-local delivery behind a phone number from another country. We would rather publish ours, because a household organising its week around an arrangement that does not exist is worse off than one told no at the start.

The pattern is straightforward. The common examined subjects at IGCSE level are reliably covered and match quickly. Diploma Standard Level across the mainstream subjects is generally available. Higher Level sciences and Higher Level Mathematics are in demand and the four to five o'clock weekday window is the most contested in this time zone, so a specific hour may not be free even where the subject is. The less common Diploma languages, Higher Level Computer Science and a handful of specialist options are genuinely thin, and for some combinations there may be nothing at all.

When there is no match, there are three honest alternatives and one dishonest one. The honest options are a different day or hour, a tutor working from another time zone where the subject is better covered, or a shorter block aimed at a specific component rather than a weekly arrangement. The dishonest option is to put a generalist in front of a Higher Level paper and hope, which happens routinely in this market and is discovered around the February mock.

The table below is what we would actually tell a household in this district, by subject and level. It is deliberately specific about match times, because vagueness about availability is how families end up waiting three weeks for a tutor who was never coming.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies across two regulators
paragraphs: Whichever side of the boundary your child is schooled, the mandatory UAE subjects apply. Private schools are not obliged to follow a specific national curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That federal rule is the reason these subjects sit on the timetable of every international school in the country, and it does not change when you cross an emirate line.

What does change is the published detail. Dubai's authority has issued unusually specific public guidance, which states that these subjects must be implemented by the start of the relevant academic year, requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students on the grounds of different curriculum expectations and language of instruction, prohibits combining the two groups, specifies Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, and calculates instructional time on a forty-minute lesson unit with the advice that no mandatory subject lesson should run under twenty-five minutes. Abu Dhabi schools sit under a different authority and the same federal requirement, so that guidance is worth reading as context rather than as the local rule.

There is one constraint that directly affects tutoring. For the mandatory subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry is not permitted. That is why legitimate support in these subjects is focused on language skill, script fluency and the specific assessment the school uses, rather than on supplying alternative material. A tutor offering their own curriculum for these subjects is offering something that is not allowed.

And the equivalency point, which costs families real grades when missed: Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five accredited subjects the Ministry requires on the GCSE and IGCSE track. A student who counts them towards the five can reach the end of Year 11 a subject short of what their university file needs, and that is a discovery with no good remedy.
bullets: The mandatory subjects apply on both sides of the boundary
Dubai's authority publishes the most detailed public guidance on them
