sections.heading: Where a tutor stops on assessed work
paragraphs: Every programme available to a household here carries work produced away from the examination hall: a Diploma internal assessment in each subject, the Extended Essay at 4,000 words, the Theory of Knowledge essay at 1,600, the MYP Personal Project, coursework in some IGCSE subjects. That work must be the student's own, and a breach is recorded against the student. It can cost a diploma outright.

A tutor interrogates the research question until it can be answered inside the word limit. A tutor says that a planned method will not generate data capable of supporting a conclusion, before any data exists. A tutor reads a draft against the published criteria, names the criterion that is currently unevidenced, teaches the missing skill and returns the work. A tutor asks a student to justify a paragraph aloud, which exposes borrowed reasoning faster than any detection tool.

A tutor does not supply text, rewrite a section into something the student could not have produced, edit a draft to completion, or hand over a topic, structure or data set ready-made. Nothing is bought in from anywhere. One operation in this market sells completed Diploma internal assessments outright, and it is sold hardest to families under pressure, which in a district with long commutes and tight schedules describes a great many households.

We also do not supply or reproduce subject guides, past papers, mark schemes or grade-boundary tables from the IB, Cambridge or Pearson. They belong to the boards and your child's school holds them legitimately. A provider advertising a library of board documents has told you how it treats rules generally, which is worth knowing before anything is paid.
bullets: Questions, methods and criteria coaching, placed as early as possible
Feedback against published criteria, on the student's own text only
No supplied text, no rewriting to completion, no ready-made topics or data
Board materials referenced and linked, never redistributed

sections.heading: Starting from Al Samha
paragraphs: Three pieces of information before anything is booked. Which school and in which emirate, because that establishes the regulator, the board and the calendar. The actual bus times, both directions, because that determines which slots are real and which are theoretical. And the most recent marked work in the subject that worries you, because it distinguishes a content gap from a technique problem from a child who is simply exhausted by a commute.

That third distinction matters more out here than anywhere. A student scoring poorly after two hours on a bus and a seven o'clock session is not necessarily a student with an academic problem, and treating fatigue as a knowledge gap means buying lessons that cannot work. Sometimes the correct recommendation is to move the session to Saturday morning and buy nothing else at all, and when the evidence says that, we say it.

Then a diagnostic session rather than an introduction. The tutor works through the script with your child, establishes what is happening, and writes down what a term of work would consist of and in which slot. You keep that plan whether or not you continue with us. If a move across the boundary is on the horizon, the plan also records the board and syllabus codes so that the question gets asked of the receiving school in advance.

Finally, the market note every parent in the UAE should have. Individuals providing private lessons need a private tuition work permit from the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years, with eligibility covering teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Operating without one carries fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule has been published, so treat any amount quoted to you as unverified. The permit is federal, so it does not change if your household crosses the boundary.
bullets: School and emirate first, because they set regulator, board and calendar
Real bus times decide which slots exist; theoretical ones collapse
Fatigue and knowledge gaps look the same on a report and need different answers
The MoHRE permit is federal and free; ask about it wherever you are

process.title: Name the school and the emirate
process.description: Which school, and on which side of the boundary. That establishes the regulator whose inspection report applies, the examination board the school enters for, and the calendar your child is actually working to. Two children in the same street out here can be on entirely different academic years.

process.title: Write down the real bus times
process.description: Both directions, as they actually run rather than as the school timetable describes them. A two-hour daily commute decides which slots exist and which are fiction, and it is the reason weekend-led patterns work out here where weekday evening hours collapse by November.

process.title: Send the last marked work
process.description: Where marks left the page distinguishes a content gap from a technique habit from plain exhaustion. Those three need completely different responses, and only one of them is solved by buying lessons. The script tells us which, and occasionally it tells us to recommend nothing.

process.title: Check coverage before building the week
process.description: We confirm whether the subject, level and hour you want exist in this time zone before you arrange anything around them. For rare Higher Level subjects the answer is sometimes no, and a clear no at the first conversation is worth more than a three-week wait for a tutor who was never coming.

process.title: Fix a weekend-led pattern and measure it
process.description: One long weekend block for the heavy work, one short weekday review, set work in between, and a measurement on a real paper after about twelve weeks. If the marks have not moved, the plan changes or the tutor does. The pattern is chosen to survive a late bus, not to look tidy.

whyPoints.title: The regulator map, published in full
whyPoints.description: Five authorities oversee private schools across the UAE, and for a boundary household knowing which applies is practical rather than academic. None of the competitor pages examined names the Abu Dhabi regulator at all, and only one mentions Sharjah's, so this is simply not published in this market.

whyPoints.title: Coverage limits disclosed up front
whyPoints.description: Higher Level sciences are hour-dependent, Higher Level Computer Science is thin, and some Diploma languages may have no match. We publish that table rather than concealing it, because a household that plans its week around an arrangement that does not exist has been actively harmed.

whyPoints.title: Built for a two-hour commute
whyPoints.description: Weekend mornings carry the heavy work because they are the only hours not downstream of the bus. Weekday slots stay short and single-purpose. Treating a tired student as a weak student is the commonest misdiagnosis out here, and it leads families to buy exactly the wrong thing.

whyPoints.title: Rates attributed, and distance-neutral
whyPoints.description: Every dirham band here names who published it and when. Online rates do not vary with distance from the city, while a visiting tutor asked to drive to Al Samha prices two hours of travel into one hour of teaching, which narrows the pool as well as raising the price.

whyPoints.title: No borrowed authority, either side of the line
whyPoints.description: We explain what ADEK and KHDA each do and point to the Ministry for equivalency. IB Gram holds no accreditation, licence or partnership from either authority, from the Ministry, or from the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, operates no UAE office, and claims none of it anywhere.

whyPoints.title: Honest about when to buy nothing
whyPoints.description: Sometimes the right advice is to move the session to Saturday, ask the school for its free support, and spend nothing further. We would rather give that advice and be recommended than sell a weekly hour that the commute was always going to defeat.

faqs.question: Which authority regulates my child's school if we live in Al Samha?
faqs.answer: The Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the Abu Dhabi emirate, including Al Samha, Al Ain and Al Dhafra. If your child is schooled over the Dubai boundary, the Knowledge and Human Development Authority applies instead. These are two separate bodies with their own inspection frameworks and their own published guidance, so the report that applies to your child's school is the one issued by the authority for the emirate the school sits in, not the one you live in.

faqs.question: Can I compare a Dubai school's inspection rating with an Abu Dhabi one?
faqs.answer: Not directly, and it is a mistake worth avoiding. Each authority runs its own inspection framework and publishes its own ratings, so a band awarded in one emirate is a different measurement from a band awarded in the other. Comparing two schools across the boundary by their published ratings alone compares two incomparable things. Read each authority's own report for the specific school, look at the phase and the subjects your child will study, and treat the overall band as background rather than as a score.

faqs.question: Which emirates do not have their own education regulator?
faqs.answer: Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah, where the Ministry of Education plays a pivotal role in supervising private schools directly. Dubai has the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, Abu Dhabi has the Department of Education and Knowledge, Sharjah has the Sharjah Private Education Authority and Ras Al Khaimah has the Department of Knowledge. Those five arrangements cover the whole country, and knowing which applies lets a parent find the right report and the right contact point in minutes rather than weeks.

faqs.question: Does moving from an Abu Dhabi school to a Dubai one break an IGCSE course?
faqs.answer: Not if the board is the same, because an IGCSE from Cambridge or Pearson is the same qualification wherever it is sat. What breaks a course is a change of board, since Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 are different examinations with different papers and different tiering. Before accepting any new place, ask the receiving school in writing for the examination board and full syllabus code for every examined subject. That single question prevents the most expensive mistake available to a mobile household.

faqs.question: How long is the school bus run from the northern suburbs?
faqs.answer: Two hours a day in total is normal for a child travelling to a Khalifa City, Al Raha or Yas Island school, and occasionally more, because the route serves several communities before and after yours. The academic consequence is bigger than the lost time: the student arrives home at the lowest point of their energy curve having done nothing restful. Demanding work scheduled into that state produces frustration and a misleading impression that the child cannot cope with the course.

faqs.question: Should we choose a closer school even if it is less well regarded?
faqs.answer: It deserves more weight than most families give it. A school thirty minutes closer buys back roughly two hours a day for five years, which is a very large academic asset, and it buys back the specific hours that are most useful for independent study. That is not an argument for ignoring quality. It is an argument for comparing a published rating difference, which may not even be comparable across emirates, against ten hours a week of your child's best time.

faqs.question: Why does the four to five o'clock slot get taken so quickly?
faqs.answer: Because it is the most contested hour in this time zone. Every family in the country wants the slot immediately after school, which means demand for popular subjects at that hour exceeds the supply of specialists who teach them. For a household out here the practical answer is usually a weekend-led pattern: the long block at the weekend where availability is better and energy is higher, plus a short weekday review in whatever slot exists. That combination is also academically better, not merely easier to book.

faqs.question: What if you have no tutor for Higher Level Computer Science?
faqs.answer: Then we say so at the first conversation rather than taking a deposit against an availability we cannot confirm. Higher Level Computer Science is one of the thinner subjects in this time zone, along with some Diploma languages and a handful of specialist combinations. The alternatives we can offer are a tutor working from another time zone, a component-focused block rather than a weekly arrangement, or a clear no. What we will not do is put a generalist in front of a Higher Level paper and hope.

faqs.question: Does a tutor permit change if we move to another emirate?
faqs.answer: No. The private tuition work permit is issued by the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, which makes it federal rather than emirate-level, so it applies wherever in the UAE the tutoring happens. It is granted free of charge for two years and the eligibility list is broad, covering registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Ask any tutor whether they hold it; the question costs nothing.

faqs.question: Do tutors travel to Al Samha for home lessons?
faqs.answer: Not through us. IB Gram does not make home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India, and Abu Dhabi lessons run one-to-one over live video. Independent in-home tutors do exist, and from this district the economics are poor: most of the emirate's teaching staff live a long way south, so a visiting tutor prices an hour of travel in each direction into the rate, which pushes it towards the top of the AED 180 to 500 market band and shrinks the available pool sharply.

faqs.question: Are the mandatory UAE subjects different in Dubai and Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: The requirement is the same because it is federal: private schools must teach Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside their licensed curriculum. What differs is the published detail. Dubai's authority issues unusually specific guidance, including separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students, Standard Arabic as the language of instruction in defined cases, and instructional time calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit. Abu Dhabi schools sit under their own authority with the same federal requirement underneath.

faqs.question: Do Arabic and Islamic Education count towards the equivalency subjects?
faqs.answer: No, and this is the detail that costs families real grades. On the British track the Ministry of Education requires five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at no less than grade E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five. One accredited A Level at grade E or better, or two AS Levels at the same grade, is also required. A student counting the mandatory subjects towards the five can finish Year 11 a subject short with no good remedy available.

faqs.question: My child is exhausted rather than struggling. Is tutoring the answer?
faqs.answer: Often not, and this is the commonest misdiagnosis in districts with long commutes. A student scoring poorly after two hours on a bus and a seven o'clock session may have no academic problem at all, and buying weekly lessons into that situation cannot work because the hour itself is the problem. The honest first interventions are moving the work to a weekend morning, shortening the weekday slot to a single defined task, and asking the school what support it offers during the day. Sometimes the correct recommendation is to spend nothing.

faqs.question: What should we ask a receiving school before transferring mid-year?
faqs.answer: Two questions. First, the examination board and full syllabus code for every examined subject, because a board change mid-course wastes much of the preparation already done. Second, what internally assessed work is already in progress and how the school handles a transfer part-way through a component, since Diploma internal assessments, Extended Essay supervision and subject combinations are all school-specific. If the household move has any flexibility, finishing the examination year where the course started is usually worth real inconvenience.

faqs.question: Is there any free support we should use before paying for a tutor?
faqs.answer: Almost certainly. Ask the school directly what it provides: a homework club, a supervised library hour, subject support sessions, revision classes before a series. Many schools run several of these and most parents never ask. For a student whose real problem is two hours of commuting and nowhere settled to work, a supervised hour inside the school day is worth more than a paid hour at home in the evening, and it costs nothing at all.

abu-dhabi/al-samha.closingHeading: Name the school, the emirate and the bus times
abu-dhabi/al-samha.closingBody: Those three facts decide almost everything for a household in Al Samha. The school and emirate establish which authority's inspection report applies, which board your child sits and which calendar binds them. The bus times decide which tutoring slots are real rather than theoretical, which out here usually points to a weekend-led pattern. Send those three along with the most recent marked work and the first session becomes a diagnosis rather than an introduction, including an honest answer about whether lessons are what your child needs at all. Everything we deliver runs one-to-one over live video, so no part of the plan depends on anyone driving up the coast at five o'clock.

intro.heading: The hours nobody timetables
paragraphs: Count the Diploma Programme honestly and the arithmetic is uncomfortable. Six subjects, three internal assessments at Higher Level and three more at Standard, a four-thousand-word Extended Essay, a Theory of Knowledge essay and exhibition, and a CAS portfolio. Of that list, the school timetables the teaching and perhaps six supervision meetings. Everything else happens in a bedroom in Al Shamkha between seven and eleven at night, unsupervised, by a seventeen-year-old who has never written a scientific report before and is about to write one that counts.

At IGCSE the shape is different and the gap is just as wide. A Year 11 student is carrying eight to ten subjects, each with a two-year back-catalogue, and the school's revision programme starts in the final term. Past-paper practice is where the grade is actually decided, and almost all of it is done alone. Students who attempt papers untimed with their notes open produce a mark that tells nobody anything, then feel ambushed in the real thing. That is a technique failure, not a knowledge failure, and it is fixable in about four sessions, because the fix is a habit rather than a syllabus. The subjects where this bites hardest are the tiered ones, maths and the sciences, where the long structured questions on the higher papers reward a student who has learned to read the command word, allocate the minutes and move on when a part is not coming.

Al Shamkha adds its own constraint. This is a large mainland villa community out towards Al Falah and Zayed City, and few families here have a private international school inside the district. Children travel, often twenty to forty minutes each way, which compresses the evening further. A household that gets home at five has four usable hours before a sensible bedtime, and school homework, the mandatory Arabic and Islamic studies work, and whatever internal assessment is due all compete for the same block.

The mandatory stream deserves naming because it is routinely forgotten in planning. Private schools in the Emirates are not obliged to follow any particular curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and must still comply with the Ministry's general regulations. For a student in a British or IB school in Al Shamkha that means real periods, real homework and real reporting in subjects that sit outside the qualification they are working towards, and for Arab students the first-language Arabic course is taught and assessed in Standard Arabic.

Tutoring here is therefore not generic help with maths. It is paid supervision of the unsupervised hours: the report format taught before the first attempt, papers sat under timed conditions and marked against the published scheme, and a calendar that counts backwards from an entry deadline rather than forwards from today. Every lesson runs one-to-one over live video, because the specialist who can teach the Chemistry internal assessment criteria is chosen for that skill, not for living near Al Shamkha.

abu-dhabi/al-shamkha.programmesIntro: Three stages account for nearly every enquiry from this district. What follows is what each one hands to the student rather than to the teacher, because that is the part a tutor can actually change.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four criteria per subject, each marked out of eight, with descriptors rather than percentages. The student-time work here is the open-ended task: an investigation, a design cycle, a piece of reflective writing. Students who have never been shown a descriptor in plain English write something competent and score in the middle band for years without understanding why.
programmes.countryNote: Al Shamkha students moving between an MYP school and a GCSE school find the content similar and the reporting unrecognisable. The useful tutoring intervention is short and specific: take one marked task, read the descriptors aloud, and rewrite the piece to hit the next band. Two sessions of that usually moves a criterion score more than a term of general subject help.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The internal assessments carry roughly a fifth to a quarter of most subject grades and are produced almost entirely outside lessons. The Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge are graded together towards the diploma points. All of it lands in the same stretch of Year 13, alongside university applications and predicted grades.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi schools enter the May session, so for an Al Shamkha student the real pressure point is the autumn of Year 13 rather than the spring. Internal assessment drafts, the Extended Essay final submission and predicted grades converge there. Confirm every IB date with the school's Diploma coordinator or on ibo.org, because secondary sources for IB session dates are not reliable enough to plan a year around.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Eight to ten subjects, tiered in maths and the sciences on Cambridge specifications, with a fixed entry deadline months before the first paper. The student-time work is the back-catalogue: two years of content to re-learn and a stack of past papers to sit properly. Grades move when the practice is timed and marked, not when the notes are re-read.
programmes.countryNote: Cambridge runs June and November series with a March series for some specifications, and allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones. Cambridge states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. Check which zone the school sits in before trusting any timetable printed from the internet.

abu-dhabi/al-shamkha.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects Al Shamkha households ask about most, described by the component that costs them marks rather than by a syllabus summary.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Paper 3 at Higher Level is an extended investigation and the single component students practise least, because the school rarely has time to set a full one. Proof by induction and the harder calculus questions reward written justification; an unexplained correct answer collects a minority of the marks available.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistical routines on the graphical display calculator decide whole questions: regression, chi-squared, hypothesis testing. Students who never drilled the calculator sequences lose marks they knew the theory for. Higher Level adds matrices, graph theory and Voronoi diagrams, none of it familiar from IGCSE.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: The internal assessment is the component most often left too late. A twelve-page report with its own criteria, written by a student who has not been taught the format, is the normal first draft. Organic mechanisms and energetics carry the heaviest Higher Level content load.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Uncertainty handling separates the top two grades from the rest, in Paper 2 and again in the practical report. Fields and circuits are where the quantitative work gets genuinely hard, and where students who learned definitions rather than relationships stop being able to progress.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Marks go on precision of language and on statistics. A six-mark question on transport across membranes needs the right terms in the right sequence. The internal assessment requires a statistical test chosen and justified, which catches out students who picked biology to avoid maths.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580
subjects.description: Extended sits on Papers 2 and 4; Core on Papers 1 and 3. They are different papers, so practice material does not transfer between tiers. A Core entry caps the grade whatever happens on the day, which is why the tier conversation belongs in Year 10.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 and Pearson 4PH1
subjects.description: Electricity, moments and momentum account for most marks lost. The Cambridge alternative-to-practical paper tests experimental reasoning on paper, and rewards a student who has learned to criticise someone else's method rather than recite their own.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language and First Language English
subjects.description: The two courses grade very differently and the choice has consequences years later for university entry conditions. ESL rewards accurate controlled writing; First Language English rewards register, structure and reading inference under time pressure.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language
subjects.levels: The mandatory stream, MYP and DP Language A
subjects.description: Assessed on grammar, classical and modern texts and formal written register, in Standard Arabic. Arab students in international schools sit this course, and the recurring gap is between confident spoken dialect and examined written Standard Arabic, which are separate skills.

sections.heading: What the school day covers, and what it hands back
paragraphs: An Al Shamkha parent who feels that the school is teaching properly and the grades are still sliding is usually right on both counts. Schools are resourced to deliver the taught syllabus to a class. They are not resourced to supervise six individual internal assessments per student, to mark forty past papers a term per child, or to sit beside a seventeen-year-old while she learns what a scientific report looks like. Those tasks are handed to the student, and the student is the least experienced person in the arrangement.

The effect is invisible until it is not. A Year 12 who is fine in class produces a first internal assessment draft that scores badly, not because the chemistry is wrong but because the report has no hypothesis stated in testable terms, no uncertainty treatment and no evaluation worth the name. A Year 11 revising diligently by re-reading notes sits a mock and scores two grades below the predicted. Both students worked. Neither was taught the thing they were being assessed on.

This is a different diagnosis from the one most tutoring is sold against. The question is not whether your child understands enzymes or quadratics. It is which specific assessed skill is unpractised, and whether it is being practised in conditions that resemble the exam. That is also why a tutor who asks for a recent marked paper before quoting is more useful than one who asks which subject you want.

sections.heading: Core or Extended: the tier decision Al Shamkha families make too late
paragraphs: On Cambridge IGCSE specifications in maths and the sciences, students are entered for either the Core or the Extended tier, and the two are not the same examination. The Core entry caps the available grade. That is not a judgement about a child; it is an administrative fact with a deadline attached, and it is the single most consequential decision taken in Year 10 for a student who may later want a Diploma place or a British sixth form.

The decision gets made late for an understandable reason. Teachers want as much evidence as possible before committing, parents do not want to limit a child, and the entry deadline feels distant until it is not. For the March 2027 series, Cambridge sets final entries at 27 November 2026 - more than two months before the first paper on 3 February 2027. After that date the tier is effectively fixed, and the supplementary content on the Extended papers represents roughly a term of additional teaching.

A tutor's useful role here is diagnostic rather than persuasive. Sit the student on a past Paper 2 and a past Paper 4 under timed conditions, mark both against the published scheme, and the conversation stops being about confidence and becomes about marks. If the Extended paper produces a weak but recoverable score with eight months left, the honest advice is usually to commit to Extended and work. If it produces nothing at all in Year 11 spring, Core may genuinely protect a pass.

The same logic applies to the English choice between First Language English and English as a Second Language, and to the Pearson Edexcel specifications, which are structured differently again. The common thread is that these choices are reversible only before an entry deadline, and that the deadline is published by the board months in advance for exactly this reason.

sections.heading: The exam calendar counted backwards
paragraphs: No competing page found for this kind of search names an exam session, an entry deadline or a results date. That absence is strange, because the dates are the plan. A tutoring arrangement built forwards from today produces a vague number of hours; one built backwards from a published entry deadline produces a sequence with checkpoints in it.

Cambridge runs its International GCSE, O Level and International A Level examinations in a June series and a November series, with a March series for some specifications and Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. Every centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, and Cambridge is explicit that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong one. Before planning around any timetable, confirm the school's zone with the examinations officer.

Pearson Edexcel International GCSE examinations are available in May and June and again in November each year. The November 2026 final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026, while November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026 - a lag that any retake plan has to absorb, because the decision to re-enter often has to be made before the previous result is in hand. Pearson also publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, so the live official timetable is the only version worth working from.

IB dates are deliberately absent from the table below. Abu Dhabi schools sit the May session, and that much is safe to say. Specific session and results dates for the IB have not been confirmed from the IB's own site for this page, so confirm each one with your school's Diploma coordinator or on ibo.org before building a revision plan around it. A tutoring provider quoting IB dates without naming its source is guessing, and a guess that moves a revision plan by two weeks is worse than no date at all.

sections.heading: Where the marks actually go, subject by subject
paragraphs: Generic revision advice fails because marks are lost in specific, diagnosable places. In Cambridge IGCSE maths at Extended tier, the recurring losses are in transformations of graphs, vectors, and the long structured questions on Paper 4 where a student does the hard step and then fails to answer the question that was asked. In physics it is electricity and the moments and momentum questions; in chemistry it is mole calculations and the qualitative analysis tables learned as a list rather than as chemistry.

At Diploma level the pattern moves from content to method. In Analysis and Approaches the losses are in justification: the assumption unstated, the step unexplained, the conclusion not tied back to the question. In the sciences they are in uncertainty, in the evaluation sections of the internal assessment, and in the habit of describing a graph rather than arguing from it. In economics it is diagram accuracy under time pressure, and in English it is the unseen text on Paper 1, which schools have least time to drill.

Across every subject there is one shared loss that costs more than any topic: unanswered questions. A student who runs out of time on the last twelve marks has lost more than a student who misunderstood a topic, and the cause is pacing rather than knowledge. Timed practice with a visible clock is the only thing that fixes it, and it is the thing students avoid most, because it feels worse than reading notes.

The practical consequence for an Al Shamkha family is that the first session should produce a list, not a plan. Which paper, which question numbers, which marks, which cause. Everything after that is just working through the list in order of how many marks each item is worth, which is both duller and more effective than a general revision programme.

sections.heading: What tutoring costs around Al Shamkha, with the sources named
paragraphs: Most pages competing for this search publish no price. Where a figure does appear it is often in US dollars, which no household in this district pays in. The bands below are AED, drawn from providers' own published rate pages and from Bestimate's 2026 Dubai tutoring cost table, and they describe the market rather than IB Gram's own quote.

A budget online tutor, usually a university student, sits between AED 45 and 150 an hour; EdFlik advertises from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from the low thirties. A qualified subject tutor working online sits between AED 150 and 300; Unitors publishes IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. A tutor travelling to a home runs AED 180 to 500 once travel is accounted for, with Bestimate quoting 180 to 350 and independent home tutors 200 to 500. An IB, IGCSE or A Level specialist sits at AED 200 to 450 and above, and TutorChase publishes AED 270. A premium named tutor can reach AED 650, which BartyED states openly.

Monthly figures are more useful for budgeting. Bestimate's estimates for one weekly hour run AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 in the middle, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year support. Advertised packages have included around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour visits at home. Those two numbers, side by side, are the clearest statement available of what travel costs.

For coursework supervision the market quotes blocks rather than months, and that is the honest shape of the work: a research question, a format, two rounds of feedback, done. IB Gram quotes after a consultation and a trial lesson, because an hour of Higher Level chemistry internal assessment supervision and an hour of Year 8 maths are different purchases and a single advertised rate would misrepresent one of them.

sections.heading: How a one-to-one online lesson actually runs from Al Shamkha
paragraphs: Parents in this district reasonably want to know what they are buying before the first session, because online tutoring covers everything from a recorded video library to a genuine one-to-one lesson. What runs here is the latter: one tutor, one student, live video, a shared whiteboard, and a document camera or phone stand pointed at paper when the work has to be handwritten, which in maths and the sciences it usually does.

A typical hour has a shape. The first ten minutes review the practice set since the last session, with specific errors pulled out. The middle forty are new teaching or worked questions, written out live rather than talked about, because a student watching a solution appear learns more than a student listening to one described. The last ten set the next practice and record what was covered. Annotated pages are saved and sent afterwards, so the student has the marked version rather than a memory of it.

The requirements are modest and worth checking before the trial. A laptop or tablet rather than a phone, wired or strong wireless internet, headphones, a pen and paper in frame, and a room where a door closes. In a villa that is usually straightforward. The one thing that reliably spoils a lesson is a shared family screen in a living room with a television on, and it is worth solving before paying for the hour.

IB Gram does not run home visits in the UAE - that service exists only in India - and every Emirates lesson is online. The practical gain for Al Shamkha specifically is the size of the pool. A household here is forty minutes from the island and further from anywhere else, so a requirement for a Higher Level chemistry specialist on a Tuesday at six has a very short list of local candidates and a long list of online ones.

sections.heading: UAE equivalency for a British curriculum student
paragraphs: Families in Al Shamkha planning on a UAE university need the Ministry of Education equivalency rules, and this is one of the areas where competing pages are either silent or wrong. For the British track, a student must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, and must submit proof of one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade.

Two details matter and are frequently misreported. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects for the GCSE and IGCSE count. And the number is five, not six: at least one page ranking for these queries tells UAE parents they need six IGCSE subjects, which is not what the published clarification says. If a provider cannot tell you where its number came from, treat the number as unverified.

For the American track the same clarification sets English proficiency through a score of 5 in the academic IELTS, 61 in the TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, with mathematics requiring at least 450 in the SAT Math test before applying. No IB points threshold appears in that source, so no figure for the IB is published on this page. Anyone quoting one should be asked for the moe.gov.ae page it came from.

Two further points, said plainly. Equivalency and attestation are processes run by the Ministry and the emirate authorities, not services IB Gram performs, and nothing on this page should be read as a guarantee about an outcome. And tutoring is not a requirement for equivalency, university admission or school progression; it is a way of raising a grade. Anyone framing a regulatory process as a reason you must buy tuition is selling urgency rather than teaching.

sections.heading: Past papers, mark schemes and what we will not send you
paragraphs: A request that arrives most weeks from exam-year families is for a bundle of past papers, mark schemes and syllabus documents to keep. The answer is no, and the reason is worth stating because several providers in this market answer yes. Examination papers, mark schemes, grade boundary tables and subject guides are the copyright of Cambridge, Pearson and the IB. Reproducing them or supplying them as downloads is infringement, and for unreleased material it is also an examination-security problem.

What works instead is both legal and more useful. Papers are referenced precisely - series, paper number, question number - and linked to the official source, which for Cambridge and Pearson means the boards' own sites and for IB material means the school's subject teacher or coordinator, who has legitimate access. Schools hold licences that parents do not, and the student's own teacher is frequently the fastest route to the right paper.

In a lesson the paper is on screen under the tutor's own legitimate access, worked through question by question, and what the student keeps is their own attempt with annotation on it. That is the artefact that has value anyway. A folder of unattempted papers changes nothing; one marked paper with the four recurring errors circled changes the next one.

The same principle governs grade boundaries. Published boundaries vary by series and are released by the boards; a tutor quoting a fixed percentage for a grade 7 across all series is inventing a constant that does not exist. The useful version of that conversation is about marks on this paper, not about an imagined threshold.

process.title: Send a recent marked paper, not a subject name
process.description: The fastest diagnosis comes from a mock or a piece of marked coursework. Which questions lost marks, and why, tells a specialist more in five minutes than a description of the problem does in an hour. If nothing marked exists, the trial lesson starts with a short timed paper instead.

process.title: Confirm the board, the code and the tier
process.description: Cambridge 0580 Extended is a different purchase from Pearson 4MA1, and Analysis and Approaches is a different purchase from Applications and Interpretation. The school's entry confirmation or the header on a past paper settles it. For Cambridge entries, ask the examinations officer which timetable zone the school sits in.

process.title: Set the slot against the real arrival time
process.description: For an Al Shamkha household the commute decides the schedule. We ask what time the last child is genuinely home, which evenings are already taken, and whether Ramadan timing will move the slot later in the year. A slot that ignores the school run collapses within a month.

process.title: Trial lesson with the tutor who would teach the term
process.description: One hour with the matched specialist rather than a conversation with a coordinator. It ends with a short written view: whether the problem is content, technique or pacing, and what the first four sessions would do about it. If the match is wrong we rematch instead of arguing.

process.title: Work the calendar backwards each term
process.description: Entry deadlines, mock windows, the school's internal coursework dates and the series the student is entered for all go on one sheet, and the plan runs back from them. That is also when a retake or review-of-results decision gets diarised, rather than discovered after the window has closed.

whyPoints.title: The unsupervised hours are the product
whyPoints.description: The tutoring here is aimed squarely at the components the school hands to the student: internal assessments, the Extended Essay, timed paper practice. That is where marks are being lost in this district, and it is a narrower and more fixable target than general subject support.

whyPoints.title: Dates from the boards, not from a blog
whyPoints.description: Every entry deadline and results date on this page is attributed to Cambridge or Pearson. Where a date could not be confirmed from an official source, as with the IB sessions, it is left out and you are pointed at the coordinator instead of given a guess.

whyPoints.title: Marked against the published scheme
whyPoints.description: Practice papers are marked against the official mark scheme rather than a tutor's impression, which is the only way the resulting number means anything. The output of a session is a list of marks lost and causes, not an encouraging comment.

whyPoints.title: Legal about materials
whyPoints.description: No papers, mark schemes or syllabus documents are supplied as downloads, because they belong to the boards. They are referenced, linked and worked through in the lesson, and the student keeps their own annotated attempt.

whyPoints.title: Clear about coursework boundaries
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches the subject, explains the criteria, questions the research scope and gives feedback on work the student wrote. No supplied text, at any stage, in any component. The student signs an authenticity declaration and the consequences of a breach fall on them.

whyPoints.title: Scheduled around a mainland commute
whyPoints.description: Lesson times are built from the household's real arrival time, including Ramadan adjustments and the later post-Iftar slots many families prefer. The flexibility exists because nobody is driving anywhere, which is the practical benefit of an online format in a district this far out.

faqs.question: How much of the IB Diploma is actually done outside lessons?
faqs.answer: More than most parents expect. Six subject internal assessments, a four-thousand-word Extended Essay, a Theory of Knowledge essay and exhibition and a CAS portfolio are all produced largely in the student's own time, with the school providing teaching and a limited number of supervision meetings. The internal assessments alone carry roughly a fifth to a quarter of each subject grade. For a student in Al Shamkha with a long daily commute, those hours compete directly with homework and the mandatory Arabic stream, which is why the work slips rather than being done badly.

faqs.question: Is there an IB school inside Al Shamkha itself?
faqs.answer: Families in this district generally travel for private international schooling. The nearest significant concentration of Cambridge IGCSE places sits around Mohammed Bin Zayed City, while British sixth forms and full IB continuum schools are mostly in Khalifa City and the Al Raha corridor, twenty-five to forty minutes away depending on the junction. Check your own child's school against the Department of Education and Knowledge listing rather than a directory, because ADEK licenses and inspects private schools in the emirate and its record is the authoritative one.

faqs.question: What does an online tutor cost for an Al Shamkha family?
faqs.answer: The published market bands in AED are the right starting point. A qualified subject tutor working online runs roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, with Unitors advertising IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. Specialists in IB, IGCSE or A Level sit at AED 200 to 450 and above, and TutorChase publishes AED 270. Budget university-student tutors start nearer AED 45 to 65. IB Gram quotes after a consultation and trial lesson rather than publishing one rate, because coursework supervision and Year 8 maths are not the same hour of work.

faqs.question: My child's school says she is on track but her mocks say otherwise. Which is right?
faqs.answer: Usually both, measuring different things. Classwork measures understanding with support available; a mock measures performance alone, to time, with no notes. A student can genuinely understand the material and still lose twenty per cent of the available marks to pacing, unanswered final questions and not answering the question asked. The fix is not more content teaching. It is timed papers marked against the published scheme until the gap between the two measurements closes, which generally takes four to six properly run sessions.

faqs.question: Should my child be entered for Cambridge IGCSE Core or Extended?
faqs.answer: Decide it on evidence, in Year 10, not in the spring of Year 11. Core caps the grade available on most syllabuses at C or 5, so a student who may want a Diploma place or a British sixth form needs Extended. Sit a past Paper 2 and a past Paper 4 under timed conditions, mark both against the official scheme, and the decision becomes arithmetic rather than opinion. Remember the deadline: for the March 2027 series Cambridge sets final entries at 27 November 2026, after which the tier is effectively fixed.

faqs.question: When do IGCSE entries actually close?
faqs.answer: Months before the papers, which surprises families every year. Cambridge sets final entries for the March 2027 series at 27 November 2026, with the examination period running 3 February to 4 March 2027 and forecast grades due 27 February 2027. Pearson's International GCSE November 2026 final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026. Both boards publish their own timetables and Pearson issues provisional versions ahead of each series, so work only from the live official document and confirm the detail with your school's examinations officer.

faqs.question: Does the distance from Al Shamkha to school affect when lessons can start?
faqs.answer: It is the main factor. A twenty-five to forty-minute run each way means the household's real arrival time is well after the school's finishing time, and a slot booked at 16:00 will be missed repeatedly. Most families here settle between 17:00 and 19:00, with Year 11 and above sometimes later still. Because every lesson is online and nobody is driving, the slot can be set against the last arrival rather than an average, and it can move later during Ramadan without renegotiating a route.

faqs.question: How many hours a week should a Year 11 in this district be studying alone?
faqs.answer: There is no honest universal number, and anyone quoting one is guessing. What can be said is the shape: across eight to ten IGCSE subjects, the hours that change a grade are timed question practice, not reading. Two focused hours spent answering past-paper questions and marking them properly beats five hours of notes. By the spring term most students who do well have sat at least two complete papers in each major subject under exam conditions, which is a measurable target rather than an hours figure.

faqs.question: What are the UAE equivalency requirements for a British curriculum student?
faqs.answer: The Ministry of Education requires five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus proof of one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. One page ranking for these searches tells parents six IGCSE subjects are needed, which does not match the published clarification. Equivalency is handled by the authorities, not by any tutoring provider, so verify your own case with them.

faqs.question: Are Arabic and Islamic education counted in the five subjects for equivalency?
faqs.answer: No. The published clarification states that Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects for the GCSE and IGCSE count. That does not make them optional at school: private schools in the Emirates teach Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside whatever international curriculum they are licensed for, and those subjects are taught, assessed and reported. The distinction is narrow but useful when a family is planning which subjects to protect in Year 11, and it is worth confirming against the Ministry's own page.

faqs.question: Can a tutor mark past papers against the official mark scheme?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is the most valuable thing a tutor does with an exam-year student. The scheme is used as the examiner would use it, so the student sees exactly which mark was awarded for which statement and which were not available for an unexplained answer. What a tutor cannot do is tell you a fixed percentage that equals a grade 7 or an A star, because boundaries are set per series by the board and vary. Marks on this paper are real information; an invented constant threshold is not.

faqs.question: Will you send us past papers and mark schemes to keep?
faqs.answer: No. Examination papers, mark schemes, grade boundary tables and subject guides are the copyright of Cambridge, Pearson and the IB, and reproducing or distributing them is infringement. What happens instead is that papers are referenced precisely by series and question number and linked to the official source, worked through on screen during the lesson, and the student keeps their own annotated attempt. Your child's school holds licensed access and the subject teacher is often the fastest legitimate route to a specific paper.

faqs.question: What happens in the November IGCSE series, and who sits it?
faqs.answer: Both Cambridge and Pearson run a November series alongside the main summer one. It is used by students retaking a subject, by candidates whose school year runs differently, and occasionally by private candidates. Pearson's November 2026 final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. That lag matters for planning, because a decision to re-enter frequently has to be made before the previous grade is in hand. Confirm entry arrangements with the school's examinations officer well ahead.

faqs.question: How do you report progress to parents in Al Shamkha?
faqs.answer: With a short written note after each session saying what was covered, what was marked and what to practise, plus the student's annotated work. What you will not get is a weekly percentage or a progress score, because a number invented by the person being paid is not evidence. The real measures are external: marks on timed papers against the published scheme, criterion scores on returned school work, and mock results. Those are the figures worth tracking across a term, and they are the ones we work against.

faqs.question: Does my child need tutoring to get UAE equivalency?
faqs.answer: No, and any provider implying otherwise is manufacturing urgency about a regulatory process. Equivalency depends on holding the required certificates at the required grades, and it is administered by the Ministry of Education and the emirate authorities. Tutoring can help a student reach a grade they would otherwise miss, which is a genuine reason to hire one. It is not a step in the equivalency procedure, it confers no standing with the authorities, and nobody can guarantee an outcome in a process they do not run.

abu-dhabi/al-shamkha.closingHeading: Bring the marked paper, and we will work backwards from the deadline
abu-dhabi/al-shamkha.closingBody: The useful first move for an Al Shamkha family is not choosing a tutor but identifying the component. Send a recent marked paper or a piece of returned coursework, tell us the board and the syllabus code, and say what time the house is genuinely quiet. From there the plan is mechanical: a specialist in that paper, a slot that survives the commute, timed practice marked against the official scheme, and a calendar counted backwards from the published entry deadline. Lessons run one-to-one over live video, every figure and date on this page names its source, and if the right specialist is not free in your window we will say so.

abu-dhabi/al-wahda.tutorsIntro: These tutors work at the level of the individual script: which tier a student should actually sit, which board their school enters them for, and how many creditable points a six-mark question needs. Those are the questions a large set cannot answer student by student.

intro.heading: A crowded cohort teaches content well and feedback badly
paragraphs: Al Wahda is central Abu Dhabi island: mid-rise apartment blocks around Al Wahda Mall, Hazza Bin Zayed Street running through it, Airport Road along one edge, and a dense residential population that is heavily South Asian, Arab and Filipino. The schools serving this district are among the largest in the emirate, and several run year groups that would be two or three forms in a European school. That size has consequences, and they are not the ones parents assume.

Large schools generally teach content thoroughly. They have specialists in every subject, they have been entering candidates for the same syllabus codes for years, and their departmental schemes of work are well drilled. What they cannot do, arithmetically, is give one student sustained individual feedback. A teacher with a hundred and twenty IGCSE students cannot mark four drafts of one essay, cannot sit beside one child while they attempt a timed paper, and cannot have an extended conversation about whether that child should be on the Core or the Extended tier.

So the gap in Al Wahda is not a teaching gap. It is a feedback and decision gap, and it shows up in a very particular pattern: a student who understands the material in class, scores respectably on homework, and then produces an examination mark two bands lower than anyone expected. Nothing in the classroom failed. What failed is that nobody ever told this specific child that their six-mark answers contain three creditable points, or that they are spending eleven minutes on a question worth four marks.

This page is therefore built around the decisions a crowded cohort leaves to the family. Which tier the student should sit, since Cambridge Core caps at grade C and that ceiling is permanent. Which board the school actually enters for, because Cambridge and Pearson examine the same subject with different papers and different tiering. How many marks an answer should contain and how many minutes it should take. Whether a set change is worth asking for, and how to ask. And for the significant number of Al Wahda families whose children moved from an Indian or Pakistani board into IGCSE, what actually changes in the assessment rather than in the syllabus.

Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, which is the right format for this kind of work. A marked script on a shared screen, with the mark scheme open beside it and the lost marks circled one by one, is a more useful hour than any amount of content re-delivery, and it is the hour a large cohort cannot give your child. It is also, in apartment housing, the only format that does not require the household to surrender its one quiet room to a visitor for ninety minutes.

One more thing is worth saying before the detail. A large school is not a worse school, and a family in this district should not approach a head of department as though something has gone wrong. The schools here enter big cohorts for the same syllabus codes year after year, and that experience is an asset. What a parent can add is the one thing the school does not have time to produce: a diagnosis of their own individual child, written down, on paper, from the evidence in their own marked work.

abu-dhabi/al-wahda.programmesIntro: This district spans international and national-board provision, so the programme notes below are about what each route leaves to the individual student once a large class has done its work.

programmes.name: IGCSE
programmes.description: Two-year courses examined externally, offered here by both Cambridge International and Pearson Edexcel. Cambridge tiers several subjects into Core and Extended with different papers and a different grade ceiling; Pearson tiers mathematics as Foundation and Higher. The tier a student sits is decided by the school and is the single most consequential academic decision of Year 10.
programmes.countryNote: Al Wahda schools enter large IGCSE cohorts, which means tier decisions are often made on class performance against a cohort rather than on an individual diagnosis. A parent who brings marked evidence to that conversation changes it. A parent who brings an opinion usually does not.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. In the current science guides the internal assessment carries 20% of the subject grade, and the Mathematics exploration the same, so a meaningful fifth of each grade is coursework produced away from the classroom.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma students from this district usually travel to a school in Al Mushrif, Al Bateen or out to Khalifa City, since Diploma provision in the immediate area is limited. That commute shortens the usable evening, which is why coursework supervision here tends to be weekend work rather than weekday.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups marked against four lettered criteria, each out of eight, with process assessed as well as product. In a large set the criteria are explained once to the class and then applied to thirty pieces of work, which leaves individual students unclear about what a specific criterion actually wants from them.
programmes.countryNote: The MYP is the programme where crowded-cohort feedback loss shows earliest, because criterion marking only makes sense when someone explains your own work back to you. A single session decoding a returned task against the rubric often changes a student's marks more than a term of subject lessons.

programmes.name: A Level
programmes.description: Linear, with all assessment at the end of the course and minimal coursework in most subjects. Narrow and deep in three or four subjects, which suits students who already have examination technique and punishes those who do not, since there is no coursework component to absorb a weak paper.
programmes.countryNote: For British-route families in Al Wahda the A Level matters for Ministry of Education equivalency, which requires one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or better, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, alongside five IGCSE or GCSE subjects at no less than E or grade 3.

abu-dhabi/al-wahda.subjectsIntro: Requests from this district concentrate in mathematics and the sciences, with English language close behind. The notes below name the syllabus codes, because the code decides the papers and the papers decide the work.

subjects.name: Mathematics (IGCSE)
subjects.levels: Cambridge 0580 Core and Extended · Pearson 4MA1 Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: Cambridge Core sits papers 1 and 3 with a ceiling at grade C; Extended sits papers 2 and 4 and reaches A*. Pearson 4MA1 tiers as Foundation and Higher instead. The tier is the grade ceiling, so a wrongly placed student cannot recover the top grades however hard they work.

subjects.name: Physics (IGCSE)
subjects.description: Electricity and waves are the predictable weak strands in large sets, because they need repeated individual correction rather than a good explanation. The alternative-to-practical paper rewards experimental conventions almost nobody drills, and it is learnable in a few hours.

subjects.name: Chemistry (IGCSE)
subjects.description: Moles, electrolysis and the qualitative analysis tables separate the top grades. Moles in particular fail individually rather than as a class: each student misunderstands a different step, which is exactly the error type a crowded cohort cannot diagnose.

subjects.name: Biology (IGCSE)
subjects.description: Content-heavy and seemingly safe, which is why students over-rely on recall and lose the data and application marks. The reliable loss is answering an explain command with a description, and it is a technique fix rather than a content one.

subjects.name: First Language English
subjects.description: Directed writing and reading response papers that reward structure and precise textual reference. Teachers in large sets can mark a handful of practice essays per student per year; a student needs considerably more than that to change a grade.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language
subjects.description: Register control and accurate structure carry more weight than vocabulary range. For students whose home language is not English, this is often where the fastest grade movement is available, and it is almost entirely technique.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Standard Level sits two papers at 40% each with a 20% exploration; Higher Level adds Paper 3 at 20%. Paper 3's extended investigation is unlike textbook work and is almost never practised in class, because there is not time in a full set.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics with the graphic display calculator used throughout. Marks go on interpretation rather than on calculation: a correct output with no sentence saying what it means in context earns the method and nothing else.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diploma Standard Level runs Paper 1 at 30%, Paper 2 at 40% and the portfolio at 30%, with Paper 3 added at Higher Level. The three-commentary portfolio is highly coachable and the commonest failure is a commentary whose diagram does no analytical work.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: The internally assessed project requires real organisational evidence. Students in large cohorts often choose the same handful of accessible companies, which produces generic analysis that the criteria do not reward.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first and additional language
subjects.description: Mandatory alongside the international curriculum under the federal rules, with different expectations and a different language of instruction for Arab and non-Arab students, and schools required to teach those groups separately.

subjects.name: Combined and Coordinated Sciences
subjects.description: Three sciences compressed into fewer papers, so one weak strand drags the whole award. Diagnosis by strand before buying lessons prevents families paying for three subjects when the problem sits in one.

abu-dhabi/al-wahda.regionsIntro: Al Wahda sits in the middle of the island, so most of the districts that matter are within a short drive, and the school choice is usually made across these.

regions.name: Al Nahyan
regions.note: Immediately adjacent, with several of the large schools this district uses, including Indian-board and British-curriculum provision. Short enough that many Al Wahda children walk or take a ten-minute bus, which leaves the afternoon unusually intact.

regions.name: Al Karamah
regions.note: The district behind Al Wahda towards the south of the island, residential and well served by the same bus routes. Families here face the same afternoon shape and often share tutors and timings with Al Wahda households.

regions.name: Al Mushrif
regions.note: The nearest cluster with substantial IB Diploma provision, including Abu Dhabi International School. For an Al Wahda Diploma student this is typically where the commute goes, and it is a manageable one by local standards.

regions.name: Al Zahiyah
regions.note: North-east towards the port and the mangroves, dense and central with older school provision. Relevant mainly because it shares the same traffic pattern along Al Salam Street in the late afternoon.

regions.name: Al Bateen
regions.note: West across the island, with Al Bateen Academy and the American Community School. The drive is genuinely cross-island, which pushes a weekday session for a Bateen-schooled Al Wahda child towards five o'clock.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City
regions.note: Mainland district with the emirate's deepest Indian and Pakistani curriculum provision. Several Al Wahda families school here for continuity with a national board, which makes the board-transition question a live one in this area.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Out along the highway, with the largest British and IB capacity in the emirate. An Al Wahda family choosing Khalifa City has accepted a long bus run, and that decision effectively moves tutoring to the weekend.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Across the bridge to the east, apartment-based with its own schools. Growing in relevance for Al Wahda families as island capacity shifts, and the commute is short enough to keep a weekday session viable.

schoolClusters.city: Al Wahda, Al Nahyan and Al Karamah
schoolClusters.note: The large central-island schools this district actually uses, spanning Indian-board, British and mixed provision. These are the cohorts where content delivery is strong and individual feedback is thinly spread, which is the gap this page is about.

abu-dhabi/al-wahda.modesIntro: The three patterns below correspond to the three things a crowded cohort leaves undone: nobody marks enough of your child's work, nobody makes the tier or set decision individually, and nobody drills answer technique.

modes.title: Marked-script sessions
modes.description: The hour is spent on work your child has already produced, marked against the official scheme with the lost marks circled one at a time. Over four or five sessions a pattern emerges that no single teacher comment reveals, and the pattern is almost always tariff discipline, command terms or pacing rather than content.
bullets: Student's own script and the official scheme side by side on screen
Lost marks identified individually, not summarised
An error log kept across sessions so the pattern becomes visible
Content taught only where the script proves it is missing

modes.title: Tier and set diagnosis
modes.description: A short block, usually two or three sessions, aimed at a single decision: Core or Extended, Foundation or Higher, which set the student should be in, whether Higher Level is realistic. The output is written evidence a parent can take into a conversation with the school rather than an opinion.
bullets: Diagnostic questions drawn from both tiers of the same syllabus
A written summary of what the student can and cannot currently do
Clear about the grade ceiling each tier imposes
Designed to inform the school's decision, not to override it

modes.title: Technique drilling before a session
modes.description: Short, repeated work on answer construction in the weeks before examinations: counting creditable points against the tariff, reading command terms correctly, allocating minutes per mark. This is the highest-return work available to a capable student who keeps underperforming, and it is rarely taught in a full class.
bullets: Tariff-to-answer-length matching practised question by question
Command terms separated and drilled until they are automatic
Full papers under genuine timing, then dissected
Repeated on the same paper type to prove the change held

sections.heading: What a set of twenty-eight can deliver, and what it cannot
paragraphs: Start with the arithmetic rather than with a complaint about class sizes. A secondary teacher in a large Al Wahda school might carry four or five examination sets. If each set is twenty-six to thirty students, that teacher is responsible for well over a hundred candidates. Marking one full past paper for all of them, properly, with individual comments, is several days of work. Doing it four times a year is not possible alongside teaching, and no amount of good intention changes that.

What the same teacher does deliver is considerable. Content coverage to a departmental scheme of work, modelled technique, a bank of resources, mock examinations, predicted grades and a judgement about tier and set that is informed by years of entering candidates. Those are real assets, and a parent who treats a large school as deficient misreads the situation.

The specific losses are narrow and identifiable. Individual error patterns go unnoticed, because spotting that one student consistently loses the final two marks of structured questions requires looking at that student's scripts repeatedly. Tier and set decisions are made on relative performance in a cohort rather than on a diagnosis of the individual. Coursework drafts get one read rather than three. And answer technique, which is learned by correction rather than by explanation, barely gets corrected at all.

Those four losses are exactly what one weekly hour of individual attention can cover, which is why tutoring works well in this district and works best when it does not try to be school. A tutor re-teaching the syllabus to an Al Wahda student is duplicating something the school already does competently. A tutor marking that student's script line by line is doing the thing nobody else can.
bullets: A teacher with a hundred and twenty candidates cannot mark four papers each
Large schools do deliver content, resources and experienced tier judgements
The losses are individual error patterns, decisions, draft reads and technique
Tutoring here should cover the gap, not duplicate the teaching

sections.heading: Core or Extended: the decision that sets the grade ceiling
paragraphs: Cambridge tiers several IGCSE subjects, and the tier is not a difficulty setting. It is a grade ceiling. A student entered for the Core tier in Mathematics 0580 sits papers 1 and 3 and cannot be awarded higher than grade C however well they perform. Extended candidates sit papers 2 and 4 and can reach A*. Pearson handles the same problem differently, tiering 4MA1 into Foundation and Higher, with a comparable ceiling effect.

In a large cohort this decision is usually made on where a student sits relative to their classmates at the end of Year 9 or early in Year 10. That is a reasonable administrative method and a poor individual one. A student who was weak in Year 9 because they joined mid-year, or because a particular topic was missed, can look like a Core candidate and be an Extended one. A student who coasted on strong arithmetic can look Extended and collapse on the algebra in Paper 4.

What a parent can usefully do is bring evidence. A short diagnostic drawn from both tiers of the same syllabus shows what the student can actually do on Extended-style questions, as opposed to how they compare with twenty-seven others. That document changes a conversation with a head of department, because it is the kind of evidence the school would gather itself if it had time.

Two warnings. First, the ceiling is real: a university or a sixth form asking for grade B is not available to a Core candidate, so this decision closes doors quietly. Second, moving a student up a tier late in Year 11 is a genuine risk, because Extended papers assume content Core courses do not cover. The right time for this conversation is early in Year 10, which is also when nobody is thinking about it.

sections.heading: Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel: the same subject, two different examinations
paragraphs: Parents in this district frequently do not know which board their child is entered for, and in a large school nobody volunteers it. It matters more than almost anything else a tutor needs to know, because the papers are structured differently, the tiering works differently, and past-paper practice on the wrong board is close to wasted effort.

Cambridge codes its syllabuses numerically, so Mathematics is 0580, Physics 0625, Chemistry 0620, Biology 0610, First Language English 0500 and English as a Second Language 0510 or 0511. Pearson uses an alphanumeric system: 4MA1 for Mathematics, 4PH1 Physics, 4CH1 Chemistry, 4BI1 Biology and 4EA1 for English Language A. Those codes are the single most useful thing a parent can put in writing when asking for help, because they remove all ambiguity about what the child is actually sitting.

There are also session differences that affect planning. Cambridge runs June and November series, with a March series available in some regions, and every centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones with its own timetable version. Cambridge states that using the correct zone timetable is essential and that it cannot accept responsibility for a candidate who misses an examination after using the wrong one. Pearson runs May and June plus November, publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, and released June 2026 results to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students the following day.

The practical instruction is short. Ask the school, in writing, for the board and the full syllabus code of every examined subject, and for the centre's Cambridge zone where relevant. Keep that list. Give it to any tutor you engage. It costs nothing and it prevents the most expensive mistake available in this market.

sections.heading: Mark tariffs and answer length: the arithmetic students never do
paragraphs: Here is the most reliable finding from reading marked scripts in large cohorts. Capable students lose marks in a pattern, and the pattern is almost never ignorance. It is an answer that contains fewer creditable points than the question is worth, written at a length the student felt was sufficient, in a time they never budgeted.

A six-mark question needs six distinct creditable points. Students write a dense, articulate paragraph containing three ideas and score three, then cannot understand the mark. A two-mark question needs two points and no more, and a student who writes a paragraph has spent four minutes earning two marks that two sentences would have earned. Across a ninety-minute paper, that pattern alone accounts for a whole grade band in both directions.

The fix is mechanical and it is taught in one session, then drilled. Read the tariff before reading the question. Count the points you intend to make. Allocate roughly a minute per mark plus reading time. Check the count before moving on. None of that requires subject knowledge, which is why it is such a cheap intervention and why so few students have ever had it explained to them individually.

The table below is the version we use on screen with a student and their own script. It works for both boards and for Diploma papers, because the underlying logic is the same: marks are awarded for discrete creditable points, and the tariff tells you how many are wanted.
